title: BxAgents
body: Get Started View on GitHub BxAgents is a conventions-based AI agent framework for BoxLang , built on ColdBox and BX AI . You describe an agent with files and folders, not a framework's API surface, and bxAgents build assembles a real, runnable ColdBox application out of it: a web app with fourteen pages, an API with an OpenAPI document, twelve kinds of gateway, routines, a vault, backups, and tests that need no API key. Watch the web app Just over three minutes through the whole web app, narrated: the left menu and every page. The answers come from a scripted demo model, so they are canned. Captions are on. Everything the build gives you Build Folders are the API . A wizard and eight starters. Sub-agents you can also talk to directly. Skills from a registry, or saved by the agent with your approval. Tests with no tokens. Run A web app with a left menu and fourteen pages. A terminal chat with 36 slash commands. Routines people make by asking. Schedules , approvals, a packaged .bxa and six deploy targets. Remember Memory in the chat database for every agent, per person, the same in the terminal, the web app and the API. Per-person notes and shared notes about the agent's work. A data home with volumes, and backups with restore. Connect Twelve gateway types , and routines that deliver to them. An API with 88 routes, OpenAPI and a BoxLang client. MCP in both directions, with per-person sign-in and seven built-in connectors . A vault with an activity log. Operate Admin and member roles, tokens and people, allowedIPs and a rate limit. Five logs . The agent tree, its files and its token usage. Gateway state with a reconnect button. bxAgents doctor . Extend Extensions add commands, keys, status items, listeners, schedulers, page slots, CLI verbs, tools, skills and gateway types. Interceptors , modules and a class-based Agent.bx . What you can build Pick the problem, write one file. Most of these have a working example in examples/ . You need to You write You get Answer people where they are gateways/slack.bx A Slack bot over Socket Mode (also Telegram, Discord, Teams, WhatsApp, Twilio SMS, GitHub, Signal and email) Run a job every morning schedules/Digest.bx A task with .everyDayAt() that calls run() , started with the app, no cron daemon Let other systems call it agentApi in Agent.yml One HTTP API at /__bxagents with an OpenAPI document and a BoxLang client, open on your machine or behind tokens; plus gateways/expose.bx for a REST path of your choosing, or an MCP server Keep a human in the loop a tool that needs approval The run waits for approve or reject, in the terminal, the web app or a gateway Let people schedule their own work routines: enabled: true A person asks, the agent makes a routine, a heartbeat runs it, reports are saved, and a summary can go to a gateway chat Give each specialist a seat subagents/researcher/ A sub-agent in the web app's Talk to menu and /agent , with its own memory Connect it to your accounts vault: {} API keys and logins sealed in the database, typed in a hidden box and never shown to the model; each person can keep their own Let each person sign in to a service oauth: on an mcpServers entry Mail, calendars and ticket systems that ask each person to sign in: one click, tokens sealed in the database, the agent acts as them Add your own commands extensions/hello.bx A chat command, key, status item or listener, in the terminal chat, the web app and gateways Test without spending tokens tests/specs/AgentSpec.bx mockResponses() and agent matchers: specs run in CI with no API key and no network Ship it anywhere bxAgents package A portable .bxa and deploy targets : local, SSH, FTP, SFTP, Docker, DigitalOcean Assembled at build time Discovery, validation and code generation run once , not on every boot. What you run afterwards is a plain ColdBox app. Folders are the API Agent.yml and instructions.md are the only required files. Every other convention folder is optional and only shapes the output if it exists. Tools and skills Drop an @AITool -annotated function into tools/ , or a SKILL.md folder into skills/ - both are discovered and wired for you. Agents all the way down subagents/ nests the exact same convention tree, so a team of specialists is just more folders - built leaf-first. Twelve gateway types Telegram, Slack, Discord, Email, WhatsApp, Teams, Twilio, GitHub and Signal, plus http , cli and mock . A web app, generated Ask for it in a gateways/ entry and the build produces a themeable app with a left menu and fourteen pages: chat, conversations, routines, registry, connectors, memory, vault, settings, and for admins the agent, gateways, logs, access and data. A full-screen terminal chat bxAgents chat keeps your scrollback and has sessions, routines, notes, @file and picture attachments, 36 slash commands, a context meter and recording. It can start its own server or connect to a deployed one. Build one in four steps 1 Install BoxLang CommandBox install-bx-module bx-agents box install bx-agents 2 Scaffold bxAgents new my-agent --model=openai/gpt-5 Then edit instructions.md and add whichever convention folders you need. 3 Build bxAgents build Discovery, validation, manifest, code generation - into .build/ (the code in app/ , the web root in public/ ). 4 Talk to it bxAgents chat # or serve it over HTTP: bxAgents serve --port=8080 Start from something, not nothing At a terminal, new asks what the agent should do and writes the project to match ( the wizard ); add <kind> adds a tool, skill, gateway or other piece later. A template is a preset you build on, not a limit: pick one of 8 built-in templates, clone an existing GitHub repo, or install a ForgeBox package instead. 8 built-in templates --template=webui-chat|slack-bot|telegram-bot|github-bot|mcp-server|scheduled|multi-agent - real, working content layered on the same base skeleton. Clone a GitHub repo --repo=owner/repo - a bundled JGit client clones it; no git binary required. Install from ForgeBox --forgebox=<slug> - talks to ForgeBox's REST API directly; no box CLI required. See Agent Templates for every generated file in detail, and how to publish your own. A web app you didn't have to build Set exposes: "webui" on a gateway and the build emits the whole app: a left menu with fourteen pages, streaming chat with a Talk to menu for sub-agents, conversations you can filter, routines and their reports, a registry of tools, skills and volumes, memory and notes, a vault, light and dark theming and a phone layout. Admins also get Agent, Gateways, Logs, Access and Data and backups. It is wired to your agent through the same HTTP API your own code can call. It is generated CSS and generated markup, themeable from a gateways/ entry , with no front-end build step of your own. The page-by-page guide shows every page. What build actually produces Your convention tree, and the plain ColdBox application build turns it into. your-agent/ ├── Application.bx # your settings and hooks ├── Agent.yml # name, model, description ├── instructions.md # the system prompt ├── tools/ # @AITool functions ├── skills/ # SKILL.md capabilities ├── subagents/ # nested agent trees ├── gateways/ # HTTP/MCP/chat exposure ├── schedules/ # BoxLang schedulers ├── mcp/ # MCP servers you host ├── interceptors/ # lifecycle hooks └── modules/ # module dependencies .build/ ├── miniserver.json ├── app/ the code (not served) │ ├── Application.bx │ ├── bxagents/ Application.bx Scheduler.bx │ ├── config/ Coldbox.bx WireBox.bx Router.bx │ ├── schedules/ agent/ tools/ skills/ mcp/ │ └── handlers/ interceptors/ ├── public/ the web root (the only served folder) │ ├── Application.bx │ └── index.bxm ├── lib/ coldbox/ modules/ └── runtime/ boxlang.json modules/bx-agents Why assemble at build time instead of at request time? Most agent frameworks wire tools, skills, routes and schedules together at request time , on every boot. BxAgents does the opposite: bxAgents build runs discovery, validation and code generation exactly once, producing a plain ColdBox application in .build/ : the code in app/ , the web root in public/ . Starting it - via bxAgents serve , a real boxlang-miniserver process, or a portable .bxa deployed anywhere BoxLang runs - is then just booting an ordinary app. No convention scanning, no dynamic file walking, no build-time work deferred into the request path. Start with one file Only Agent.yml is required. instructions.md is optional - set instructions directly in the YAML, or drop the file in and let the build wire it in. Every other folder only affects the generated output if it exists and has content in it - so you add conventions as you actually need them. YAML by default, a class when you need code Agent.yml holds the agent's settings - most agents are a few lines of it. When the definition needs code (hooks, dynamic instructions, tools registered in code), Agent.bx extends BX AI's own AiAgent directly - the build instantiates your class, so what you write is what runs. See Agent.yml and Agent.bx . Reach it from anywhere Gateways Nine push-style gateways - Telegram, Slack, Discord, Email, WhatsApp Cloud, Teams, Twilio, GitHub and Signal - coordinated by one session with reject / queue / steer / interrupt policies. Each person and each thread has their own conversation, and slash commands work there too. HTTP and MCP Every agent serves an HTTP API (88 routes) with an OpenAPI document, open on your machine or behind tokens, allowedIPs and a rate limit. Host local MCP servers from mcp/ so other clients can call your tools. Ship it Package a portable .bxa and deploy it with local , ssh , docker , digitalocean , ftp or sftp - secrets stay environment variables, never build artifacts. Check your setup at any time Where to go next Installation Install BoxLang, BX AI and BxAgents. Quick Start Scaffold, build and chat with your first agent. Conventions One page per convention folder, start to finish. The Build Pipeline Exactly what build does, in order. CLI Reference Every one of the 29 verbs and its flags. Agent Templates Every built-in starter, GitHub/ForgeBox sourcing, and publishing your own. Deployment & Secrets Package a .bxa and ship it, safely. Every convention folder also has a working, buildable sample under examples/ .

Install from ForgeBox `--forgebox=` - talks to ForgeBox's REST API directly; no `box` CLI required.](/next/agent-templates/index.html)

title: A Model That Needs No Key
body: A Model That Needs No Key Every lesson from here on builds one agent, Acme support , an assistant that answers questions about orders, returns and shipping. To follow along you do not need an OpenAI or Anthropic account. You will run a small scripted model on your own machine: a server that speaks the same protocol as a real model, but only replays answers the course wrote for it. Your agent cannot tell the difference, and when you do have a key, swapping it in is a two-line change (the last section shows it). What you will have at the end A running scripted model, a new project called acme-support that builds, and an answer from it in your terminal. About 15 minutes. 1. Get the course kit The kit is a folder with the scripted model and its answers. Make a workspace and unpack it: mkdir -p ~/bxagents-course cd ~/bxagents-course curl -LO https://bxagents.ai/assets/course/bxagents-course-kit.zip unzip bxagents-course-kit.zip If you cloned the BxAgents repository you can copy tools/course/kit/ instead and call the copy kit . On Windows, use WSL: the commands of this course are for a Unix shell. cd ~/bxagents-course ls kit README.md checkpoints demos fakellm.bxs resume.sh 2. Start the scripted model Open a second terminal (call it Terminal 1 ) and leave it running: cd ~/bxagents-course/kit boxlang fakellm.bxs fakellm listening on http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1 (script: <anything>/demos/model.json) It listens on port 8080, which is where BxAgents looks for an openai-compatible model by default. Its answers live in kit/demos/model.json ; open it later to see how little there is to it. Use an absolute path if you pass `--script` If you start it with a script of your own, give a path ( --script=$PWD/my.json ). A path that does not exist where you are is looked up next to fakellm.bxs . 3. Create the agent Back in Terminal 2: cd ~/bxagents-course bxAgents new acme-support --model=openai-compatible/fast-model --skipInstall --no-banner Created new BX Agents project [acme-support] at <anything>/acme-support --model is a provider/model slug: the provider is openai-compatible (any server that speaks the OpenAI chat protocol) and fast-model is a name the scripted model accepts for any request. --skipInstall skips installing the test framework for now ( Testing Your Agent does it). Write flag values without spaces BoxLang 1.19.0's launcher splits every argument at spaces, so --message="Where is my order" arrives as --message=Where and the rest is read as something else. Until that is fixed, keep the values of flags free of spaces ( --message=refund ). What you type into the chat, or into a curl -d '{...}' body, is not affected. See Quoting flag values . 4. Build it and ask it something cd acme-support bxAgents build Build succeeded: <anything>/acme-support/.build/app bxAgents invoke --message=hello Hello from the practice model. I am scripted: I only say what the course told me to say. invoke runs exactly one turn and prints the answer, which makes it the easiest thing to put in a script. Ask something the script has a rule for, and then something it does not: bxAgents invoke --message=refund bxAgents invoke --message=anything Returns are free for **30 days** after delivery. Refunds land within **5 working days**. Sale items are final, but a damaged item is always replaced. I can help with orders, returns and shipping. (Answered by fast-model.) The second answer is the script's default . It names fast-model , the model your agent asked for, so two agents on different model names can be told apart later. --json prints the answer the way a program would read it: bxAgents invoke --message=hello --json {"response":"Hello from the practice model. I am scripted: I only say what the course told me to say."} Now try the full-screen chat. Type hello , then exit (or press Ctrl+C): bxAgents chat What just happened bxAgents new wrote a folder: Agent.yml (the definition), instructions.md (the system prompt) and empty convention folders. The three lines of Agent.yml that matter now: name: acme-support provider: openai-compatible model: fast-model bxAgents build assembled a runnable app in .build/ . You never edit it. When you asked a question, the agent sent a request to http://localhost:8080/v1 , where the scripted model answered. Stop the model in Terminal 1 (Ctrl+C) and ask again: the agent reports that it cannot reach its model. The model really is just a service. When you have a real key Nothing else in the course changes. # A Model That Needs No Key

Every lesson from here on builds one agent, **Acme support** , an assistant that answers questions
about orders, returns and shipping. To follow along you do not need an OpenAI or Anthropic account.
You will run a small **scripted model** on your own machine: a server that speaks the same protocol as a
real model, but only replays answers the course wrote for it. Your agent cannot tell the difference, and
when you do have a key, swapping it in is a two-line change (the last section shows it).
> **What you will have at the end**
>
> A running scripted model, a new project called `acme-support` that builds, and an answer from it in
> your terminal. About 15 minutes.

## 1. Get the course kit

The kit is a folder with the scripted model and its answers. Make a workspace and unpack it:

```bash
mkdir -p ~/bxagents-course
cd ~/bxagents-course
curl -LO https://bxagents.ai/assets/course/bxagents-course-kit.zip
unzip bxagents-course-kit.zip
```

If you cloned the BxAgents repository you can copy `tools/course/kit/` instead and call the copy `kit`.
On Windows, use WSL: the commands of this course are for a Unix shell.

```bash
cd ~/bxagents-course
ls kit
```

```text
README.md
checkpoints
demos
fakellm.bxs
resume.sh
```

## 2. Start the scripted model

Open a second terminal (call it **Terminal 1**) and leave it running:

```bash
cd ~/bxagents-course/kit
boxlang fakellm.bxs
```

```text
fakellm listening on http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1 (script: <anything>/demos/model.json)
```

It listens on port 8080, which is where BxAgents looks for an `openai-compatible` model by default. Its
answers live in `kit/demos/model.json`; open it later to see how little there is to it.
> **Use an absolute path if you pass \`--script\`**
>
> If you start it with a script of your own, give a path (`--script=$PWD/my.json`). A path that does not
> exist where you are is looked up next to `fakellm.bxs`.

## 3. Create the agent

Back in Terminal 2:

```bash
cd ~/bxagents-course
bxAgents new acme-support --model=openai-compatible/fast-model --skipInstall --no-banner
```

```text
Created new BX Agents project [acme-support] at <anything>/acme-support
```

`--model` is a `provider/model` slug: the provider is `openai-compatible` (any server that speaks the OpenAI
chat protocol) and `fast-model` is a name the scripted model accepts for any request. `--skipInstall` skips
installing the test framework for now ([Testing Your Agent](/next/course/19-testing-your-agent/index.html) does it).
> **Write flag values without spaces**
>
> BoxLang 1.19.0's launcher splits every argument at spaces, so `--message="Where is my order"` arrives
> as `--message=Where` and the rest is read as something else. Until that is fixed, keep the values of
> flags free of spaces (`--message=refund`). What you type *into* the chat, or into a `curl -d '{...}'`
> body, is not affected. See [Quoting flag values](/next/cli-reference/index.html#quoting-flag-values).

## 4. Build it and ask it something

```bash
cd acme-support
bxAgents build
```

```text
Build succeeded: <anything>/acme-support/.build/app
```

```bash
bxAgents invoke --message=hello
```

```text
Hello from the practice model. I am scripted: I only say what the course told me to say.
```

`invoke` runs exactly one turn and prints the answer, which makes it the easiest thing to put in a script.
Ask something the script has a rule for, and then something it does not:

```bash
bxAgents invoke --message=refund
bxAgents invoke --message=anything
```

```text
Returns are free for **30 days** after delivery. Refunds land within **5 working days**. Sale items are final, but a damaged item is always replaced.
I can help with orders, returns and shipping. (Answered by fast-model.)
```

The second answer is the script's `default`. It names `fast-model`, the model your agent asked for, so two
agents on different model names can be told apart later. `--json` prints the answer the way a program would
read it:

```bash
bxAgents invoke --message=hello --json
```

```text
{"response":"Hello from the practice model. I am scripted: I only say what the course told me to say."}
```

Now try the full-screen chat. Type `hello`, then `exit` (or press Ctrl+C):

```bash
bxAgents chat
```

## What just happened

* `bxAgents new` wrote a folder: `Agent.yml` (the definition), `instructions.md` (the system prompt) and
  empty convention folders. The three lines of `Agent.yml` that matter now:

  ```yaml
  name: acme-support
  provider: openai-compatible
  model: fast-model
  ```

* `bxAgents build` assembled a runnable app in `.build/`. You never edit it.

* When you asked a question, the agent sent a request to `http://localhost:8080/v1`, where the scripted
  model answered. Stop the model in Terminal 1 (Ctrl+C) and ask again: the agent reports that it cannot
  reach its model. The model really is just a service.

## When you have a real key

Nothing else in the course changes. Replace two lines of `Agent.yml` and put your key in `.env` (the
[last lesson](/next/course/capstone/index.html) does this properly):

```yaml
provider: openai
model: gpt-5
```

A real model words its answers in its own way, so what you see will differ from the "You see" blocks in this
course. What does not differ is what the files do.

## Checkpoint

`acme-support/` builds and answers `hello`. If you get lost in a later lesson, `kit/resume.sh <lesson>` puts
the project back to the state after that lesson, and you rebuild.

Next: [Scaffolding Your First Agent](/next/course/04-scaffolding-your-first-agent/index.html)

body: Agent Templates bxAgents new creates a project one of three mutually exclusive ways - see CLI Reference for the exact flag syntax and validation rules. This page goes deep on all three: exactly what each built-in --template generates, what a --repo / --forgebox source needs to look like to work as a project source, and how to build and publish one of your own. A template is the shape a project starts from. The new wizard lets you pick one (a single agent, a team, a scheduled agent, an MCP server) and then adds the tools, MCP servers, channels and deploy target you choose on top, so a template and those choices combine. The channel starters below ( slack-bot , telegram-bot , github-bot , webui-chat ) are the same thing as picking that channel in the wizard. bxAgents new my-agent --model=openai/gpt-5 --template=<name> # a built-in starter bxAgents new my-agent --repo=owner/repo-name # clone a GitHub repo bxAgents new my-agent --forgebox=some-package-slug # install a ForgeBox package Every path lands on the same thing: a directory containing an agent definition (an Agent.yml , or a class-based Agent.bx ) at its root, ready for bxAgents build . What differs is where that definition (and everything around it) comes from. The 8 built-in --template starters Every template starts from the exact same base skeleton - Agent.yml , instructions.md , a root Application.bx and box.json , the empty convention folders ( tools , skills , subagents , gateways , schedules , mcp , interceptors and modules ), a ready-to-run tests/ folder, a .env (with room for your API keys), a .gitignore and the standard dotfiles - then layers a small, specific amount of pre-wired content on top. Add --class to any --template to get the class-based Agent.bx form of the root definition (and of the subagents the multi-agent template scaffolds) instead of Agent.yml ; everything else is unchanged. None of them need a validator change: each one's extra content reuses a config shape ProjectValidator already accepts, so a scaffolded project of any template validates cleanly by construction. minimal The bare skeleton. Nothing extra. webui-chat A browser chat UI at /chat. slack-bot A Slack Socket Mode channel adapter. telegram-bot A Telegram long-poll channel adapter. github-bot A GitHub issue/PR webhook adapter. mcp-server An example tool exposed as an MCP server. scheduled A real ColdBox Scheduler calling the agent. multi-agent Two subagents, wired via subAgents. minimal The default when --template is omitted entirely. This IS the base skeleton described above - no extra files. Use it when you're starting from a blank agent and adding conventions yourself as you need them. webui-chat Adds gateways/webui.bx , exposing the built-in web chat UI at /chat ( bxAgents add gateway web writes the same content to gateways/web.bx ; the file name does not matter): // gateways/webui.bx class { function configure() { return { exposes : "webui", path : "/chat" }; } } After bxAgents build && bxAgents serve , the agent is reachable at http://localhost:8080/chat - the web app (a chat and the pages around it) backed by a generated SQLite-based conversation store. No apiKeyEnvVar / users are configured out of the box, so the page is open by default; see The web chat UI for locking it down. slack-bot Adds gateways/slack.bx , a push-style Slack channel adapter (Socket Mode - a persistent websocket, no public webhook needed): // gateways/slack.bx class { function configure() { return { type : "slack", botTokenEnvVar : "SLACK_BOT_TOKEN", appTokenEnvVar : "SLACK_APP_TOKEN" }; } } Also appends matching stub lines to .env : # Slack gateway (gateways/slack.bx) - see https://api.slack.com/apps SLACK_BOT_TOKEN=xoxb-... SLACK_APP_TOKEN=xapp-... Fill in both real values from a Slack app with Socket Mode enabled before bxAgents serve - see Slack for the app-configuration steps. telegram-bot Adds gateways/telegram.bx , a push-style Telegram channel adapter (long-poll via getUpdates ): // gateways/telegram.bx class { function configure() { return { type : "telegram", botTokenEnvVar : "TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN" }; } } Also appends a matching stub line to .env : # Telegram gateway (gateways/telegram.bx) - from @BotFather TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN=... Get a token from @BotFather and drop it in before serving. github-bot Adds gateways/github.bx , a push-style GitHub channel adapter (webhook-driven, @mention -gated issue/PR comment threads): // gateways/github.bx class { function configure() { return { type : "github", tokenEnvVar : "GITHUB_TOKEN", webhookSecretEnvVar : "GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET", botNameEnvVar : "GITHUB_BOT_NAME" }; } } Also appends matching stub lines to .env : # GitHub gateway (gateways/github.bx) - a PAT with repo/issues+PR read+write scope GITHUB_TOKEN=... GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET=... GITHUB_BOT_NAME=... GITHUB_TOKEN needs a PAT with repo + issues/PR read-write scope; GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET is whatever you set the repo's webhook signing secret to; GITHUB_BOT_NAME is the account name the bot replies as, used to gate on @mention . See GitHub for the webhook setup. mcp-server Adds an example MCP tool server plus a gateway entry exposing it: // mcp/exampleServer.bx class { function configure() { return { description : "Example MCP tool server", version : "1.0.0" }; } } // gateways/mcpExpose.bx class { function configure() { return { exposes : "mcp", path : "/mcp", target : "exampleServer" }; } } target names the mcp/* entry to expose - here, the example server above. After build / serve , any MCP-speaking client can connect at /mcp . The example server registers no tools yet: write @AITool functions under tools/ and list their names in a tools: [ ... ] array in mcp/exampleServer.bx (or add more mcp/*.bx files), per mcp/ . scheduled Adds a BoxLang scheduler calling the agent on a daily schedule: // schedules/Example.bx class { function configure() { task( "example" ) .everyDayAt( "00:00" ) .call( () => run( "Give me a status update" ) ) .withNoOverlaps() } } ( run() sends the message to the project's default agent, the root agent. The build gives the class its helpers, so there is no extends .) This is real schedules/ content, not a placeholder - edit configure() to add or change tasks with BoxLang's task DSL ( every(...) , everyDayAt(...) , onWeekdays(...) , etc.), or add more files. A six-field cron(...) works; a five-field one does not fire on BoxLang 1.19.0 (see Cron ). multi-agent The one template that changes the root Agent.yml itself, rather than only adding files alongside it. It declares two subagents with a subAgents list: # Agent.yml name: my-agent provider: openai model: gpt-5 subAgents: [ researcher, writer ] environments: # `bxAgents test` builds against this override by default (see # BaseAgentSpec.bx) so a fresh project's tests need no API key or # network access - swap the model to test against a real provider. test: model: mock/mock-model ...and scaffolds both as real, working subagent folders: subagents/ ├── researcher/ │ ├── Agent.yml │ └── instructions.md └── writer/ ├── Agent.yml └── instructions.md Each subagent's own Agent.yml is a complete, buildable agent (always against the mock provider - a subagent here is a demonstration of the delegation shape, not a working agent out of the box): # subagents/researcher/Agent.yml name: researcher description: "Gathers facts on a topic. Does not write final prose - that's the writer's job." model: mock/mock-model researcher gathers facts; writer turns findings into final prose - a minimal two-role delegation example. See subagents/ for how the subAgents list (folder names to wire) differs from super.init() 's own subAgents argument in a class-based Agent.bx (already-built AiAgent instances), and the multi-agent-team example for a fuller walkthrough. Sourcing a project from GitHub ( --repo ) bxAgents new my-agent --repo=owner/repo-name # or a full URL: bxAgents new my-agent --repo=https://github.com/owner/repo-name.git Instead of scaffolding from a built-in template, --repo clones an existing repository and uses it as the new project directly. Cloning is done with a bundled JGit dependency ( org.eclipse.jgit:org.eclipse.jgit , from Maven Central) - no git binary needs to be installed or on PATH ; the git client ships inside the module's own jar. What makes a repo a valid template: an Agent.yml (or Agent.bx ) at the repository's root, same as any scaffolded project. Beyond that, there's no special manifest or marker file to add - any BxAgents project (yours, a colleague's, an example from examples/ ) is already a valid --repo source as-is. What happens on clone, in order: owner/repo-name shorthand resolves to https://github.com/owner/repo-name.git ; a value already containing :// or starting with git@ is used as-is (so a self-hosted GitLab/Bitbucket/etc. HTTPS URL works too, not just GitHub). Refuses to run if the target directory already exists and is not empty - nothing is ever cloned over existing files. Clones shallow ( --depth=1 - only the current state, no history) via JGit's cloneRepository() . Always deletes the resulting .git folder afterward, unconditionally - no flag to keep it. This is deliberate: a template repo's own git history and origin remote have no legitimate reason to survive into a fresh project, and leaving them in place is a real foot-gun (your project's first git init /commit/push could otherwise interact with the template's upstream repo instead of your own). If you genuinely want the source repo's git history, clone it manually with git clone instead of using bxAgents new --repo . Verifies an Agent.yml or Agent.bx exists at the cloned root - if not, the whole operation fails with a clear error naming what's missing, rather than leaving behind a half-usable, non-BxAgents directory. Warning Cloning is anonymous HTTPS only - no credentials are passed to JGit today, so a private repository will fail to clone. Use a public repo, or clone a private one manually and bxAgents new isn't the right tool for that case yet. --model , --name , and --description are not required or used with --repo - the cloned project already defines its own Agent.yml or Agent.bx (and therefore its own name/model). Passing --name / --description anyway produces a warning in the output rather than an error, and is otherwise ignored. The scaffolded- tests/ 's automatic box install step (and --skipInstall ) also don't apply here - a cloned project's own tests/ folder, if it has one, is left exactly as cloned. Sourcing a project from ForgeBox ( --forgebox ) bxAgents new my-agent --forgebox=some-package-slug Installs a ForgeBox package - CommandBox's package registry, which can host a full app/project template, not just a library - and uses it as the new project. This talks to ForgeBox's own public REST API ( https://www.forgebox.io/api/v1 ) directly, using BoxLang's native bx:http / http() support - no box CLI is required . What makes a ForgeBox entry a valid template: an Agent.yml (or Agent.bx ) at the root of its published archive (or nested exactly one folder deep - see the unwrapping note below). ForgeBox has a dedicated bxagents entry type for exactly this ("BxAgents" in the ForgeBox UI) - browsing it is the fastest way to find a starting point - but bxAgents new --forgebox itself doesn't filter or care about an entry's declared type at all when installing; it only cares whether the downloaded archive, once extracted, contains an Agent.yml or Agent.bx . What happens on install, in order: Refuses to run if the target directory already exists and is not empty . GET /entry/<slug> looks up the package. A slug that doesn't exist fails clearly and immediately - no download is attempted. Resolves the current release's download URL from the entry's own latestVersion.downloadURL (falling back to the newest entry in its versions array if that's somehow missing). Downloads the archive and extracts it with BoxLang's own built-in extract() BIF (zip support - no bespoke unzip code involved). Unwraps one level of nesting automatically , if present: many ForgeBox archives (matching a typical GitHub zip export) wrap their entire contents in one top-level folder. If extraction produces exactly one top-level entry and it's a directory, its contents are moved up so the target directory itself ends up as the project root. Verifies an Agent.yml or Agent.bx exists at the (possibly unwrapped) root - if not, the whole operation fails, since a ForgeBox slug could just as easily be an unrelated library rather than a project template. Same as --repo : --model / --name / --description are not required (warned-and-ignored if passed anyway - the installed project defines its own), and the auto- box install / --skipInstall step doesn't apply. Publishing your own template A BxAgents template - whether you'll share it via GitHub, ForgeBox, or both - is just an ordinary BxAgents project (an Agent.yml at its root, plus whatever conventions it uses) with the specifics filled in for someone else to copy and adapt, rather than left as placeholders for you personally. 1. Build the project Start from any of the 8 built-in starters above (or from scratch) and shape it into what you want people to start from: bxAgents new my-template --model=openai/gpt-5 --template=<closest starting point> A few things worth doing deliberately, since someone else will bxAgents new --repo=... / --forgebox=... this and expect it to just work: Keep Agent.yml generic and buildable out of the box. Don't hardcode a real API key or point at a paid-only model by default - the test environment's mock/mock-model override (already scaffolded) means bxAgents test still works with zero setup even if the real model needs a key nobody but you has yet. Ship a real instructions.md describing the agent's actual purpose, not the generic "You are a helpful AI agent" placeholder new scaffolds by default. Document required env vars in .env as commented stub lines ( SLACK_BOT_TOKEN=xoxb-... , etc.) exactly like the slack-bot / telegram-bot / github-bot templates do above - it's the first thing someone reads after cloning. Verify it from cold , the same way a stranger would receive it: rm -rf .build dist , then bxAgents build && bxAgents test (and bxAgents doctor to catch anything env/dependency-related) from a completely fresh checkout. Never commit .build/ , dist/ , or a real .env - the scaffolded .gitignore already covers all three; keep it. 2a. Publish it to GitHub Nothing BxAgents-specific is needed - push the project to a public GitHub repository with Agent.yml at the root (or push a subtree; --repo only unwraps ForgeBox's own single-nesting convention, not arbitrary repo layouts, so keep Agent.yml at the actual repo root). Anyone can then run: bxAgents new my-agent --repo=your-org/your-template-repo A short "Getting Started" section in the repo's own README.md (what env vars to set, which model to point at) goes a long way, since --repo doesn't read or surface anything from the README itself - it's purely for the human cloning it. 2b. Publish it to ForgeBox ForgeBox packages are described by a box.json at the project root - the same file CommandBox's own package system uses everywhere else. At minimum: { "name": "My BxAgents Template", "slug": "my-bxagents-template", "version": "1.0.0", "type": "bxagents", "shortDescription": "A short description of what this agent template does", "private": false } slug is the unique name people install with ( --forgebox=my-bxagents-template ) - it's also what getEntry() looks up, so pick one you're happy to keep. type should be bxagents - ForgeBox's own dedicated entry type for BxAgents projects/templates (run box forgebox types to see it alongside every other type). bxAgents new --forgebox itself never inspects type when installing, but declaring it correctly is what gets your template listed under ForgeBox's own "BxAgents" category instead of a generic one, so people can actually find it by browsing. Add descriptive keywords too (e.g. "boxlang" , "ai-agent" ), since that's what full-text search uses. version should be bumped ( box bump --patch / --minor / --major , from inside the template's own folder) each time you publish a change - bxAgents new --forgebox always installs whatever latestVersion currently resolves to. Then, from inside the project: box forgebox register # once, if you don't already have a ForgeBox account box publish publish reads readme / instructions / changelog files from the folder by convention and publishes them as the entry's description/installation notes/changelog - worth having a real README.md for the same reason as the GitHub path above. Once published, anyone can run: bxAgents new my-agent --forgebox=my-bxagents-template Info bxAgents new --forgebox already unwraps one level of nesting automatically (see above), so you don't need box.json 's createPackageDirectory: false setting for this specific path to work - that flag only matters for box install 's own separate install conventions, not this module's installer.
