A value of the wrong type (a text where a list belongs, say) and an empty value (`model:` with nothing after it) are errors too.
> **The person who installs your agent can change these**
>
> Every setting except `name` and `data.home` can be overridden or added to from `~/.bxagents/Agent.yml` (every agent) and `~/.bxagents/<agent>/Agent.yml` (one agent), when the agent is built and again when a built app starts. See [layered settings](/next/conventions/layered-settings/index.html).

## Tools

An agent gets its own `tools/` folder, and nothing else, unless it asks. The tools other modules provide (bx-ai's built-ins, `bx-playwright`, ...) are a catalog: they are available, but an agent only has the ones its `tools:` list names. Every entry is `item@module`, the key bx-ai keeps them under:

```yaml
name: support
model: openai/gpt-5
tools:
  - now@bxai            # one tool from one module
  - "*@bxplaywright"    # every tool that module registered (quote it: * starts a YAML alias)
```

|          Entry           |         Gives the agent          |
|--------------------------|----------------------------------|
| `item@module`            | that one tool                    |
| `*@module`, or `@module` | every tool the module registered |

* **Default.** No `tools:` means only the agent's own `tools/`. This holds for every [subagent](/next/conventions/subagents/index.html) too: each one has its own `tools/` and its own `tools:`.
* **Naming a module validates it.** If the module is not installed, or has no such tool, `build` and the generated app fail with a message that lists what the module does provide.
* **A bare name is an error.** `now` fails with a hint to write `now@bxai`. bx-ai would otherwise resolve it to whichever module registered a tool called `now` first.
* **Own tools win.** If a tool in the agent's `tools/` has the same name as a module tool it selected, the own tool is used and the module tool is left out, with a warning in the `bxagents-tools` log.
* **Each tool once.** Listing a tool twice, or listing it along with a `*@module` that covers it, attaches it once.

### Tool options

`toolOptions` configures the tools of a module, keyed by **module name** . Two modules take options: `bxai`, for its [file tools](#file-tools), and `bxplaywright`, whose options are those of bx-playwright's `playwright()`: a `profile` (a name, or a list of names) and settings such as `headless`, `baseURL`, `browser`, `viewport` or `device`.

```yaml
tools:
  - "*@bxplaywright"
toolOptions:
  bxplaywright:
    profile: mobile
    headless: false
    baseURL: ${env.APP_URL:http://localhost:8080}
```

* **Each agent gets its own browser.** The browser tools bx-playwright registers share one browser for the whole app. An agent that lists `bxplaywright` tools does not get those: it gets a fresh set built for it alone (`playwright( profile, options ).aiTools()`), so a root agent and its subagent never drive the same page. The browser opens when one of its tools is first used, not at startup. `*@bxplaywright` works with no `toolOptions` at all and uses the module's own settings.
* **Environment values.** ``${env.NAME}` and `${env.NAME:default}`` are replaced with the environment variable when the app starts, never at build time, so a secret or a per-machine setting stays out of the project. A variable that is not set and has no default fails the agent at startup, naming it.
* **Checked at build time.** A key that is not a module the agent lists tools from, a module that takes no options, a key written as `item@module`, or an option bx-playwright does not have (the message lists the valid ones) is a `build` error.
* The module-wide settings (where browsers are installed, the default profile) stay in bx-playwright's own settings, not here.

### File tools

bx-ai has 19 file tools (`readFile`, `writeFile`, `listDirectory`, `searchFiles`, `deleteFile`, `zipFiles` and more), but it registers none of them. In BxAgents an agent gets them by listing them **and** naming the folders they may use in `toolOptions.bxai.allowedPaths`:

```yaml
tools:
  - readFile@bxai
  - listDirectory@bxai
toolOptions:
  bxai:
    allowedPaths:
      - tmp                  # the system temp folder
      - cwd                  # the folder the agent is started from
      - /data/reports        # or an absolute path
```

* **Each agent gets its own tools, locked to its own folders.** A path outside them is refused (`..` tricks included), and the tools are never put in the shared registry where another agent could pick them up.
* **No folders, no tools.** The tools exist only when `allowedPaths` is set, and an empty list is a build error, because bx-ai reads an empty list as "any path". Listing `readFile@bxai` with no `allowedPaths` fails with a message saying so.
* `now@bxai`, `httpGet@bxai`, `webSearch@bxai` and the rest of bx-ai's registered tools keep working as before, with or without `toolOptions.bxai`. `*@bxai` includes the file tools once `allowedPaths` is set.
* An entry may be `${env.NAME}` to take a folder from the environment.
* `bxAgents new` can write all of this for you: see [the new wizard](/next/guides/new-wizard/index.html).

![The Memory page: your notes, the agent's shared notes and conversation memory](/next/assets/webui/webui-memory.png)

## Notes

An agent can keep short notes: things about the user ("prefers short answers") and things about its own work ("the repo uses Gradle"). They are off until the block is there:

```yaml
notes: {}
```

```yaml
notes:
  provider: sqlite        # built in. Or a class implementing INotesProvider
  user:  { limit: 1400 }  # characters of user notes that go into the prompt
  agent: { limit: 2200 }  # characters of agent notes
  tool: true              # give the agent the note_remember and note_forget tools (default true)
  approveForget: true     # a person approves what the agent forgets (default true)
```

|       Key       | Default  |                                                                                                                                   Notes                                                                                                                                    |
|-----------------|----------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `provider`      | `sqlite` | `sqlite` keeps one row per note in the [shared chat database](/next/conventions/web-ui/index.html#the-sqlite-store). Any other value is the name of a class that implements `INotesProvider` and is created with `( config, agentName )`, for a notes service of your own. |
| `user.limit`    | 1400     | Characters of notes about the user, a whole number from 100 to 20000. Each user has their own.                                                                                                                                                                             |
| `agent.limit`   | 2200     | Characters of notes about the agent's work, a whole number from 100 to 20000. Shared by everyone who talks to it.                                                                                                                                                          |
| `tool`          | `true`   | `remember` (save or replace a note) and `forget` (remove one). Without them the notes are read-only for the agent and a person manages them.                                                                                                                               |
| `approveForget` | `true`   | A run that wants to `forget` stops for [approval](/next/cli-reference/index.html#chat), like any tool that needs it. Saving a note needs none.                                                                                                                             |

How it works:

* Both scopes go into the system prompt as short lists, oldest first, within their limits. They are read once per conversation, so the prompt stays the same turn to turn (a provider's prompt cache keeps working) and a note saved now shows from the next conversation.
* A note is one line of at most 500 characters. Nothing is dropped silently: a note that does not fit the limit is refused, and the agent is told how full the notes are so it can replace or forget an older one.
* **Who a user is** : it is the name of the [access token](/next/conventions/agent-bx/index.html#access-tokens-for-a-deployed-agent) the caller used, or `local` when the route is open. `local` is also who you are in `bxAgents chat` (`--user=NAME` changes it), so the terminal, the web page and the API share one set of conversations and notes on an open server. The agent scope belongs to the agent's `name`.
* The terminal chat, the web chat and the server share one file, `chat.db` in the [data home](/next/conventions/data/index.html) (`~/.bxagents/<agent name>/chat.db` by default; see [the SQLite store](/next/conventions/web-ui/index.html#the-sqlite-store)).

Manage them yourself with `/remember` and `/notes` in [`chat`](/next/cli-reference/index.html#chat), with [`bxAgents notes`](/next/cli-reference/index.html#notes) from a shell, or over HTTP through the [run-control routes](/next/conventions/agent-bx/index.html#run-control).

## Instructions

The agent's instructions are its system prompt. Put them in an `instructions.md` beside `Agent.yml`, the usual choice because the file is plain Markdown and easy to edit:

```text
my-agent/
├── Agent.yml
└── instructions.md
```

For a short prompt you can write them inline instead:

```yaml
name: greeter
model: openai/gpt-5
instructions: |
  You greet people by name.
  Keep it to one sentence.
```

If both exist, **`instructions.md` wins** - the file is the more deliberate choice, so a stray `instructions:` line cannot override it. If neither exists, `build` fails and says so.

## Environments

`environments` holds overrides keyed by environment name. It is the YAML spelling of the environment-override methods (`production()`) an `Agent.bx` can declare:

```yaml
name: support
model: openai/gpt-5

environments:
  production:
    model: openai/gpt-5-mini
  staging:
    description: Staging copy
```

The active environment is chosen with this precedence, highest first:

1. the `--environment` CLI flag (`bxAgents build --environment=production`)
2. the `BX_AGENTS_ENV` environment variable
3. `development`

Only the block for the active environment is applied, on top of the top-level settings; keys it does not mention are left alone. Each block accepts the same keys as the top level, except `environments` itself.

`bxAgents test` builds against the `test` environment, which is why a scaffolded project carries a `test` block pointing at the `mock` provider: its tests need no API key or network access.
> **Note**
>
> An `Agent.yml` cannot compute its environment. The `detectEnvironment()` method described under [Environment overrides](/next/conventions/agent-bx/index.html#environment-overrides) needs code, so a project that needs it uses an `Agent.bx`.

The overrides then merge with `boxlang.json`, `boxlang-{environment}.json`, `miniserver.json` and `miniserver-{environment}.json` exactly as described in [Merge semantics](/next/conventions/agent-bx/index.html#merge-semantics).

## Requirements

Reading YAML needs the `bx-yaml` module, **1.1.0 or later** . BxAgents bundles it, so there is nothing to install. Global YAML tags (such as `!!java.io.File`) are rejected, so a cloned project's `Agent.yml` cannot make the build instantiate arbitrary Java classes.

## YAML or Agent.bx?

|                         Use                         |                                                                   When                                                                   |
|-----------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `Agent.yml`                                         | The agent is configuration: a name, a model, instructions, memory, subagents. This is almost every agent.                                |
| [`Agent.bx`](/next/conventions/agent-bx/index.html) | The definition itself needs code: hooks, dynamic instructions, tools registered in code, an overridden method, or `detectEnvironment()`. |

You can start with YAML and switch later: create the `Agent.bx`, move the settings across, and delete the `Agent.yml`.

title: Application.bx
body: Application.bx A project has its own Application.bx at its root. It is where the settings and lifecycle hooks of your app live. It extends a class BxAgents generates on every build, which holds the base: // Application.bx class extends="bxagents.Application" { } bxAgents new writes this file. A project without one gets the thin class above, so older projects keep building. bxagents.Application is the name you write; the build points it at the generated class ( app.bxagents.Application , below), so a file written for an older BxAgents needs no change. Where it ends up The built app follows the ColdBox BoxLang template : the web root is .build/public and the code is .build/app . The Application.bx the server loads is .build/public/Application.bx . It is derived from the template's own public/Application.bx and changed to suit , and it ends as a thin class that extends the generated base, .build/app/bxagents/Application.bx : // .build/public/Application.bx (yours, or this when the project has none) class extends="app.bxagents.Application" { } What is derived from the template's file, in the template's own terms, and lives in the generated base: the COLDBOX_APP_ROOT_PATH , COLDBOX_APP_MAPPING and COLDBOX_WEB_MAPPING settings ( /app and / ), the call of new coldbox.system.Bootstrap( ... ) followed by loadColdbox() in onApplicationStart() , and onRequestStart() handing the request to the bootstrap. What is changed: the lifecycle is not in the web root: it is in the base, so public/ holds a thin class and the logic is not served; the app's name , sessions, the web UI's datasource and this.schedulers are generated from the project; the data home, the logs and bx-ai's settings are set up before ColdBox loads, and the tools, MCP servers, gateways and interceptors are registered once it has; the template's onApplicationEnd() , onSessionStart() , onSessionEnd() and onMissingTemplate() are not carried (a class that extends the base can define them); three hooks are added, before() , after() and beforeRequest() . The template's own file is still in the module (it is vendored, see templates/coldbox-boxlang/VERSION ) and is what the build lays out first; the generator then replaces it. What the generated base does On every build the base class is written into .build/app/bxagents/ and sets up: the app name , sessions (on when there is a web UI) and the web UI's database; the data home, the logs, and bx-ai's settings (applied before ColdBox loads, because the agents are built while it loads); ColdBox, started from onApplicationStart() ; tools, MCP servers, gateways and interceptors , registered once ColdBox has loaded; this.schedulers , listing the project's schedules/ as app.schedules.<Name> . It starts with a comment saying it is generated. Do not edit it: the next build overwrites it. Override a hook, or add a setting Your class loads after the base, so a setting you assign wins, and a method you define replaces the base's. To add to a hook instead of replacing it, call super : // Application.bx class extends="bxagents.Application" { this.sessionTimeout = createTimeSpan( 0, 4, 0, 0 ) // once ColdBox has loaded (and the tools, gateways and interceptors are registered) function after() { super.after() application.startedAt = now() } } The three hooks: Hook Runs before() at the start of the app's start, before ColdBox loads: the data home, the logs, bx-ai's settings after() once ColdBox has loaded: tools, MCP servers, gateways, interceptors, the web store beforeRequest() at the start of every request, before ColdBox gets it (it waits for a request body the server has not finished reading) Warning Replacing a hook without calling super removes what it holds (with before() , no data home and no bx-ai settings; with after() , no tools or gateways). Call the super method unless that is what you mean. You can still override onApplicationStart() and onRequestStart() themselves (your class is the Application) and call super.onApplicationStart() ; the hooks are the lighter way to add to them. The bxagents name bxagents.Application and bxagents.Scheduler are the names you write. In the built app they are the classes under .build/app/bxagents/ , reached through the template's /app mapping: app.bxagents.Application and app.bxagents.Scheduler . The build rewrites the extends of your Application.bx and of your schedulers, so the files they extend are copied with the app and nothing depends on the module being installed where the app runs. The generated classes exist after a build. Before the first bxAgents build , an IDE cannot follow bxagents.Application ; the class itself is not in your project. Paths The base lives one folder down, so it resolves paths from the app folder, not from its own location. The web root / is .build/public now, so expandPath( "/" ) is not the app: use expandPath( "/app" ) (the template's mapping) for a file in the app, for example expandPath( "/app/config/agent-settings.json" ) .
headings: Override a hook, or add a setting

markdown:
# box.json

BxAgents already bundles BX AI, ColdBox and the other modules agents use, so most agents need nothing more. When an agent needs a package that is not bundled, for example `bx-playwright` for browser tools, list it in a `box.json` at the project root and install it yourself:

```json
{
  "name": "support-bot",
  "dependencies": {
    "bx-playwright": "*"
  },
  "devDependencies": {
    "testbox": "*"
  }
}
```

BxAgents never installs anything. Install packages the way you normally do, with CommandBox (`box install`) or the BoxLang binary (`install-bx-module bx-playwright --local`), from the project root. `bxAgents new` scaffolds a `box.json` for you, with TestBox as a development dependency installed into `lib/testbox`, and a `.gitignore` that already ignores `lib/` and `boxlang_modules/`. Commit `box.json`; keep the installed folders out of version control.

## Where installed packages go

|                  What                  |        Folder in the project        |                                                                                What `build` does with it                                                                                 |
|----------------------------------------|-------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| BoxLang modules (`bx-playwright`, ...) | `boxlang_modules/`                  | BoxLang loads this folder from the project root, so `chat`, `invoke` and `test` find them. `build` copies it to `.build/boxlang_modules`, so `serve` and a packaged `.bxa` carry it too. |
| ColdBox libraries and modules          | `lib/coldbox`, `lib/modules/<name>` | Copied into the app over the bundled ones, so a project can add or override a library.                                                                                                   |
| Test tools (TestBox, ...)              | `lib/<name>` or `tests/`            | Not copied: the app does not need them.                                                                                                                                                  |

## Development dependencies

A BoxLang module that is only in `devDependencies` is left out of `.build`, and the build says which. A module is matched to `box.json` by the `slug` in its own `box.json`, or by its folder name (`bxplaywright` for `bx-playwright`). One listed in both sections is kept.

## Using an installed module

A module that registers tools, such as `bx-playwright`, is used by naming its tools in the agent's [`tools`](/next/conventions/agent-yaml/index.html#tools). If the module is not installed, the error says how to install it:

```yaml
tools:
  - "*@bxplaywright"
```

> **Note**
>
> `box.json` is different from [`modules/`](/next/conventions/modules/index.html), which holds ColdBox modules that are part of your project's own source.

title: Building Your Agent
body:
Building Your Agent With Agent.yml and instructions.md in place, build your project: bxAgents build This runs the full build pipeline - config resolution, discovery, validation, code generation, manifest normalization - and writes a real ColdBox application to .build/ , laid out like the ColdBox BoxLang template (the code in app/ , the web root in public/ ), plus .build/manifest.json . The five phases, in order flowchart TD A["1 · Resolve config"] --> B["2 · Discover"] B --> C{"3 · Validate"} C -->|"any error"| X["Build throws.
.build/app is never written"] C -->|"clean"| D["4 · Generate"] D --> E["5 · Normalize + write manifest"] E --> F[".build/manifest.json
+ .build/app and .build/public"] style C fill:#fff3cd,stroke:#856404 style X fill:#f8d7da,stroke:#721c24 style F fill:#d4edda,stroke:#155724 Resolve config - loads Agent.yml (or a class-based Agent.bx , calling its configure() ) and the active environment override, then deep-merges any boxlang.json / boxlang-{env}.json . Discover - walks the project and enumerates every convention folder into raw entries. Pure discovery - no interpretation of file contents yet. Validate - collects every error (never fails fast) plus warnings: duplicate tool/skill/model/subagent names, circular references, bad model/provider config, and more. If any errors were collected, the build throws here - .build/app is never written or touched. Generate - only reached once validation is clean. Interceptors, gateways, MCP, the router, the agent API handler, the web UI (if any), the core app skeleton, a verbatim copy of tools/ / skills/ , the bundled ColdBox libraries, and the scheduler, in that order. Normalize + write the manifest - produces the canonical .build/manifest.json . If your project fails validation build fails with every collected error, not just the first one - a duplicate tool name and an unknown model provider in the same project both get reported in one run. Idempotency Rebuilding an unchanged project produces byte-identical output, down to the manifest's per-file content hashes. This is the entire point of paying the assembly cost once, at build time, instead of deferring it into every request. Useful flag: --verbose bxAgents build --verbose Prints one line per build phase live as it runs - what got resolved/discovered/ validated, per-phase counts, which agents ended up registered in config/WireBox.bx and under which names, whether a scheduler was found, and a final timing line. Silent otherwise, so it costs nothing when you don't need it. Try it cd ~/bxagents-course/acme-support bxAgents build --verbose ... Build succeeded: /acme-support/.build/app You should see a .build/ directory appear, with app/ (the code) and public/ (the only folder a server serves), and a manifest describing exactly what went into it. Two commands check a project without running it: inspect reports what the source says, and doctor checks the machine and the project: bxAgents doctor [ OK ] BoxLang [ OK ] bx-ai [ OK ] Agent definition found at [] [ OK ] Project structure validates cleanly [ OK ] Data home [] (convention) can be written Everything checks out. doctor is the first thing to run when something does not work: it names a missing key, a bad Agent.yml or a folder it cannot write. You'll talk to this built agent in the next lesson. Full reference: The Build Pipeline . Checkpoint Nothing in the source changed; acme-support/ is built. Next: Talking to Your Agent

# Building Your Agent With `Agent.yml` and `instructions.md` in place, build your project: ```bash bxAgents build ``` This runs the full build pipeline - config resolution, discovery, validation, code generation, manifest normalization - and writes a real ColdBox application to `.build/`, laid out like the ColdBox BoxLang template (the code in `app/`, the web root in `public/`), plus `.build/manifest.json`. ## The five phases, in order ```mermaid flowchart TD A["1 · Resolve config"] --> B["2 · Discover"] B --> C{"3 · Validate"} C -->|"any error"| X["Build throws.
.build/app is never written"] C -->|"clean"| D["4 · Generate"] D --> E["5 · Normalize + write manifest"] E --> F[".build/manifest.json
+ .build/app and .build/public"] style C fill:#fff3cd,stroke:#856404 style X fill:#f8d7da,stroke:#721c24 style F fill:#d4edda,stroke:#155724 ``` 1. **Resolve config** - loads `Agent.yml` (or a class-based `Agent.bx`, calling its `configure()`) and the active environment override, then deep-merges any `boxlang.json`/`boxlang-{env}.json`. 2. **Discover** - walks the project and enumerates every convention folder into raw entries. Pure discovery - no interpretation of file contents yet. 3. **Validate** - collects **every** error (never fails fast) plus warnings: duplicate tool/skill/model/subagent names, circular references, bad model/provider config, and more. If any errors were collected, the build throws here - `.build/app` is never written or touched. 4. **Generate** - only reached once validation is clean. Interceptors, gateways, MCP, the router, the agent API handler, the web UI (if any), the core app skeleton, a verbatim copy of `tools/`/`skills/`, the bundled ColdBox libraries, and the scheduler, in that order. 5. **Normalize + write the manifest** - produces the canonical `.build/manifest.json`. ## If your project fails validation `build` fails with **every** collected error, not just the first one - a duplicate tool name and an unknown model provider in the same project both get reported in one run. ## Idempotency Rebuilding an unchanged project produces **byte-identical** output, down to the manifest's per-file content hashes. This is the entire point of paying the assembly cost once, at build time, instead of deferring it into every request. ## Useful flag: `--verbose` ```bash bxAgents build --verbose ``` Prints one line per build phase live as it runs - what got resolved/discovered/ validated, per-phase counts, which agents ended up registered in `config/WireBox.bx` and under which names, whether a scheduler was found, and a final timing line. Silent otherwise, so it costs nothing when you don't need it. ## Try it ```bash cd ~/bxagents-course/acme-support bxAgents build --verbose ``` ```text ... Build succeeded: /acme-support/.build/app ``` You should see a `.build/` directory appear, with `app/` (the code) and `public/` (the only folder a server serves), and a manifest describing exactly what went into it. Two commands check a project without running it: `inspect` reports what the source says, and `doctor` checks the machine and the project: ```bash bxAgents doctor ``` ```text [ OK ] BoxLang [ OK ] bx-ai [ OK ] Agent definition found at [] [ OK ] Project structure validates cleanly [ OK ] Data home [] (convention) can be written Everything checks out. ``` `doctor` is the first thing to run when something does not work: it names a missing key, a bad `Agent.yml` or a folder it cannot write. You'll talk to this built agent in the next lesson. Full reference: [The Build Pipeline](/next/build-pipeline/index.html). ## Checkpoint Nothing in the source changed; `acme-support/` is built. title: Call your agent from code
body: Call your agent from code Every built agent serves one HTTP API at /__bxagents . The web chat page, the terminal chat and the gateways use the same one, so anything they do, your program can do. This guide is the tour; every route, with its request and answer, is in the OpenAPI document the server hands out, and the settings are in agentApi . Two and a half minutes: open mode and its startup warning, token mode, the guards, the BoxLang client, the OpenAPI document, the web page, the terminal chat and gateway sessions. The agent answers are canned (the mock provider), and the gateway part runs the gateway session tests. The project in examples/api-agent/ runs everything below. Open or behind a token Two ways to run, chosen by agentApi in Agent.yml . Settings Who may call Open (the default) nothing Anyone who can reach the port. Everyone is one user, local . Keep it on 127.0.0.1 ; serve prints a warning when an open API listens on every interface. Token tokenEnvVar: MY_SECRET , and/or tokens: true Callers that send x-bxagents-token . The shared secret is an admin; issued tokens are chat or admin . Everything else gets 401 . You can also narrow who may call with allowedIPs and cap how often with rateLimit ; both work open or closed. agentApi: tokenEnvVar: TOKEN_FOR_ADMIN # the NAME of an environment variable tokens: true # also accept tokens made with `bxAgents token create` manageTokens: true # an admin may make and revoke tokens over the API embeds: false # no embeds: leaves out the embed routes (default true) Connections When an mcpServers entry has oauth ( connect ), the API has the sign in routes. They act for the caller: nothing a caller sends can name somebody else. Route GET /connect The services, and whether the caller is connected to each. Never a token POST /connect { "name": "mail" } starts a sign in and answers { "authorizationUrl" } to send the caller to POST /connect/remove { "name": "mail" } forgets the caller's sign in GET /connect/callback Where the provider sends the browser back. Open , because the single use state says who it is. Shows a small page With curl export T="x-bxagents-token: $TOKEN_FOR_ADMIN" curl -H "$T" http://127.0.0.1:8080/__bxagents/whoami curl -H "$T" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"input":"What can you do?"}' \ http://127.0.0.1:8080/__bxagents/invoke invoke answers { "success": true, "output": "...", "threadId": "..." } . Send conversationId to carry on a conversation; the agent remembers it for you. With BoxLang import bxModules.bxagents.models.api.AgentApiClient; agentClient = new AgentApiClient( url = "http://127.0.0.1:8080", token = getSystemSetting( "TOKEN_FOR_ADMIN" ) ); first = agentClient.invoke( "What can you do?" ); println( first.output ); // the text as it is written agentClient.stream( "Say it shorter.", ( text ) => print( text ), first.threadId ); Build the client with named arguments. There is one method for each route: invoke , stream , events , resume , cancel , steer , sessions , history , export , notes , preferences , command , tokens and the rest. A bad request comes back as { success: false, error, code } ; a refused token, a missing route or a server failure is thrown. Pass path when the server moved the API with agentApi.path , and source to name your program in the conversation list. What a turn accepts Besides input , conversationId , threadId and attachments , a turn request may carry two structs: Field What is used options profile only: the name of an offered profile ( GET /profiles ). Any other name is a 400 bad_profile . params Everything the model accepts ( temperature , top_p , max_tokens , stop , seed , response_format , reasoning settings and so on), except model , messages , contents , system and tools , and any key that starts with _ at any depth. Everything else is dropped without an error, and the server logs the names it ignored (never the values). This is a security rule. A key such as options._resumeContext would make the model library run tool calls the request supplies without asking for approval, and options.apiKey would swap the server's key. In params , model would pick a model the server did not offer, messages or contents would replace the conversation, system could set the prompt, and tools would add tools the agent was not given. The person, thread and conversation come from the token and the request, never from options . Pictures go in attachments , as [ { "name": "a.png", "mime": "image/png", "data": "<base64>" } ] . A request has no images field: it holds paths to files on the server, so the server ignores it (and logs that it did) and reads no file; only the terminal that runs the agent in its own process attaches files by path. Streams stream and events answer server-sent events: each frame is event: <name> then data: <json> . Frame Meaning thread First frame: the run's id, for cancel , steer and resume . chunk A piece of what the model is saying. tool A tool call started ( running ) or finished ( ok ). events only. suspended The run paused for approval. Answer with resume . events only. error The run failed. done Last frame. stream carries thread , chunk and done . events carries all of them, and the client turns them into events for your callback: thread , delta , reasoning , tool , suspended , error . Run control The thread id from a run's first frame is what cancel and steer take. A run belongs to the caller that started it, so the same id from another caller reaches nothing ( cancelled: false , steered: false ), and two callers can use the same thread id without sharing a run. A paused run can only be resumed by the caller who started it. Call Does cancel( threadId ) Stops it. steer( threadId, input ) Adds a message to a run that is going. pending( threadId ) and resume( threadId, decision ) Approve, reject or edit what a paused run wants to do. Conversations, notes and settings Conversations belong to the caller too: sessions() lists them, newest first (an admin may pass all = true for everyone's), and createSession , renameSession , forkSession , deleteSession , history and export work on one. notes() and preferences() keep what the agent should remember about the caller. command( "/context" ) runs any slash command the caller may use. Routines When the app has routines on, capabilities.routines is true in GET /agent , and the client has routines() , routine( name ) , createRoutine() , updateRoutine() , pauseRoutine() , resumeRoutine() , runRoutine() , deleteRoutine() , routineReports() , routineReport() , deleteRoutineReport() and cleanRoutineReports() . The routes are /routines , /routines/get , /routines/update , /routines/pause , /routines/resume , /routines/run , /routines/delete , /routines/reports , /routines/report , /routines/reports/delete and /routines/reports/clean , all in the OpenAPI document under Routines . People see their own routines; an admin adds all=1 (or all=true ) to list everyone's, and anyone else who asks for it gets 403 forbidden , as on /sessions . A clean-up removes nothing unless the request says "apply": true . capabilities.admin says whether the caller is an admin. Access tokens over the API With manageTokens: true an admin can make tokens without a shell on the server: made = agentClient.createToken( name = "ci", scope = "chat", expires = "90d" ); println( made.token ); // shown once; the server keeps only a fingerprint agentClient.revokeToken( "ci" ); The same list, create and revoke are on the Tokens tab of the web app 's Access page ( <path>/access/tokens , shown to admins on a server that allows it). A chat token gets 403 . Leave manageTokens off and the routes do not exist. Every route Every path is under /__bxagents (or your agentApi.path ). The table was written from the one list in ApiContract.bx that the build makes the routes and the OpenAPI document from; the document a running server hands out at GET /openapi is the authority, and it also has the request and answer shapes. Admin routes answer 403 to a caller who is not an admin; Open routes need no token even on a closed API. There are 88 routes (97 verb and path pairs); the token routes are there only with manageTokens: true . Turns Route Who Does POST /invoke Caller One whole turn: the agent's answer once it is done. POST /stream Caller One turn as a stream of thread, chunk and done frames (the small subset of events). POST /batch Caller Several inputs, one after another, in one conversation. POST /events Caller One turn as the full stream: thread, chunk, tool, suspended, error and done frames. About the agent Route Who Does GET /info Caller What is served: name, model and the routes of the agent. GET /tools Caller The tools the agent has. GET /health Open Is the server up. GET /profiles Caller The models a caller may ask for with options.profile. GET /whoami Caller Who the server takes the caller to be: id, scope and where the call came from. GET /volumes Caller The folders the agent may use, by name and mode. GET /logs/stream Admin One log, live: lines frames with what is written from now on, and reset when the file was rotated. Ends after ten minutes. GET /logs Admin The agent's logs: which there are, or the last lines of one. POST /gateways/reconnect Admin Stops and starts one gateway in place, so a fixed credential or a dropped connection does not need an app restart. GET /gateways Admin The gateways and the state of each: connected, which credentials are set (never their values), last activity, last error and the chats each has talked to (ids and when, never text). GET /skills/read Caller One skill's SKILL.md text with its origin, size and when it was saved. GET /skills Caller The skills the agent can load: name, description and whether the project or the agent wrote it. GET /agent/composition Admin How the agent is put together in one call: what comes in, its parts, the agent tree, what goes out and the tools that ask first. GET /agent/files Admin The project's own files that are safe to show (Agent.yml, instructions, tools, skills, subagents, gateways), by relative path and size. # Call your agent from code

Every built agent serves one HTTP API at `/__bxagents`. The web chat page, the terminal chat and the gateways use the same one, so anything they do, your program can do. This guide is the tour; every route, with its request and answer, is in the [OpenAPI document](#the-openapi-document) the server hands out, and the settings are in [agentApi](/next/conventions/agent-bx/index.html#the-always-on-agent-route).

*Two and a half minutes: open mode and its startup warning, token mode, the guards, the BoxLang client, the OpenAPI document, the web page, the terminal chat and gateway sessions. The agent answers are canned (the mock provider), and the gateway part runs the gateway session tests.*

The project in [`examples/api-agent/`](https://github.com/ortus-boxlang/bx-agents/tree/development/examples/api-agent) runs everything below.

## Open or behind a token

Two ways to run, chosen by `agentApi` in `Agent.yml`.

|                    |                    Settings                     |                                                                        Who may call                                                                         |
|--------------------|-------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Open (the default) | nothing                                         | Anyone who can reach the port. Everyone is one user, `local`. Keep it on `127.0.0.1`; `serve` prints a warning when an open API listens on every interface. |
| Token              | `tokenEnvVar: MY_SECRET`, and/or `tokens: true` | Callers that send `x-bxagents-token`. The shared secret is an admin; issued tokens are `chat` or `admin`. Everything else gets `401`.                       |

You can also narrow who may call with `allowedIPs` and cap how often with `rateLimit`; both work open or closed.

```yaml
agentApi:
  tokenEnvVar: TOKEN_FOR_ADMIN   # the NAME of an environment variable
  tokens: true                   # also accept tokens made with `bxAgents token create`
  manageTokens: true             # an admin may make and revoke tokens over the API
  embeds: false                  # no embeds: leaves out the embed routes (default true)
```

## Connections

When an `mcpServers` entry has `oauth` ([connect](/next/conventions/connect/index.html)), the API has the sign in routes. They act for the caller: nothing a caller sends can name somebody else.

|          Route          |                                                                                                                         |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `GET /connect`          | The services, and whether the caller is connected to each. Never a token                                                |
| `POST /connect`         | `{ "name": "mail" }` starts a sign in and answers `{ "authorizationUrl" }` to send the caller to                        |
| `POST /connect/remove`  | `{ "name": "mail" }` forgets the caller's sign in                                                                       |
| `GET /connect/callback` | Where the provider sends the browser back. **Open** , because the single use `state` says who it is. Shows a small page |

## With curl

```bash
export T="x-bxagents-token: $TOKEN_FOR_ADMIN"

curl -H "$T" http://127.0.0.1:8080/__bxagents/whoami

curl -H "$T" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     -d '{"input":"What can you do?"}' \
     http://127.0.0.1:8080/__bxagents/invoke
```

`invoke` answers `{ "success": true, "output": "...", "threadId": "..." }`. Send `conversationId` to carry on a conversation; the agent remembers it for you.

## With BoxLang

```javascript
import bxModules.bxagents.models.api.AgentApiClient;

agentClient = new AgentApiClient( url = "http://127.0.0.1:8080", token = getSystemSetting( "TOKEN_FOR_ADMIN" ) );

first = agentClient.invoke( "What can you do?" );
println( first.output );

// the text as it is written
agentClient.stream( "Say it shorter.", ( text ) => print( text ), first.threadId );
```

Build the client with named arguments. There is one method for each route: `invoke`, `stream`, `events`, `resume`, `cancel`, `steer`, `sessions`, `history`, `export`, `notes`, `preferences`, `command`, `tokens` and the rest. A bad request comes back as `{ success: false, error, code }`; a refused token, a missing route or a server failure is thrown. Pass `path` when the server moved the API with `agentApi.path`, and `source` to name your program in the conversation list.

## What a turn accepts

Besides `input`, `conversationId`, `threadId` and `attachments`, a turn request may carry two structs:

|   Field   |                                                                                                                    What is used                                                                                                                    |
|-----------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `options` | `profile` only: the name of an [offered profile](/next/conventions/agent-bx/index.html#agentapi) (`GET /profiles`). Any other name is a `400` `bad_profile`.                                                                                       |
| `params`  | Everything the model accepts (`temperature`, `top_p`, `max_tokens`, `stop`, `seed`, `response_format`, reasoning settings and so on), except `model`, `messages`, `contents`, `system` and `tools`, and any key that starts with `_` at any depth. |

Everything else is dropped without an error, and the server logs the names it ignored (never the values). This is a security rule. A key such as `options._resumeContext` would make the model library run tool calls the request supplies without asking for approval, and `options.apiKey` would swap the server's key. In `params`, `model` would pick a model the server did not offer, `messages` or `contents` would replace the conversation, `system` could set the prompt, and `tools` would add tools the agent was not given. The person, thread and conversation come from the token and the request, never from `options`.

Pictures go in `attachments`, as `[ { "name": "a.png", "mime": "image/png", "data": "<base64>" } ]`. A request has no `images` field: it holds paths to files on the server, so the server ignores it (and logs that it did) and reads no file; only the terminal that runs the agent in its own process attaches files by path.

## Streams

`stream` and `events` answer server-sent events: each frame is `event: <name>` then `data: <json>`.

|    Frame    |                              Meaning                               |
|-------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `thread`    | First frame: the run's id, for `cancel`, `steer` and `resume`.     |
| `chunk`     | A piece of what the model is saying.                               |
| `tool`      | A tool call started (`running`) or finished (`ok`). `events` only. |
| `suspended` | The run paused for approval. Answer with `resume`. `events` only.  |
| `error`     | The run failed.                                                    |
| `done`      | Last frame.                                                        |

`stream` carries `thread`, `chunk` and `done`. `events` carries all of them, and the client turns them into events for your callback: `thread`, `delta`, `reasoning`, `tool`, `suspended`, `error`.

## Run control

The thread id from a run's first frame is what `cancel` and `steer` take. A run belongs to the caller that started it, so the same id from another caller reaches nothing (`cancelled: false`, `steered: false`), and two callers can use the same thread id without sharing a run. A paused run can only be resumed by the caller who started it.

|                           Call                           |                          Does                          |
|----------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------|
| `cancel( threadId )`                                     | Stops it.                                              |
| `steer( threadId, input )`                               | Adds a message to a run that is going.                 |
| `pending( threadId )` and `resume( threadId, decision )` | Approve, reject or edit what a paused run wants to do. |

## Conversations, notes and settings

Conversations belong to the caller too: `sessions()` lists them, newest first (an admin may pass `all = true` for everyone's), and `createSession`, `renameSession`, `forkSession`, `deleteSession`, `history` and `export` work on one. `notes()` and `preferences()` keep what the agent should remember about the caller. `command( "/context" )` runs any [slash command](/next/guides/slash-commands/index.html) the caller may use.

## Routines

When the app has [routines](/next/conventions/routines/index.html) on, `capabilities.routines` is `true` in `GET /agent`, and the client has `routines()`, `routine( name )`, `createRoutine()`, `updateRoutine()`, `pauseRoutine()`, `resumeRoutine()`, `runRoutine()`, `deleteRoutine()`, `routineReports()`, `routineReport()`, `deleteRoutineReport()` and `cleanRoutineReports()`. The routes are `/routines`, `/routines/get`, `/routines/update`, `/routines/pause`, `/routines/resume`, `/routines/run`, `/routines/delete`, `/routines/reports`, `/routines/report`, `/routines/reports/delete` and `/routines/reports/clean`, all in the [OpenAPI document](#the-openapi-document) under **Routines** . People see their own routines; an admin adds `all=1` (or `all=true`) to list everyone's, and anyone else who asks for it gets `403 forbidden`, as on `/sessions`. A clean-up removes nothing unless the request says `"apply": true`. `capabilities.admin` says whether the caller is an admin.

![The Access page of the web app, which is a client of this API: the token list and the form that makes a token](/next/assets/webui/webui-access.png)

## Access tokens over the API

With `manageTokens: true` an admin can make tokens without a shell on the server:

```javascript
made = agentClient.createToken( name = "ci", scope = "chat", expires = "90d" );
println( made.token );        // shown once; the server keeps only a fingerprint
agentClient.revokeToken( "ci" );
```

The same list, create and revoke are on the **Tokens** tab of the [web app](/next/conventions/web-ui/index.html)'s Access page (`<path>/access/tokens`, shown to admins on a server that allows it). A `chat` token gets `403`. Leave `manageTokens` off and the routes do not exist.

## Every route

Every path is under `/__bxagents` (or your `agentApi.path`). The table was written from the one list in `ApiContract.bx` that the build makes the routes and the OpenAPI document from; the document a running server hands out at `GET /openapi` is the authority, and it also has the request and answer shapes. **Admin** routes answer `403` to a caller who is not an admin; **Open** routes need no token even on a closed API.

There are 88 routes (97 verb and path pairs); the token routes are there only with `manageTokens: true`.

| `POST /connectors/options`    | Caller | Changes the caller's option values for one connector.                                                                                                                                                                        |
| `GET /connectors/tools`       | Caller | The tools a connected connector brings and which the caller has on.                                                                                                                                                          |
| `POST /connectors/tools`      | Caller | Switches tools: one, all of them, or only the ones that read.                                                                                                                                                                |

### Notes

|        Route         |  Who   |                                                           Does                                                           |
|----------------------|--------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `POST /notes/clear`  | Caller | Removes every note of one scope and says how many: the caller's own (user) or the agent's (agent, which takes an admin). |
| `POST /notes/update` | Caller | Changes a note.                                                                                                          |
| `POST /notes/remove` | Caller | Removes a note.                                                                                                          |
| `POST /notes`        | Caller | Adds a note.                                                                                                             |
| `GET /notes`         | Caller | The notes about the caller and about the agent's own work.                                                               |

### Embeds

|         Route          |  Who  |                                                        Does                                                        |
|------------------------|-------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `GET /embeds/get`      | Admin | One embed, never its key.                                                                                          |
| `POST /embeds/update`  | Admin | Changes an embed (the fields not sent keep their value); enabled false turns it off.                               |
| `POST /embeds/rotate`  | Admin | Gives an embed a new signing key: every open visitor session stops working.                                        |
| `GET /embeds/snippets` | Admin | The text to paste on the other website (HTML, iframe, web component, curl).                                        |
| `GET /embeds/usage`    | Admin | What an embed did in the last 7 days: messages, requests refused for a wrong origin, requests refused for a limit. |
| `POST /embeds`         | Admin | Makes an embed.                                                                                                    |
| `GET /embeds`          | Admin | The embeds, never a key, and the names of the tools an embed may list.                                             |

These are the admin side. See [Embeds](/next/conventions/embeds/index.html) for what visitors use.

### Tokens

|         Route         |  Who  |                Does                |
|-----------------------|-------|------------------------------------|
| `POST /tokens/revoke` | Admin | Stops a token working.             |
| `POST /tokens`        | Admin | Makes an access token.             |
| `GET /tokens`         | Admin | The access tokens, never a secret. |

## Errors

Every error is `{ "success": false, "error": "text for people", "code": "machine_code" }`.

| Status |                                                                            Codes                                                                            |
|--------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 400    | `bad_request`, `bad_profile`, `bad_attachment`                                                                                                              |
| 401    | `unauthorized`                                                                                                                                              |
| 403    | `forbidden`, `csrf`, `not_your_run`                                                                                                                         |
| 404    | `not_found`, `no_notes`                                                                                                                                     |
| 405    | `method_not_allowed`                                                                                                                                        |
| 409    | `busy` (a run is already going in that conversation)                                                                                                        |
| 429    | `rate_limited` from a token check; the `rateLimit` guard (cbSecurity's Throttle) answers `{ "error": true, "messages": [...] }` with a `Retry-After` header |

## The OpenAPI document

```bash
curl -H "$T" http://127.0.0.1:8080/__bxagents/openapi > agent-api.json
```

It is an OpenAPI 3 document of the routes this server really has: every route, what it takes and answers, the token header on a closed API, and the stream frames. Feed it to a client generator or an API tool such as Swagger UI or Postman. The routes, the document and the BoxLang client are all made from one list, and a test fails when they disagree.

# Chat walkthroughs

Six short sessions, each about two minutes. They assume an agent you have already built; if you have not, start with the [quick start](/next/getting-started/quick-start/index.html). Every key and command used here is listed in [The terminal UI](/next/guides/terminal-ui/index.html) and [Slash commands](/next/guides/slash-commands/index.html).

*The keys, prompt styles, context, name, fork and sessions in one run. The answers in these recordings come from a scripted demo model, so they are canned. Everything else is the real screen.*

## 1. Your first conversation

```bash
bxAgents build
bxAgents chat
```

1. Type a question and press **Enter**. The answer streams in; any tool the agent calls is shown with its arguments and how long it took.
2. Press **Shift+Enter** for a second line before sending.
3. Type `/` and look at the menu, or `?` for the keys. Type `/tools` to see what the agent can call.
4. Press **Esc** while the agent is working to stop it at its next step. Type while it works to **steer** it: your message is added to the run.
5. `/copy` puts the last answer on the clipboard.
6. `/exit`, or **Ctrl+C** on an empty box, to leave.

Scroll up afterwards: the conversation is ordinary terminal text.

## 2. Pick a conversation up again

```bash
bxAgents chat --continue          # the latest one, with its history
```

Inside a chat:

1. `/name Quarterly plan` names this conversation.
2. `/fork Other approach` copies it, messages and all, and carries on in the copy. The original stays as it was.
3. `/sessions` lists your conversations, numbered. `/resume 2` goes back to number 2 and shows what was said.
4. `/export plan.html` saves the conversation as a page. A `.md` name saves Markdown.

![The conversation list after naming and forking](/next/assets/tui/chat-sessions.png)

*After `/name` and `/fork`: three conversations, numbered, with their message counts.*

Messages are kept in the agent's [memory](/next/conventions/agent-yaml/index.html#settings), so a conversation can be picked up again only as far as that memory lasts. The default `cache` memory is lost when the process ends; a `file` or `jdbc` memory is not.

## 3. Try another model

Needs more than one [profile](/next/conventions/models/index.html#profiles) in the project.

1. `/model` shows the model in use.
2. `/profile` lists the profiles; pick one with the arrows. Or `/profile fast` goes straight to it. The conversation, tools and instructions stay; only the model changes.
3. `/ping` checks the model answers, and says how long it took or why it did not.
4. `/default` goes back to the app's default.

## 4. Notes the agent keeps

Needs a [`notes`](/next/conventions/agent-yaml/index.html#notes) block in `Agent.yml`.

1. `/remember I prefer short answers` keeps a note about you. The agent sees it in every conversation.
2. `/notes` opens the notes screen. **a** adds, **e** edits, **d** removes (after a yes), **Tab** switches between your notes and the agent's, **Esc** goes back.
3. `/notes stats` shows how many characters you use of the limit and the rough tokens they add to every conversation.

## 5. Show it a file or a picture

1. Type `@` and a list of files under your folder opens. Keep typing to narrow it; **Tab** takes one. The file's content goes with your message.
2. `@diagram.png` sends a picture. A profile that sets `vision: false` makes the chat refuse it with a message instead of a provider error.
3. **Ctrl+Shift+V** pastes a picture from the clipboard.
4. `!git diff --stat` runs a command on your machine and sends what it printed along with your next message. `!!` shows it without sending.
5. `/context` shows how big the context is and what it is made of: system prompt, tool definitions, notes and messages. The output of a `!command` waiting for your next message counts too.

## 6. Make the chat your own

1. `/prompt` shows the message box looks and widgets. `/prompt box` changes the look and `/prompt top +git -clock` changes the top bar, for this chat only. To set it for the project, use a [`tui:` block](/next/guides/terminal-ui/index.html#the-look-of-the-message-box) in `Agent.yml`.
2. `?` alone, `F1`, or `/keys`, opens a panel with every key and the name of its action; type to narrow it. To change one, put it in `~/.bxagents/Agent.yml`: `chat:` then `keys:` then, for example, `newline: ctrl+n`. See [Change a key](/next/guides/terminal-ui/index.html#change-a-key).
3. `/extensions` lists what the [extensions](/next/guides/first-extension/index.html) added: commands, keys and more. After you edit one, `/reload` loads it again without leaving the chat.
4. `/record demo.cast` starts saving the screen as an asciicast file, and `/record stop` ends it. Or start with `bxAgents chat --record=demo.cast`.
5. `/stats` shows the tokens the model calls used, once `usage: true` is set in `Agent.yml`. `/stats enable` writes that line for you.

## The wizard in the same style

*The `new` wizard from the name to the finished project.*

`bxAgents new my-agent` is the other screen. Arrow keys or `j`/`k` move, **Space** ticks, **Enter** confirms, **Esc** goes back one question and **Ctrl+C** cancels without creating anything. The last screen prints the one-line command that would build the same project with no questions. The full tour is in [the new wizard](/next/guides/new-wizard/index.html).

title: CLI Reference
body: CLI Reference Usage: bxAgents <command> [options] (or boxlang module:bxAgents <command> [options] - see Installation .) Global flags These are handled before verb dispatch and never reach a verb. Flag Effect -h , --help , help Show the task-grouped command overview and exit 0. Use bxAgents serve --help or bxAgents help serve for focused usage, options, defaults, and examples. Help is accepted in any position and never runs the command, including clean --help . The overview is also printed (exit 1) if no command is given. -v , --version Print bxAgents v{version} and exit 0. Only meaningful as the very first token, so it never collides with package --version=1.0.0 . --no-color Disable help's color and bold styling. --no-banner Hide the overview's logo. Focused command help never shows the logo. Help groups commands by task instead of presenting one alphabetical wall of text. At an interactive terminal, headings use bold brand cyan, commands and flags use bold, and supporting text is muted. Descriptions wrap with hanging indents to fit COLUMNS (80 columns when unset). Pipes, NO_COLOR , and TERM=dumb receive plain text without ANSI escapes. Quoting flag values BoxLang 1.19.0's boxlang launcher script splits every argument at spaces, so --description="Daily standup" arrives as --description=Daily ( --description "a b c" and "--description=a b c" too). Single quotes, backslashes and %20 do not help either: there is no way to type a value with a space through the bxAgents command until this is fixed upstream. A message that is split this way is not rejected, it is mis-read: bxAgents invoke --message="Where is order 48213, and can I still return it?" fails with No build found at [.../is/.build] , because is was taken as the project folder. Two ways round it: Start the module through Java, which keeps the quoting. Define this once in your shell, and every example on these pages that quotes a value with spaces works as typed (replace the path with the BoxLang runtime jar, boxlang-<version>.jar , in the lib folder of your BoxLang install): bxAgents() { java -cp /path/to/boxlang-1.19.0.jar ortus.boxlang.runtime.BoxRunner module:bxagents "$@"; } Or run it in one line: java -cp /path/to/boxlang-1.19.0.jar ortus.boxlang.runtime.BoxRunner module:bxagents new my-agent --description="a b c" . Write the value without spaces ( --description=Daily-standup ) and fill the text in the generated file afterwards. The banner At an interactive terminal, bxAgents --help and the end of the new wizard greet you with the BxAgents name in block letters, painted left to right in the Ortus brand gradient, cyan ( #00DBFF ) to green ( #00FF78 ), matching BxRig. It is never written to a pipe or a file. Alternative themes remain available: Ocean, Fire, Sunset, Purple, Mint, Gray, Forest and Gold. Setting Effect NO_COLOR , --no-color Same shape, no color TERM=dumb , output that is not UTF-8, or a terminal narrower than the art (75 columns) One plain line instead --no-banner , or BXAGENTS_BANNER=off No banner BXAGENTS_BANNER_THEME=Ocean Select an alternative theme; unset or Brand uses the brand gradient Every verb accepts --projectRoot=<path> (or a bare positional path as the first non-flag argument) to target a project other than the current directory. Precedence: --projectRoot flag > first positional argument > current working directory. Argument syntax Follows BoxLang's own documented CLI conventions: Form Result --option true --option=value / --option="quoted value" value (surrounding quotes stripped) -o=value short form with a value -o short form, true -abc combined shorthand: a , b , c all true --!option / --no-option negation, false anything else a positional (the first becomes the project-root fallback) Repeated options: last one wins. Note the first row: a bare --option is a boolean , not a way to pass the next token as its value. A flag that requires a value ( --model , --message , --password , --environment , --port , ...) is therefore rejected with an error when written bare, rather than silently becoming true : $ bxAgents new my-agent --model openai/gpt-5 Error: --model requires a value - write it as `--model=<value>`. Always use the --flag=value form. The space-separated form is not supported. Tab completion completions/ holds ready-made completion scripts for bash, fish and PowerShell. See Installation for the one-line setup of each. Verbs An example below that quotes a value with spaces ( --description="..." , --message="..." , --when="..." ) needs the Java form from Quoting flag values when it is run through the bxAgents launcher. new Scaffold a new agent project. add Add a tool, interceptor, schedule, MCP server, gateway, subagent, skill, extension and more to an existing project. skills Find, install, update and remove skills from skills.boxlang.io. build Run the full build pipeline. test Run your project's own tests/specs via TestBox. serve Launch a real boxlang-miniserver process. chat Interactive REPL against the built agent. invoke One non-interactive turn - for scripting/CI. package Package a built project into a .bxa. deploy Ship to a real deployment target. hash-password Hash a plaintext password for a webui users entry. token Issue, list and revoke access tokens for a deployed agent. embed Put the agent on another website, for anonymous visitors. users List the web page's accounts and choose who is an admin. notes Read and manage the notes an agent keeps. models List the models a project can talk to and test that they answer. sessions List, rename, fork, delete, export and import the conversations in the chat database. stats What the model calls used: tokens by model, provider, day or user, once the project turns usage on. vault The secrets the agent uses, sealed in the chat database: list, add, edit, remove, status, audit. connect Sign in to the MCP servers that ask each person to sign in. connectors The catalog of known connectors that ships with BX Agents: list them, show one, check the files. routines The scheduled routines: list, add, edit, pause, run, reports and clean-up. data Where the agent keeps everything, how big each part is, and the volumes it may use. logs List the agent's logs and show the last lines of one. backup Zip the chat database, files and skills in the data home. restore Put a backup back; what was there is kept as before-restore. inspect Report how the agent is composed, from its source. extensions List the extensions the chat loads, and install, update, remove or link more. clean Remove a project's .build/ and dist/ output. doctor Diagnose the runtime and project before build/serve surprise you. new Create a new agent project one of three mutually exclusive ways: scaffold it (answering questions at a terminal, or with flags), clone a GitHub repo, or install a ForgeBox package. # At a terminal: answer questions (see the new wizard guide) bxAgents new my-agent # Scaffold from flags (default template: minimal) bxAgents new my-agent --model=openai/gpt-5 [--template=minimal|webui-chat|slack-bot|telegram-bot|github-bot|mcp-server|scheduled|multi-agent] [--name=...] [--description=...] [--class] [--skipInstall] # A model on your own machine: LM Studio (1234) or llama-server (8080), no key bxAgents new my-agent --model=openai-compatible/qwen/qwen3.6-35b-a3b --base-url=http://127.0.0.1:1234/v1 # The same, adding what the wizard would have offered bxAgents new my-agent --model=claude --with=time,search --search=brave --mcp=github --channels=web,telegram --guard=flag # Clone an existing GitHub repo bxAgents new my-agent --repo=owner/repo-name # Install a ForgeBox package bxAgents new my-agent --forgebox=some-package-slug With no --model , no --repo and no --forgebox , at a terminal, new runs the wizard . --no-wizard or --yes turns it off, --wizard turns it on even with a --model , and --no-tui asks the same questions as numbered lines. A --model on its own never starts it, since scripts have always had to pass one. The wizard's flags ( --with , --search , --files , --files-dir , --base-url , --temperature , --max-tokens , --timeout , --memory , --mcp , --connectors , --channels , --web-auth , --guard , --prompt , --widgets , --widgets-bottom , --deploy and the deploy details) are listed in the wizard guide ; a bad value names the flag and what it accepts. They need Agent.yml , so they cannot be combined with --class . --template , --repo , and --forgebox name three different project SOURCES - exactly one applies. Combining any two of them is an error. --template mode (the default when no source flag is passed at all - minimal ): --model is required when no questions are asked - a provider/model slug (see the model slug ). --name defaults to the target directory's own basename. Refuses to run if the target already contains an Agent.yml or an Agent.bx . Creates Agent.yml , instructions.md , a root Application.bx (extends the class every build generates; never overwritten), every convention folder (empty), a root box.json ( testbox as a development dependency, installed into lib/testbox ), a ready-to-run tests/ folder ( tests/specs/AgentSpec.bx ), a .env (commented API key stubs only; it deliberately does not set BOXLANG_HOME ), a .gitignore ( .env and .env.* , .build/ , dist/ , data/chat.db* (a leftover: the chat database lives in the data home , outside the project), lib/ , boxlang_modules/ , .agents/skills/ , editor files), and the standard dotfiles .editorconfig , .gitattributes , .bxlint.json , .markdownlint.json and a .boxlang.json listing every bx-ai setting at its default (the BoxLang runtime reads it when run from the project root; edit the values there). Never overwrites a file that already exists. BoxLang and boxlang-miniserver load a .env from the project root themselves, so the file also works for your API keys; BxAgents never reads, copies or packages it. --class (a bare boolean flag, like the others described above) writes the class-based Agent.bx instead of the default Agent.yml , for agents whose definition needs code (hooks, dynamic instructions). It applies to the root and to any subagents a template scaffolds, and only to --template mode - not to --repo / --forgebox . --template picks one of 8 built-in starters, each layering a bit of pre-wired content on top of the base skeleton above (see Agent Templates for every generated file in full, plus how --repo / --forgebox sources work and how to publish your own): minimal - the bare skeleton, nothing extra. webui-chat - adds a gateways/webui.bx exposing the web chat UI at /chat . slack-bot - adds a gateways/slack.bx channel adapter, plus matching SLACK_BOT_TOKEN / SLACK_APP_TOKEN stub lines in .env . telegram-bot - adds a gateways/telegram.bx channel adapter, plus a matching TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN stub line in .env . github-bot - adds a gateways/github.bx channel adapter, plus matching GITHUB_TOKEN / GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET / GITHUB_BOT_NAME stub lines in .env . mcp-server - adds an example mcp/exampleServer.bx tool server and a gateways/mcpExpose.bx entry exposing it as an MCP server at /mcp . scheduled - adds a schedules/Example.bx scheduler calling the agent on a daily cron schedule. multi-agent - adds a subAgents list to the root Agent.yml declaring two subagents ( researcher , writer ), each scaffolded as its own real subagents/<name>/Agent.yml + instructions.md . Also runs box install in the new project root, so bxAgents test works immediately with no separate install step. This is best-effort: if box isn't on PATH or the install fails, new still succeeds - the message just tells you to run it yourself. Pass --skipInstall to opt out of this step entirely. --repo mode ( --repo=owner/repo-name or a full URL): clones the repo via a bundled JGit dependency - no git binary needs to be installed. Always clones shallow (depth 1) and always strips the resulting .git folder afterward, so the new project starts with a clean history rather than staying tied to the template repo's own remote. Refuses to run into a directory that already exists and is non-empty, and fails clearly if no Agent.yml or Agent.bx is found in the cloned repo. --forgebox mode ( --forgebox=<slug> ): installs a ForgeBox package by talking to ForgeBox's own REST API directly (no box CLI required). Fails clearly if the slug doesn't exist, the download fails, or the installed package has no Agent.yml or Agent.bx at its root (unwrapping one level of nesting first, since many ForgeBox archives wrap their contents in a single top-level folder). Only --template mode needs --model ; --repo / --forgebox never require it, since the source project already defines its own. --name / --description are ignored (with a warning in the output) when --repo / --forgebox is used - the cloned/installed project defines its own. The box install convenience step (and --skipInstall ) only ever apply to --template mode - a cloned/installed project's own box.json (if it has one at all) is left untouched. add Add one thing to a project that already exists, asking the same questions new asks. Today that is a tool , an interceptor , a schedule , an mcp server, a gateway , a subagent , a skill , a profile , a provider , a capability or an extension . bxAgents add # pick what to add bxAgents add tool # asks for the name, function, description and arguments bxAgents add tool WeatherTools --function=getWeather --description="Get the weather for a city" --args="city, days:numeric" bxAgents add tool Pinger --agent=researcher # into subagents/researcher/tools/ bxAgents add tool Pinger --dry-run # show the file, write nothing The positional arguments are the kind and the name, so the project is found by --projectRoot=<path> or the current folder only. At a terminal, whatever is not given as a flag is asked, in the full-screen UI (or numbered lines with --no-tui ). With --yes , in a pipe or in CI nothing is asked: flags and defaults are used, and a required answer that is missing names the flag to pass. Questions end on a review of the files that will be written. Cancelling, with Esc or Ctrl+C, changes nothing. Nothing is overwritten. If a file already exists none are written and the error names it; --force replaces it. At a terminal the review offers to replace instead. --dry-run prints each file with its text and writes nothing. add tool Creates tools/<Name>.bx with one @AITool function in the shape bx-ai documents : a docblock describing each argument, the annotation carrying the description the model reads, and typed required arguments from which bx-ai builds the tool's schema. Flag Meaning --name=<Name> The file name, or the second positional. Letters, digits and underscores, starting with a letter. --agent=<subagent> Whose tool it is. Asked only when the project has subagents; . (the default) is the root agent. --function=<name> The function the model calls. Defaults to the file name with a lower-case first letter. --description=<text> What the tool does. The model reads it to decide when to call the tool. Without it, and with nothing to ask, the file gets a TODO description and the output reminds you to replace it. --args=<list> Comma separated, each name or name:type ( string by default; numeric , boolean , array , struct , date and any also work). A tool belongs to the agent whose folder it is in and is attached to that agent automatically. Two tool files of one agent may not share a name, even in different subfolders, so a clash is refused here instead of at the next build . Check the result with bxAgents inspect --section=tools . add interceptor Creates interceptors/<Name>.bx with one method for each interception point you pick, and the @scope that the build splits on . bxAgents add interceptor AuditLogger --points=preProcess,onException --description="Log every request" bxAgents add interceptor AiWatch --scope=runtime --points=beforeAIModelInvoke,onAIError Flag Meaning --name=<Name> The file name, or the second positional. A name another interceptor already uses is refused. --scope=agent\|runtime agent (the default) is a ColdBox interceptor registered with the generated app when it starts; its methods take ( event, interceptData, rc, prc ) . runtime listens to the events bx-ai announces in the BoxLang runtime and takes the event data as its one argument; BxAgents copies it to .build/runtime-interceptors but does not register it for you. --points=<list> Comma separated interception points. The picker offers the common ones; any ColdBox core point ( agent ) or bx-ai event ( runtime ) can be named here, and a name that is not a point for that scope is refused. Defaults to preProcess ( agent ) or beforeAIModelInvoke ( runtime ). --description=<text> One line for the class's docblock. Optional. add schedule Adds a scheduler to schedules/ that sends an agent a message on a schedule. Three things are asked: when it runs, what it says to the agent, and which agent. Overlapping runs are always prevented ( .withNoOverlaps() ). Each schedule is its own file, schedules/<Name>.bx , so adding one never edits another. bxAgents add schedule --when="weekdays 08:30" --prompt="Summarize yesterday's findings" bxAgents add schedule digest --when="0 9 * * 1-5" --prompt="Check for new tickets" --agent=researcher bxAgents add schedule # asks how often, the details, a name, and what to say Flag Meaning --when=<phrase or cron> When it runs: one of the phrases below, or a cron expression. At a terminal, leave it out and you are asked how often, then the details. --prompt=<text> The message sent to the agent each time. --name=<name> The task's name, or the second positional. It also names the file: daily-digest writes schedules/DailyDigest.bx . Defaults to a name made from the phrase. A task name already used in schedules/ is refused. --agent=<subagent> Which agent runs it. Asked only when the project has subagents; . (the default) is the root agent, which the file calls with run() . Another agent is called with agent( "name" ).run() by its declared name , so renaming the agent means editing the file. Phrase Runs Written as every 15 minutes , every 2 hours , every 1 days At that interval .every( 15, "minutes" ) , .every( 2, "hours" ) , .every( 1, "days" ) hourly , hourly :15 Every hour, on the hour or at that minute .everyHour() , .everyHourAt( 15 ) daily 09:00 Every day at that time .everyDayAt( "09:00" ) weekdays 08:30 , weekends 10:00 Monday to Friday, or Saturday and Sunday .onWeekdays( "08:30" ) , .onWeekends( "10:00" ) weekly mon 09:00 Once a week ( mon tue wed thu fri sat sun ) .everyWeekOn( 1, "09:00" ) monthly 1 09:00 Once a month on that day, 1 to 28 so that no month skips it .everyMonthOn( 1, "09:00" ) first-business-day 09:00 , last-business-day 17:00 On that business day of each month .onFirstBusinessDayOfTheMonth( "09:00" ) 0 9 * * 1-5 , 0 30 8 * * MON-FRI Any cron expression: five fields, or six with seconds in front .cron( "..." ) with six fields (a leading 0 is added to a five-field one), checked by BoxLang's own parser. Only the six-field form fires on BoxLang 1.19.0 Times are 24 hour HH:mm in the scheduler's timezone.
