### `new` Create a new agent project one of three mutually exclusive ways: scaffold it (answering questions at a terminal, or with flags), clone a GitHub repo, or install a ForgeBox package. ```bash # At a terminal: answer questions (see the new wizard guide) bxAgents new my-agent # Scaffold from flags (default template: minimal) bxAgents new my-agent --model=openai/gpt-5 [--template=minimal|webui-chat|slack-bot|telegram-bot|github-bot|mcp-server|scheduled|multi-agent] [--name=...] [--description=...] [--class] [--skipInstall] # A model on your own machine: LM Studio (1234) or llama-server (8080), no key bxAgents new my-agent --model=openai-compatible/qwen/qwen3.6-35b-a3b --base-url=http://127.0.0.1:1234/v1 # The same, adding what the wizard would have offered bxAgents new my-agent --model=claude --with=time,search --search=brave --mcp=github --channels=web,telegram --guard=flag # Clone an existing GitHub repo bxAgents new my-agent --repo=owner/repo-name # Install a ForgeBox package bxAgents new my-agent --forgebox=some-package-slug ``` * With no `--model`, no `--repo` and no `--forgebox`, at a terminal, `new` runs the [wizard](/next/guides/new-wizard/index.html). `--no-wizard` or `--yes` turns it off, `--wizard` turns it on even with a `--model`, and `--no-tui` asks the same questions as numbered lines. A `--model` on its own never starts it, since scripts have always had to pass one. The wizard's flags (`--with`, `--search`, `--files`, `--files-dir`, `--base-url`, `--temperature`, `--max-tokens`, `--timeout`, `--memory`, `--mcp`, `--connectors`, `--channels`, `--web-auth`, `--guard`, `--prompt`, `--widgets`, `--widgets-bottom`, `--deploy` and the deploy details) are listed in the [wizard guide](/next/guides/new-wizard/index.html#without-the-wizard); a bad value names the flag and what it accepts. They need `Agent.yml`, so they cannot be combined with `--class`. * `--template`, `--repo`, and `--forgebox` name three different project SOURCES - exactly one applies. Combining any two of them is an error. * **`--template` mode** (the default when no source flag is passed at all - `minimal`): * `--model` is **required** when no questions are asked - a `provider/model` slug (see [the model slug](/next/conventions/agent-bx/index.html#the-model-slug)). * `--name` defaults to the target directory's own basename. * Refuses to run if the target already contains an `Agent.yml` or an `Agent.bx`. * Creates [`Agent.yml`](/next/conventions/agent-yaml/index.html), `instructions.md`, a root [`Application.bx`](/next/conventions/application-bx/index.html) (extends the class every build generates; never overwritten), every convention folder (empty), a root [`box.json`](/next/conventions/box-json/index.html) (`testbox` as a development dependency, installed into `lib/testbox`), a ready-to-run [`tests/`](/next/conventions/testing/index.html) folder (`tests/specs/AgentSpec.bx`), a `.env` (commented API key stubs only; it deliberately does not set `BOXLANG_HOME`), a `.gitignore` (`.env` and `.env.*`, `.build/`, `dist/`, `data/chat.db*` (a leftover: the chat database lives in the [data home](/next/conventions/data/index.html), outside the project), `lib/`, `boxlang_modules/`, `.agents/skills/`, editor files), and the standard dotfiles `.editorconfig`, `.gitattributes`, `.bxlint.json`, `.markdownlint.json` and a `.boxlang.json` listing every bx-ai setting at its default (the BoxLang runtime reads it when run from the project root; edit the values there). Never overwrites a file that already exists. BoxLang and `boxlang-miniserver` load a `.env` from the project root themselves, so the file also works for your API keys; BxAgents never reads, copies or packages it. * `--class` (a bare boolean flag, like the others described above) writes the class-based [`Agent.bx`](/next/conventions/agent-bx/index.html) instead of the default `Agent.yml`, for agents whose definition needs code (hooks, dynamic instructions). It applies to the root and to any subagents a template scaffolds, and only to `--template` mode - not to `--repo`/`--forgebox`. * `--template` picks one of 8 built-in starters, each layering a bit of pre-wired content on top of the base skeleton above (see [Agent Templates](/next/agent-templates/index.html) for every generated file in full, plus how `--repo`/`--forgebox` sources work and how to publish your own): * `minimal` - the bare skeleton, nothing extra. * `webui-chat` - adds a `gateways/webui.bx` exposing the [web chat UI](/next/conventions/gateways/index.html) at `/chat`. * `slack-bot` - adds a `gateways/slack.bx` channel adapter, plus matching `SLACK_BOT_TOKEN`/`SLACK_APP_TOKEN` stub lines in `.env`. * `telegram-bot` - adds a `gateways/telegram.bx` channel adapter, plus a matching `TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN` stub line in `.env`. * `github-bot` - adds a `gateways/github.bx` channel adapter, plus matching `GITHUB_TOKEN`/`GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET`/`GITHUB_BOT_NAME` stub lines in `.env`. * `mcp-server` - adds an example `mcp/exampleServer.bx` tool server and a `gateways/mcpExpose.bx` entry exposing it as an MCP server at `/mcp`. * `scheduled` - adds a [`schedules/Example.bx`](/next/conventions/schedules/index.html) scheduler calling the agent on a daily cron schedule. * `multi-agent` - adds a `subAgents` list to the root `Agent.yml` declaring two [subagents](/next/conventions/subagents/index.html) (`researcher`, `writer`), each scaffolded as its own real `subagents//Agent.yml` + `instructions.md`. * Also runs `box install` in the new project root, so `bxAgents test` works immediately with no separate install step. This is best-effort: if `box` isn't on `PATH` or the install fails, `new` still succeeds - the message just tells you to run it yourself. Pass `--skipInstall` to opt out of this step entirely. * **`--repo` mode** (`--repo=owner/repo-name` or a full URL): clones the repo via a bundled [JGit](https://www.eclipse.org/jgit/) dependency - no `git` binary needs to be installed. Always clones shallow (depth 1) and always strips the resulting `.git` folder afterward, so the new project starts with a clean history rather than staying tied to the template repo's own remote. Refuses to run into a directory that already exists and is non-empty, and fails clearly if no `Agent.yml` or `Agent.bx` is found in the cloned repo. * **`--forgebox` mode** (`--forgebox=`): installs a [ForgeBox](https://www.forgebox.io) package by talking to ForgeBox's own REST API directly (no `box` CLI required). Fails clearly if the slug doesn't exist, the download fails, or the installed package has no `Agent.yml` or `Agent.bx` at its root (unwrapping one level of nesting first, since many ForgeBox archives wrap their contents in a single top-level folder). * Only `--template` mode needs `--model`; `--repo`/`--forgebox` never require it, since the source project already defines its own. * `--name`/`--description` are ignored (with a warning in the output) when `--repo`/`--forgebox` is used - the cloned/installed project defines its own. * The `box install` convenience step (and `--skipInstall`) only ever apply to `--template` mode - a cloned/installed project's own `box.json` (if it has one at all) is left untouched. ### `add` Add one thing to a project that already exists, asking the same questions `new` asks. Today that is a `tool`, an `interceptor`, a `schedule`, an `mcp` server, a `gateway`, a `subagent`, a `skill`, a `profile`, a `provider`, a `capability` or an `extension`. ```bash bxAgents add # pick what to add bxAgents add tool # asks for the name, function, description and arguments bxAgents add tool WeatherTools --function=getWeather --description="Get the weather for a city" --args="city, days:numeric" bxAgents add tool Pinger --agent=researcher # into subagents/researcher/tools/ bxAgents add tool Pinger --dry-run # show the file, write nothing ``` * The positional arguments are the kind and the name, so the project is found by `--projectRoot=` or the current folder only. * At a terminal, whatever is not given as a flag is asked, in the full-screen UI (or numbered lines with `--no-tui`). With `--yes`, in a pipe or in CI nothing is asked: flags and defaults are used, and a required answer that is missing names the flag to pass. * Questions end on a review of the files that will be written. Cancelling, with Esc or Ctrl+C, changes nothing. * **Nothing is overwritten.** If a file already exists none are written and the error names it; `--force` replaces it. At a terminal the review offers to replace instead. * `--dry-run` prints each file with its text and writes nothing. #### `add tool` Creates `tools/.bx` with one `@AITool` function in the shape [bx-ai documents](/next/conventions/tools/index.html): a docblock describing each argument, the annotation carrying the description the model reads, and typed `required` arguments from which bx-ai builds the tool's schema. | Flag | Meaning | |------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------| | `--name=` | The file name, or the second positional. Letters, digits and underscores, starting with a letter. | | `--agent=` | Whose tool it is. Asked only when the project has subagents; `.` (the default) is the root agent. | | `--function=` | The function the model calls. Defaults to the file name with a lower-case first letter. | | `--description=` | What the tool does. The model reads it to decide when to call the tool. Without it, and with nothing to ask, the file gets a `TODO` description and the output reminds you to replace it. | | `--args=` | Comma separated, each `name` or `name:type` (`string` by default; `numeric`, `boolean`, `array`, `struct`, `date` and `any` also work). | A tool belongs to the agent whose folder it is in and is attached to that agent automatically. Two tool files of one agent may not share a name, even in different subfolders, so a clash is refused here instead of at the next `build`. Check the result with `bxAgents inspect --section=tools`. #### `add interceptor` Creates `interceptors/.bx` with one method for each interception point you pick, and the `@scope` that [the build splits on](/next/conventions/interceptors/index.html). ```bash bxAgents add interceptor AuditLogger --points=preProcess,onException --description="Log every request" bxAgents add interceptor AiWatch --scope=runtime --points=beforeAIModelInvoke,onAIError ``` | Flag | Meaning | |--------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------| | `--name=` | The file name, or the second positional. A name another interceptor already uses is refused. | | `--scope=agent\|runtime` | `agent` (the default) is a ColdBox interceptor registered with the generated app when it starts; its methods take `( event, interceptData, rc, prc )`. `runtime` listens to the events bx-ai announces in the BoxLang runtime and takes the event data as its one argument; BxAgents copies it to `.build/runtime-interceptors` but does not register it for you. | | `--points=` | Comma separated interception points. The picker offers the common ones; any ColdBox core point (`agent`) or bx-ai event (`runtime`) can be named here, and a name that is not a point for that scope is refused. Defaults to `preProcess` (`agent`) or `beforeAIModelInvoke` (`runtime`). | | `--description=` | One line for the class's docblock. Optional. | #### `add schedule` Adds a [scheduler](/next/conventions/schedules/index.html) to `schedules/` that sends an agent a message on a schedule. Three things are asked: when it runs, what it says to the agent, and which agent. Overlapping runs are always prevented (`.withNoOverlaps()`). Each schedule is its own file, `schedules/.bx`, so adding one never edits another. ```bash bxAgents add schedule --when="weekdays 08:30" --prompt="Summarize yesterday's findings" bxAgents add schedule digest --when="0 9 * * 1-5" --prompt="Check for new tickets" --agent=researcher bxAgents add schedule # asks how often, the details, a name, and what to say ``` | Flag | Meaning | |---------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------| | `--when=` | When it runs: one of the phrases below, or a cron expression. At a terminal, leave it out and you are asked how often, then the details. | | `--prompt=` | The message sent to the agent each time. | | `--name=` | The task's name, or the second positional. It also names the file: `daily-digest` writes `schedules/DailyDigest.bx`. Defaults to a name made from the phrase. A task name already used in `schedules/` is refused. | | `--agent=` | Which agent runs it. Asked only when the project has subagents; `.` (the default) is the root agent, which the file calls with `run()`. Another agent is called with `agent( "name" ).run()` by its declared `name`, so renaming the agent means editing the file. | | Phrase | Runs | Written as | |-------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------| | `every 15 minutes`, `every 2 hours`, `every 1 days` | At that interval | `.every( 15, "minutes" )`, `.every( 2, "hours" )`, `.every( 1, "days" )` | | `hourly`, `hourly :15` | Every hour, on the hour or at that minute | `.everyHour()`, `.everyHourAt( 15 )` | | `daily 09:00` | Every day at that time | `.everyDayAt( "09:00" )` | | `weekdays 08:30`, `weekends 10:00` | Monday to Friday, or Saturday and Sunday | `.onWeekdays( "08:30" )`, `.onWeekends( "10:00" )` | | `weekly mon 09:00` | Once a week (`mon` `tue` `wed` `thu` `fri` `sat` `sun`) | `.everyWeekOn( 1, "09:00" )` | | `monthly 1 09:00` | Once a month on that day, 1 to 28 so that no month skips it | `.everyMonthOn( 1, "09:00" )` | | `first-business-day 09:00`, `last-business-day 17:00` | On that business day of each month | `.onFirstBusinessDayOfTheMonth( "09:00" )` | | `0 9 * * 1-5`, `0 30 8 * * MON-FRI` | Any cron expression: five fields, or six with seconds in front | `.cron( "..." )` with six fields (a leading `0` is added to a five-field one), checked by BoxLang's own parser. Only the six-field form fires on BoxLang 1.19.0 | Times are 24 hour `HH:mm` in the scheduler's timezone. A phrase is never written as a five-field `.cron()`: on BoxLang 1.19.0 that does not fire (see [Cron](/next/conventions/schedules/index.html#cron)). * An existing file of the same name is a conflict and nothing is written; `--force` replaces it. * Schedulers run while the app is served (`bxAgents serve`). Check the result with `bxAgents inspect --section=schedule`. #### `add mcp` Adds an MCP server in either direction: one the agent **calls** (written into `Agent.yml`), or one the project **hosts** (`mcp/.bx`). ```bash bxAgents add mcp client github # a server from the catalog the new wizard uses (or --direction=client) bxAgents add mcp client --url=https://mcp.acme.dev/mcp --name=acme --auth=bearer --env=ACME_TOKEN bxAgents add mcp server tools --description="My tools" bxAgents add mcp # asks which way ``` **`add mcp client`** adds an entry to the agent's `mcpServers:` list. A name from the catalog (`github`, `stripe`, `notion`, `atlassian`, `cloudflare`, `supabase`, `git`) fills in the address and the sign-in, or for a server that runs as a program on this machine (`git`) the `command` to start it and what it needs on the PATH; otherwise give `--url`. Without a terminal, name the server as the positional or give `--url`. | Flag | Meaning | |--------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------| | `--server=` | A catalog server by name, instead of the positional. | | `--url=
` | A server not in the catalog. An address with a user name, password or key in it is refused: the secret belongs in an environment variable. | | `--name=

title: Composing Subagents
body:
Composing Subagents subagents/ holds nested agents - each an ordinary BxAgents project of its own, with its own Agent.yml + instructions.md , and optionally its own tools/ , skills/ , etc. my-agent/ ├── Agent.yml # subAgents: [ researcher ] ├── instructions.md └── subagents/ └── researcher/ ├── Agent.yml └── instructions.md A subagent is wired to its parent by name, declared in the parent's Agent.yml this is the subagents/ folder name : subAgents: [ researcher ] At build time, bx-ai's addSubAgent() wraps each built subagent instance as a callable tool on the parent automatically - there's no separate tool-wrapping step to write yourself. Flat on disk, a graph in config Every subagent - no matter how deeply another subagent's own config references it - lives directly under the root project's subagents/ folder. A subagent's own declared subAgents names reference sibling entries in that same root-level folder, never a folder nested under itself. flowchart LR subgraph disk["ON DISK - always flat"] direction TB R1["subagents/A/"] R2["subagents/B/"] R3["subagents/C/"] end subgraph declared["DECLARED - each agent definition's own subAgents list"] direction TB GA["A"] --> GB["B"] --> GC["C"] end subgraph built["BUILT - leaf-first"] direction TB O1["1. build C"] --> O2["2. build B
with the built C"] --> O3["3. build A
with the built B"] end disk -.-> declared declared -.-> built A cycle in the declared graph ( A -> B -> A ) is rejected at validation, before anything is generated. A diamond (two parents sharing one descendant) is fine. Two different names, two different jobs The folder name under subagents/ is what subAgents: [ "..." ] references - purely a build-time wiring concern. The subagent's own declared name (its definition's name field) is what you retrieve it by at runtime - every agent in the tree is registered in config/WireBox.bx under this name, so a schedules/ scheduler (or anything else WireBox-aware) reaches it with getInstance( "TheAgentName" ) . These two names can differ, and often will. Because name is now also a WireBox binding key, it must be unique across the whole project - build fails validation if two agents share one. Try it Acme support gets two helpers: a researcher that looks things up and a writer that words the final reply. Each is a folder with its own Agent.yml and instructions.md , and each picks one of the profiles from Models and Profiles . ( bxAgents add subagent researcher --profile=fast writes the same frame and wires it in for you.) name: researcher description: Looks things up and writes a short summary with sources. profile: fast You research a question and answer with a short summary and the sources you used. name: writer description: Turns facts into a friendly reply for a customer. profile: planner You write the final reply to a customer from the facts you are given. Be brief and friendly. Wire them to the root agent, with the folder names, at the end of Agent.yml : subAgents: [ researcher, writer ] Rebuild and look at what the root agent can use. Each subagent arrived as a tool called delegate_to_ : cd ~/bxagents-course/acme-support bxAgents build bxAgents invoke --message=capabilities Build succeeded: /acme-support/.build/app I can use these tools: delegate_to_researcher, delegate_to_writer The scripted model has a rule for research and one for write : each delegates a task to that subagent. The subagent answers with the model of its profile, which the default answer names, so you can see who did the work: bxAgents invoke --message=research bxAgents invoke --message=write The researcher answered: I can help with orders, returns and shipping. (Answered by fast-model.) The writer answered: I can help with orders, returns and shipping. (Answered by planner-model.) In the web app and in the terminal chat you can also talk to a subagent directly. The Talk to menu in the bar above the conversation lists the main agent and each subagent; pick one and the next message goes to it, a banner says who you are talking to, and every agent keeps its own memory. In the terminal the same thing is /agent . Checkpoint acme-support/subagents/ has researcher/ and writer/ , and Agent.yml ends with subAgents: [ researcher, writer ] . kit/resume.sh 11-composing-subagents restores them; rebuild after. Full reference: subagents/ . Next: Routines and Reports

markdown:
# Connect: services that ask each person to sign in
> The seven ready-made services (GitHub, Stripe, Notion, Atlassian, Cloudflare, Supabase, Git) are [connectors](/next/conventions/connectors/index.html) and need nothing in `Agent.yml`. This page is for services you write yourself under `mcpServers`.

Some [MCP servers](/next/conventions/mcp/index.html) do not take a fixed key. Mail, calendars and ticket systems ask **each person** to sign in with OAuth, and then accept a token that expires and is renewed. Add `oauth` to the server's entry in `Agent.yml` and BX Agents does the rest: the person signs in once, their tokens are **sealed in the chat database** with the [vault](/next/conventions/vault/index.html) key, and the agent uses **their** tokens when it acts for them. The model never sees a token.

```yaml
# Agent.yml
mcpServers:
  - name: mail
    url: https://mail.example.com/mcp
    oauth:
      scopes: [ mail.read ]
```

`oauth: true` is enough for a server that tells us what we need. The entry needs a `name`, because people type it.

The sign in above is real, against a small fake mail service ([`tools/demo/fake-oauth-mcp.bxs`](https://github.com/ortus-boxlang/bx-agents/tree/development/tools/demo)); the agent's first answer is scripted.

## What you write

|     Key under `oauth`      |                                                                                                      Meaning                                                                                                       |
|----------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `scopes`                   | A list of scopes to ask for. Left out: what the server asks for, else everything it supports                                                                                                                       |
| `clientId`, `clientSecret` | A client you registered with the provider yourself. Left out: the client registers itself. `clientSecret` must be an ``${env.NAME}` or `${vault.NAME}`` placeholder: a secret written in the file is a build error |
| `clientMetadataUrl`        | The `https` address of your Client ID Metadata Document, for providers that support them                                                                                                                           |
| `clientName`               | The name shown on the sign in page when the client registers itself                                                                                                                                                |
| `redirectUri`              | Where the provider sends the person back. Left out: your public address, the [API path](/next/guides/agent-api/index.html) and `/connect/callback`                                                                 |

A server with `oauth` cannot also have `token`, `user` or `password`. Everything is checked when the project is built.

## Signing in

Each way asks the same questions of the same place, so they never disagree about who is connected.

|     Where      |                                                                               How                                                                                |
|----------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Web page       | The **Connectors** page, **In Agent.yml** tab: a row per service with *Connect* or *Disconnect*. The sign in opens in a new tab; the page notices when it worked |
| Terminal chat  | `/connect` lists the services, `/connect mail` prints an address and waits for the browser in the background, `/connect mail remove` forgets it                  |
| Command line   | `bxAgents connect` lists, `bxAgents connect mail` signs in, `bxAgents connect mail --remove` forgets. See [`connect`](/next/cli-reference/index.html#connect)    |
| Chat platforms | `/connect mail` sends an address that works once, for ten minutes. Open it in a browser and sign in                                                              |
| HTTP           | `GET /connect`, `POST /connect`, `POST /connect/remove` on the [agent API](/next/guides/agent-api/index.html)                                                    |

![The terminal chat after /connect: not connected, the address to open, then connected](/next/assets/tui/connect-chat.png)

When a person has not signed in to a service, the agent is told which one and how to connect, in one short line, so it can say so instead of "I cannot read your mail". The tools of a service appear in the same running agent once somebody has signed in; there is no restart.

## Trying it on a chat platform

A person reaches the agent from Telegram, Slack and the other [gateways](/next/conventions/gateways/index.html), and `/connect` works there too. The browser is the part to plan for: the provider sends it back to **your server**, so the server needs an address the person's browser can open. On your own machine, give it one with a tunnel.

1. **A gateway.** For Telegram, `gateways/telegramChannel.bx` with `type: "telegram"` and `botTokenEnvVar: "TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN"` (see [Telegram](/next/conventions/gateways/telegram/index.html)). Make the bot with @BotFather and `export TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN=...`.
2. **A service that asks people to sign in** , with `oauth` on its `mcpServers` entry as above.
3. **A public address.** Start a tunnel to the port you serve on, `export BXAGENTS_PUBLIC_URL=https://your-tunnel.example.com`, and register `https://your-tunnel.example.com/__bxagents/connect/callback` with the provider.
4. **Build and serve:** `bxAgents build` then `bxAgents serve`.
5. **In the chat with the bot:** send `/connect`, then `/connect mail`. The bot answers with an address that works once, for ten minutes. Open it in a browser, allow access, and send `/connect` again: the service is *connected*.

The person is the platform's own id for them (a Telegram user id, a Slack member id). Their tokens are kept under it, so each person on the platform signs in once. Send `/connect` in a private chat with the bot, not in a group: anyone in a group can open a link posted there.

## Where the browser comes back to

After the person signs in, the provider sends their browser to an address you register with it.

* **A served agent** receives it at `<your public address><API path>/connect/callback`, for example `https://agent.example.com/__bxagents/connect/callback`. Set `BXAGENTS_PUBLIC_URL` to the address people reach the server at, and register that callback with the provider.
* **The terminal** has no public address. `bxAgents connect` and `/connect` open a small listener on `127.0.0.1`, on a free port, for a few minutes, catch the one redirect and close it. Providers that follow RFC 8252 accept any port on the loopback address. For one that does not, give the port you registered: `bxAgents connect mail --port=8765`.

The callback is the one public route of the connect routes. It is safe because it carries no person: the **single use `state`** that the sign in started with says who it was for, and it is used once and expires after ten minutes. Nothing in the address names anyone.

## Whose tokens

A turn runs as the person who asked, so the agent uses that person's tokens. A person never uses another's. A run with nobody behind it, such as a [schedule](/next/conventions/schedules/index.html), finds no tokens and gets no tools from that service.

The list of a service's tools is the same for everyone, so when the app starts it is asked for as **the person who signed in last**. If nobody has, the agent starts without those tools and gets them when the first person signs in.
> **Note**
>
> Signing in on the web page does not sign the same human in on a chat platform: each place knows the person by its own id (`local`, a Slack user id), so each is its own sign in. Say so to the people who use both.

## Where the tokens are

Tokens, the client registration and a sign in waiting for its callback are rows of the `oauth_records` table, each **sealed with the vault key** (AES-256-GCM) and bound to its row, so a value copied onto another row does not open. The key is the vault's: `BXAGENTS_VAULT_KEY`, or the key file beside the database. Losing the key means everyone signs in again, and a changed key is reported by name. `bxAgents vault status` says where it comes from.

bx-ai's own token stores keep tokens as plain text; this is why BX Agents brings its own.

## Limits

* OAuth is for web servers (HTTP). A server that runs as a program takes its credentials from its environment.
* A link sent in a group chat can be used by anyone in it: ask people to use `/connect` in a private chat with the bot.
* The sign in follows the [MCP authorization specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest/basic/authorization): PKCE (S256) is required, and a provider that does not offer it is refused.

title: Connecting Chat Platforms
body:
Connecting Chat Platforms The other kind of gateways/* entry - one with a type key instead of exposes - registers a bx-ai IGateway , a channel adapter for external delivery or human-in-the-loop approval. This is a real "chat bot" connection, distinct from the REST exposure you built in Exposing Your Agent over HTTP and MCP . Two request-driven types: mock and cli mock is test-only. cli is bx-ai's own built-in human-in-the-loop approval channel - a blocking stdin/stdout prompt, and what HumanInTheLoopMiddleware attaches by default when no gateway is specified. http - your own webhook endpoint // gateways/slack.bx class { function configure() { return { type : "http", secretEnvVar : "SLACK_WEBHOOK_SECRET" }; } } secretEnvVar names an environment variable holding the signing secret - never the secret value itself . It's resolved live at server startup, so it's never present in generated source or a packaged .bxa either. This gets real routes, from a single route( "/gateways" ).toAiGateway() in the generated router: POST /gateways/:gateway/events , GET /gateways/:gateway/events (the platform's URL verification handshake), GET /gateways/interactions/:requestID , and POST /gateways/interactions/:requestID/decisions . Nine push-style platforms Telegram, Slack, Discord, Email, WhatsApp Business Cloud, Microsoft Teams, Twilio SMS, GitHub, and Signal each hold their own connection (long-poll, websocket, webhook, or SSE) and push inbound messages to your agent as they arrive: // gateways/telegramChannel.bx class { function configure() { return { type : "telegram", botTokenEnvVar: "TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN" }; } } Every platform follows the same secrets stay external rule - every *EnvVar key names an environment variable, resolved live, never a literal in generated code. One GatewaySession ties them together Any project with at least one push-style gateway gets a generated start-up statement in the generated base Application that builds a single bx-ai GatewaySession bundling every push-style gateway, bound to your project's root agent: flowchart TD M["a message arrives on thread T"] --> B{"is a run already

# Connecting Chat Platforms The other kind of `gateways/*` entry - one with a `type` key instead of `exposes` - registers a bx-ai `IGateway`, a channel adapter for external delivery or human-in-the-loop approval. This is a real "chat bot" connection, distinct from the REST exposure you built in [Exposing Your Agent over HTTP and MCP](/next/course/13-exposing-http-and-mcp/index.html). ## Two request-driven types: `mock` and `cli` `mock` is test-only. `cli` is bx-ai's own built-in human-in-the-loop **approval** channel - a blocking stdin/stdout prompt, and what `HumanInTheLoopMiddleware` attaches by default when no gateway is specified. ## `http` - your own webhook endpoint ```javascript // gateways/slack.bx class { function configure() { return { type : "http", secretEnvVar : "SLACK_WEBHOOK_SECRET" }; } } ``` `secretEnvVar` names an environment variable holding the signing secret - **never the secret value itself** . It's resolved live at server startup, so it's never present in generated source or a packaged `.bxa` either. This gets real routes, from a single `route( "/gateways" ).toAiGateway()` in the generated router: `POST /gateways/:gateway/events`, `GET /gateways/:gateway/events` (the platform's URL verification handshake), `GET /gateways/interactions/:requestID`, and `POST /gateways/interactions/:requestID/decisions`. ## Nine push-style platforms Telegram, Slack, Discord, Email, WhatsApp Business Cloud, Microsoft Teams, Twilio SMS, GitHub, and Signal each hold their own connection (long-poll, websocket, webhook, or SSE) and push inbound messages to your agent as they arrive: ```javascript // gateways/telegramChannel.bx class { function configure() { return { type : "telegram", botTokenEnvVar: "TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN" }; } } ``` Every platform follows the same `secrets stay external` rule - every `*EnvVar` key names an environment variable, resolved live, never a literal in generated code. ## One GatewaySession ties them together Any project with at least one push-style gateway gets a generated start-up statement in the generated base `Application` that builds a single bx-ai `GatewaySession` bundling every push-style gateway, bound to your project's root agent: ```mermaid flowchart TD M["a message arrives on thread T"] --> B{"is a run already
in flight on T?"} B -->|"no"| D["dispatch a new turn"] B -->|"yes"| P{"policy"} P -->|"reject"| R["Immediate 'busy' reply"] P -->|"queue (default)"| Q["Enqueue, runs after the current turn"] P -->|"steer"| ST["Spliced into the SAME run"] P -->|"interrupt"| I["Cancel current turn, then run this one"] style D fill:#d4edda,stroke:#155724 style R fill:#f8d7da,stroke:#721c24 ``` Control the policy from `Agent.yml`: ```yaml gatewaySession: policy: queue # both optional, these are the defaults maxQueueDepth: 50 ``` > **Warning** > > v1 limitation: exactly one `GatewaySession`, always bound to the project's root > agent - a project with subagents can't yet route different gateways to different > subagents. ## Every person has their own conversation The agent is told who is writing (the platform and their id there, such as `slack:U123`) and which conversation it is: the chat, plus its thread when the platform has them (a Telegram forum topic, a Slack thread). So memory, `/notes`, `/remember` and the conversation list are kept apart per person and per thread. Two people in one channel do not share a memory, and neither do two chats on two platforms. The list is stored in the same `chat.db` (in the agent's data home) the web page uses, marked with the platform it started on; an admin can see it with `GET /__bxagents/sessions?all=1`. ## Commands in a chat A message that is a slash command is answered by BxAgents and never reaches the model. A safe set is on by default: `/help`, `/tools`, `/model`, `/info`, `/ping`, `/remember`, `/notes` and `/connect`. The conversation commands (`/new`, `/clear`, `/compact`, `/sessions`, `/resume`) are off, because most chats are one long conversation; turn them on with `conversation: true`. Each platform shows the commands its own way (Telegram's `/` menu, Discord application commands, Slack slash commands, buttons on WhatsApp, a numbered list on SMS). ```yaml gatewaySession: commands: conversation: true # also /new, /clear, /compact, /sessions, /resume prefixes: { slack: "!" } # a different one-character prefix for one gateway ``` Pictures and text files sent on Telegram, Discord, Slack, WhatsApp and Twilio MMS reach the agent with the message (`gatewaySession.attachments: false` switches that off). ## Adding a platform, or your own `bxAgents add gateway` adds a platform the way the `new` wizard does: it writes the `gateways/` file, an empty `.env` line for each credential and the setup steps that happen outside the project (a bot token, a public address). `bxAgents doctor` reports credentials that are still not set. If a platform is not in the list, an [extension](/next/course/18-interceptors-and-modules/index.html) can bring a new gateway type. ## Try it A chat platform needs an account on that platform, which the course cannot give you, and the `mock` and `cli` types are test and approval channels, not chat. What you can do offline is see exactly what adding a platform would write, without writing it. `--dry-run` prints the files and the line for `.env`: ```bash cd ~/bxagents-course/acme-support bxAgents add gateway telegram --dry-run ``` ```text Would create gateways/telegram.bx ... Would append to .env ... TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN= ... ``` That is the whole change for Telegram: one small file that names the variable, and an empty line for the token. The token itself would go in `.env` (never in the file), and `bxAgents doctor` reports a credential that is still not set. If you have a disposable bot token, drop `--dry-run`, put the token in `.env`, rebuild and `bxAgents serve`: message the bot and the same Acme agent answers, with its tools, skills and notes. The other eight platforms follow the same shape, and a message there reaches the same agent, so the commands (`/help`, `/tools`, `/remember`, `/notes`) you used in the terminal work in the chat too. ## Checkpoint Nothing in `acme-support/` changed in this lesson (the dry run writes nothing). Full reference: [gateways/](/next/conventions/gateways/index.html). Next: [Hosting and Consuming MCP Servers](/next/course/17-hosting-mcp-servers/index.html)

body: Connector catalog This page is written from the connector files in src/main/bx/catalog/connectors/ ( tools/generate-connector-docs.bxs ), so it says what the product does. See connectors for how they work, and how to add one . libraries Datadog sign in or token medium Search logs, metrics, traces, monitors and dashboards in Datadog Excalidraw no sign in low Draw hand-drawn style diagrams and sketches Git a local program (an from an agent Supabase sign in or token high Database, SQL, migrations, projects and branches Vercel sign in high Search Vercel docs, manage projects, inspect deployments and logs, and query Web sign in high List event types and meetings, create scheduling links and bookings, read meeting notes Canva sign in (your own app) medium Create, find, edit, comment on and export Canva designs and assets ClickUp sign in high Search, create and update tasks, documents and chat messages Gamma sign in medium Create, search, edit and export presentations, documents and webpages HyperFrames by HeyGen sign in medium Create, revise and render videos from a text description Linear sign in or token medium Find, create and update issues, projects, documents and comments Notion sign in or token medium Search, read, create and update pages and databases RingCentral Chat sign in high Team messaging chats, direct conversations, teams and posts in RingEX RingCentral Phone sign in high Call logs, contacts, messages, presence and SMS in RingEX Slack sign in (your own app) or token high Search channels and people, read threads, send messages, canvases, files and lists Whop sign in high Search the Whop docs and read or change live Whop data Sales Connector Connects with Risk What it does HubSpot sign in (your own app) high Search and update CRM records, activities, content and campaigns in HubSpot Meltwater sign in or token low Media and social mentions, saved searches and insights from Meltwater Finance Connector Connects with Risk What it does Bigdata.com token low Search financial news, filings, earnings transcripts and analyst research Daloopa sign in or token low Company financials, KPIs, filings and earnings transcripts S&P Global sign in low Financial data and company research from the Kensho LLM-ready API Stripe sign in or token high Customers, invoices, subscriptions, refunds and documentation search Analytics Connector Connects with Risk What it does Mixpanel sign in medium Run reports on events, funnels and retention, and browse dashboards Social Media Connector Connects with Risk What it does Buffer sign in or token high Read channels and queue, schedule and edit posts, capture ideas and pull post analytics Metricool sign in or token high Manage brands, read social analytics and schedule posts Advertising Connector Connects with Risk What it does X Ads sign in (your own app) high Read X Ads accounts and analytics, and create and manage campaigns Apps Connector Connects with Risk What it does Wix sign in or token high Search Wix documentation and make API calls on your Wix sites Zapier sign in or token high Run actions in the apps connected to your Zapier account Details Cloudflare cloudflare . The Cloudflare API: DNS, Workers, rules and more. Listed under Developer. Connects with: sign in or token. Risk: high. Three tools (search, execute and docs) reach more than 2,500 endpoints, so turning tools on or off does not limit it. Only the scopes of the sign in or the permissions of the token do. It can change DNS, Workers and rules and create billable resources. Address: https://mcp.cloudflare.com/mcp Sign in: OAuth with the scopes user:read , account:read . Token: sealed in the vault as CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN , only for mcp.cloudflare.com . A Cloudflare API token, user or account. Scope it to the accounts and zones the agent should touch. Documentation . Checked on 2026-11-14. Context7 context7 . Up-to-date documentation and code examples for libraries. Listed under Developer. Connects with: token. Risk: low. Reads public library documentation. The library name and the question the agent asks are sent to Context7's servers. Address: https://mcp.context7.com/mcp Token: sealed in the vault as CONTEXT7_API_KEY , only for mcp.context7.com . A Context7 API key (starts with ctx7sk), made on the dashboard at context7.com. The server also answers without one, at much lower rate limits. Documentation . Checked on 2026-11-26. Datadog datadog . Search logs, metrics, traces, monitors and dashboards in Datadog. Listed under Developer. Connects with: sign in or token. Risk: medium. Reads logs, metrics, traces and other observability data, and some tools can change things such as dashboards, notebooks and monitors in the person's organization. Access follows the person's Datadog permissions. Address: https://{site}/v1/mcp (the host is one of 7, see the option below) Sign in: OAuth. Token: sealed in the vault as DATADOG_MCP_TOKEN , only for mcp.datadoghq.com , mcp.us3.datadoghq.com , mcp.us5.datadoghq.com , mcp.datadoghq.eu , mcp.ap1.datadoghq.com , mcp.ap2.datadoghq.com , mcp.uk1.datadoghq.com . A Personal Access Token or Service Access Token made in Datadog. It is sent as a bearer token. Option What it does Goes to For site The MCP address for the site where your Datadog organization is hosted. Check the address you use to sign in to Datadog. One of: mcp.datadoghq.com (US1), mcp.us3.datadoghq.com (US3), mcp.us5.datadoghq.com (US5), mcp.datadoghq.eu (EU1), mcp.ap1.datadoghq.com (AP1), mcp.ap2.datadoghq.com (AP2), mcp.uk1.datadoghq.com (UK1). host site every way in Documentation . Checked on 2026-11-27. Excalidraw excalidraw . Draw hand-drawn style diagrams and sketches. Listed under Developer. Connects with: no sign in. Risk: low. A public server run by a third party with no account. Whatever the agent sends to draw a diagram goes to that server. It does not reach the person's own data. Address: https://mcp.excalidraw.com/mcp Sign in: none. A person switches it on for themselves, and no secret is stored. Documentation . Checked on 2026-11-27. Git git . Read, search and change local Git repositories. Listed under Developer. Connects with: a local program (an admin). Risk: medium. Can add, reset, commit, merge and switch branches. Described by its authors as in early development. Without a repository set it can reach every repository the process can. Runs: uvx mcp-server-git==2026.11.11 on the machine the agent runs on. It needs uvx on the PATH. Install uv ( https://docs.astral.sh/uv/ ) so the agent can start this server. It runs on the machine the agent runs on, in the folder you start the agent from. Sign in: none. A person switches it on for themselves, and no secret is stored. Option What it does Goes to For repository A path inside a Git working tree. The server then works only in that repository. Left empty, it can read and write any repository the process can reach. arg --repository every way in Documentation . Checked on 2026-11-17. GitHub github . Repositories, issues, pull requests, Actions and code search. Listed under Developer. Connects with: token. Risk: high. Can create pull requests, push files, merge, delete files and trigger Actions. Prefer a fine-grained token with read access first. Address: https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/ Token: sealed in the vault as GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN , only for api.githubcopilot.com . A personal access token. Give it only the repositories and permissions the agent needs. Option What it does Goes to For toolsets A comma separated list of the GitHub toolsets to enable, for example issues,pull_requests. Left empty, the server's default set is used. header X-MCP-Toolsets every way in readonly Turns off every tool that changes something. header X-MCP-Readonly every way in Documentation . Checked on 2026-11-14. Netlify netlify . Create, deploy and manage Netlify sites from an agent. Listed under Developer. Connects with: sign in. Risk: high. Can create and change sites and publish deploys in the person's Netlify account, which can reach production sites. Start with a test site. Address: https://mcp.netlify.com/mcp Sign in: OAuth. Documentation . Checked on 2026-11-26. Supabase supabase . Database, SQL, migrations, projects and branches. Listed under Developer. Connects with: sign in or token. Risk: high. Runs SQL and migrations and can create paid projects. Read only is on by default; add a project to limit it to one. Table data can carry prompt injection, so never give it to end users. Address: https://mcp.supabase.com/mcp Sign in: OAuth. Token: sealed in the vault as SUPABASE_ACCESS_TOKEN , only for mcp.supabase.com . A personal access token. Option What it does Goes to For project_ref Limits the connector to one project and turns off the account tools. query project_ref every way in read_only Runs queries as a read only Postgres user. On by default. query read_only every way in features A comma separated list of the tool groups to enable. Left empty, the server's default groups are used. query features every way in Documentation . Checked on 2026-11-14. Vercel vercel . Search Vercel docs, manage projects, inspect deployments and logs, and query Web Analytics. Listed under Developer. Connects with: sign in. Risk: high. Can manage projects and deployments in the person's Vercel account, which can reach production sites. Start with a test team or project. Address: https://mcp.vercel.com Sign in: OAuth. Documentation . Checked on 2026-11-26. Asana asana . Search, read, create and update tasks, projects and comments in Asana. Listed under Productivity. Connects with: sign in (your own app). Risk: medium. Can create and change tasks, projects and comments in the workspaces the person can reach. Address: https://mcp.asana.com/v2/mcp Sign in, with your own app: the service takes no dynamic client registration, so an admin registers an app and sets ASANA_CLIENT_ID and ASANA_CLIENT_SECRET in the agent's vault or environment. In the Asana developer console create a new app of type MCP app, add the redirect address (the public address of this app followed by /__bxagents/connect/callback) on its OAuth page, and under Manage distribution allow the workspaces that will use it. Asana does not accept dynamic client registration. Scopes: default . Documentation . Checked on 2026-11-27. Atlassian (Jira and Confluence) atlassian . Jira work items, Confluence pages, Bitbucket. Listed under Productivity. Connects with: sign in or token. Risk: medium. Creates and updates work items and pages and posts comments. Address: https://mcp.atlassian.com/v2/mcp Sign in: OAuth. Token: sealed in the vault as ATLASSIAN_API_TOKEN , only for mcp.atlassian.com . A service account API key, sent as a Bearer token. An organization admin must allow API token sign in first. Personal API tokens use Basic authentication and are not supported here. Tokens are not tied to one site and some tools are missing. Documentation . Checked on 2026-11-14. Box box . Search and read files and folders, ask Box AI, create folders and comments. Listed under Productivity. Connects with: sign in (your own app). Risk: medium. Can create folders, comments and new file versions, and some tools can change file properties or create shared links. Tools that write are off by default in Box. People can only reach content they already have access to. Address: https://mcp.box.com Sign in, with your own app: the service takes no dynamic client registration, so an admin registers an app and sets BOX_CLIENT_ID and BOX_CLIENT_SECRET in the agent's vault or environment. A Box admin opens Integrations in the Admin Console, configures the Box MCP server, adds Integration Credentials, copies the client id and secret, enters the redirect address (the public address of this app followed by /__bxagents/connect/callback) and selects the access scopes. Box also lists docgen.readwrite, which needs an Enterprise Advanced license. Scopes: root_readwrite , ai.readwrite . Documentation . Checked on 2026-11-27. Calendly calendly . List event types and meetings, create scheduling links and bookings, read meeting notes. Listed under Productivity. Connects with: sign in. Risk: high. Can book and cancel meetings, create event types, mark no-shows and invite people to the organization, which can send emails to other people. Address: https://mcp.calendly.com Sign in: OAuth with the scopes mcp:scheduling:read , mcp:scheduling:write . Documentation . Checked on 2026-11-26. Canva canva . Create, find, edit, comment on and export Canva designs and assets. Listed under Productivity. Connects with: sign in (your own app). Risk: medium. Can create and edit designs, upload assets, add comments and move items between folders in the person's own Canva account. Address: https://api.canva.com/connect/v1/mcp Sign in, with your own app: the service takes no dynamic client registration, so an admin registers an app and sets CANVA_CLIENT_ID and CANVA_CLIENT_SECRET in the agent's vault or environment. In the Canva Developer Portal create an app, open Outside Canva, turn on Canva MCP under Integration methods, copy the client id, generate a client secret, and add the redirect address (the public address of this app followed by /__bxagents/connect/callback) under Redirect URLs. Each person signs in with their own Canva account. Scopes: profile:read , design:meta:read , design:content:read , design:content:write , folder:read , folder:write , brandtemplate:meta:read , brandtemplate:content:read , brandtemplate:content:write , comment:read , comment:write , asset:read , asset:write , brandkit:read , help:answers:read , help:answers:write . Documentation . Checked on 2026-11-27. ClickUp clickup . Search, create and update tasks, documents and chat messages. Listed under Productivity. Connects with: sign in. Risk: high. Can create and change tasks and documents and post chat messages that other people in the workspace see. It has no delete tools. Address: https://mcp.clickup.com/mcp Sign in: OAuth. Documentation . Checked on 2026-11-26. Gamma gamma . Create, search, edit and export presentations, documents and webpages. Listed under Productivity. Connects with: sign in. Risk: medium. Can create and edit gammas in the workspace and uses the workspace's credits when it generates or edits. Address: https://mcp.gamma.app/mcp Sign in: OAuth. Documentation . Checked on 2026-11-26. HyperFrames by HeyGen hyperframes . Create, revise and render videos from a text description. Listed under Productivity. Connects with: sign in. Risk: medium. Creates and renders videos in the person's HeyGen account, which can use credits. The documentation calls this connector a beta. Address: https://mcp.heygen.com/mcp/hyperframes/ Sign in: OAuth. Documentation . Checked on 2026-11-26. Linear linear . Find, create and update issues, projects, documents and comments. Listed under Productivity. Connects with: sign in or token. Risk: medium. Can create and change issues, projects, documents and comments in the workspace. Use a read-only key to limit it. Address: https://mcp.linear.app/mcp Sign in: OAuth with the scopes read , write . Token: sealed in the vault as LINEAR_API_KEY , only for mcp.linear.app . A Linear API key, or an OAuth access token from your own Linear OAuth app. A key with only the Read permission gives read-only access. Documentation . Checked on 2026-11-26. Notion notion . Search, read, create and update pages and databases. Listed under Productivity. Connects with: sign in or token. Risk: medium. Can edit and delete pages and databases. Address: https://mcp.notion.com/mcp Sign in: OAuth. Token: sealed in the vault as NOTION_MCP_TOKEN , only for mcp.notion.com . A token made by a workspace owner under New MCP token in the developer portal. Business and Enterprise plans only. Documentation . Checked on 2026-11-14. RingCentral Chat ringcentral-chat . Team messaging chats, direct conversations, teams and posts in RingEX. Listed under Productivity. Connects with: sign in. Risk: high. Can read and post messages in your chats and teams as you. This is a RingCentral Labs preview. Address: https://mcp.labs.ringcentral.com/ringex/team-chat Sign in: OAuth with the scopes ReadAccounts , TeamMessaging . Documentation . Checked on 2026-11-26. RingCentral Phone ringcentral-phone . Call logs, contacts, messages, presence and SMS in RingEX. Listed under Productivity. Connects with: sign in. Risk: high. Can read call history and messages and send SMS from your number. This is a RingCentral Labs preview. Address: https://mcp.labs.ringcentral.com/ringex/phone Sign in: OAuth with the scopes ReadAccounts , ReadContacts , ReadCallLog , AI , ReadMessages , ReadPresence , SMS . Documentation . Checked on 2026-11-26. Slack slack . Search channels and people, read threads, send messages, canvases, files and lists. Listed under Productivity. Connects with: sign in (your own app) or token. Risk: high. Can send and schedule messages as the person, add reactions, create channels and canvases, upload files and read private channels and direct messages the token reaches. Use a test workspace first, and give the token read scopes only to start with. Address: https://mcp.slack.com/mcp Sign in, with your own app: the service takes no dynamic client registration, so an admin registers an app and sets SLACK_CLIENT_ID and SLACK_CLIENT_SECRET in the agent's vault or environment. Register a Slack app at api.slack.com/apps that is internal to your workspace or published in the Slack Marketplace (Slack refuses MCP for other apps, and does not accept dynamic client registration). Add the user scopes listed, and add the app public address followed by /__bxagents/connect/callback as a redirect URL. Scopes: search:read.public , search:read.private , search:read.mpim , search:read.im , search:read.files , search:read.users , files:read , files:write , emoji:read , chat:write , channels:history , groups:history , mpim:history , im:history , channels:read , groups:read , im:read , mpim:read , channels:write , groups:write , im:write , mpim:write , reactions:read , reactions:write , canvases:read , canvases:write , users:read , users:read.email , lists:read , lists:write . Token: sealed in the vault as SLACK_MCP_TOKEN , only for mcp.slack.com . A Slack user token (xoxp-...) of a Slack app that is internal to your workspace or published in the Slack Marketplace, with only the scopes the agent needs (docs.slack.dev lists the scopes of each tool). Slack does not accept dynamic client registration, so there is no sign in, and an app that is neither internal nor published is refused. (not verified yet) Documentation . Checked on 2026-11-27. Whop whop . Search the Whop docs and read or change live Whop data. Listed under Productivity. Connects with: sign in. Risk: high. Asks for admin access and works on production data only. It can change products, plans and payments data. There is no sandbox. Address: https://mcp.whop.com/mcp Sign in: OAuth with the scopes admin . Documentation . Checked on 2026-11-26. HubSpot hubspot . Search and update CRM records, activities, content and campaigns in HubSpot. Listed under Sales. Connects with: sign in (your own app). Risk: high. Can create and change CRM records, publish landing pages and blog posts, and create or schedule social posts. Use read access only to start with. Address: https://mcp.hubspot.com Sign in, with your own app: the service takes no dynamic client registration, so an admin registers an app and sets HUBSPOT_CLIENT_ID and HUBSPOT_CLIENT_SECRET in the agent's vault or environment. In HubSpot go to Development, then MCP Connectors, and create an MCP connector with the redirect address (the public address of this app followed by /__bxagents/connect/callback). Copy its client id and client secret. The account must be on the HubSpot developer platform, and an admin connects first. Scopes come from what the person grants at install. Documentation . Checked on 2026-11-27. Meltwater meltwater . Media and social mentions, saved searches and insights from Meltwater. Listed under Sales. Connects with: sign in or token. Risk: low. Reads your saved searches, tags and media and social data. Which tools you get depends on your Meltwater package. Address: https://api.meltwater.com/v2/mcp Sign in: OAuth with the scopes tools:read , tools:call . Token: sealed in the vault as MELTWATER_API_KEY , only for api.meltwater.com . It is sent in the apikey header. Make an API token in the Meltwater app (see API Credentials in the Meltwater developer portal) and paste it here. Your plan must include Meltwater MCP. Documentation . Checked on 2026-11-27. Bigdata.com bigdata . Search financial news, filings, earnings transcripts and analyst research. Listed under Finance. Connects with: token. Risk: low. Reads financial documents and market data. It cannot change anything. You need a Bigdata.com account. Address: https://mcp.bigdata.com/ Token: sealed in the vault as BIGDATA_API_KEY , only for mcp.bigdata.com . It is sent in the x-api-key header. Make an API key in the Bigdata.com Developer Platform under API Keys (platform.bigdata.com/api-keys) and paste it here. Documentation . Checked on 2026-11-27. Daloopa daloopa . Company financials, KPIs, filings and earnings transcripts. Listed under Finance. Connects with: sign in or token. Risk: low. Reads financial data, filings and stock prices. It cannot change anything. You need a Daloopa account. Address: https://mcp.daloopa.com/server/mcp Sign in: OAuth. Token: sealed in the vault as DALOOPA_API_KEY , only for mcp.daloopa.com . It is sent in the X-API-KEY header. Use your Daloopa API key. Daloopa sales or support gives you one. The key is sent as is, with no token step. Documentation . Checked on 2026-11-27. S&P Global spglobal . Financial data and company research from the Kensho LLM-ready API. Listed under Finance. Connects with: sign in. Risk: low. Reads financial and market data. It cannot change anything. You need a Kensho account. Address: https://kfinance.kensho.com/integrations/mcp Sign in: OAuth with the scopes kensho:app:kfinance , offline_access . Documentation . Checked on 2026-11-26. Stripe stripe . Customers, invoices, subscriptions, refunds and documentation search. Listed under Finance. Connects with: sign in or token. Risk: high. Moves money. Its write tool covers POST, PATCH, PUT and DELETE. Stripe asks for human confirmation on refunds and outbound payments. Address: https://mcp.stripe.com Sign in: OAuth with the scopes mcp . Token: sealed in the vault as STRIPE_AGENT_API_KEY , only for mcp.stripe.com . An agent API key with the smallest set of permissions. Use a sandbox account first. Stripe stops accepting full-access secret keys and restricted keys without the Agent tag on 2026-11-30. Option What it does Goes to For connectedAccount The id of a connected account (acct_...) to act as. Platform agent API keys only; OAuth cannot act as a connected account. header Stripe-Account a token Documentation . Checked on 2026-11-14. Mixpanel mixpanel . Run reports on events, funnels and retention, and browse dashboards. Listed under Analytics. Connects with: sign in. Risk: medium. Reads analytics data, and can also create, edit and delete dashboards, tags and event definitions in the person's project. The admin picks the region that matches the project. Address: https://{region}/mcp (the host is one of 3, see the option below) Sign in: OAuth. Option What it does Goes to For region The region where your Mixpanel project stores its data. One of: mcp.mixpanel.com (US), mcp-eu.mixpanel.com (EU), mcp-in.mixpanel.com (India). host region every way in Documentation . Checked on 2026-11-27. Buffer buffer . Read channels and queue, schedule and edit posts, capture ideas and pull post analytics. Listed under Social Media. Connects with: sign in or token. Risk: high. Can schedule, edit and delete posts that go out to the connected social channels. Use a test channel first. Address: https://mcp.buffer.com/mcp Sign in: OAuth. Token: sealed in the vault as BUFFER_API_KEY , only for mcp.buffer.com . A Buffer API key made in Settings, API at publish.buffer.com/settings/api. It reaches every organization and channel in the account. Documentation . Checked on 2026-11-26. Metricool metricool . Manage brands, read social analytics and schedule posts. Listed under Social Media. Connects with: sign in or token. Risk: high. Can schedule and publish posts to the connected social accounts and change brand settings. Plan limits still apply. Address: https://ai.metricool.com/mcp Sign in: OAuth with the scopes mcp:read , mcp:write . Token: sealed in the vault as METRICOOL_API_KEY , only for ai.metricool.com . It is sent in the X-Mc-Auth header. Copy your Metricool API key from Account Settings, then API (app.metricool.com/user-settings/api) and paste it here. Documentation . Checked on 2026-11-27. X Ads x-ads . Read X Ads accounts and analytics, and create and manage campaigns. Listed under Advertising. Connects with: sign in (your own app). Risk: high. Can create and change campaigns, line items, audiences and creatives, and activate campaigns that spend money. New campaigns start paused. Address: https://ads-api.x.com/mcp Sign in, with your own app: the service takes no dynamic client registration, so an admin registers an app and sets X_ADS_CLIENT_ID (a public client has no secret) in the agent's vault or environment. In the X Developer Console create or reuse an app with Read and Write permission, type Native App (public client, PKCE, no secret), and add the redirect address (the public address of this app followed by /__bxagents/connect/callback). Enable Ads API access under Project Access, and copy the OAuth 2.0 client id. Scopes: ads.read , ads.write , offline.access . Documentation . Checked on 2026-11-27. Wix wix . Search Wix documentation and make API calls on your Wix sites. Listed under Apps. Connects with: sign in or token. Risk: high. Can change site content, store data and other settings through the Wix APIs, including on a live site. Address: https://mcp.wix.com/mcp Sign in: OAuth with the scopes offline_access . Token: sealed in the vault as WIX_API_KEY , only for mcp.wix.com . It is sent alone in the Authorization header. Make an API key in your Wix account (API Keys page in the Wix developer docs) and paste it here. The key is sent alone, without Bearer. Also fill in your Wix account ID below. Option What it does Goes to For wix_account_id The ID of your Wix account. Needed with an API key. header wix-account-id a token Documentation . Checked on 2026-11-27. Zapier zapier . Run actions in the apps connected to your Zapier account. Listed under Apps. Connects with: sign in or token. Risk: high. Can run any action you enable in Zapier, such as sending email and messages or changing records in other apps. Enable only the actions you need. Address: https://mcp.zapier.com/api/v1/connect Sign in: OAuth. Token: sealed in the vault as ZAPIER_MCP_TOKEN , only for mcp.zapier.com . A connection token. Create a server at mcp.zapier.com, then generate its token. It is shown once and stays valid until you regenerate it. Documentation . Checked on 2026-11-26.

# Connector catalog

This page is written from the connector files in `src/main/bx/catalog/connectors/` (`tools/generate-connector-docs.bxs`), so it says what the product does. See [connectors](/next/conventions/connectors/index.html) for how they work, and [how to add one](/next/conventions/connectors/index.html#adding-a-connector).

## Developer

| [Cloudflare](#cloudflare) | sign in or token           | high   | The Cloudflare API: DNS, Workers, rules and more                                           |
| [Context7](#context7)     | token                      | low    | Up-to-date documentation and code examples for libraries                                   |
| [Datadog](#datadog)       | sign in or token           | medium | Search logs, metrics, traces, monitors and dashboards in Datadog                           |
| [Excalidraw](#excalidraw) | no sign in                 | low    | Draw hand-drawn style diagrams and sketches                                                |
| [Git](#git)               | a local program (an admin) | medium | Read, search and change local Git repositories                                             |
| [GitHub](#github)         | token                      | high   | Repositories, issues, pull requests, Actions and code search                               |
| [Netlify](#netlify)       | sign in                    | high   | Create, deploy and manage Netlify sites from an agent                                      |
| [Supabase](#supabase)     | sign in or token           | high   | Database, SQL, migrations, projects and branches                                           |

## Finance

|         Connector          |  Connects with   | Risk |                               What it does                                |
|----------------------------|------------------|------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------|

| [Daloopa](#daloopa)        | sign in or token | low  | Company financials, KPIs, filings and earnings transcripts                |
| [S\&P Global](#sp-global)  | sign in          | low  | Financial data and company research from the Kensho LLM-ready API         |
| [Stripe](#stripe)          | sign in or token | high | Customers, invoices, subscriptions, refunds and documentation search      |

## Analytics

|       Connector       | Connects with |  Risk  |                            What it does                             |
|-----------------------|---------------|--------|---------------------------------------------------------------------|

## Social Media

|        Connector        |  Connects with   | Risk |                                      What it does                                       |
|-------------------------|------------------|------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|

| [Metricool](#metricool) | sign in or token | high | Manage brands, read social analytics and schedule posts                                 |

## Advertising

|    Connector    |     Connects with      | Risk |                            What it does                            |

## Apps

|     Connector     |  Connects with   | Risk |                         What it does                          |
