title: Each Person's Own Settings
body: Each Person's Own Settings You wrote Agent.yml , and somebody else installs the agent. They want it to answer in French, or to drop a tool, or to use their own model, and they should not have to edit your files (and lose their edits on the next update). BxAgents lets a person keep their own settings in a file of their own, layered over yours. What you will build A personal settings file that adds an instruction and removes a tool, seen working in the agent, then taken away again. About 15 minutes. Three files called Agent.yml <project>/Agent.yml the author's file (yours) ~/.bxagents/Agent.yml the person's file, for every agent on this machine ~/.bxagents/<agent>/Agent.yml the person's file, for one agent The person's files win over the author's, so the person who runs the agent has the last word . In full, first match wins: the flag of one run ~/.bxagents/<agent>/Agent.yml ~/.bxagents/Agent.yml the project: environments.<env> , then Agent.yml the default <agent> is the agent's data home, ~/.bxagents/acme-support , the folder that holds the conversations and notes. How a value is combined A person's file does not have to repeat the whole project. A plain value replaces, a mapping merges key by key, and markers on a key say what to do with a list or a text: Written as Result a plain value, or a list replaces key+: with a list appends to the list below key+: with text appends to the text below, after a blank line (for instructions ) key-: with a list removes those entries from the list below key: ~ removes the key 1. Look before you change Your project's agent has these tools, one of them now , from Giving Your Agent Tools : cd ~/bxagents-course/acme-support bxAgents build bxAgents invoke --message=capabilities Build succeeded: <anything>/acme-support/.build/app I can use these tools: <anything>now<anything> 2. Write a person's file Imagine you are the person who installed Acme support. Make a file for this one agent, with an instruction added after the project's and one tool taken away: mkdir -p ~/.bxagents/acme-support cat > ~/.bxagents/acme-support/Agent.yml <<'EOF' instructions+: Always answer in French. tools-: [ now@bxai ] EOF bxAgents invoke --message=capabilities bxAgents invoke --message=system | grep French ... <anything>instructions (append) from <anything>/.bxagents/acme-support/Agent.yml <anything>tools (remove) from <anything>/.bxagents/acme-support/Agent.yml ... I can use these tools: <anything> Always answer in French. The agent started with the person's lines applied: every setting that came from a person's file is named, with the file, so nothing is silent. The tools line the model received has lost now , and your project's file is untouched. Take the personal file away and the agent is yours again: rm ~/.bxagents/acme-support/Agent.yml bxAgents invoke --message=capabilities I can use these tools: <anything>now<anything> From the chat A person does not have to write the file by hand. In the terminal chat, /settings model ollama/qwen3 writes a setting to the agent's own file, --global writes it to the file for every agent, and /settings tools+ [ now@bxai ] adds to a list ( /settings tools+ reset takes that entry out of the file again). It edits only its own lines, keeps the rest of the file, comments included, and puts the file back when the result would not be valid. /info lists each setting that came from a person's file. (The web app's Settings page is for appearance, the model picker and the account; the layered files are written from the chat or by hand.) What to remember A build bakes the machine's files. If you ship an agent, build it on a machine without your own ~/.bxagents/Agent.yml , or read the lines the build prints. A built app reads the files again when it starts , over the author's settings as the build saved them, so a zip or a container can be adjusted on the machine that runs it. markdown:
# Each Person's Own Settings

You wrote `Agent.yml`, and somebody else installs the agent. They want it to answer in French, or to drop a tool,
or to use their own model, and they should not have to edit your files (and lose their edits on the next update).
BxAgents lets a person keep their own settings in a file of their own, layered over yours.
> **What you will build**
>
> A personal settings file that adds an instruction and removes a tool, seen working in the agent, then taken away
> again. About 15 minutes.

## Three files called `Agent.yml`

```text
<project>/Agent.yml             the author's file (yours)
~/.bxagents/Agent.yml           the person's file, for every agent on this machine
~/.bxagents/<agent>/Agent.yml   the person's file, for one agent
```

The person's files win over the author's, so **the person who runs the agent has the last word**. In full, first match
wins:

1. the flag of one run
2. `~/.bxagents/<agent>/Agent.yml`
3. `~/.bxagents/Agent.yml`
4. the project: `environments.<env>`, then `Agent.yml`
5. the default

`<agent>` is the agent's data home, `~/.bxagents/acme-support`, the folder that holds the conversations and notes.

## How a value is combined

A person's file does not have to repeat the whole project. A plain value replaces, a mapping merges key by key, and
markers on a key say what to do with a list or a text:

|        Written as        |                               Result                               |
|--------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------|
| a plain value, or a list | replaces                                                           |
| `key+:` with a list      | appends to the list below                                          |
| `key+:` with text        | appends to the text below, after a blank line (for `instructions`) |
| `key-:` with a list      | removes those entries from the list below                          |
| `key: ~`                 | removes the key                                                    |

## 1. Look before you change

Your project's agent has these tools, one of them `now`, from [Giving Your Agent Tools](/next/course/09-giving-your-agent-tools/index.html):

```bash
cd ~/bxagents-course/acme-support
bxAgents build
bxAgents invoke --message=capabilities
```

```text
Build succeeded: <anything>/acme-support/.build/app
I can use these tools: <anything>now<anything>
```

## 2. Write a person's file

Imagine you are the person who installed Acme support. Make a file for this one agent, with an instruction added after
the project's and one tool taken away:

```bash
mkdir -p ~/.bxagents/acme-support
cat > ~/.bxagents/acme-support/Agent.yml <<'EOF'
instructions+: Always answer in French.
tools-: [ now@bxai ]
EOF
bxAgents invoke --message=capabilities
bxAgents invoke --message=system | grep French
```

```text
...
<anything>instructions (append) from <anything>/.bxagents/acme-support/Agent.yml
<anything>tools (remove) from <anything>/.bxagents/acme-support/Agent.yml
...
I can use these tools: <anything>
Always answer in French.
```

The agent started with the person's lines applied: every setting that came from a person's file is named, with the
file, so nothing is silent. The tools line the model received has lost `now`, and your project's file is untouched.
Take the personal file away and the agent is yours again:

```bash
rm ~/.bxagents/acme-support/Agent.yml
bxAgents invoke --message=capabilities
```

```text
I can use these tools: <anything>now<anything>
```

## From the chat

A person does not have to write the file by hand. In the terminal chat, `/settings model ollama/qwen3` writes a setting
to the agent's own file, `--global` writes it to the file for every agent, and `/settings tools+ [ now@bxai ]` adds to a
list (`/settings tools+ reset` takes that entry out of the file again). It edits only its own lines, keeps the rest of
the file, comments included, and puts the file back when the result would not be valid. `/info` lists each setting that
came from a person's file. (The web app's **Settings** page is for appearance, the model picker and the account; the
layered files are written from the chat or by hand.)

## What to remember

* **A build bakes the machine's files.** If you ship an agent, build it on a machine without your own `~/.bxagents/Agent.yml`, or read the lines the build prints.
* **A built app reads the files again when it starts** , over the author's settings as the build saved them, so a zip or a container can be adjusted on the machine that runs it. Some keys cannot change at start, because they are generated into the app (`agentApi`, `gatewaySession`, `routines`, `subAgents`, `data`); the app says so in its log.
* **What a person's file may not say:** `name`, `data.home` and `environments`. Secrets stay as `${env.X}` or `${vault.X}` placeholders, never values.
* **An unknown key is an error here too**, and a built app that finds a bad file at start refuses to start and names it.

## Checkpoint

No file of the project changed, and the personal file is gone. `acme-support/` is as the previous lesson left it.

Full reference: [Layered settings](/next/conventions/layered-settings/index.html) and [Settings of the terminal chat](/next/guides/terminal-ui/index.html#settings).

Next: [Logs, Usage and Backups](/next/course/operating-it/index.html)

title: Embeds
body: Embeds Status This page is the spec for increment 1. Built so far: the record and its store, the admin routes, the bxAgents embed verb, and the public routes (config, session, events, cancel, history, frame) with the origin check, the signed session and the limits. Everything in this increment is built: the embed filter, the widget, the hosted page and the Embeds admin page. Anything marked proposed is open to change. An embed lets a visitor of another website chat with your agent. An admin defines it in the web app (Admin, Embeds), copies a snippet, and pastes it into the other site. Increment 1 supports one case: an anonymous docs agent . The visitor is not signed in, may only ask questions, and the agent may only use the tools the embed lists. Out of scope for now: signed-in visitors (identity tokens), approvals, the temporary history mode, host-side helpers, extension hooks, bot protection, variables and context. See it About a minute: an admin makes an embed, a visitor chats from another website, and the admin looks at the counters, rotates the key and disables it. The answers come from a scripted demo model, so they are canned. Narrated, with captions. The record An embed lives in the agent's database , next to the access tokens. It is never written in Agent.yml : it is changed from the web app while the agent runs, and it holds a key. { id "emb_7Kq2xV9nR4" generated; public, like a site key; not a secret name "Docs helper" enabled true expires optional date an expired embed answers like an unknown one keyVersion 1 goes up when the key is rotated target { agent, profile } which agent and which model profile answer look { title, welcome, placeholder, suggestions[<=3], color, position, theme, icon } tools [ "docs_search" ] names; the ONLY tools a visitor's turn may use limits { allowedOrigins[], perVisitorPerMinute, dailyMessages, maxMessageChars } } The signing key is kept beside the record on the server and is never returned by any route. Only look is ever sent to a browser. Every field is validated on save and again on use. Field Rule id emb_ plus 10 characters from [A-Za-z0-9] , made by the server allowedOrigins at least one; each exactly scheme://host[:port] , no path, no wildcard, no null tools each must be a tool the agent has; an unknown name is refused on save and ignored on use perVisitorPerMinute default 10 dailyMessages default 200, for the whole embed maxMessageChars default 2000 look.color #rrggbb only; look.position bottom-right or bottom-left ; look.theme light , dark or auto ; look.icon one of chat (the default), question , sparkle , headset , book look.suggestions up to 3 strings, each up to 120 characters The server uses only the stored record . A page can send an agent, profile, model, tool list, limit or user id and it changes nothing. Routes All sit under the agent API path ( /__bxagents unless moved), so <api> below. Public (for visitors) GET <api>/embed/widget.js the script and the <bx-agent> element GET <api>/embed/<id>/config look and text only; origin checked; always revalidated POST <api>/embed/<id>/session origin checked, rate limited; answers { token, expiresAt } POST <api>/embed/<id>/events Authorization: Bearer <token>; body { input, conversationId? }; answers an SSE stream POST <api>/embed/<id>/cancel Bearer; body { threadId }; stops the visitor's own run (proposed) GET <api>/embed/<id>/history Bearer; ?conversationId=...; the visitor's own saved chat (proposed) GET <api>/embed/<id>/frame the hosted chat page for an iframe; CSP frame-ancestors OPTIONS on each of the above the CORS preflight, answered for listed origins only cancel and history are added to the proposed list because the brief says a visitor can stop its own run and read its own saved chats, and those need a route each. Where they sit. The public routes are outside the token gate and the address guards of the agent API ( models/api/Guards.bx : AllowedIPs@cbsecurity and Throttle@cbsecurity ), and have their own checks. Reasons, from reading Guards.bx and Authenticator.bx : Throttle@cbsecurity counts by IP in one counter shared by the whole API ( bxagents-api ). A crowd of visitors behind one proxy would spend the budget the admin and the web app need. allowedIPs is meant to keep a private API private. Visitors come from anywhere. The token check proves a caller who holds a token. A visitor holds none, and gets a signed session instead. An embed route never reaches an admin route, because it is a different set of handlers and the caller it builds has the embed scope (below). Admin (admin scope only) Like every other route of the agent API, the id goes in the query or the body, not in the path. GET <api>/embeds list, with the names of the tools an embed may list POST <api>/embeds create; the answer carries the new id GET <api>/embeds/get?id= one embed, without the key POST <api>/embeds/update body { id, ...fields }; fields not sent keep their value; { enabled: false } turns it off POST <api>/embeds/rotate body { id }; new signing key; every open session stops working GET <api>/embeds/snippets?id=&base= the HTML script tag, iframe, web component and curl, with the id filled in GET <api>/embeds/usage?id= counters for the last 7 days: messages, refused for a wrong origin, refused for a limit They are in ApiContract , so the OpenAPI document and the route specs have them. Embed management needs the app's shared database; without one the routes answer not_found . Admin scope is the gate, and agentApi.embeds: false is a master switch: with it the admin routes and the seven public routes are not written at all, the page leaves the menu and the OpenAPI document does not list them (see the master switch ). CLI: bxAgents embed create|list|show|disable|rotate . They are added to ApiContract , so the OpenAPI document and the route specs pick them up. A visit, step by step The page loads widget.js from the agent: <script src="https://agent.example/__bxagents/embed/widget.js" data-embed="emb_..." defer></script> . The widget works out its base address from its own script URL. At connect time the widget reads its attributes (not properties set later by page script) and calls GET /config . The server answers only if the Origin header is on the embed's list, with Access-Control-Allow-Origin set to that origin. On the first message it calls POST /session . The server checks the origin and the per-visitor limit, makes a visitor id and answers a signed session token . POST /events sends the message with Authorization: Bearer <token> . The server checks the token, the origin it was issued to, the limits and the length, then runs the agent in process and re-emits its frames as SSE. An empty message frame every 30 seconds is forwarded, so a long silent run survives a proxy's 60 second read timeout. The widget keeps a readable transcript in localStorage (the server also stores the chat under the visitor, see below). The session token A signed token (the jwt class of cbsecurity's jwtcfml, which takes a key on each call), HS256, signed with the embed's own key. Claims: emb (the embed id), v (the visitor id), o (the origin it was issued to), exp (1 hour), kv (the key version). A token is refused with 401 when the signature is wrong, it is expired, emb is another embed, o is not the Origin of this request, kv is not the current key version, or it is missing. The same token sent from another origin is refused. Limits run on the server's clock , never on a time the client sends: Limit Over it per visitor, per minute 429 with Retry-After daily messages for the embed 429 message longer than maxMessageChars 400 The embed caller and its scope Today a Caller ( models/api/Caller.bx ) has scope chat or admin . This adds a third, least-privilege scope embed . An embed caller has id v:<visitorId> and is built from the verified session, never from the request body. An embed caller can An embed caller can never send a message ( events ) read or write notes, memory or the vault stream and stop its own run read another visitor's conversations or runs read its own saved chats reach any admin, token, log, backup, settings, gateway, routine or connector route choose the agent, profile, model, params or tools of a turn Run ids are already scoped by caller ( TurnRunner hands bx-ai u:<caller id>:<thread id> ), so a visitor cannot reach another visitor's run even if it guesses the id. Conversation ids are issued by the server , never trusted from the client: c-<first 12 characters of the visitor id>-<client label> , where the label is the client's own text cut to a-z0-9- and 24 characters. A spike found that two callers sharing a client-chosen id silently lose the second one's listing. History in this increment: conversations are stored under the visitor like any other caller's. The temporary mode is a later increment. The embed filter A middleware that ships with the agent and is always on . A request that is not an embed call is left alone. For an embed call only the tools on the embed's list may run. Proven by a spike ( plans/embed-filter-findings.md ), it does both: beforeLLMCall removes the unlisted tools from dataPacket.tools , so the model is never offered them. beforeToolCall rejects a call to an unlisted tool, so a model that names one anyway (from training or an earlier turn) gets a refusal and the tool body never runs. Hiding alone is not a guard. How it knows. TurnRunner sets options.usageMetadata.embedId on a turn whose caller has the embed scope, after it has dropped everything a client sent (a client cannot send it). usageMetadata is a property of every bx-ai request, so the filter reads chatRequest.getUsageMetadata().embedId in both hooks. A request with none is not an embed turn: the filter returns at once and reads no database. It reads the embed's list for each call, so an admin's change takes effect at once, and it fails closed: an embed that is off, expired, gone or unreadable allows no tool. A tool is compared without its @module suffix ( now@bxai on the list is now to the model). It is attached to every agent the build makes, the main one and each sub-agent. Measured on a served app (scripted model, an agent with docs_search and a delete_all that writes a file): asked which tools it had, the model said docs_search to a visitor of an embed that lists only that, and delete_all, docs_search, loadSkill, skill_save to the admin on the same agent. Asked to wipe, the visitor's turn left no file; the admin's turn created it. Threat model Visitors are anonymous and anyone on the internet can become one, so the Origin check is not authentication . What the Origin check does. It stops a browser on an unlisted site from reading the config or getting a session, and (with the origin bound into the token) from reusing a token it was handed. CORS headers are only sent for listed origins, and the hosted frame can only be embedded by listed sites ( frame-ancestors ). What it does not do. The Origin header is set by the browser, so any program ( curl , a script) can send whatever it likes. It does not stop a person from calling the embed directly. Do not rely on it for that. What does protect you , in order of importance: The tool list. A visitor's turn can only use the tools the embed lists. Do not list a tool you would not let a stranger run. The embed scope. Even a fully scripted attacker can only chat. No notes, memory, vault, other chats or admin routes. The limits. Per visitor per minute, a daily cap for the whole embed, a maximum message length. The daily cap is also the cost cap. Server-side truth. The record decides the agent, profile, model and tools. A forged userId , agent , profile or tools in a body changes nothing. Key rotation and disable. Rotating the key ends every session at once. A disabled or expired embed answers like an unknown one (same status, same body), so a visitor cannot tell which ids exist. Accepted for now: a script can mint many visitor ids (each session call is rate limited, but not by identity). The daily cap bounds the damage. Bot protection is a later increment. Prompt injection through a visitor's message is possible for any agent that takes text: keep the tool list to read-only tools. SSE( cors : origin ) also sends Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true . The embed routes use no cookies , so credentials are not needed and the embed routes send the CORS headers by hand without it. Measured on a served app Run against a built app with a scripted model (a throwaway demo, not a real model): A visitor's message streamed as 35 content deltas in 44 frames ( thread , chunk , two tool , done ), with Access-Control-Allow-Origin set to the visitor's own website and no Access-Control-Allow-Credentials . The CORS headers set before SSE() survive. With the API behind a token, a visitor's session token on GET /embeds , /notes , /vault , /sessions , /logs , /info , /tools and POST /invoke gives 401 , also when sent as x-bxagents-token . The public routes work with no x-bxagents-token at all. A forged signature, no token, a token from another listed website and a garbage token give 401 ; an unlisted website gives 403 ; 2001 characters give 400 ; the sixth message in a minute (limit 5) gives 429 . Every response of the app carries X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN from the app's own security headers. The frame route also sends frame-ancestors ; whether a browser lets another website frame it is tested in a real browser, not assumed. An open API (no agentApi token) lets anyone call the admin routes, as it always has. Before an embed goes on the public internet, give the API a token. Visitors are not affected by it: they do not use it. chunk frames carry the model's own tool-call arguments ( delta.tool_calls ), as they do for every client of the stream; the tool frames a visitor gets carry the tool's name, its status and the time it took, not its arguments. The widget widget.js is one file of plain JavaScript with no dependencies: a <bx-agent> element with a shadow root, a launcher and a panel (or, with mode="page" , the chat filling the page). Attributes: embed , base (taken from the script's own address when left out), mode , storage ( local or none ), storage-key and credentials . They are read once, when the element connects , because the saved transcript is restored then; a page script that sets them later changes nothing. headers (an async function) and onUnauthorized are properties read at each request. It sends bx-done and bx-error events. Accessibility: the launcher is a real button with aria-expanded ; the panel is a labelled dialog; opening moves focus to the input and Esc closes and gives it back to the launcher; the conversation is a role="log" that is not read piece by piece while streaming, and the finished answer is announced once from a status region; colours come from tokens with the text colour chosen for contrast on the embed's colour; prefers-reduced-motion and prefers-color-scheme are respected; answers are shown as text, never as HTML. Measured in Chromium against real loopback servers on other ports (an allowed website on 9100, another on 9200): the allowed website got the launcher, focus moved to the input and back on Esc, the answer arrived as 35 DOM updates (not one block), and the transcript came back after a reload; the other website got no launcher, because its config request was refused with no CORS header; the hosted frame drew on the allowed website and Chromium blocked it on the other ( frame-ancestors ), although the app also sends X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN . The hosted page runs on the agent's own origin, so a request from it is from that origin: a browser sends no Origin header on a same-origin GET , so the agent reads Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin (which a page script cannot set) as "from my own origin". The agent's own origin is accepted whether or not the embed lists it. A visitor who opens the frame address directly is a visitor like any other. The pictures below are from that run. A disabled or expired embed stops showing its bubble at the next page load: config is sent with Cache-Control: no-cache , so a browser asks again every time. (A 30 second cache was tried first. A recording of the tour showed the bubble staying on the website for up to 30 seconds after Disable, so it was removed.) Known limit: a visitor's conversation belongs to its session (one hour, kept in localStorage so a reload keeps it). After it expires the widget still shows the saved transcript, but the agent starts without the earlier messages. The hosted frame GET /embed/<id>/frame returns the chat page for an <iframe> , with Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors <the allowed origins> . A site that is not listed cannot frame it. The page loads the same widget. The Embeds admin page Built as described below; see also The web app . It is checked with axe (light, dark, desktop and phone) and with browser tests that make an embed, refuse bad websites, watch the preview follow the form, copy a snippet, rotate the key and turn it off. A page in the web app ( bxagentsui ), under Admin , next to Gateways, admin scope only, themed like the other pages (system, light, dark) and usable by keyboard. + Embeds ------------------------------------------------------------------------+ | [ Docs helper on ] [ Pricing bot off ] [ New embed ] | +----------------------------------------------+-----------------------------------+ | Agent name, agent, profile | Live preview of the widget | | Look & text title, placeholder, welcome, | (updates as you type) | | up to 3 suggestions, color, | | | position, theme, icon | Snippet [HTML][iframe][web | | What visitors can use [x] docs_search | component][curl] [Copy]| | [ ] note_remember (all off=none)| | | Allowed websites (chips, no wildcards) | Last 7 days | | Limits per minute, per day, max chars | messages | wrong origin | limit | | [Save] [Disable] [Rotate key...] | | +----------------------------------------------+-----------------------------------+ The counters are real numbers read from stored usage, or an honest empty state ("No visits yet"). They are never invented. The button icon look.icon picks the glyph on the widget's button from a fixed set: chat (the speech bubble, and the default for every embed that has none), question , sparkle , headset and book . The widget draws them itself from its own SVG; an unknown name is refused on save ("look.icon is one of: ..."), and the widget falls back to the bubble for any other value. It is a name, never markup or a URL, so an embed cannot make a visitor's page load an image from somewhere else. The editor shows the five as a radio group. A custom image (a URL, with a rule on which hosts) is not built. The master switch agentApi: embeds: false # default true With embeds: false the build writes no embed route (public or admin), GET /__bxagents/capabilities says embeds: false (so the web app hides the Embeds page), the OpenAPI document leaves the embed operations out and AgentService.embeds() answers nothing. The embed tables stay in the database, and the tool filter stays attached (nothing can be an embed caller without the routes). Anything but a boolean is a build error. Open points (proposed, tell me if you disagree) agentApi.embeds: false to turn embeds off. Built, see the master switch . The daily cap and the counters are kept in the database ( embed_usage , one row per embed per day), so a restart does not reset the cap. The per-minute window is in memory. Built: the table and the counters. The window comes with the public routes. The signing key is stored as it is in the embeds table, not sealed like a vault secret: a stolen database file would let someone mint sessions, which an anonymous visitor can already get. It is never returned by any route. "Visitors who hit the limit" is shown as requests refused for a limit , a count of refusals, because counting distinct visitors would need to store visitor ids.

> **Status**
>
> This page is the **spec** for increment 1. Built so far: the record and its store, the admin routes, the `bxAgents embed`
> verb, and the public routes (config, session, events, cancel, history, frame) with the origin check, the signed session and

Out of scope for now: signed-in visitors (identity tokens), approvals, the temporary history mode, host-side helpers, extension

## See it

*About a minute: an admin makes an embed, a visitor chats from another website, and the admin looks at the counters, rotates the key and disables it. The answers come from a scripted demo model, so they are canned. Narrated, with captions.*

## The record

An embed lives in the agent's **database** , next to the access tokens. It is never written in `Agent.yml`: it is changed from the
web app while the agent runs, and it holds a key.

```text
{
  id         "emb_7Kq2xV9nR4"     generated; public, like a site key; not a secret
  name       "Docs helper"
  enabled    true
  expires    optional date        an expired embed answers like an unknown one
  keyVersion 1                    goes up when the key is rotated
  target     { agent, profile }   which agent and which model profile answer
  look       { title, welcome, placeholder, suggestions[<=3], color, position, theme, icon }
  tools      [ "docs_search" ]    names; the ONLY tools a visitor's turn may use
  limits     { allowedOrigins[], perVisitorPerMinute, dailyMessages, maxMessageChars }
}
```

The signing key is kept beside the record on the server and is **never** returned by any route. Only `look` is ever sent to a
browser. Every field is validated on save and again on use.

|         Field         |                                                                                            Rule                                                                                            |
|-----------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `id`                  | `emb_` plus 10 characters from `[A-Za-z0-9]`, made by the server                                                                                                                           |
| `allowedOrigins`      | at least one; each exactly `scheme://host[:port]`, no path, no wildcard, no `null`                                                                                                         |
| `tools`               | each must be a tool the agent has; an unknown name is refused on save and ignored on use                                                                                                   |
| `perVisitorPerMinute` | default 10                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| `dailyMessages`       | default 200, for the whole embed                                                                                                                                                           |
| `maxMessageChars`     | default 2000                                                                                                                                                                               |
| `look.color`          | `#rrggbb` only; `look.position` `bottom-right` or `bottom-left`; `look.theme` `light`, `dark` or `auto`; `look.icon` one of `chat` (the default), `question`, `sparkle`, `headset`, `book` |
| `look.suggestions`    | up to 3 strings, each up to 120 characters                                                                                                                                                 |

The server uses **only the stored record**. A page can send an agent, profile, model, tool list, limit or user id and it changes
nothing.

## Routes

All sit under the agent API path (`/__bxagents` unless moved), so `<api>` below.

### Public (for visitors)

```text
GET  <api>/embed/widget.js        the script and the <bx-agent> element
GET  <api>/embed/<id>/config      look and text only; origin checked; always revalidated
POST <api>/embed/<id>/session     origin checked, rate limited; answers { token, expiresAt }
POST <api>/embed/<id>/events      Authorization: Bearer <token>; body { input, conversationId? }; answers an SSE stream
POST <api>/embed/<id>/cancel      Bearer; body { threadId }; stops the visitor's own run          (proposed)
GET  <api>/embed/<id>/history     Bearer; ?conversationId=...; the visitor's own saved chat      (proposed)
GET  <api>/embed/<id>/frame       the hosted chat page for an iframe; CSP frame-ancestors
OPTIONS on each of the above      the CORS preflight, answered for listed origins only
```

`cancel` and `history` are added to the proposed list because the brief says a visitor can stop its own run and read its own
saved chats, and those need a route each.

**Where they sit.** The public routes are **outside** the token gate and the address guards of the agent API
(`models/api/Guards.bx`: `AllowedIPs@cbsecurity` and `Throttle@cbsecurity`), and have their own checks. Reasons, from reading
`Guards.bx` and `Authenticator.bx`:

* `Throttle@cbsecurity` counts by IP in **one counter shared by the whole API** (`bxagents-api`). A crowd of visitors behind one proxy would spend the budget the admin and the web app need.
* `allowedIPs` is meant to keep a private API private. Visitors come from anywhere.
* The token check proves a caller who holds a token. A visitor holds none, and gets a signed session instead.

An embed route never reaches an admin route, because it is a different set of handlers and the caller it builds has the
`embed` scope (below).

### Admin (admin scope only)

Like every other route of the agent API, the id goes in the query or the body, not in the path.

```text
GET  <api>/embeds               list, with the names of the tools an embed may list
POST <api>/embeds               create; the answer carries the new id
GET  <api>/embeds/get?id=       one embed, without the key
POST <api>/embeds/update        body { id, ...fields }; fields not sent keep their value; { enabled: false } turns it off
POST <api>/embeds/rotate        body { id }; new signing key; every open session stops working
GET  <api>/embeds/snippets?id=&base=   the HTML script tag, iframe, web component and curl, with the id filled in
GET  <api>/embeds/usage?id=     counters for the last 7 days: messages, refused for a wrong origin, refused for a limit
```

They are in `ApiContract`, so the OpenAPI document and the route specs have them. Embed management needs the app's shared database;
without one the routes answer `not_found`. Admin scope is the gate, and `agentApi.embeds: false` is a master switch: with it the admin routes and the seven public routes are not written at all, the page leaves the menu and the OpenAPI document does not list them (see [the master switch](#the-master-switch)).

CLI: `bxAgents embed create|list|show|disable|rotate`. They are added to `ApiContract`, so the OpenAPI document and the route
specs pick them up.

## A visit, step by step

1. The page loads `widget.js` from the agent: `<script src="https://agent.example/__bxagents/embed/widget.js" data-embed="emb_..." defer></script>`. The widget works out its base address from its own script URL.
2. At connect time the widget reads its **attributes** (not properties set later by page script) and calls `GET /config`. The server answers only if the `Origin` header is on the embed's list, with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` set to that origin.
3. On the first message it calls `POST /session`. The server checks the origin and the per-visitor limit, makes a visitor id and answers a signed **session token**.
4. `POST /events` sends the message with `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. The server checks the token, the origin it was issued to, the limits and the length, then runs the agent **in process** and re-emits its frames as SSE. An empty `message` frame every 30 seconds is forwarded, so a long silent run survives a proxy's 60 second read timeout.
5. The widget keeps a readable transcript in `localStorage` (the server also stores the chat under the visitor, see below).

## The session token

A signed token (the `jwt` class of cbsecurity's jwtcfml, which takes a key on each call), HS256, signed with the **embed's own**
key. Claims: `emb` (the embed id), `v` (the visitor id), `o` (the origin it was issued to), `exp` (1 hour), `kv` (the key version).

A token is refused with **401** when the signature is wrong, it is expired, `emb` is another embed, `o` is not the `Origin` of this
request, `kv` is not the current key version, or it is missing. The same token sent from another origin is refused.

Limits run on the **server's clock**, never on a time the client sends:

|                 Limit                 |         Over it          |
|---------------------------------------|--------------------------|
| per visitor, per minute               | `429` with `Retry-After` |
| daily messages for the embed          | `429`                    |
| message longer than `maxMessageChars` | `400`                    |

## The embed caller and its scope

Today a Caller (`models/api/Caller.bx`) has scope `chat` or `admin`. This adds a third, least-privilege scope **`embed`** . An
embed caller has id `v:<visitorId>` and is built from the verified session, never from the request body.

|      An `embed` caller can      |                            An `embed` caller can never                             |
|---------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| send a message (`events`)       | read or write notes, memory or the vault                                           |
| stream and stop **its own** run | read another visitor's conversations or runs                                       |
| read **its own** saved chats    | reach any admin, token, log, backup, settings, gateway, routine or connector route |
|                                 | choose the agent, profile, model, params or tools of a turn                        |

Run ids are already scoped by caller (`TurnRunner` hands bx-ai `u:<caller id>:<thread id>`), so a visitor cannot reach another
visitor's run even if it guesses the id.

**Conversation ids are issued by the server** , never trusted from the client: `c-<first 12 characters of the visitor id>-<client label>`, where the label is the client's own text cut to `a-z0-9-` and 24 characters. A spike found that two callers sharing a
client-chosen id silently lose the second one's listing.

History in this increment: conversations are stored under the visitor like any other caller's. The temporary mode is a later increment.

## The embed filter

A middleware that ships with the agent and is **always on** . A request that is not an embed call is left alone. For an embed call
only the tools on the embed's list may run. Proven by a spike (`plans/embed-filter-findings.md`), it does both:

* `beforeLLMCall` removes the unlisted tools from `dataPacket.tools`, so the model is never offered them.
* `beforeToolCall` rejects a call to an unlisted tool, so a model that names one anyway (from training or an earlier turn) gets a refusal and the tool body never runs.

Hiding alone is not a guard.

**How it knows.** `TurnRunner` sets `options.usageMetadata.embedId` on a turn whose caller has the `embed` scope, after it has dropped everything a client sent (a client cannot send it). `usageMetadata` is a property of every bx-ai request, so the filter reads `chatRequest.getUsageMetadata().embedId` in both hooks. A request with none is not an embed turn: the filter returns at once and reads no database. It reads the embed's list for each call, so an admin's change takes effect at once, and it fails closed: an embed that is off, expired, gone or unreadable allows no tool. A tool is compared without its `@module` suffix (`now@bxai` on the list is `now` to the model). It is attached to every agent the build makes, the main one and each sub-agent.

**Measured on a served app** (scripted model, an agent with `docs_search` and a `delete_all` that writes a file): asked which tools it had, the model said `docs_search` to a visitor of an embed that lists only that, and `delete_all, docs_search, loadSkill, skill_save` to the admin on the same agent. Asked to wipe, the visitor's turn left no file; the admin's turn created it.

## Threat model

Visitors are anonymous and anyone on the internet can become one, so **the Origin check is not authentication**.

**What the Origin check does.** It stops a *browser* on an unlisted site from reading the config or getting a session, and (with
the origin bound into the token) from reusing a token it was handed. CORS headers are only sent for listed origins, and the hosted
frame can only be embedded by listed sites (`frame-ancestors`).

**What it does not do.** The `Origin` header is set by the browser, so any program (`curl`, a script) can send whatever it likes.
It does not stop a person from calling the embed directly. Do not rely on it for that.

**What does protect you**, in order of importance:

1. **The tool list.** A visitor's turn can only use the tools the embed lists. Do not list a tool you would not let a stranger run.
2. **The `embed` scope.** Even a fully scripted attacker can only chat. No notes, memory, vault, other chats or admin routes.
3. **The limits.** Per visitor per minute, a daily cap for the whole embed, a maximum message length. The daily cap is also the cost cap.
4. **Server-side truth.** The record decides the agent, profile, model and tools. A forged `userId`, `agent`, `profile` or `tools` in a body changes nothing.
5. **Key rotation and disable.** Rotating the key ends every session at once. A disabled or expired embed answers like an unknown one (same status, same body), so a visitor cannot tell which ids exist.

**Accepted for now:** a script can mint many visitor ids (each session call is rate limited, but not by identity). The daily cap
bounds the damage. Bot protection is a later increment. Prompt injection through a visitor's message is possible for any agent that
takes text: keep the tool list to read-only tools.

`SSE( cors : origin )` also sends `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. The embed routes use **no cookies**, so credentials
are not needed and the embed routes send the CORS headers by hand without it.

## Measured on a served app

Run against a built app with a scripted model (a throwaway demo, not a real model):

* A visitor's message streamed as 35 content deltas in 44 frames (`thread`, `chunk`, two `tool`, `done`), with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` set to the visitor's own website and no `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials`. The CORS headers set before `SSE()` survive.
* With the API behind a token, a visitor's session token on `GET /embeds`, `/notes`, `/vault`, `/sessions`, `/logs`, `/info`, `/tools` and `POST /invoke` gives `401`, also when sent as `x-bxagents-token`. The public routes work with no `x-bxagents-token` at all.
* A forged signature, no token, a token from another listed website and a garbage token give `401`; an unlisted website gives `403`; 2001 characters give `400`; the sixth message in a minute (limit 5) gives `429`.
* Every response of the app carries `X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN` from the app's own security headers. The frame route also sends `frame-ancestors`; whether a browser lets another website frame it is tested in a real browser, not assumed.
* **An open API (no `agentApi` token) lets anyone call the admin routes, as it always has.** Before an embed goes on the public internet, give the API a token. Visitors are not affected by it: they do not use it.

`chunk` frames carry the model's own tool-call arguments (`delta.tool_calls`), as they do for every client of the stream; the `tool` frames a visitor gets carry the tool's name, its status and the time it took, not its arguments.

## The widget

`widget.js` is one file of plain JavaScript with no dependencies: a `<bx-agent>` element with a shadow root, a launcher and a panel (or, with `mode="page"`, the chat filling the page). Attributes: `embed`, `base` (taken from the script's own address when left out), `mode`, `storage` (`local` or `none`), `storage-key` and `credentials`. They are read **once, when the element connects** , because the saved transcript is restored then; a page script that sets them later changes nothing. `headers` (an async function) and `onUnauthorized` are properties read at each request. It sends `bx-done` and `bx-error` events.

Accessibility: the launcher is a real button with `aria-expanded`; the panel is a labelled dialog; opening moves focus to the input and Esc closes and gives it back to the launcher; the conversation is a `role="log"` that is not read piece by piece while streaming, and the finished answer is announced once from a status region; colours come from tokens with the text colour chosen for contrast on the embed's colour; `prefers-reduced-motion` and `prefers-color-scheme` are respected; answers are shown as text, never as HTML.

Measured in Chromium against real loopback servers on other ports (an allowed website on 9100, another on 9200): the allowed website got the launcher, focus moved to the input and back on Esc, the answer arrived as 35 DOM updates (not one block), and the transcript came back after a reload; the other website got no launcher, because its `config` request was refused with no CORS header; the hosted frame drew on the allowed website and Chromium blocked it on the other (`frame-ancestors`), although the app also sends `X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN`.

The hosted page runs on the agent's own origin, so a request from it is from that origin: a browser sends no `Origin` header on a same-origin `GET`, so the agent reads `Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin` (which a page script cannot set) as "from my own origin". The agent's own origin is accepted whether or not the embed lists it. A visitor who opens the frame address directly is a visitor like any other.

The pictures below are from that run.

![The Embeds editor: the agent, the look and text on the left, and on the right the preview, which is the real widget drawn from the form](/next/assets/webui/webui-embeds-editor.png)

![A wildcard website is refused in words before anything is saved](/next/assets/webui/webui-embeds-wildcard-refused.png)

![The snippet panel with the HTML snippet, its note and Copy](/next/assets/webui/webui-embeds-snippet.png)

![A visitor on another website: the chat bubble and a streamed answer](/next/assets/webui/webui-embeds-visitor.png)

![The last seven days: real counters](/next/assets/webui/webui-embeds-counters.png)

![Rotate key asks first](/next/assets/webui/webui-embeds-rotate.png)

A disabled or expired embed stops showing its bubble at the next page load: `config` is sent with `Cache-Control: no-cache`, so a browser asks again every time. (A 30 second cache was tried first. A recording of the tour showed the bubble staying on the website for up to 30 seconds after Disable, so it was removed.)

Known limit: a visitor's conversation belongs to its session (one hour, kept in `localStorage` so a reload keeps it). After it expires the widget still shows the saved transcript, but the agent starts without the earlier messages.

## The hosted frame

`GET /embed/<id>/frame` returns the chat page for an `<iframe>`, with `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors <the allowed origins>`. A site that is not listed cannot frame it. The page loads the same widget.

## The Embeds admin page

Built as described below; see also [The web app](/next/conventions/web-ui/index.html#embeds). It is checked with axe (light, dark, desktop and phone) and with browser tests that make an embed, refuse bad websites, watch the preview follow the form, copy a snippet, rotate the key and turn it off.

A page in the web app (`bxagentsui`), under **Admin**, next to Gateways, admin scope only, themed like the other pages (system,
light, dark) and usable by keyboard.

```text
+ Embeds ------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| [ Docs helper    on  ]  [ Pricing bot  off ]   [ New embed ]                      |
+----------------------------------------------+-----------------------------------+
| Agent        name, agent, profile            |  Live preview of the widget       |
| Look & text  title, placeholder, welcome,    |  (updates as you type)            |
|              up to 3 suggestions, color,     |                                   |
|              position, theme, icon           |  Snippet   [HTML][iframe][web     |
| What visitors can use   [x] docs_search      |            component][curl] [Copy]|
|              [ ] note_remember (all off=none)|                                   |
| Allowed websites   (chips, no wildcards)     |  Last 7 days                      |
| Limits       per minute, per day, max chars  |  messages | wrong origin | limit  |
| [Save] [Disable] [Rotate key...]             |                                   |
+----------------------------------------------+-----------------------------------+
```

The counters are real numbers read from stored usage, or an honest empty state ("No visits yet"). They are never invented.

## The button icon

`look.icon` picks the glyph on the widget's button from a fixed set: `chat` (the speech bubble, and the default for every embed that
has none), `question`, `sparkle`, `headset` and `book`. The widget draws them itself from its own SVG; an unknown name is refused
on save ("look.icon is one of: ..."), and the widget falls back to the bubble for any other value. It is a name, never markup or a
URL, so an embed cannot make a visitor's page load an image from somewhere else. The editor shows the five as a radio group. A custom
image (a URL, with a rule on which hosts) is not built.

## The master switch

```yaml
agentApi:
  embeds: false      # default true
```

With `embeds: false` the build writes no embed route (public or admin), `GET /__bxagents/capabilities` says `embeds: false` (so the web app
hides the Embeds page), the OpenAPI document leaves the embed operations out and `AgentService.embeds()` answers nothing. The embed
tables stay in the database, and the tool filter stays attached (nothing can be an embed caller without the routes). Anything but a boolean is a build error.

## Open points (proposed, tell me if you disagree)

1. `agentApi.embeds: false` to turn embeds off. *Built, see [the master switch](#the-master-switch).*
2. The daily cap and the counters are kept in the database (`embed_usage`, one row per embed per day), so a restart does not reset the cap. The per-minute window is in memory. *Built: the table and the counters. The window comes with the public routes.*
3. The signing key is stored as it is in the `embeds` table, not sealed like a vault secret: a stolen database file would let someone mint sessions, which an anonymous visitor can already get. It is never returned by any route.
4. "Visitors who hit the limit" is shown as **requests refused for a limit**, a count of refusals, because counting distinct visitors would need to store visitor ids.

# Example: A Minimal Agent

The smallest complete BxAgents project is [`examples/minimal-agent/`](https://github.com/ortus-boxlang/bx-agents/tree/development/examples/minimal-agent) - a few files that show the whole shape of a project: an `Agent.yml`, instructions, one [tool](/next/conventions/tools/index.html), and one [skill](/next/conventions/skills/index.html). Every other example in this guide series builds on exactly this shape.

## The project

```text
minimal-agent/
├── Agent.yml
├── instructions.md
├── tools/
│   └── Greeter.bx
└── skills/
    └── greeting/
        └── SKILL.md
```

`Agent.yml` declares a name, description, and model - the `provider/model` slug (see [The model slug](/next/conventions/agent-bx/index.html#the-model-slug)) - and nothing else is required. Need code in the definition (hooks, dynamic instructions)? The class-based [`Agent.bx`](/next/conventions/agent-bx/index.html) is the advanced alternative.

```yaml
name: minimal-agent
description: "The smallest complete BX Agents project: one tool, one skill."
model: mock/mock-model
```

`instructions.md` is the system prompt - a plain Markdown file, copied in as-is at build time:

```markdown
## Minimal Agent

You are a friendly assistant. When someone tells you their name, use the
`sayHello` tool to greet them, and follow the greeting skill's guidance
on tone.
```

## The tool

Any `class` under `tools/` with an `@AITool`-annotated function becomes a callable tool automatically - no registration step, no config entry. `tools/Greeter.bx`:

```javascript
class {

	@AITool( "Say hello to someone by name." )
	function sayHello( name ) {
		return "Hello, " & arguments.name & "!";
	}

}
```

The string passed to `@AITool` is the tool's description, sent to the model exactly as written - see [Tools](/next/conventions/tools/index.html) for how BoxLang argument types map to the JSON schema the model sees.

## The skill

A skill under `skills/<name>/SKILL.md` is guidance the model can pull in when it decides it's relevant - not always-on like `instructions.md`. `skills/greeting/SKILL.md`:

```markdown
---
name: greeting
description: How to greet people warmly.
---

Always greet the user warmly and use their name if known.
```

See [Skills](/next/conventions/skills/index.html) for how `description` drives when a skill actually gets used.

## Build and run

```bash
cd examples/minimal-agent
bxAgents build
bxAgents chat
```

`build` assembles everything above into a plain ColdBox application in `.build` (`app/` and `public/`) (see [The Build Pipeline](/next/build-pipeline/index.html)); `chat` starts an isolated BoxLang process with `.build/runtime/boxlang.json` and `.build/runtime` as its home, then loads the generated agent and opens the [terminal chat](/next/guides/terminal-ui/index.html). Type `/` to see the commands, and `/tools` to see that `sayHello` is there. Try:

```text
My name is Ada.
```

The model should reach for the `sayHello` tool and reply warmly, per the skill's guidance - both from a single sentence of instructions plus a small tool and a one-line skill. With the `mock` model this example ships with, the reply is a fixed one: set a real `provider/model` in `Agent.yml` to see the tool called. `bxAgents inspect` lists the agent, its tool and its skill without a build.

## Where to go next

* [Example: A Multi-Agent Team](/next/guides/example-multi-agent-team/index.html) - the same shape, with subagents delegating to each other.
* [Example: A Scheduled Agent](/next/guides/example-scheduled-agent/index.html) - the same shape, woken by a schedule instead of a chat prompt.
* [Tools](/next/conventions/tools/index.html) and [Skills](/next/conventions/skills/index.html) for the full conventions these two files follow.

# Example: A Multi-Agent Team

[`examples/multi-agent-team/`](https://github.com/ortus-boxlang/bx-agents/tree/development/examples/multi-agent-team) is a root agent with two [subagents](/next/conventions/subagents/index.html) - `researcher` and `writer` - each auto-wrapped as a callable tool on the root agent by bx-ai's own `aiAgent()`. Delegation is entirely the model's decision at runtime; nothing in this project hard-codes which subagent handles which message.

## The project

```text
multi-agent-team/
├── Agent.yml
├── instructions.md
└── subagents/
    ├── researcher/
    │   ├── Agent.yml
    │   └── instructions.md
    └── writer/
        ├── Agent.yml
        └── instructions.md
```

Every `subagents/<name>/` folder is itself a complete mini-agent - its own `Agent.yml`, its own `instructions.md`, and (not used here, but supported) its own `tools/`/`skills/`.

## Declaring the team

The root `Agent.yml` names the subagents to wire in with `subAgents`:

```yaml
# Agent.yml
name: multi-agent-team
description: A root agent delegating to a researcher and a writer subagent.
model: mock/mock-model

# The list of `subagents/` FOLDER names to wire at build time.
subAgents: [ researcher, writer ]
```

`subAgents` is resolved against folder names under `subagents/`; each folder's own `Agent.yml` declares its own `name`, `description`, and `model` independently:

```yaml
# subagents/researcher/Agent.yml
name: researcher
description: Gathers facts on a topic.
model: mock/mock-model
```

```yaml
# subagents/writer/Agent.yml
name: writer
description: Turns research into polished prose.
model: mock/mock-model
```

## Instructions divide the responsibility

Each agent's `instructions.md` is deliberately scoped to its own job - the root coordinates, and each subagent is told explicitly what it does *not* do, so the model doesn't try to do everything in one hop:

```markdown
<!-- instructions.md (root) -->
## Team Lead

You coordinate a small team. Delegate research questions to the `researcher`
subagent and drafting/writing tasks to the `writer` subagent, then combine
their output into a final answer.
```

```markdown
<!-- subagents/researcher/instructions.md -->
## Researcher

You gather and summarize facts on a topic, citing your reasoning. You do
not write final prose - that's the writer's job.
```

```markdown
<!-- subagents/writer/instructions.md -->
## Writer

You turn research notes into clear, polished prose. You do not do your
own research - you rely on what the researcher provides.
```

## How the build wires it up

`ColdBoxAppGenerator` builds the tree **leaf-first** : `researcher` and `writer` are constructed first, and the already-built instances are passed into the root agent's own construction, so the root's `aiAgent()` call receives real subagent objects rather than names to resolve later. See [Subagents](/next/conventions/subagents/index.html) for the full leaf-first build order and how each subagent gets registered under its own name in WireBox (not just the root).

## Build and run

```bash
cd examples/multi-agent-team
bxAgents build
bxAgents chat
```

Ask something that clearly needs both roles, e.g. `Give me three facts about the BoxLang language, then turn them into a short paragraph.` A real model would typically call `researcher` first, then `writer`, then compose the final answer - the `mock` provider this example ships with won't actually delegate (it returns a fixed response with no tool calls), so swap in a real `provider/model` slug (see [The model slug](/next/conventions/agent-bx/index.html#the-model-slug)) to see real delegation happen. `bxAgents inspect` prints the agent and subagent tree, with each model and tools, before you build.

## Where to go next

* [Example: A Minimal Agent](/next/guides/example-minimal-agent/index.html) if you haven't seen the base project shape yet.
* [Subagents](/next/conventions/subagents/index.html) for cycle detection, nested subagent trees, and per-subagent tools/skills.
* [Example: Building a Slack Bot](/next/guides/example-slack-bot/index.html) to see a similar agent reachable over a real chat platform instead of the terminal chat.

# Example: A Scheduled Agent

[`examples/scheduled-agent/`](https://github.com/ortus-boxlang/bx-agents/tree/development/examples/scheduled-agent) wakes an agent nightly with a BoxLang scheduler under `schedules/` - plain [Schedules](/next/conventions/schedules/index.html) code with BoxLang's own task DSL (`.every()`, `.everyDayAt()`, `.onWeekdays()` and the rest).

## The project

```text
scheduled-agent/
├── Agent.yml
├── instructions.md
└── schedules/
    └── Nightly.bx
```

`Agent.yml` is the same shape as every other example - nothing special is needed on the agent side to be schedule-driven:

```yaml
name: scheduled-agent
description: An agent that wakes up on a daily schedule via schedules/.
model: mock/mock-model
```

## The scheduler

`schedules/Nightly.bx` is a plain class. The build adds the base class that provides `task()` and `run()`:

```javascript
class {

	function configure() {
		task( "nightly" )
			.everyDayAt( "00:00" )
			.call( () => run( "cleanup" ) )
			.withNoOverlaps()
	}

}
```

The full BoxLang task DSL is available - `every()`, `everyDayAt()`, `onWeekdays()`, `withNoOverlaps()`, `onFailure()` and the rest, not a subset BxAgents reimplements (see [`schedules/`](/next/conventions/schedules/index.html)). A six-field `cron()` works too, but a five-field one never fires on BoxLang 1.19.0 (see [Cron](/next/conventions/schedules/index.html#cron)).

`run( "cleanup" )` sends the message to the project's default agent, the root agent. To reach a subagent, use `agent( "TheAgentName" ).run( ... )`: every agent in a project's tree is registered under its own declared `name`.

## Instructions for the scheduled prompt

The instructions describe what the agent should do when `run( "cleanup" )` fires - there's no difference, from the agent's point of view, between a scheduled wake-up and a chat message; both are just a `run()` call with some input text:

```markdown
## Scheduled Agent

You run periodic housekeeping prompts. When asked to "cleanup", summarize
what a cleanup pass would involve for a typical project.
```

## Build and run

Unlike a plain `bxAgents chat` (which loads the agent in the chat process and never boots ColdBox), schedulers only start with the served app, so this one needs `serve`. `bxAgents chat --server` also starts the app, as a throwaway local server, and chats with it:

```bash
cd examples/scheduled-agent
bxAgents build
bxAgents serve
```

The `nightly` task fires automatically once `serve` is running - no separate cron daemon, no OS-level `cron` entry. BoxLang's own scheduler drives it, on the schedule declared in `Nightly.bx`.

To add another schedule to your own project, run `bxAgents add schedule`. It asks when (for example `daily 09:00` or `every 15 minutes`), what to tell the agent and which agent, and writes `schedules/<Name>.bx` using the task's own methods (`daily 09:00` becomes `.everyDayAt( "09:00" )`). A cron expression you type is written as a six-field `.cron()`, because a five-field one does not fire on BoxLang 1.19.0. `bxAgents inspect` lists the schedules a project has.
> **Info**
>
> `build` checks the scheduler's file name and that it is a class, but not the *contents* of `configure()` - a typo in an `agent()` call or a reference to an agent name that doesn't exist will pass `build` cleanly and only surface once the generated app actually boots.

## Where to go next

* [Schedules](/next/conventions/schedules/index.html) for the helpers a scheduler gets, the ways to say when it runs and the cron note.
* [Example: A Minimal Agent](/next/guides/example-minimal-agent/index.html) if you haven't seen the base project shape yet.
* [Example: Building a Web Chat Agent](/next/guides/example-web-chat-agent/index.html) for an agent reachable interactively instead of on a timer.

# Example: Building a Slack Bot

[`examples/slack-gateway-agent/`](https://github.com/ortus-boxlang/bx-agents/tree/development/examples/slack-gateway-agent) connects an agent to a real Slack app via a push-style `gateways/` entry with `type: "slack"`. Slack uses **Socket Mode** - a persistent websocket the gateway holds open itself - so unlike a webhook-driven platform (WhatsApp Cloud, Teams, Twilio, GitHub), there's no public route to expose or `curl`; the gateway reaches out to Slack, not the other way around. See [Push-style gateways](/next/conventions/gateways/index.html) for how this category differs from `exposes: "agent"`/`"webui"` HTTP exposure.

## The project

```text
slack-gateway-agent/
├── Agent.yml
├── instructions.md
└── gateways/
    └── slackChannel.bx
```

`Agent.yml` is the same shape as every other example:

```yaml
name: slack-gateway-agent
description: An agent reachable as a real Slack app via gateways/, over Socket Mode.
model: mock/mock-model
```

## The gateway

`gateways/slackChannel.bx` declares the platform type and where its credentials come from - **environment variable names**, not the secrets themselves, so nothing sensitive ever lands in the generated app or version control:

```javascript
class {

	function configure() {
		return {
			type          : "slack",
			botTokenEnvVar: "SLACK_BOT_TOKEN",   // xoxb-... - chat.postMessage/chat.update scope
			appTokenEnvVar: "SLACK_APP_TOKEN"    // xapp-... - apps.connections.open scope (Socket Mode)
		};
	}

}
```

At build time, `GatewayGenerator` turns this into a registered `SlackGateway` instance and wires it into the project's single, project-wide `GatewaySession`. At runtime, `SlackGateway.onConnect()` opens the Socket Mode websocket as soon as `GatewaySession` starts.

## Instructions

```markdown
## Slack Gateway Agent

You are a helpful workspace assistant, reachable as a Slack app. Use
Slack-flavored formatting sparingly (bold with `*asterisks*`, not markdown `**`).
```

Nothing here is Slack-API-specific beyond a formatting note - the agent's own logic doesn't know or care which gateway is delivering its replies.

## 1. Create a Slack app

At [api.slack.com/apps](https://api.slack.com/apps), create an app "from scratch":

1. **Socket Mode** - enable it, generate an app-level token with the `connections:write` scope (`xapp-...`) → this becomes `SLACK_APP_TOKEN`.
2. **OAuth \& Permissions** - add the `chat:write` bot scope, install the app to your workspace, copy the Bot User OAuth Token (`xoxb-...`) → this becomes `SLACK_BOT_TOKEN`.
3. **Event Subscriptions** - enable it and subscribe to the `message.im` (and/or `message.channels`) bot event, so the app actually receives message events over the socket.
4. Optional: **Slash Commands** for the chat commands, and the `files:read` scope to let the agent read files people share (see below).

## 2. Configure and run

```bash
export SLACK_BOT_TOKEN="xoxb-..."
export SLACK_APP_TOKEN="xapp-..."
cd examples/slack-gateway-agent
bxAgents build
bxAgents serve
```

DM the bot, or mention it in a channel it's in. Replies stream back token-by-token via a placeholder message that `SlackGateway` posts immediately and then updates in place with `chat.update` as tokens arrive - the same incremental-reveal effect the [web chat UI](/next/conventions/web-ui/index.html) gives you in a browser, produced here entirely through Slack's own message-editing API.
> **Info**
>
> There's no `curl`-able entrypoint for this one - message the app for real in Slack to see it work. This is true of every persistent-connection gateway (Telegram's long-poll, Slack/Discord's websockets); only the webhook-driven platforms (WhatsApp Cloud, Teams, Twilio, GitHub) generate a route you can hit locally with a hand-computed signature - each of those examples' own README shows how.

## What people can do in the chat

* **Everyone has their own conversation.** The agent is told who is writing (`slack:U123`) and which conversation it is: the channel, plus the thread when there is one. Two people in the same channel do not share a memory, and each Slack thread keeps its own. Conversations are stored in the `chat.db` of the agent's [data home](/next/conventions/data/index.html), marked with `source` Slack.
* **Commands.** By default the bot answers `/help`, `/tools`, `/model`, `/info`, `/ping`, `/remember`, `/notes` and `/connect` itself, without calling the model. Slack keeps typed `/word` messages for its own commands, so a bot never receives them. Either create a slash command in the Slack app (an umbrella `/agent`, so `/agent model fast` runs `/model fast`, or one per command) and the answer is shown only to the person who typed it, or set another prefix in `Agent.yml`:

```yaml
gatewaySession:
  commands:
    prefixes: { slack: "!" }     # then type !help
    conversation: true           # also turns on /new, /clear, /compact, /sessions and /resume
```

* **Files.** A text file or a picture shared in a message goes to the agent with it. This needs the `files:read` scope on the Slack app.

See [Commands in a gateway](/next/conventions/gateways/index.html#commands-in-a-gateway) for every option.

## What's proven, and what isn't

`SlackGatewaySpec.bx` exercises the gateway's inbound/outbound logic - chunking, HITL approvals, reconnect handling - entirely against an injectable test seam, never a real Slack connection; a separate smoke test confirms the BoxLang-to-Java WebSocket interop itself works correctly (a real connection attempt to an unreachable address fails with a plain `ConnectException`, not an interop error). No test in this repo has completed a real Socket Mode handshake against Slack's actual servers. The steps above are exactly the manual verification that gap calls for.

## Where to go next

* [Slack](/next/conventions/gateways/slack/index.html) for the full gateway convention - reconnect model, HITL correlation, chunking limits.
* [Example: A Multi-Agent Team](/next/guides/example-multi-agent-team/index.html) to combine a gateway-reachable agent with subagent delegation.
headings: What people can do in the chat

title: Example: Building a Web Chat Agent
body: Example: Building a Web Chat Agent examples/webui-agent/ generates a complete, themed browser chat page for an agent from a single gateways/* entry with exposes: "webui" - the v1 web chat UI . No frontend code to write, no Node/npm in the build, no separate deploy step for a SPA - the app is a ColdBox module BxAgents copies, already built, into the generated app. This is the one example in this guide series with real screenshots, because it's the one kind of BxAgents example whose output is actually a browser page. The images below show the current page layout, captured from a demo app (title "Acme Assistant", blue accent), so the title, tagline and colors differ from this example's own config. The page is the same: only the branding comes from the gateway file. The project webui-agent/ ├── Agent.yml ├── instructions.md ├── gateways/ │ └── chat.bx └── resources/ └── webui/ └── theme.css Agent.yml is the same shape as every other example: name: webui-agent description: An agent reachable through the v1 web chat UI via gateways/. model: mock/mock-model The gateway: branding and theme, all in config gateways/chat.bx is where the actual page comes from - exposes: "webui" is the trigger, and everything else is optional branding: class { function configure() { return { exposes : "webui", path : "/chat", apiKeyEnvVar: "CHAT_UI_API_KEY", // optional - omit entirely to leave the agent API open (dev-mode) // --------------------------------------------------------------- // Branding // --------------------------------------------------------------- title : "Acme Support", subtitle : "Orders, returns and shipping", icon : "🛟", // an emoji, an image URL/path ("/logo.svg", "https://..."), or "phosphor:<name>" ("phosphor:lightning") welcome : "Hi! Ask me about an order, a return, or shipping times.", placeholder: "Ask about your order...", footer : "Answers are generated and may be wrong - check anything important.", // --------------------------------------------------------------- // Stream detail - both default to true // --------------------------------------------------------------- showReasoning: true, // the model's thinking, as a collapsed "Thinking" strip showToolCalls: true, // each tool call as a collapsed chip (name + arguments) // --------------------------------------------------------------- // Theme - every key maps to a CSS custom property on the page. // --------------------------------------------------------------- theme: { accent : "0f766e", accentFg: "ffffff", radius : "10px", font : "Inter, system-ui, sans-serif", maxWidth: "68%", dark: { accent : "2dd4bf", accentFg: "05201c" } } }; } } Other branding keys you can add: suggestions (up to four short texts, shown as buttons under the welcome message on an empty conversation; one click sends it) and icon: "phosphor:<name>" for an icon from the page's own set. With no icon the header shows a robot. suggestions: [ "Where is my order?", "How do I return something?" ], Colors are written as bare hex with no leading # ( "0f766e" , not "#0f766e" ) - BoxLang starts string interpolation at a hash in both single- and double-quoted strings, so a literal one has to be doubled to parse at all. Bare hex sidesteps that entirely; see the comment in the file itself for the full reasoning, and The web chat UI for anything the theme tokens don't cover (that goes in resources/webui/theme.css , inlined last and wins). Build and run cd examples/webui-agent bxAgents build bxAgents serve --port=8080 Open http://localhost:8080/chat/ . You get the left menu, the conversation sidebar, the streaming transcript, and a header and composer in the colors of your theme : Dark mode The theme.dark overrides ( accent / accentFg ) apply when the page switches to dark, from the switch in the header or the Appearance card of Settings - everything else is the same CSS, just re-tokened: Narrow screens The page is responsive with no separate mobile build - at a narrow viewport, the transcript keeps its full width and the menu becomes a drawer instead of squeezing the content: The header and the bar above the conversation The header holds the agent's icon, title and subtitle, a light or dark switch, and either the Password button (the key, on an agent without accounts like this one) or who is signed in and Sign out . On the Chat page, the bar above the conversation holds the model picker (only when the gateway lists profiles ), the context ring (click it for what is sent to the model), any status chips from extensions, and the Fork , Export and Compact buttons. Everything else is a page of the menu on the left, each at its own address ( /chat/memory , /chat/vault , /chat/settings , ...); see the web app, page by page . In the message box, the paperclip attaches a picture or a text file (you can also paste or drop them), the lightning button opens the / commands menu, and the arrow sends. While the agent works the arrow steers the run and a stop button appears. The optional API key This example ships apiKeyEnvVar set . It is the agent API's shared secret, so every call to /__bxagents must carry a matching x-bxagents-token header - the app's pages ( /chat/ ) stay reachable regardless, since a browser's plain page navigation can't send a custom header, and the app is exactly what prompts you for the key: export CHAT_UI_API_KEY="a-real-secret" bxAgents build bxAgents serve --port=8080 The page loads fine either way, but a call without the matching key gets a 401 and the page opens its Password dialog by itself (once per page load) - type a-real-secret and choose Save , which loads the page again with it. The key button in the header opens the dialog any time, and Forget it removes the saved value. The password is kept in the browser's localStorage until you forget it. Delete the apiKeyEnvVar line entirely to leave the UI open instead (fine for local dev, never for a public deployment). Access tokens for administrators With agentApi: { tokens: true, manageTokens: true } in Agent.yml , a caller with an admin token sees the Access page ( /chat/access/tokens ). Its Tokens tab lists tokens, creates one (a name, a scope of chat or admin , and how long it lasts, such as 90d ), shows the secret once for you to copy, and revokes tokens. manageTokens is off by default and a chat token gets 403 . The same thing from a shell is bxAgents token create|list|revoke . One API for the page, the terminal and the gateways path: "/chat" is only where the app's pages are served. The page calls the agent API at /__bxagents , which derives the visitor's identity server-side only , rather than trusting a caller-supplied userId the way ColdBox's toAi() does, and which the terminal chat and the gateways use too. See Conversation identity for the full reasoning. What's proven, and what isn't The generator output itself - the web app module and its config/bxagentsui.json , the sign-in pieces when there are accounts, its registration from Application.bx - is proven by real generator specs and confirmed to compile and instantiate. Over real HTTP, runColdBoxIntegrationTests.bxs proves /__bxagents/health and, further, the shared-preferences round trip ( /__bxagents/preferences/set + /__bxagents/preferences ) between two independent callers. The screenshots above were captured from the real generated page, not a hand-built mockup - but do at least one real bxAgents serve + browser check of your own theme/branding choices before depending on them in production. Where to go next The web chat UI for the full picture - human-in-the-loop approvals, compaction, steer-while-streaming, the SQLite-backed conversation store. Example: A Minimal Agent if you haven't seen the base project shape yet. Example: Building a Slack Bot for an agent reachable on a chat platform instead of a browser.
