# extensions/

An **extension** adds to BxAgents without changing it: chat commands (`/deploy`, `/roll 2d6`), listeners for the events of the chat and of bx-ai, schedules that run when the agent is served, and pieces of the [web page](#the-web-page-slots-and-web). It is a class that looks and behaves like a ColdBox `ModuleConfig`: it has a `configure()`, an `onLoad()` and an `onUnload()`, its settings come from `Agent.yml`, and things are handed to it with `$inject`.

One file is a whole extension:

```text
extensions/
  hello.bx             /hello
  roll.bx              /roll, /coin
  standup/             a folder is an extension too
    Extension.bx
    commands/Standup.bx
    schedulers/Reminder.bx
```

A working project with all of these is [`examples/extensions-agent`](https://github.com/ortus-boxlang/bx-agents/tree/development/examples/extensions-agent).

## The smallest extension

`extensions/hello.bx`. The file name is the extension's name.

```text
class {

	function configure() {
		variables.settings = { greeting : "Hello" }
	}

	@Command( "hello" )
	@Hint( "say hello: /hello <name>" )
	function greet( agentContext, commandArguments ) {
		return agentContext.reply().ok( "#settings.greeting#, #commandArguments#!" )
	}

}
```

Run `bxAgents chat` and type `/hello Ada`. `/extensions` lists what is loaded.

A command method is called with the `agentContext` (the conversation and nothing else; the same object the built-in commands get) and the text after the command name. It returns a `Reply` or just a string. If it throws, the person sees a warning that names the extension and the chat carries on.

### The Reply API

Build a reply by chaining methods on `agentContext.reply()`. Every method returns the reply, so they chain. The terminal, the web page and the gateways each draw the blocks their own way.

**Single-style blocks** --- the whole block is one color:

|         Method         |                       What it draws                        |
|------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------|
| `.text( s )`           | Muted gray text (the default)                              |
| `.text( s, "accent" )` | Teal accent text                                           |
| `.ok( s )`             | Green text (success)                                       |
| `.warn( s )`           | Amber text (warning)                                       |
| `.header( s )`         | Accent header for a section                                |
| `.line( s )`           | A printed line; `.line()` with no argument is a blank line |
| `.blank()`             | A blank line (alias for `.line()`)                         |

**Mixed-style lines** --- different colors within one line. Start with `.styled()`, chain segment methods, then `.print()` to commit the line:

```js
agentContext.reply()
    .styled()
        .accentBold( "/deploy" )
        .text( "  " )
        .muted( "ship it to production" )
        .print()
```

Segment methods: `.text( s )` (plain), `.muted( s )` (gray), `.accent( s )` (teal), `.accentBold( s )` (bold teal), `.ok( s )` (green), `.warn( s )` (amber), `.error( s )` (red), `.bold( s )` (bold). For a style chosen at runtime: `.segment( s, styleName )`.

Dynamic compound styles work too, like CommandBox's print helper --- combine foreground, background and modifiers in the method name:

```js
.styled().boldRedOnBlue( "CRITICAL" ).text( "  " ).muted( "disk full" ).print()
```

Recognized tokens: foreground (`accent`, `ok`, `muted`, `warn`, `error`, `plain`, `black`, `red`, `green`, `yellow`, `blue`, `magenta`, `cyan`, `white`, `gray`), background (`onBlack` through `onWhite`), modifiers (`bold`, `dim`, `italic`, `underlined`, `blink`, `reversed`, `hidden`, `crossedout`).

**Convenience methods** --- shortcuts for common patterns, each produces a mixed-style line:

|             Method              |                     What it draws                     |
|---------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------|
| `.commandLine( name, hint )`    | Bold teal name + gray hint (for `/help`-style lists)  |
| `.labelValue( label, value )`   | Gray label + teal value (for `/info`-style facts)     |
| `.statusLine( label, boolean )` | Gray label + green "on" or red "off"                  |
| `.indent( text )`               | Indented gray text (like CommandBox's `indentedLine`) |
| `.bullet( text )`               | Teal dot + gray text                                  |
| `.divider()`                    | A horizontal rule                                     |

**Structured blocks:**

|           Method            |                            What it draws                            |
|-----------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `.keyValues( rows )`        | Label-value pairs; `rows` is `[ [ label, value ], ... ]`            |
| `.grid( columns, rows )`    | A table; `columns` is `[ { width, align }, ... ]`                   |
| `.choose( title, options )` | Buttons to pick from; `options` is `[ { label, hint, line }, ... ]` |
| `.transcript( messages )`   | Conversation messages; `messages` is `[ { role, text }, ... ]`      |
| `.file( name, mime, text )` | A file for the client to save or download                           |
| `.screen( name )`           | Opens a terminal-only screen (e.g. `"notes"`, `"vault"`)            |

**Effects** --- things the caller does to its own state:

|            Method            |              What it does               |
|------------------------------|-----------------------------------------|
| `.reset()`                   | Clears the conversation from the screen |
| `.conversation( id, title )` | Switches to another conversation        |
| `.quit()`                    | Leaves the chat                         |

All methods return the reply, so they chain:

```js
return agentContext.reply()
    .header( "Deploy status" )
    .statusLine( "Connected", true )
    .labelValue( "Target", "production" )
    .styled().ok( "3 services" ).muted( " running" ).print()
    .blank()
    .indent( "Type /deploy run to start." )
```

## Annotations

Annotations are normal BoxLang annotations on a method. Each one can be written four ways, and every BxAgents annotation takes all four:

| Written |                  Means                   |                                                        Example                                                         |
|---------|------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| bare    | defaults; the name comes from the method | `@Command` on `function roll()` is `/roll`                                                                             |
| simple  | the main value                           | `@Command( "deploy" )`                                                                                                 |
| array   | several                                  | `@Alias( [ "dice", "d" ] )`                                                                                            |
| struct  | every option                             | `@Command( { name : "deploy", hint : "plan it", admin : true, aliases : [ "ship" ], transports : [ "tui", "web" ] } )` |

Shorthand annotations say one option each: `@Hint( "..." )`, `@Admin`, `@Alias( ... )`, `@Transports( [ "tui", "web" ] )`. A struct option wins over a shorthand, and the clash is shown in `/extensions`. Annotation names ignore case.

`transports` are where the command runs: `tui` (the terminal chat), `web` (the web page and the HTTP command route) and `gateway` (chat platforms). The default is all three. A chat platform only answers the commands its gateway allows (`gatewaySession.commands.allow`), and a command with `@Admin` only runs for the people listed as admins there.

## Settings

The extension says its defaults in `configure()`, as a module does:

```text
function configure() {
	variables.settings = { target : "staging", environments : [ "staging", "production" ] }
}
```

The people who use it change them under the extension's name in `Agent.yml`:

```yaml
extensions:
  deploy:
    target: production
```

A person can set their own values in `~/.bxagents/Agent.yml` (same `extensions:` block); their values win over the project's, because the person who runs the agent has the last word (see [layered settings](/next/conventions/layered-settings/index.html)). Nested structs merge key by key, arrays and simple values replace. In the extension, `settings` is the merged struct.

## Lifecycle

|    Method     |                                           When                                           |
|---------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `configure()` | once, first. Sets `variables.settings`. No work here                                     |
| `onLoad()`    | after the settings are merged and everything is injected. Open connections, start timers |
| `onUnload()`  | when the chat or the server ends. Release them                                           |

`this.title`, `this.author`, `this.webURL`, `this.description`, `this.version` and `this.enabled` are read as in a module config, and `this.dependencies = [ "other-extension" ]` loads that extension first. An extension that throws while it loads is shown as failed in `/extensions` with the reason; the others still load.

## Injection

Every class of an extension has ``$inject( name, object )`. It puts the object in both the `this` and the `variables` scopes. For private only: `$inject( name, object, "variables" )``. `$read( name )` reads a `variables` entry from outside.

BxAgents injects two things before `onLoad()`: `settings` and `log` (`log.info( "..." )`, `.warn()`, `.error()`; what an extension logs is also in `/extensions`). To share an object between the files of an extension, create it in `onLoad()` and `$inject` it where it is needed. The same call is how a test hands an extension a fake.

## A folder extension

A folder has the same shape as an agent project:

```text
extensions/standup/
  Extension.bx        required: it is what makes the folder an extension (the module config: properties, configure(), onLoad(), onUnload())
  commands/           one class per command, like the built-in ones
  schedulers/         BoxLang scheduler classes, started when the agent is served
  web/                styles, scripts and other files for the web page (see below)
```

A class in `commands/` extends `models.chat.commands.BaseCommand@bxagents` and says its `name()`, `hint()`, `transports()` and `run( context, args )`. `settings` and `log` are injected into it.

## Schedulers

A class in `schedulers/` is a **BoxLang scheduler** : a class with a `configure()` that defines tasks through the `scheduler` property BoxLang gives it, like any other BoxLang scheduler. When the agent is served (`bxAgents serve`, a `.bxa`, a deployed server) it starts in the runtime's scheduler service. Like every class of an extension it is given `settings` (the defaults with the values from `Agent.yml`) and `log` before `configure()` runs:

```text
class {

	function configure() {
		scheduler.task( "standup-reminder" )
			.call( () => log.info( "Standup time for #settings.channel#" ) )
			.everyDayAt( settings.at )
			.withNoOverlaps()
	}

}
```

The BoxLang scheduler lifecycle methods (`onStartup()`, `onShutdown()`, `onAnyTaskError()` and the rest) work as usual. Each scheduler is registered as `extension-<extension>-<scheduler>`, and a scheduler that fails to start is reported on its extension in `/extensions` while the others still run. The terminal chat does not start schedulers: they belong to the served agent.

## Listening to events

An extension is also an interceptor. A method named after an event listens to it, exactly like a BoxLang or ColdBox interceptor:

```text
class {

	function onChatInput( data ) {
		if ( data.text contains "password" ) {
			data.cancel( "That looks like a password, so it was not sent." )
		}
	}

	function onAIError( data ) {
		log.warn( "the model failed" )
	}

}
```

Two things can be listened to:

* **bx-ai events** (`beforeAIAgentRun`, `afterAIModelInvoke`, `onAIError`, `beforeAIToolExecute` and the rest). They fire wherever the agent runs.
* **Chat events**, announced by BxAgents:

|                   Event                   |                                    When                                     |                     `data` has                     |               A listener can                |
|-------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------|
| `onChatSessionStart` / `onChatSessionEnd` | the terminal chat opens or closes                                           | `agent`, `transport`                               |                                             |
| `onChatInput`                             | before a message is sent                                                    | `text`, `transport`                                | `cancel( reason )`, or `replace( newText )` |
| `onChatTurnStart` / `onChatTurnEnd`       | around one turn of the agent                                                | `text`, `transport` (`reply`, `status` at the end) |                                             |
| `onChatConversationChange`                | `/new`, `/resume`, `/clear`, `/fork` or `/compact` changed the conversation | `line`, `transport`                                |                                             |
| `onChatCommandBefore`                     | before any command, on every transport                                      | `line`, `name`, `arguments`, `transport`           | `cancel( reason )`                          |
| `onChatCommandAfter`                      | after any command, on every transport                                       | `line`, `name`, `reply`, `transport`               | `replace( newReply )`                       |

The session, input, turn and conversation events are the terminal chat's; the two command events fire in the terminal, the web page and on chat platforms alike. A listener that throws is caught: it can never stop a turn, the listeners after it still run, and the error is shown in `/extensions`.

`@On` binds a method with another name, or many events at once, and takes the four forms an annotation takes:

```text
@On( [ "beforeAIToolExecute", "afterAIToolExecute" ] )
function toolCalled( data ) { log.info( "a tool ran" ) }
```

`@On` naming an event the runtime does not know is reported in `/extensions`, not ignored.

### `interceptors` and `customInterceptionPoints`

As in a module config, `configure()` can name classes from the extension's folder to register, each with its own properties, and points of its own to announce:

```text
function configure() {
	variables.interceptors = [ { class : "interceptors.Audit", properties : { level : "info" } } ]
	variables.customInterceptionPoints = [ "onAuditRecorded" ]
}
```

`interceptors/Audit.bx` listens with methods named after events and has `settings`, `log` and `properties` injected. Any extension can then listen to `onAuditRecorded`, and the one that owns it announces it with `BoxAnnounce( "onAuditRecorded", { ... } )`. `extensions.disable` takes `extension:method` to turn one listener off.

ColdBox events (`preProcess`, `postProcess` and the rest) are not part of the terminal chat; they fire only in a served agent.

## Keys and status

`@Key` binds keys in the terminal chat to a method. On a command method it runs that command, with the same rules and events as typing it; on any other method it calls the method with the `agentContext` and an empty text and shows what it returns. `@Hint` (or `hint` in the struct form) says what it does.

```js
@Command
@Hint( "count a pulse" )
@Key( "ctrl+g" )
function pulse( agentContext, commandArguments ) { ... }

@Key( { keys : [ "ctrl+y", "alt+y" ], hint : "reset the count" } )
function resetPulse( agentContext, commandArguments ) { ... }
```

A key is named `extension:method` (`pulse:pulse`). `/keys` lists it with the built-in ones, and a person can give it other keys under `chat: keys:` in `~/.bxagents/Agent.yml`. A key a built-in action already uses, or an earlier extension holds, is refused with a sentence that says so. A typed draft stays in the box while a key runs. Keys are for the terminal chat; the web page and chat platforms have commands.

`@Status` is a piece of status next to the size of the context: a method that returns a short text, asked each time the box is drawn in the terminal and after each change to the conversation on the web page (chips in the bar above the conversation, see [Status items](#status-items)). Return an empty string to show nothing. It must be quick; one that throws is left out and the reason is put on its extension once.

```js
@Status
function beats( agentContext ) {
	return variables.beats > 0 ? "beat #variables.beats#" : ""
}
```

`extensions.disable` takes `extension:method` for a key or a status item too.

## `register( registry )`

What annotations cannot say, because it is worked out in code, is said as calls. If the class has a `register( registry )` method it is called once, right after `configure()`:

```js
function register( registry ) {
	registry.command( "deploy", { run : ( agentContext, commandArguments ) => ..., hint : "ship it", admin : true, aliases : [ "ship" ] } )
	registry.key( "ctrl+d", "/deploy", { hint : "ship it" } )                    // a key that runs a command line
	registry.key( "ctrl+o", ( agentContext ) => "opened", { name : "open", hint : "open it" } )   // or any function
	registry.status( "branch", ( agentContext ) => "main" )
	registry.on( "onChatCommandAfter", ( data ) => ... )                         // an event, or an array of them
}
```

## Prefixes and `@` sources

Both are for the terminal chat only.

`@Prefix` claims the start of a line in the message box. The method gets the `agentContext` and the text after the prefix. It answers one of two ways: a `Reply` (or a string) is shown and nothing is sent, and `{ send : "text" }` is sent to the agent as the message, after `onChatInput` has seen it.

```js
@Prefix( "%" )
@Hint( "ask for an explanation: % why is the sky blue" )
function explain( agentContext, text ) {
	return { send : "Explain this in one short paragraph: #text#" }
}

@Prefix( "=" )
function count( agentContext, text ) {
	return agentContext.reply().ok( "#text.listToArray( ' ' ).len()# words" )
}
```

`/`, `!`, `#` and `@` are the chat's own, and a lone `?` asks for the keys; a prefix that starts with one of them, is empty or has a space is refused with a sentence. The longest prefix wins. Two extensions on one prefix are a warning and the later layer wins.

`@Source( "ticket" )` brings content along with a message the way `@path` brings a file. Write `@ticket:TCK-1` (or `@ticket:"two words"`) and the method is called with the `agentContext` and the query. It returns `{ name, content }`, an array of them or a string; the content goes with the message and the mention stays in it. `@Suggest( "ticket" )` on another method is optional: it returns the values the menu offers as the person types after the colon. It is asked on keystrokes, so it must be quick; one that throws gives no suggestions and the reason is put on its extension once. A source name can be anything that starts with a letter, since files are plain `@path`.

```js
@Source( "ticket" )
function ticket( agentContext, query ) { return { name : "ticket #query#", content : tickets[ query ] } }

@Suggest( "ticket" )
function ticketNames( agentContext, query ) { return tickets.keyArray() }
```

Written as calls: `registry.prefix( "%", ( agentContext, text ) => ..., { hint : "..." } )` and `registry.source( "ticket", ( agentContext, query ) => ..., { hint : "...", suggest : ( agentContext, query ) => [ ... ] } )`.

The person chooses the prefix or the name, by the id `extension:method`, in `~/.bxagents/Agent.yml`:

```yaml
chat:
  prefixes:
    desk:explain: "?%"
  sources:
    desk:ticket: issue
```

A choice that cannot be used is reported and the extension's own is kept. `extensions.disable` takes `extension:method` for these too.

## Asking the person

A command, key or prefix can put a question to the person while it runs:

```js
var title    = agentContext.ask( "Title of the ticket?", { default : commandArguments, help : "A short sentence." } )
var priority = agentContext.choose( "Priority?", [ "low", "normal", { value : "high", label : "high", hint : "someone is blocked" } ] )
if ( agentContext.confirm( "Make the #priority# ticket?" ) ) { ... }
```

`ask()` returns the text, `choose()` returns the value picked, and `confirm()` is true only for a yes. Esc gives `null` (`false` for `confirm()`). Questions work in the terminal chat only. Where nobody can answer (the web page, chat platforms, a server) they answer at once with `null` (`false`) instead of waiting, and `agentContext.canAsk()` tells you beforehand so a command can say so.

## Reloading

`/reload` loads the extensions again without leaving the chat: it runs `onUnload()` of what was loaded, reads `~/.bxagents/Agent.yml` and the `extensions:` settings of `Agent.yml` anew, and loads what is found, with its commands, keys, status items, prefixes, sources and listeners. An extension that fails to load is reported and left out; the others load. It is for admins and works in the terminal chat only: a served app registers schedulers and ColdBox listeners when it starts, so restart it instead.

## The web page: slots and `web/`

An extension can add to the [web app](/next/conventions/web-ui/index.html) four ways: **slots** (a string the server draws in a place of the Chat page), **status items** (chips above the conversation), **commands** (in the page's `/` menu), and **files in `web/`** (styles and scripts linked into every page). The terminal chat has no page, so slots and `web/` files are ignored there.

### Slots

A slot puts a string in a named place of the Chat page. The method is called with the `agentContext` and returns the string:

|   Place    |                           Where on the Chat page                            |
|------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `header`   | the bar above the conversation, after the context size and the status chips |
| `sidebar`  | under the list of conversations                                             |
| `composer` | in the message box, before the Attach button                                |

```js
@Slot( "header" )
function badge( agentContext ) { return variables.pings > 0 ? "#variables.pings# pings" : "" }

@Slot( { place : "sidebar", html : true } )
function about( agentContext ) { return "<strong>Panel</strong><br>Use the Ping button." }
```

An empty string shows nothing. A place other than these three is refused when the extension loads. Written as a call: `registry.slot( "header", ( agentContext ) => "...", { html : false, name : "badge" } )`. `extensions.disable` takes `extension:method` for a slot.

**Text or markup.** The string is shown as text (`textContent`): `<b>` shows as `<b>`. Only a slot that says `html : true` has its string put into the page as markup (`innerHTML`). That is the author saying the markup is their own. The page does not clean it, so it must never carry what a visitor typed, a model wrote or a service sent: pass any such value through `encodeForHTML()`. The slot places are outside Alpine (`x-ignore`), so `x-`, `:` and `@` attributes in a slot do nothing; behaviour belongs in a script of `web/`.

**When it is drawn.** The page asks for every slot in one request, `GET /__bxagents/slots?conversationId=` (the agent API's path, which `agentApi.path` can move), behind the same sign-in or token as the rest of the API. It asks when the Chat page opens and after each turn, command and change of conversation, at the same moments it reads the context size. Each draw replaces what the server drew before and leaves what a script added alone. A slot that throws is left out and the reason is put on its extension once. When no extension has a slot, `GET /agent` says `capabilities.slots: false` and the page does not ask.

### Status items

`@Status` (see [Keys and status](#keys-and-status)) is shown on the web page too: a chip for each item, in the bar above the conversation, read from `GET /__bxagents/status?conversationId=` at the same moments as the slots. An empty string shows no chip.

### Commands

A `@Command` whose `transports` include `web` (the default) is offered on the Chat page: in the menu that `/` opens and behind the lightning button, with the extension's name as a badge (`GET /commands`). Enter runs the line on the server with `POST /command` (`{ line, conversationId }`) and the page draws the `Reply`: text, a table, or buttons to pick from. A command that asks the person something gets `null` at once on the page (see [Asking the person](#asking-the-person)). A script runs one with `bxagents.runCommand( "/ping" )`, as if it were typed.

### Files in `web/`

`web/` is a folder inside a folder extension. Every file in it (images and fonts too, in subfolders as well) is served at `<path>/ext/<name>/<file>`, where `<path>` is the `webui` gateway's path: `extensions/panel/web/logo.png` is `/chat/ext/panel/logo.png`. The file is read from the extension itself in the built app (`<app>/extensions/<name>/web/`); nothing is copied next to the page.

```text
extensions/panel/
  Extension.bx
  web/
    panel.css       linked into every page
    panel.js        linked into every page
    logo.png        served at <path>/ext/panel/logo.png
    img/icon.svg    served at <path>/ext/panel/img/icon.svg, not linked
```

* The `*.css` and `*.js` files that sit directly in `web/` are linked into **every page** of the app, in file name order: styles in the head, after the app's own; scripts at the end of the body, deferred, after the app's own script. Files in subfolders are served but not linked.
* Like the page's own scripts and styles, these files are not behind the sign-in. Do not put anything secret in `web/`.
* An address is checked before any file is read: the extension is a plain folder name, the file a relative path with no `..`, no part that starts with a dot and no backslash, and the file must be inside the extension's `web/` folder. Anything else, a missing file, or an extension turned off in `extensions.disable` answers 404.
* Which files are linked is written by `bxAgents build`, so build again after you add or rename one.
* Only the project's own `extensions/` bring `web/` files (see [What stays in the project](#what-stays-in-the-project)).

A script runs on every page, but the slot places, the open conversation and the commands exist only on the Chat page. Elsewhere `bxagents.slot()` gives a box that is not in the page, `conversationId()` is `""` and `runCommand()` does nothing. Check for the Chat page's message box (`document.getElementById( "input" )`) if a script should only run there.

### The `bxagents` object

The page makes one object, `window.bxagents`, before the extensions' deferred scripts run. Its members are fixed (a browser test keeps them so):

|            Member             |                                                                                                          What it does                                                                                                          |
|-------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `bxagents.apiBase`            | the agent API's path (`/__bxagents`, or what `agentApi.path` says), for your own `fetch` calls                                                                                                                                 |
| `bxagents.slot( place )`      | a new box of your own in `header`, `sidebar` or `composer` to draw into. Another place throws an error                                                                                                                         |
| `bxagents.runCommand( line )` | runs a slash command as if it were typed, and shows its answer in the conversation. Does nothing while a turn runs                                                                                                             |
| `bxagents.onRefresh( fn )`    | calls `fn()` after each draw of the slots and status chips: when the Chat page opens and after each turn, command and change of conversation. A listener that throws is logged in the browser console and the others still run |
| `bxagents.refresh()`          | asks the Chat page to read the slots, the status chips and the context size now                                                                                                                                                |
| `bxagents.conversationId()`   | the id of the conversation in view, or `""`                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| `bxagents.icon( name )`       | the markup of one of the page's [Phosphor icons](https://phosphoricons.com) (`bxagents.icon( "robot" )`), sized by the text around it. The names are in `tools/webui-vendor/icons.json`                                        |

There is no event bus and no other member. `plug` and `notify` are the page's own, not part of the contract. A call to the API from a script goes to `bxagents.apiBase + "/..."` on the same origin, so the sign-in cookie goes with it. A call that changes something must also send the header `x-bxagents-csrf: 1`. On an agent with an API password and no accounts, a script's own `fetch` does not carry the password: run a command instead.

### Theming

The page's colours, shapes and fonts are CSS custom properties. Use them in your CSS and it follows light and dark, the visitor's accent and the gateway's `theme` block:

|                 Variable                  |                                What it is                                 |
|-------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `--bg`, `--surface`, `--input-bg`         | the page, a card or panel, a text box                                     |
| `--fg`, `--muted`, `--border`             | text, quieter text, lines                                                 |
| `--accent`, `--accent-fg`                 | the brand colour, and text on it                                          |
| `--accent-soft`, `--accent-ink`, `--ring` | a light tint of the accent, the accent as text or an icon, the focus glow |
| `--radius`, `--radius-sm`                 | large and small corners                                                   |
| `--font`, `--font-mono`, `--font-size`    | the text font, the code font, the base size                               |

The dark theme sets the same variables on `:root[data-theme="dark"]`, so a rule that uses them needs no dark copy. The gateway's [`theme` block](/next/conventions/web-ui/index.html#branding-and-theming) and the project's `resources/webui/theme.css` come after the extensions' styles in the page, so the operator's choices win over an extension's. Do not hard-code a colour: it breaks the dark theme and the operator's brand.

### A worked example: the panel extension

The dev agent of the web app (`ui/dev/agent/extensions/panel`) uses all of it: a header slot that counts pings, a sidebar slot with markup, a `/ping` command, and a script that adds a **Ping** button to the message box.

```text
extensions/panel/
  Extension.bx
  web/
    panel.css
    panel.js
```

`Extension.bx`:

```js
class {

	function configure() {
		variables.settings = { name : "panel" }
		variables.pings = 0
	}

	// shown as text in the bar above the conversation, next to the context size
	@Slot( "header" )
	function badge( agentContext ) {
		return variables.pings > 0 ? "#settings.name#: #variables.pings# ping#variables.pings == 1 ? '' : 's'#" : ""
	}

	// markup the author wrote, under the list of conversations
	@Slot( { place : "sidebar", html : true } )
	function about( agentContext ) {
		return "<strong>#encodeForHTML( settings.name )#</strong><br>Use the Ping button by the message box."
	}

	@Command
	@Hint( "count a ping: the web page's Ping button runs it too" )
	function ping( agentContext, commandArguments ) {
		variables.pings++
		return agentContext.reply().ok( "pong #variables.pings#" )
	}

}
```

The sidebar slot is markup, so the setting in it goes through `encodeForHTML()`: `settings.name` can be changed in `Agent.yml`.

`web/panel.css` uses the page's variables, so the button follows light, dark and the accent:

```css
.panel-button {
	font: inherit;
	padding: 0.25rem 0.6rem;
	border: 1px solid var(--border);
	border-radius: var(--radius-sm);
	background: transparent;
	color: inherit;
	cursor: pointer;
}
```

`web/panel.js` adds the button to the message box and runs the command:

```js
( function () {
	var button = document.createElement( "button" );
	button.type = "button";
	button.className = "panel-button";
	button.textContent = "Ping";
	button.title = "Run /ping";
	button.addEventListener( "click", function () { bxagents.runCommand( "/ping" ); } );
	bxagents.slot( "composer" ).appendChild( button );
} )();
```

What happens on the Chat page:

1. The page loads `panel.css` in the head and `panel.js` at the end of the body. The script finds `bxagents` there and puts the **Ping** button in the message box.
2. The page asks `GET /slots`. The header slot is empty (no ping yet), so nothing shows there; the sidebar shows **panel** in bold and the line under it.
3. A click on **Ping** runs `/ping` with `POST /command`. The answer, `pong 1`, shows in the conversation.
4. After the command the page asks for the slots again, and the header shows `panel: 1 ping`. The button stays: it is in a box of the script's own, which a draw never removes.

`/ping` typed in the message box, or in the terminal chat, counts the same way. To try it, run the web app's dev stack (see [Work on the web app](/next/guides/ui-development/index.html)) and open <http://127.0.0.1:8780/chat>.

## Tools and skills

A folder extension can carry its own tools and skills:

```text
extensions/helpdesk/
  Extension.bx
  tools/Tickets.bx             a normal bx-ai tool class
  skills/triage/SKILL.md       a normal skill folder
```

The extension stays as it is. The app reads the folders where they are (`extensions/helpdesk/tools/` in the built app) and gives the tools to the root agent as if they were in the project's own `tools/`, and adds the skills to the global skills every agent gets. Nothing is copied or merged into the project's `tools/` or `skills/`. A tool or skill of the project's own wins over an extension's of the same name, and a later extension wins over an earlier one. `extensions.disable` takes `extension:Tickets` (the tool's file name) or `extension:ticket-triage` (the skill's name) for one, or the extension's name for all of them.

## Gateway types

A class in an extension's `gateways/` folder is a gateway type, named after its file in lower case: `extensions/matrix/gateways/Matrix.bx` is the type `matrix`. It is an ordinary bx-ai gateway (see the built-in ones, which extend `ScheduledGatewayBase`); its `getName()` must be the same as its file, lower case, because that is the key bx-ai's gateway registry holds it under. A project then uses it like any other:

```js
// gateways/chat.bx
class {
	function configure() {
		return { type : "matrix", homeserver : "https://matrix.example.org", tokenEnvVar : "MATRIX_TOKEN" };
	}
}
```

Every option named `<name>EnvVar` is the name of an environment variable: the gateway receives its value as `<name>` (here `token`), and it is read when the app starts, so a secret is never a literal in the build. The app builds the gateway from the extension's own class file and registers it when it starts.

All the types come from one registry, `GatewayTypes`: the built-in ones, and whatever extensions bring. A built-in type cannot be replaced (an extension cannot take over `telegram`). Two extensions on one type is a warning and the later one wins. A file name that is not a usable type name (a letter, then letters, digits and `-`) is refused. `extensions.disable` takes `extension:Matrix` for one type or the extension's name for all of them. The gateway classes are read from the project's extensions only.

## Command line verbs

```js
@Verb( { name : "greet", valueOptions : [ "name" ] } )
@Hint( "say hello from the command line: bxAgents greet --name=Ada" )
function greet( options ) { return "Hello, #options.name ?: 'there'#!" }
```

`bxAgents greet --name=Ada` finds the verb in the extensions (modules, the person's own and the project's, loaded as in the chat) when it is not one of the module's own. The method is called with the flags as a struct, as a built-in verb gets them (`--projectRoot` is always there). It returns an exit code, a message to print, `{ exitCode, message }`, or nothing. A flag that must have a value is listed in `valueOptions`, so `--name` alone is refused as it is for a built-in verb. A method that throws is an error with exit code 1 that names the extension. A built-in verb cannot be replaced, and two extensions on one verb is a warning with the later one winning. `bxAgents help` lists the verbs extensions add. They are not in the generated shell completions, which stay as they are. `registry.verb( "greet", ( options ) => ..., { hint, valueOptions } )` is the call form, and `extensions.disable` takes `extension:method`.

## Where extensions come from

|  Layer  |                    Folder                    |                           Runs in                           |
|---------|----------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------|
| modules | `extensions/` of an installed BoxLang module | everywhere the module is installed                          |
| user    | `~/.bxagents/extensions/`                    | the terminal chat on that machine only                      |
| project | `<project>/extensions/`                      | the terminal chat, the web page, chat platforms, the server |

A later layer wins. An extension with the same name replaces the earlier one, and a command replaces an earlier command of the same name or alias, a built-in included. Both are shown in `/extensions`; nothing is replaced silently. The build copies the project's `extensions/` into the app; a served agent never reads a developer's home folder.

## Starting one

```bash
bxAgents add extension standup                       # asks what it should bring
bxAgents add extension standup --with=command,key    # or say so, for a pipe or CI
bxAgents add extension standup --with=command,tool --description="Daily standup"
```

(With the BoxLang 1.19.0 launcher a quoted value with spaces is split at the spaces; see [Quoting flag values](/next/cli-reference/index.html#quoting-flag-values).)

`add extension` writes `extensions/<name>.bx`, or `extensions/<name>/` with an `Extension.bx` when something needs a file of its own, with working stubs and a `TODO` where you fill in. `--with` takes any of `command`, `key`, `status`, `prefix`, `source`, `slot`, `verb`, `listener` (methods of the one class) and `scheduler`, `gateway`, `tool`, `skill`, `web` (files, so the extension is a folder). `--layout=file|folder` picks the shape when it can be either. Nothing is overwritten without `--force`, and `--dry-run` shows the files. It is yours: commit it with the project. Try it with `bxAgents chat` and `/reload`.

## Installing extensions

`bxAgents extensions install` puts an extension into the project from a folder, a zip, GitHub or ForgeBox.

```bash
bxAgents extensions install ./my-ext                    # a folder
bxAgents extensions install ./my-ext.zip                # a zip file
bxAgents extensions install ./greet.bx                   # a one-class extension
bxAgents extensions install acme/tools                  # GitHub: owner/repo, or owner/repo#ref
bxAgents extensions install https://github.com/acme/tools
bxAgents extensions install https://example.org/ext.zip # a zip by address
bxAgents extensions install acme-tools@1.2.0            # a ForgeBox slug, optionally with a version
bxAgents extensions install ./my-ext --system           # for you, in ~/.bxagents/extensions
```

A folder that exists wins over `owner/repo`. To say which you mean, start with `path:`, `github:`, `forgebox:` or `url:`.

An extension is code that runs when the chat or the app starts, so `install` fetches it into a temporary folder, looks at it without running anything, and shows you what it adds (commands, keys, prefixes, listeners, gateways, tools, skills, web files, verbs) and what its code mentions (files, network, processes, java). It then asks for a yes. `--yes` skips the question and is required when there is no terminal. Nothing is placed until you agree.

|      Command       |                                                                       Does                                                                       |
|--------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `install <source>` | fetch, preview, ask, place. `--name=<name>` renames it, `--force` replaces one that is there, `--system` installs for you instead of the project |
| `install`          | with no source, brings back everything `extensions.lock.json` lists                                                                              |
| `list --installed` | what was installed, where from, and whether it is `intact`, `changed` or `missing`                                                               |
| `update [name...]` | fetches again, shows the change and asks. A source pinned to a version or ref (`#v1`, `@1.2.0`) is left alone                                    |
| `remove <name>`    | deletes it and its lock entry. A folder you edited needs `--force`                                                                               |

The project keeps `extensions.lock.json` (`~/.bxagents/extensions.lock.json` with `--system`): the name, the source, the version or ref fetched, and a checksum of the files. **Commit the lock.** `bxAgents build` brings back anything in it that is missing, and refuses a package whose files no longer match their checksum. Installed extensions are not committed (see below), and the build restores them from the lock.

An installed extension is kept out of source control with one line per extension in the project's `.gitignore` (`/extensions/acme-tools/`, or `/extensions/acme.bx`), added on `install` and taken out on `remove`, only when the project has a `.gitignore`. An extension you wrote yourself in the same folder is still committed. Commit `extensions.lock.json`: it is what brings the rest back.

What `install` refuses: a zip entry with an absolute path, a `..` part or a backslash, more than 5000 files or 50 MB, a name that is not safe as a folder name, a name already there that this command did not install (unless `--force`), a BoxLang module (`ModuleConfig.bx`), and anything that is not an extension. Symbolic links and `.git` are left out. The preview is a quick read of the text, not a security review: install what you trust.

## Working on one: link it

```bash
bxAgents extensions link ./my-ext                 # ~/.bxagents/extensions/my-ext -> ./my-ext
bxAgents extensions link ./greet.bx --name=hi     # a one-class extension, under another name
bxAgents extensions unlink my-ext                 # takes the link away, never the folder
```

`link` makes a symbolic link in your own extensions folder, so the terminal chat on this machine loads the extension from where you are editing it, and `/reload` picks up a change with nothing to install again. There is no preview and no lock: the code is yours, and a link is a path on this machine, so it is not brought back on another one. A real folder or file in that place is never replaced, a name installed with `install --system` has to be removed first, and `--force` only points an existing link somewhere else. `list --installed --system` shows links beside installs, as `linked` or `broken` (the target went away). Because a link is for you, it is not part of a project and does not travel into a built app: put the extension in the project's `extensions/` (or `install` it) for that.

## Turning things off

```yaml
extensions:
  disable: [ roll, "deploy:deploy", "acme-*" ]
```

A plain name turns off the extension of that name (and any command called that); `extension:item` turns off one command; `*` matches any run of characters. Both `Agent.yml` and `~/.bxagents/Agent.yml` accept it.

## Looking at them

`/extensions` in the chat, or from the shell:

```bash
bxAgents extensions          # the list, where each came from and what it added
bxAgents extensions --json
```

## What stays in the project

Tools, skills, gateway types and `web/` files are read from the project's own `extensions/` folder, which the build copies into the app as it is. An extension in an installed module or in your own `~/.bxagents/extensions` still adds commands, keys, prefixes, listeners and verbs to the chat and the command line, but it does not travel into a built app: a server never reads a developer's home folder.

title: gateways/
body:
gateways/ gateways/*.bx / .json files under this one folder cover two distinct, unrelated things - which kind an entry is depends entirely on whether its configure() struct has an exposes key. Warning Don't confuse these with each other - an HTTP-exposed agent ( exposes: "agent" ) is a REST API for your agent; a channel-adapter gateway ( type: "http" ) is a webhook endpoint for a chat platform or human-in-the-loop approval flow. They generate completely different routes. flowchart TD F["a file under gateways/"] --> Q{"does configure() return
an 'exposes' key?"} Q -->|"yes"| E["EXPOSURE
a route into your agent"] Q -->|"no - it has a 'type' key instead"| C["CHANNEL ADAPTER
a connection to a chat platform"] E --> E1["exposes: agent
four routes of the agent API"] E --> E2["exposes: mcp
route().toMCP()"] E --> E3["exposes: webui
the web app module"] C --> C1["mock / cli / http
pull-driven: something calls US"] C --> C2["telegram, slack, discord, email, whatsapp-cloud,
teams, twilio, github, signal
push-style: holds its own connection"] C2 --> S["one GatewaySession
bound to the root agent"] style E fill:#d4edda,stroke:#155724 style C fill:#cce5ff,stroke:#004085 Tip bxAgents add gateway writes this entry for you and the .env stubs it needs, then lists the setup steps that happen outside the project. See add . 1. HTTP/MCP/web-UI exposure ( exposes: "agent" | "mcp" | "webui" ) Exposes the agent, or a local MCP server, over HTTP using ColdBox 8.1's native AI Routing DSL - or a pre-built browser chat UI, documented separately in The web chat UI . Expose the agent: // gateways/expose.bx class { function configure() { return { exposes : "agent", path : "/api/chat" }; } } Generates, in config/Router.bx , four routes served by the agent API's own handler ( handlers/AgentApi.bx , the same one as the reserved /__bxagents route ): POST /api/chat/invoke , POST /api/chat/stream (SSE), POST /api/chat/batch , GET /api/chat/info . The bare /api/chat path itself is not routable. They follow the same agentApi.access switch as the reserved route: with token , a request needs the shared secret or an issued token in x-bxagents-token , and is answered 401 without one. Expose a local MCP server (see mcp/ ): class { function configure() { return { exposes : "mcp", path : "/mcp/tools", target : "local-server" // must match an mcp/*.bx entry's file name }; } } Generates route( "/mcp/tools" ).toMCP( "local-server" ) . Expose the web chat UI: // gateways/chat.bx class { function configure() { return { exposes : "webui", path : "/chat", apiKeyEnvVar: "CHAT_UI_API_KEY" // optional - see below }; } } Installs the web app (a ColdBox module, bxagentsui ) at , and the app calls the agent API at /__bxagents (or where agentApi.path puts it), the same one the terminal chat uses, so the entry adds no API of its own. It does bring the shared SQLite store with it. Each page of the app is an address under ( /chat/settings , /chat/logs/gateways ), and an address under that is no page answers 404 . path cannot be / . The web UI is a subsystem rather than a single exposure switch - the store, conversations and preferences, branding and theming, sign-in and how the page uses the agent API are all on its own page: The web chat UI . Validation: exposes must be agent , mcp , or webui ; path is required and must be unique across every exposure entry; an mcp exposure's target is required and must match a real mcp/* entry's file name; webui 's apiKeyEnvVar is entirely optional, with no required-field check (see below). A webui entry may list profiles for the page's model picker (see Choosing the model ); each must be declared in Agent.yml , and no other kind of entry may list them. 2. Channel-adapter gateways ( type: "mock" | "cli" | "http" ) Registers a bx-ai IGateway (a channel adapter for external delivery / human-in-the-loop approval) by name - distinct from exposing the agent's own REST API. // gateways/slack.bx class { function configure() { return { type : "http", secretEnvVar : "SLACK_WEBHOOK_SECRET" }; } } secretEnvVar names an environment variable holding the signing secret - never the secret value itself . Generates, in the generated base Application 's onApplicationStart() : aiGatewayRegistry().register( aiGateway( "http", { secret : getSystemSetting( "SLACK_WEBHOOK_SECRET", "" ) } ) ) The secret is resolved live at server startup, matching this project's "secrets stay external" rule everywhere else (see Deployment & Secrets ) - it's never embedded as a literal in generated source, so it's never present in a packaged .bxa either. If the env var is unset, bx-ai's own HttpGateway treats an empty secret as "no signing configured" and rejects requests accordingly, rather than crashing at startup. Validation: type must be mock , cli , or http ; a type: "http" entry requires a secretEnvVar ; the entry's own file/base name must be unique across every channel-adapter entry. mock is test-only; cli is bx-ai's own built-in human-in-the-loop approval channel (a blocking stdin/stdout A/R/Q prompt) - it's what HumanInTheLoopMiddleware attaches by default when no gateway is specified, and is unrelated to BxAgents' own chat verb (which never touches the gateway registry at all). Any channel-adapter entry mounts the bx-ai Gateway surface : one line in config/Router.bx , using ColdBox's own toAiGateway() terminator. route( "/gateways" ).toAiGateway() That single terminator mounts the whole bx-ai Gateway surface: POST /gateways/:gateway/events inbound platform event GET /gateways/:gateway/events the platform's URL verification handshake GET /gateways/interactions/:requestID poll a pending human interaction POST /gateways/interactions/:requestID/decisions submit a human's decision GET /gateways/info what this mount serves This mount is not http -specific. http is one gateway type among many, and the surface is shared: the /interactions routes are the human-in-the-loop approval channel for every gateway, resolved through bx-ai's own gateway registry rather than per-transport. So a project whose only gateway is Telegram, Slack or Discord gets the same /gateways mount - it needs those routes exactly as much, since a paused agent has to be answerable somehow. Warning The routes only reach a running server, so a project relying on human-in-the-loop approval needs serve (or a real deployment), not plain chat . 3. Push-style gateways ( type: "telegram" / "slack" / "discord" / "email" / "whatsapp-cloud" / "teams" / "twilio" / "github" / "signal" , and friends) A different kind of channel adapter from mock / cli / http above: instead of being driven by an inbound HTTP request, a push-style gateway holds its own connection to the platform and pushes inbound messages to your agent as they arrive - the closer-to-"real chat bot" experience. Four transport shapes exist today: Long-poll (Telegram, Email): a scheduled task periodically asks the platform "anything new?" (Telegram's getUpdates , Email's IMAP poll). Persistent websocket (Slack via Socket Mode, Discord via its Gateway API): the gateway holds a live, long-running connection the platform pushes events down in real time. Webhook, pull-driven (WhatsApp Business Cloud API, Microsoft Teams, Twilio SMS, GitHub): the platform calls us over a public HTTP endpoint instead of this gateway holding its own outbound connection - no scheduler task or socket to manage. See their own subsections below. Server-Sent Events (SSE) (Signal, against a locally-run signal-cli daemon): a long-lived, one-way streaming HTTP connection the gateway holds open, reading events as they're pushed down the same response body. See its own subsection below. Signing in to a service from a chat platform A person talking to the agent through any of these can send /connect to see the services that ask them to sign in and /connect NAME to get a link that works once. The link goes to the server's public address, so set BXAGENTS_PUBLIC_URL . See connect , which walks through it with a Telegram bot. /connect also lists the built-in connectors . A token is never typed into a chat platform, so connecting a connector there points to the web page; set BXAGENTS_PUBLIC_URL so the address is right. The nine push-style platforms Each platform gets its own page: its gateways/*.bx config shape, what's required, and (where one exists) the protocol-level detail on how BxAgents talks to it. Telegram Long-poll. botTokenEnvVar only. Slack Persistent websocket, Socket Mode. Discord Persistent websocket, Gateway API, mandatory heartbeats. Email Long-poll IMAP + cbmailservices/bx-mail outbound. WhatsApp Business Cloud Webhook-driven, Meta Graph API. Microsoft Teams Webhook-driven, Bot Framework Activity protocol. Twilio SMS Webhook-driven, form-urlencoded, dual-path TwiML response. GitHub Webhook-driven, @mention -gated issue/PR comment threads. Signal Server-Sent Events, against an external signal-cli daemon. Same "secrets stay external" rule as http 's secretEnvVar : every *EnvVar key names an environment variable, resolved live via getSystemSetting() at startup, never embedded as a literal - email 's imapHost / fromAddress aren't cryptographic secrets, but the same env-var-driven convention is used for every one of its config values anyway, since they all vary per deployment. Unlike the core types, a push-style gateway's class lives inside BxAgents itself ( models/gateways/*.bx , not bx-ai), so its registration renders as a bare class path rather than a short name: aiGatewayRegistry().register( aiGateway( "bxModules.bxagents.models.gateways.TelegramGateway", { "botToken" : getSystemSetting( "TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN", "" ) } ) ) aiGatewayRegistry().register( aiGateway( "bxModules.bxagents.models.gateways.SlackGateway", { "appToken" : getSystemSetting( "SLACK_APP_TOKEN", "" ), "botToken" : getSystemSetting( "SLACK_BOT_TOKEN", "" ) } ) ) aiGatewayRegistry().register( aiGateway( "bxModules.bxagents.models.gateways.DiscordGateway", { "botToken" : getSystemSetting( "DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN", "" ) } ) ) aiGatewayRegistry().register( aiGateway( "bxModules.bxagents.models.gateways.EmailGateway", { "imapHost" : getSystemSetting( "IMAP_HOST", "" ), "imapUsername" : getSystemSetting( "IMAP_USERNAME", "" ), "imapPassword" : getSystemSetting( "IMAP_PASSWORD", "" ), "fromAddress" : getSystemSetting( "EMAIL_FROM_ADDRESS", "" ) } ) ) aiGatewayRegistry().register( aiGateway( "bxModules.bxagents.models.gateways.whatsapp.WhatsAppCloudGateway", { "accessToken" : getSystemSetting( "WHATSAPP_ACCESS_TOKEN", "" ), "phoneNumberId" : getSystemSetting( "WHATSAPP_PHONE_NUMBER_ID", "" ), "appSecret" : getSystemSetting( "WHATSAPP_APP_SECRET", "" ), "verifyToken" : getSystemSetting( "WHATSAPP_VERIFY_TOKEN", "" ) } ) ) aiGatewayRegistry().register( aiGateway( "bxModules.bxagents.models.gateways.TeamsGateway", { "appId" : getSystemSetting( "TEAMS_APP_ID", "" ), "appPassword" : getSystemSetting( "TEAMS_APP_PASSWORD", "" ) } ) ) aiGatewayRegistry().register( aiGateway( "bxModules.bxagents.models.gateways.TwilioGateway", { "accountSid" : getSystemSetting( "TWILIO_ACCOUNT_SID", "" ), "authToken" : getSystemSetting( "TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN", "" ), "from" : getSystemSetting( "TWILIO_FROM_NUMBER", "" ) } ) ) aiGatewayRegistry().register( aiGateway( "bxModules.bxagents.models.gateways.GitHubGateway", { "token" : getSystemSetting( "GITHUB_TOKEN", "" ), "webhookSecret" : getSystemSetting( "GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET", "" ), "botName" : getSystemSetting( "GITHUB_BOT_NAME", "" ) } ) ) aiGatewayRegistry().register( aiGateway( "bxModules.bxagents.models.gateways.SignalGateway", { "account" : getSystemSetting( "MY_SIGNAL_ACCOUNT", "" ) } ) ) Validation: type: "telegram" requires botTokenEnvVar ; type: "slack" requires both botTokenEnvVar and appTokenEnvVar ; type: "discord" requires botTokenEnvVar ; type: "email" requires imapHostEnvVar , imapUsernameEnvVar , imapPasswordEnvVar , and fromAddressEnvVar ; type: "whatsapp-cloud" requires accessTokenEnvVar , phoneNumberIdEnvVar , appSecretEnvVar , and verifyTokenEnvVar ; type: "teams" requires appIdEnvVar and appPasswordEnvVar ; type: "twilio" requires accountSidEnvVar , authTokenEnvVar , and fromEnvVar ; type: "github" requires tokenEnvVar , webhookSecretEnvVar , and botNameEnvVar ; type: "signal" requires accountEnvVar - all checked the same way http 's secretEnvVar is. Info Slack v1 is Socket Mode only - no public webhook endpoint is needed or generated for it (unlike http , which gets real routes - see §2 above). The Events-API/HTTP-webhook alternative Slack also supports isn't built here. Discord v1 is likewise the real Gateway API (a persistent websocket) rather than Discord's alternative HTTP Interactions Endpoint URL webhook mode - no Ed25519 signature verification is needed here as a result, since interactions arrive over the same authenticated connection rather than a public HTTP endpoint (confirmed against Discord's own docs). GatewaySession - wiring the agent to every push-style gateway Any project with at least one push-style gateway entry also gets a generated start-up statement in the generated base class's after() . It builds a single bx-ai GatewaySession (our CommandGatewaySession , which is one with commands in front of the agent) bundling every push-style gateway in the project, bound to the project's root agent, and starts it: // bxagents/Application.bx, after() (GENERATED) var wirebox = application.cbController.getWireBox() var agent = wirebox.getInstance( "GeneratedAgent" ) var gatewaySession = new "models.gateways.CommandGatewaySession@bxagents"( agent : agent, gateways : [ aiGatewayRegistry().get( "telegram" ) ], policy : "queue", maxQueueDepth: 50, commands : {}, attachments : true ) BoxAnnounce( "onGatewaySessionCreate", { session: gatewaySession } ) gatewaySession.start() application.bxaiGatewaySession = gatewaySession Info The generated variable is deliberately named gatewaySession , not session - session is a reserved BoxLang/ColdBox scope name (like request / server / url / form / cgi / thread ), and a local variable reusing one of those names can collide with the live scope instead of behaving as an ordinary local. Warning The aiGatewayRegistry().get(...) key is always the gateway TYPE string ("telegram", "slack", "discord", "email", ...) - confirmed against bx-ai's real GatewayRegistry.register() source, which always keys by the gateway class's own fixed getName() , never anything caller-supplied. A real consequence: two gateways/* entries of the same push-style type collide on the same registry slot project-wide - the second registration silently overwrites the first. There's no per-entry alias today; use a distinct type per additional platform account, or wait for multi-instance support. Control GatewaySession 's policy via an optional gatewaySession block on the root project's Agent.yml : # Agent.yml gatewaySession: # both optional - these are the defaults policy: queue maxQueueDepth: 50 policy must be one of reject / queue / steer / interrupt (bx-ai's own GatewaySession policy vocabulary, illustrated below) - checked at build time so a typo fails loudly instead of surfacing as a runtime error the first time the app boots. Warning v1 limitation: exactly one GatewaySession , always bound to the project's root agent - matches the existing precedent that exposes: "agent" HTTP exposure is also always root-agent-only. A project with subagents cannot yet route different gateways to different subagents. Commands in a gateway A message that is one of the session's slash commands is answered by BxAgents itself and never reaches the model, through the same gateway it came in on. Anything else, including a slash word that is not a command here, goes to the agent as before. A choice (a list to pick from) comes back as a numbered list with the command to type for each. By default a safe set is on: /help , /tools , /model , /info , /ping , /remember , /notes and /connect . They need no conversation of their own and change nothing shared ( /connect only gives the person who sends it a link to sign in to a service: see connect ). Narrow it, widen it or switch it off in the same gatewaySession block: # Agent.yml gatewaySession: commands: enabled: true # false switches commands off prefix: "/" # one character prefixes: { slack: "!" } # a different one-character prefix for one gateway, by name conversation: false # true also turns on /new, /clear, /compact, /sessions and /resume allow: [ help, info, tools, notes, remember, model, ping, connect ] # the default; any command that runs on a gateway admins: [ "123456789" ] # gateway user ids that may run commands marked for admins Each platform shows the same commands its own way: Platform How the commands appear Telegram The bot's / menu lists them ( setMyCommands , sent when the first message arrives). /info@yourbot in a group is read as /info Discord Registered as application commands when the bot starts, so typing / in a server lists them; each takes one optional args text. Needs the application id: Discord sends it when the bot connects, or set applicationId on the gateway entry. The answer replaces the "thinking" placeholder Slack Slack slash commands are created in the Slack app, not through the API. Define one umbrella command (default /agent , option slashCommand ): /agent model fast runs /model fast and /agent alone runs /help . Or define one Slack command per chat command ( /info ). The answer is visible only to the person who typed it. Typed /word messages never reach a Slack bot, so use prefixes below WhatsApp A "pick one" answer arrives as up to three buttons, or a list for four to ten; a tap runs that command Twilio (SMS), Signal and others A "pick one" answer is a numbered list; reply with just the number. Any other message forgets the list The prefix can differ per gateway. A Slack workspace has its own / commands, so give Slack another character: gatewaySession: commands: prefix: "/" prefixes: { slack: "!" } # by gateway name; one character each build checks the block: an unknown key, a prefix that is not one character, or an allow entry that is not a command that runs on a gateway fails before the app starts. In Telegram a group message such as /info@yourbot is read as /info . Pictures and files A picture or file sent to the bot goes to the agent with the message: pictures as image parts, text files ( .txt , .md , .json , .csv , code and the like, cut at 100,000 characters) inside the message. Other types are named back to the person as not read. At most 4 pictures of 5 MB each go with one message, and a picture sent to a profile marked vision: false is refused with that reason, the same checks as the terminal and the web page. Platform What is read Setup Telegram A photo (the largest size within 5 MB) and a document, with the caption as the text None Discord Attachments None Slack Files shared in a message The Slack app needs the files:read scope WhatsApp A picture or document, with its caption None; the media link is fetched with the access token Twilio (MMS) Media sent with the message, even with no text Media links are public unless the account turned on basic auth for media; with that on, they cannot be read Teams, Signal, Email, GitHub Not read Links must be https. A file that cannot be downloaded is named back to the person and the rest of the message goes on. Switch it off with gatewaySession.attachments: false . Whose conversation it is Each person's chats are their own. The agent is told who is writing (the platform and their id there, slack:U123 ) and which conversation it is, so the agent's memory, /notes and /remember , and the conversation list are kept apart per person. The conversation id is the gateway's name, the chat and, when the platform gives one, a thread: slack:C0123:1700000000.0001 . Two people in the same channel do not share a memory, and neither do two chats on two platforms. The conversations are stored in the same SQLite database as the web page's and the terminal's ( chat.db in the agent's data home , the same file a project with a web page uses), marked with the platform they started on ( source ). They belong to the person's own id, so they do not appear in the list of the open local user. Platform The person The chat The thread part Telegram The user id The chat id None: one conversation per chat Slack The user id The channel The thread's timestamp, or the message's own timestamp when it is not in a thread, so a message outside a thread starts a conversation of its own Discord The author's id The channel The id of the message being replied to, none for a plain message WhatsApp The sender's number The sender The id of the message quoted, if any Twilio (SMS) The sender's number The sender None Signal The sender The sender The id of the message quoted, if any Teams The sender's id Teams' own conversation id The replyToId of the activity GitHub The commenter's login repo:owner/repo:issue:N (or the review comment form) None Email The sender's address The sender's address The mail thread Conversation commands /new , /clear , /compact , /sessions and /resume are off by default, because most chats are one long conversation and a stray /clear is easy to type. They only ever act on the sender's own conversation. Turn them on with conversation: true (or list them in allow ). /new moves the chat to a fresh conversation; the old one stays on the list. Where a chat was moved to is kept in memory only, so after the app restarts the chat is back in its own conversation until it moves again. /sessions lists the conversations the person has had in this app, newest first, and /resume 2 (or an id) moves the chat back to one. The list is in the shared chat database, so it lasts across restarts; the messages last as long as the agent's memory does. /clear and /compact act on the conversation the chat is in now. In Slack each thread has its own conversation, and /new moves only that thread. What each policy actually does with a message that arrives while a turn is still running: flowchart TD M["a message arrives on thread T"] --> B{"is a run already
in flight on T?"} B -->|"no"| D["dispatch a new turn.
The reply streams back through
the gateway the message came from."] B -->|"yes"| P{"policy"} P -->|"reject"| R["Immediate 'busy' reply.
Nothing is queued - the sender must resend."] P -->|"queue
(the default)"| Q["Enqueue, up to maxQueueDepth.
Runs as its own turn once
the current one finishes."] P -->|"steer"| ST["agent.steerRun( T, text )
Spliced into the SAME run at its next
checkpoint - never a second turn."] P -->|"interrupt"| I["agent.cancelRun( T ), AND enqueue.
The current turn winds down at its next
checkpoint, then this message runs."] Q --> OVER{"queue already at
maxQueueDepth?"} I --> OVER OVER -->|"yes"| R style D fill:#d4edda,stroke:#155724 style R fill:#f8d7da,stroke:#721c24 Warning "Steer" here means Hermes Agent's non-destructive splice - the running turn keeps going and the new text is folded into it. It does not mean what Eve's turnPolicy: "steer" means (cancel the active turn and start a replacement); that behaviour is this vocabulary's interrupt . Info Neither cancelRun() nor steerRun() is instant. Both are signalled and take effect at the run's next checkpoint (before the next LLM call or tool call), so interrupt is "ask the current turn to wind down soon", not "synchronously replace it". How a push-style gateway stays connected: the shared ColdBox Scheduler Rather than a new background-loop primitive, push-style gateways reach the app's own live ColdBox scheduler singleton ( appScheduler@coldbox ; a project's own schedules/ are BoxLang schedulers and run separately) and register their own named task(s) into it dynamically - a recurring long-poll task for Telegram, for example. One shared scheduler, every push-style gateway registering its own tasks into it - never one scheduler per gateway, and never in conflict with a project's own schedules. Chats the app has heard from Each message that reaches a push-style gateway also notes its chat (the gateway's name, the chat id, who wrote, and for Teams the serviceUrl ) in the chat database. Only addresses are kept, never message text. This is how routines learn where they can write to a gateway later, since a bot cannot write to a chat that has never written to it. A reply to a command, and a reply when streaming is off, are sent under data.text as well as data.content . The gateways read text , so before this a command reply could be dropped by Telegram. Logging Every push-style gateway writes to its own gateway- log file (e.g. gateway-telegram ) via BoxLang's writeLog() , rather than one shared/default app log - so an operator can tail exactly the platform they care about without noise from everything else the app logs.
