# Guide: Work on the Web App

This guide is for people who change the [web app](/next/conventions/web-ui/index.html) itself, in this repository. To use the app in an agent you need none of it: `bxAgents build` installs it, already built.

The app is a ColdBox module, `bxagentsui`, built the cbGenesis way: handlers, views and partials in BoxLang, and the scripts and styles (Alpine.js and Sass) built by Vite. It is a client of the [agent API](/next/guides/agent-api/index.html): a handler picks a view, and the page's Alpine component reads its data from `/__bxagents`.

The rules and the full tables of building blocks are in [`ui/AGENTS.md`](https://github.com/ortus-boxlang/bx-agents/blob/development/ui/AGENTS.md). Read it before you change the app. This guide is the tour.

## Where things are

|                                              Part                                               |                         Path                         |
|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------|
| The module: `ModuleConfig.bx`, `config/Router.bx`, `handlers/`, `layouts/`, `views/`, `models/` | `src/main/bx/bxagentsui/`                            |
| Partials                                                                                        | `src/main/bx/bxagentsui/views/_components/{app,ui}/` |
| Sass: tokens, base, layouts, components, views, in that order                                   | `ui/resources/assets/scss/`                          |
| Alpine: `App.js`, `stores/`, `components/<domain>/`, `utils/`                                   | `ui/resources/assets/js/`                            |
| The Vite build, not committed (made by `./gradlew uiBuild`)                                     | `src/main/bx/bxagentsui/includes/build/`             |
| The dev agent and its scripted model                                                            | `ui/dev/agent/`, `ui/dev/model.json`                 |
| Project shapes (other paths, a password, no accounts)                                           | `ui/dev/shapes/`                                     |
| Browser tests                                                                                   | `ui/tests/e2e/`, `ui/tests/shapes/`                  |
| Tours for screenshots and video                                                                 | `ui/tests/media/`                                    |

## How an agent gets it

For each `gateways/*.bx` entry with `exposes: "webui"`, the build (`WebAppModule`) copies the module to `.build/app/modules/bxagentsui`, puts the built scripts and styles (`includes/build/assets`) where the browser fetches them, in `.build/public/includes/bxagentsui/build/assets` (the module's own folders are not under the web root), and writes `config/bxagentsui.json`: where the app is mounted (`basePath`, the entry's `path`), where the agent API is (`apiBase`), the branding, the theme, and the files of the project's extensions. `ModuleConfig.bx` reads that file when ColdBox registers the module, so the module answers at the entry's path.

The build of the scripts and styles is not committed: `./gradlew shadowJar` (through `uiBuild`) writes it to `includes/build` and the module carries it, so an agent build never runs Node. Building this repository needs Java and Node 24 (`ui/.nvmrc`); there is no way to skip it, and the build fails with what to install when Node is missing or another major.

With `BXAGENTS_UI_LINK=true` the build links the module instead of copying it (and links `public/includes/bxagentsui` to the module's `includes` folder), so a change to a view shows on the next request. `npm run stack` sets it. Only a linked module serves `<path>/_kit`, a page with every partial and magic working; a built agent answers 404 there.

## Set it up once

From the repository root:

```bash
./gradlew downloadBoxLang shadowJar
cd ui && npm install     # Node 24 (nvm use) and Java are both required
npx playwright install chromium     # if you have no Playwright browser yet
```

## Run it

```bash
npm run dev        # the dev agent, its model and the Vite dev server
npm run stack      # the dev agent and its model only, with the build of the scripts and styles (run `npm run build` first)
```

The app is at <http://127.0.0.1:8780/chat>. Sign in as `ada` (an admin) or `bob` (a member), password `demo-pass`.

In `npm run dev` a change to a view or a layout shows on reload, and a change to the Sass or a script reloads the page by itself. A change to a handler, a model or `ModuleConfig.bx` needs the stack restarted (Ctrl+C, then `npm run dev` again). `npm run dev -- --no-build` starts without building the agent again.

### The dev agent and its scripted model

The dev agent is `ui/dev/agent`, built and served by this repository's own bxAgents. Its model is scripted: `ui/dev/model.json`, served by `tools/demo/fakellm.bxs`. Nothing needs a key or the network.

|        Ask        |                  You get                   |
|-------------------|--------------------------------------------|
| "what time is it" | a call to the `now` tool, then the answer  |
| "give me a list"  | Markdown: a numbered list and a code block |
| anything else     | a plain answer that names the model        |

The agent has two profiles (`fast`, `planner`), notes, a vault, routines and one folder extension, `panel` (see [extensions](/next/conventions/extensions/index.html#a-worked-example-the-panel-extension)). It keeps its data in `ui/.stack/home`: delete that folder to start fresh. `UI_AGENT_PORT` and `UI_LLM_PORT` move the ports (8780 and 8080).

## Build

```bash
npm run build      # builds only the web app, into src/main/bx/bxagentsui/includes/build
```

The output is ignored by git. `./gradlew shadowJar` builds it too (`./gradlew uiBuild` alone), so a module build always carries a fresh one.

## Conventions

The full list is in `ui/AGENTS.md`. In short:

* **Handlers are thin.** They pick the layout and the view and check who may see the page. The data comes from the agent API through the page's Alpine component. No business logic in a handler.
* **Partials document their args** in a header comment and declare each one with `<bx:param name="args.x" default="..."/>`. Call one with `view( view = "_components/ui/name", module = "bxagentsui", args = { ... } )`.
* **Escape what the server writes** with `encodeForHTML()`. Data for the scripts goes through `PageData.json()` into a `<script type="application/json">` block, never into a script.
* **No server value inside `x-`, `:` or `@` attributes.** They run as code. Put the value in a `data-` attribute and read it in the expression (`$el.dataset.x`) or in `init()`.
* **Every colour is a token** in `abstracts/_tokens.scss`, so the dark theme and the gateway's `theme` block work.
* **One Alpine factory per file** , registered in `App.js` with `Alpine.data( "name", factory )`, with JSDoc on every function, getter and store member.
* **Bind boolean attributes to a real boolean** (`:disabled="!!t.locked"`), never to a value that can be `undefined` or `null`.
* **Accessible by default:** a skip link, a visible focus ring, dialogs that hold and give back the focus, and an `aria-label` on an icon-only button that starts with its visible text, if it has any.
* **A change needs a test:** a browser test for what a person sees, a TestBox spec for BoxLang code.

## The building blocks

Use these before you write markup or logic of your own. `ui/AGENTS.md` has each one with its args.

| Partial (`views/_components/ui/`) |                              What it is                              |
|-----------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `page-head`                       | A page's title, a line under it and its actions                      |
| `tabs`                            | A row of tabs (an ARIA tablist) bound to a component variable        |
| `search`                          | A search box with a debounce                                         |
| `chip`                            | A state or a count (`ok`, `warn`, `bad`)                             |
| `card`                            | A box that holds another view                                        |
| `field`                           | Label, control, help line and error line                             |
| `switch`                          | An on and off toggle, a real checkbox                                |
| `modal`, `drawer`                 | A native `<dialog>`, centred or at the side, that holds another view |
| `table`                           | A table that scrolls on a phone, rows from Alpine                    |
| `empty`                           | What a list shows when it has nothing                                |
| `icon`                            | One icon of the set                                                  |
| `toasts`, `confirm`               | In the layout once: the message region and the question dialog       |

|                                Magic or store                                 |                                               What it does                                               |
|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| ``$api.get( path )`, `$api.post( path, body )``                               | Calls the agent API. Answers `{ ok, status, data, error }`, never throws                                 |
| `$sse( path, { body, onEvent, signal } )`                                     | A stream of the agent API                                                                                |
| ``$confirm( { title, body, danger } )`, `$prompt( { title, label, value } )`` | The app's own dialogs; never `window.confirm` or `window.prompt`                                         |
| ``$toast.success( text )`, `$toast.error( text )``                            | A short message                                                                                          |
| `$md( text )`                                                                 | Markdown as safe HTML, the only input `x-html` takes                                                     |
| `$fmt`                                                                        | Dates, sizes and counts, the same everywhere                                                             |
| `$tabKeys( $event )`                                                          | The arrow, Home and End keys of a tab row                                                                |
| `$store.session`                                                              | What this person may use: `can( capability )`, `agentName`, `agents`; `await loaded()` first in `init()` |
| ``$store.theme`, `$store.appearance``, `$store.nav`                           | Light or dark; accent, text size and density; the folded menu and the phone drawer                       |
| `$store.password`                                                             | The password of an agent without accounts, sent with every call                                          |

`window.bxagents` is the extensions' contract, see [extensions](/next/conventions/extensions/index.html#the-bxagents-object).

## Add a page

A page is a route, a menu entry, a handler, a view and an Alpine component. Say the page is `reports`.

1. **The route.** In `config/Router.bx`, add `route( "/reports" ).to( "Reports.index" )` above the last route. The last route sends every other address to `Main.missing`, which answers 404.

2. **The menu.** In `models/Menu.bx`, add the page to `PAGES`: `{ id : "reports", title : "Reports", icon : "chart-line", group : "main", capability : "" }`. The left menu draws itself from that list. `capability` is the capability of `GET /agent` the page needs (`""` for everybody, `"a|b"` for either, `"~a"` for "unless `a` is false"). A page in the `admin` group answers 403 to a member who is signed in.

3. **The handler.** `handlers/Reports.bx` extends `BaseHandler` and has one `index()`:

   ```text
   class extends="BaseHandler" {

   	function index( event, rc, prc ) {
   		showPage( event, prc, "reports", "reports/index" )
   	}

   }
   ```

   `showPage()` answers 404 for a page that is not in the menu and 403 for an admin page to anybody else, so every page follows the same rule.
4. **The view.** `views/reports/index.bxm` starts with `<div class="pg" x-data="reportsPage">` and the `page-head` partial. A value the component needs from the server goes in a `data-` attribute, escaped with `encodeForHTML()`.

5. **The component.** `ui/resources/assets/js/components/reports/ReportsPage.js` exports one factory, `reportsPage()`, registered in `App.js` with `Alpine.data( "reportsPage", reportsPage )`. It reads its data with `$api` in `init()`. A tab or a filter the address should keep goes through `keepInAddress()` (`utils/address.js`).

6. **The styles** , if the partials are not enough: a file under `scss/views/`, used in `app.scss`, with tokens for every colour.

7. **The tests.** Add `"reports"` to `PAGES` in `ui/tests/e2e/a11y.spec.js` (and to `MEMBER_PAGES` when a member sees it), and write a browser test in `ui/tests/e2e` for what a person does on the page. Run `npm run e2e:shapes` too: a change to routes, paths or the frame must work under every project shape.

8. **The build.** `npm run build` to see it in `npm run stack`; the build is not committed, and `./gradlew shadowJar` makes it for the module.

A change to the router, the menu or a handler needs the stack restarted.

## Lint

```bash
npm run lint       # ESLint, the scripts (lint:fix fixes what it can)
npm run lint:scss  # Stylelint, the Sass (lint:scss:fix)
npm run lint:md    # markdownlint: docs/, changelog.md, readme.md and the notes in ui/
```

The rules are cbGenesis': `eslint.config.mjs`, `.stylelintrc.json`, and `.markdownlint.json` and `.bxlint.json` at the repository root. CI fails on any finding.

## Test

```bash
npm test             # the unit tests of the scripts (Vitest)
npm run e2e          # every browser test, against a stack it starts (or the one already running)
npm run e2e:headed   # the same, with the browser on screen
npm run e2e:shapes   # every page under other project shapes
```

The browser tests sign in once as each account, start every chat test on a new conversation, and fail on any error the page throws. Two of them check the whole app:

* `a11y.spec.js` runs axe-core (WCAG 2.2 AA) on every page, as an admin and a member, light and dark, desktop and phone, and with the dialogs open. A serious or critical finding fails.
* `keyboard.spec.js` checks the skip link, a visible focus ring on every Tab stop, dialogs that hold and give back the focus, and reduced motion.

`npm run e2e:shapes` builds the dev agent again for each folder of `ui/dev/shapes`, serves them side by side on ports 8791 and up, and checks that every page answers, draws its frame, links its files and extensions under its path, and talks to its API:

|     Shape      |       Path        |                        Sign in                        |
|----------------|-------------------|-------------------------------------------------------|
| `open-support` | `/support`        | none, an open API, a Phosphor icon and a theme accent |
| `password`     | `/chat`           | the API's shared secret, with the password dialog     |
| `nested-api`   | `/team/assistant` | none, with the agent API at `/team/api`               |

Add a folder to `ui/dev/shapes` (a `gateways/chat.bx` and a `shape.json`) to test another shape.

## Proof on a pull request

Each pull request that changes the app carries screenshots and a short video of the change. Write a tour in `ui/tests/media/<name>.tour.js` that walks the flow and calls `shot( "what-it-shows" )` at each step. Then, with the stack running:

```bash
npm run media -- <name>      # .stack/media/<name>/: NN-*.png, tour.mp4, tour.gif
```

Publish the folder on the `pr-media` branch, never on a code branch, under `<pr-number>/`, and link the files in the pull request: the GIF and the screenshots show inline, the MP4 is a link.

# Guide: Write Your First Extension

An [extension](/next/conventions/extensions/index.html) adds to the chat and the app without touching the framework: a command, a key, a status item, a tool, a web page slot. This guide takes one from nothing to something you can share. It needs a project (`bxAgents new` makes one).

## 1. Start it

```bash
bxAgents add extension standup --with=command,key --layout=file --description="Daily standup"
```

(With the BoxLang 1.19.0 launcher a quoted value with spaces is split at the spaces; see [Quoting flag values](/next/cli-reference/index.html#quoting-flag-values).)

That writes `extensions/standup.bx`: one class with a `/standup` command and a key, each with a `TODO` to fill in. Leave `--with` or `--layout` out at a terminal and it asks (what to bring, and one file or a folder). If you tick a scheduler, gateway, tool, skill or web files, it makes a folder (`extensions/standup/Extension.bx` plus those files) instead.

## 2. Try it

```bash
bxAgents chat
```

Type `/extensions` to see it loaded, then `/standup`. A problem in the file shows up there with its reason, so a typo is never silent. From a shell, `bxAgents extensions` prints the same list.

## 3. Change it live

Edit the command in `extensions/standup.bx`, then type `/reload` in the same chat. The change is in, with no restart. `/reload` is for admins; in your own terminal chat you are one. A setting goes in `configure()`:

```boxlang
function configure() {
	variables.settings = { greeting : "Good morning" }
}
```

Read it in the command as `settings.greeting`. `Agent.yml` (or your own `~/.bxagents/Agent.yml`) can change it without touching the code:

```yaml
extensions:
  standup:
    greeting: "Hello team"
```

## 4. Use it in every project

An extension in the project's `extensions/` belongs to that project and goes into its built app. To have one in your own terminal chat everywhere, link it:

```bash
bxAgents extensions link ./extensions/standup.bx
```

It now loads from where you edit it, in every chat on this machine, and `/reload` picks up a change.

## 5. Share it

An extension is a folder or a file, so sharing is giving someone that:

* zip the folder, or push it to a GitHub repository;
* they run `bxAgents extensions install ./standup.zip`, or `bxAgents extensions install you/standup`.

They see what it adds and what its code mentions, and say yes before anything is placed. The install is recorded in `extensions.lock.json`, which they commit; the extension itself is restored from it at build time.

## Where next

* [Extensions](/next/conventions/extensions/index.html) lists everything an extension can bring, with the exact shape of each.
* [`examples/extensions-agent`](https://github.com/ortus-boxlang/bx-agents/tree/development/examples/extensions-agent) has a working extension of each kind.

# Hosting and Consuming MCP Servers

Model Context Protocol (MCP) works in two directions in a BxAgents project, and
nothing links them - an agent consuming remote servers need not host one, and a hosted
server is only reachable if a `gateways/` entry exposes it (see
[Exposing Your Agent over HTTP and MCP](/next/course/13-exposing-http-and-mcp/index.html)).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph consume["CONSUMING - declared on Agent.yml"]
        direction LR
        AG["your agent"] -->|"calls out at runtime"| RM["a remote MCP server"]
    end
    subgraph host["HOSTING - one file per server under mcp/"]
        direction LR
        TL["tools/"] -->|"a named SUBSET"| MS["mcpServer('localServer')"]
        MS --> GW["gateways/ entry, exposes: mcp"]
    end
    style consume fill:#e7f1ff,stroke:#004085
    style host fill:#eaf6ec,stroke:#155724
```

## Consuming a remote server

Declared directly in `Agent.yml` via `mcpServers` - not a file under `mcp/`:

```yaml
mcpServers:
  - https://example.com/mcp
  - url: https://other.com/mcp
    name: other
```

A server can need a sign-in: write it as a ``${env.NAME}` placeholder (`token: "${env.GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN}"``),
never the secret itself. An entry can also start a program on the agent's machine
(`command: [uvx, mcp-server-git]`) instead of a web address, and `toolFilter` limits which tools the
agent gets. `bxAgents add mcp client` writes such an entry for you (a catalog name such as GitHub
or Notion, or `--url`), with an empty stub for the key in `.env`; the [`new` wizard](/next/guides/new-wizard/index.html)
offers the same catalog. See [mcp/](/next/conventions/mcp/index.html) for every option.

**No network connection is ever attempted at build time** - reachability is a runtime
concern, so an unreachable server at build time is not a build error. Subagents can
declare their own `mcpServers` independently.

## Hosting a local server

Each `mcp/*.bx` file is a local MCP server your project hosts, exposing a named subset
of your `tools/` (from [Giving Your Agent Tools](/next/course/09-giving-your-agent-tools/index.html)) as MCP tools:

```javascript
// mcp/localServer.bx
class {
	function configure() {
		return {
			description : "Internal tools MCP server",
			version     : "1.0.0",
			cors        : "*",             // optional
			tools       : [ "sayHello" ]   // function names of @AITool tools already under tools/
		};
	}
}
```

The entry's discovered name is its **filename** (`localServer.bx` -\> `localServer`),
not any `name` inside `configure()`. At build time the file is copied verbatim, and a
registration statement is emitted at startup.

## Exposing it over HTTP

A local server isn't reachable on its own - pair it with the `gateways/` exposure
entry you saw in [Exposing Your Agent over HTTP and MCP](/next/course/13-exposing-http-and-mcp/index.html):

```javascript
// gateways/expose-mcp.bx
class {
	function configure() {
		return {
			exposes : "mcp",
			path    : "/mcp/tools",
			target  : "localServer"
		};
	}
}
```

## Connectors: ready-made servers, signed in per person

Consuming a server by writing its address in `Agent.yml` is for services you choose. BxAgents also ships a catalog
of **connectors** : ready-made connections to seven services (GitHub, Stripe, Notion, Atlassian, Cloudflare, Supabase
and Git). Every agent offers them, and none is connected until a person connects *their own* account; the token is
sealed in [the vault](/next/course/the-vault/index.html) and locked to the service's host, and the model never sees it.

![The Connectors page: the built-in connectors, each with its risk and how it signs in](/next/assets/webui/connectors.png)

`bxAgents connectors list` shows the catalog, and `bxAgents connect github` (or the **Connectors** page of the web app)
connects one. `connectors: { only: [ github ] }` in `Agent.yml` limits what the agent offers. See
[connectors](/next/conventions/connectors/index.html) and [connect](/next/conventions/connect/index.html).

## Try it

Acme's `orderStatus` tool from [Giving Your Agent Tools](/next/course/09-giving-your-agent-tools/index.html) should be usable by other
agents too. Host it as its own MCP server. `add mcp server` writes the `mcp/` file with the tools it finds and the
`gateways/` entry that serves it (the description has no spaces, because of the launcher rule):

```bash
cd ~/bxagents-course/acme-support
bxAgents add mcp server tools --description=Acme-tools --yes
bxAgents connectors list
```

```text
+ Created  mcp/tools.bx
+ Created  gateways/toolsMcp.bx
...
ID           NAME                              HOW IN              RISK    VERIFIED
...
github<anything>
...
7 connectors. Nothing is active until a person connects one. bxAgents connectors show <id> says more.
```

`mcp/tools.bx` lists `tools: [ "orderStatus" ]` (a tool added later has to be added there), and
`gateways/toolsMcp.bx` serves it at `/mcp/tools` once the app runs. That route has no authentication of its own: keep
it off public networks or put it behind a proxy that checks a credential. Check the wiring without serving:

```bash
bxAgents build
bxAgents inspect --section=mcp
```

```text
Build succeeded: <anything>/acme-support/.build/app
...
  hosts tools<anything>Acme-tools
```

Any outside MCP client can now list and call `orderStatus`, independent of your agent's own chat interface.

## Checkpoint

`acme-support/` has `mcp/tools.bx` and `gateways/toolsMcp.bx`. `kit/resume.sh 17-hosting-mcp-servers` restores them;
rebuild after.

Full reference: [mcp/](/next/conventions/mcp/index.html).

Next: [Who Is Allowed](/next/course/users-roles-and-tokens/index.html)

title: Installation
body: Installation BxAgents is a BoxLang module. It needs two things on the machine that runs it: A BoxLang runtime. BxAgents itself. It bundles everything else it needs: bx-ai , bx-sqlite , bx-ftp , bx-mail , bx-yaml and bx-markdown as nested BoxLang modules, plus ColdBox, qb , cbsecurity , cbauth and cbmailservices for the apps it generates. There is nothing else to install. Info BxAgents needs BoxLang 1.18.0 or later , which supports the nested modules it bundles. Info serve , chat --server and invoke --server additionally need the standalone boxlang-miniserver binary on PATH . Every other verb ( build , plain chat and invoke , package , inspect , clean , new , ...) doesn't. Info To run bxAgents test the project needs TestBox in lib/testbox . new fetches it by running box install , which needs CommandBox (the box command) on PATH . Without it the project is still created, new prints a warning with the command to run later, and --skipInstall leaves the step out. Nothing else in BxAgents needs CommandBox. 1 Install BoxLang Follow the official BoxLang installation guide . The quick installer also sets up ~/.boxlang/bin on your PATH , which is where module-provided executables (like BxAgents' own bxAgents command, below) land. 2 Install BxAgents install-bx-module bx-agents This fetches the module, with its bundled dependencies, into your BoxLang modules directory ( ~/.boxlang/modules by default, or boxlang_modules/ with --local ). 3 Verify it worked bxAgents --version bxAgents --help --help lists all 29 verbs ( new , add , build , test , serve , chat , invoke , package , deploy , inspect , clean , hash-password , token , users , notes , vault , connect , connectors , sessions , routines , stats , models , doctor , skills , extensions , data , logs , backup , restore ) with a one-line summary of each. The bxAgents command BxAgents declares a native executable in its box.json : "boxlang": { "moduleName": "bxagents", "executable": "bxAgents" } The installer turns that into a bxAgents wrapper script on your PATH , so you can run: bxAgents new my-agent --model=openai/gpt-5 instead of the longer form: boxlang module:bxagents new my-agent --model=openai/gpt-5 Both are equivalent - every verb dispatches through the same ModuleConfig.bx main(args) entry point either way. This doc uses the short bxAgents <verb> form throughout. What is bundled The module zip carries its own dependencies, pinned to the stable releases it was built with. A bug fix in one of them ships as a BxAgents patch release, so nobody installs or updates them by hand. Where What Used for modules/ (nested BoxLang modules) bx-ai 3.8.0-snapshot, bx-sqlite 1.3.0, bx-ftp 1.9.0, bx-mail 1.4.15, bx-yaml 1.1.0, bx-markdown 1.1.0 The agent runtime, the web UI's SQLite store, the ftp / sftp deploy targets, the email gateway, Agent.yml , the HTML of an exported conversation lib/ (ColdBox runtime) ColdBox, qb , cbsecurity , cbauth , cbmailservices Copied into every app build generates serve points the served app at the same bundled modules. The versions above are the ones pinned in the repository's gradle.properties for this release. Adding your own libraries Put extra ColdBox libraries in a lib/ folder in your project, using the same layout as the bundled one: my-agent/ lib/ coldbox/ # replaces the bundled ColdBox modules/ cbvalidation/ # added next to the bundled modules qb/ # replaces the bundled qb build copies the bundled set first and your lib/ second, so yours wins. Tab completion The module ships tab completion for bxAgents (and bxagents ) in three shells. It completes verbs, flags, the --template and --target values, and project folders. Shell Setup bash, zsh Automatic. install-bx-module copies completions/bxAgents.bash to ~/.boxlang/completions/ and BVM sources it in new sessions. Without the installer: source <module folder>/completions/bxAgents.bash . fish cp <module folder>/completions/bxAgents.fish ~/.config/fish/completions/ PowerShell Add . "<module folder>\completions\bxAgents.ps1" to your $PROFILE . The scripts in completions/ are generated from the CLI's own verb tables, so they cannot drift from the verbs. After changing a verb or a flag in ModuleConfig.bx , regenerate them with tools/generate-completions.bxs (add --check to only verify); the spec suite fails if they are stale. See Quick Start to scaffold your first agent.

# Installation

BxAgents is a BoxLang module. It needs two things on the machine that runs it:

1. A [BoxLang](https://www.boxlang.io) runtime.
2. BxAgents itself. It bundles everything else it needs: `bx-ai`, `bx-sqlite`, `bx-ftp`, `bx-mail`, `bx-yaml` and `bx-markdown` as nested BoxLang modules, plus ColdBox, `qb`, `cbsecurity`, `cbauth` and `cbmailservices` for the apps it generates. There is nothing else to install.

> **Info**
>
> BxAgents needs BoxLang **1.18.0 or later**, which supports the nested modules it bundles.
> **Info**
>
> `serve`, `chat --server` and `invoke --server` additionally need the standalone [`boxlang-miniserver`](https://boxlang.ortusbooks.com/getting-started/running-boxlang/miniserver) binary on `PATH`. Every other verb (`build`, plain `chat` and `invoke`, `package`, `inspect`, `clean`, `new`, ...) doesn't.
> **Info**
>
> To run `bxAgents test` the project needs TestBox in `lib/testbox`. `new` fetches it by running `box install`, which needs [CommandBox](https://commandbox.ortusbooks.com) (the `box` command) on `PATH`. Without it the project is still created, `new` prints a warning with the command to run later, and `--skipInstall` leaves the step out. Nothing else in BxAgents needs CommandBox.

1

Install BoxLang

Follow the [official BoxLang installation guide](https://boxlang.ortusbooks.com/getting-started/installation). The quick installer also sets up `~/.boxlang/bin` on your `PATH`, which is where module-provided executables (like BxAgents' own `bxAgents` command, below) land.

2

Install BxAgents

```bash
install-bx-module bx-agents
```

This fetches the module, with its bundled dependencies, into your BoxLang modules directory (`~/.boxlang/modules` by default, or `boxlang_modules/` with `--local`).

3

Verify it worked

```bash
bxAgents --version
bxAgents --help
```

`--help` lists all 29 verbs (`new`, `add`, `build`, `test`, `serve`, `chat`, `invoke`, `package`, `deploy`, `inspect`, `clean`, `hash-password`, `token`, `users`, `notes`, `vault`, `connect`, `connectors`, `sessions`, `routines`, `stats`, `models`, `doctor`, `skills`, `extensions`, `data`, `logs`, `backup`, `restore`) with a one-line summary of each.

## The `bxAgents` command

BxAgents declares a native executable in its `box.json`:

```json
"boxlang": { "moduleName": "bxagents", "executable": "bxAgents" }
```

The installer turns that into a `bxAgents` wrapper script on your `PATH`, so you can run:

```bash
bxAgents new my-agent --model=openai/gpt-5
```

instead of the longer form:

```bash
boxlang module:bxagents new my-agent --model=openai/gpt-5
```

Both are equivalent - every verb dispatches through the same `ModuleConfig.bx main(args)` entry point either way. This doc uses the short `bxAgents <verb>` form throughout.

## What is bundled

The module zip carries its own dependencies, pinned to the stable releases it was built with. A bug fix in one of them ships as a BxAgents patch release, so nobody installs or updates them by hand.

|                Where                |                                                       What                                                        |                                                                      Used for                                                                       |
|-------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `modules/` (nested BoxLang modules) | `bx-ai` 3.8.0-snapshot, `bx-sqlite` 1.3.0, `bx-ftp` 1.9.0, `bx-mail` 1.4.15, `bx-yaml` 1.1.0, `bx-markdown` 1.1.0 | The agent runtime, the web UI's SQLite store, the `ftp`/`sftp` deploy targets, the email gateway, `Agent.yml`, the HTML of an exported conversation |
| `lib/` (ColdBox runtime)            | ColdBox, `qb`, `cbsecurity`, `cbauth`, `cbmailservices`                                                           | Copied into every app `build` generates                                                                                                             |

`serve` points the served app at the same bundled modules. The versions above are the ones pinned in the repository's `gradle.properties` for this release.

### Adding your own libraries

Put extra ColdBox libraries in a `lib/` folder in your project, using the same layout as the bundled one:

```text
my-agent/
  lib/
    coldbox/          # replaces the bundled ColdBox
    modules/
      cbvalidation/   # added next to the bundled modules
      qb/             # replaces the bundled qb
```

`build` copies the bundled set first and your `lib/` second, so yours wins.

## Tab completion

The module ships tab completion for `bxAgents` (and `bxagents`) in three shells. It completes verbs, flags, the `--template` and `--target` values, and project folders.

|   Shell    |                                                                                                     Setup                                                                                                     |
|------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| bash, zsh  | Automatic. `install-bx-module` copies `completions/bxAgents.bash` to `~/.boxlang/completions/` and BVM sources it in new sessions. Without the installer: `source <module folder>/completions/bxAgents.bash`. |
| fish       | `cp <module folder>/completions/bxAgents.fish ~/.config/fish/completions/`                                                                                                                                    |
| PowerShell | Add `. "<module folder>\completions\bxAgents.ps1"` to your `$PROFILE`.                                                                                                                                        |

The scripts in `completions/` are generated from the CLI's own verb tables, so they cannot drift from the verbs. After changing a verb or a flag in `ModuleConfig.bx`, regenerate them with `tools/generate-completions.bxs` (add `--check` to only verify); the spec suite fails if they are stale.

See [Quick Start](/next/getting-started/quick-start/index.html) to scaffold your first agent.

# Installing BxAgents

BxAgents is a BoxLang module. It needs two things on the machine that runs it:

1. A [BoxLang](https://www.boxlang.io) runtime.
2. BxAgents itself, which bundles everything else it needs (`bx-ai`, `bx-sqlite`, `bx-ftp`, `bx-mail`, `bx-yaml`, `bx-markdown`, and ColdBox with its modules for the apps it generates). BoxLang **1.18.0 or later** is required.

1

Install BoxLang

Follow the [official BoxLang installation guide](https://boxlang.ortusbooks.com/getting-started/installation).
The quick installer also sets up `~/.boxlang/bin` on your `PATH`, which is where
module-provided executables (like BxAgents' own `bxAgents` command) land.

2

Install BxAgents

```bash
install-bx-module bx-agents
```

This fetches the module, with its bundled dependencies, into your BoxLang modules directory (`~/.boxlang/modules`
by default, or `boxlang_modules/` with `--local`).

3

Verify it worked

```bash
bxAgents --version
bxAgents --help
```

`--help` lists all 29 verbs (`new`, `add`, `build`, `test`, `serve`, `chat`, `invoke`, `package`, `deploy`, `inspect`, `clean`, `hash-password`, `token`, `users`, `notes`, `vault`, `connect`, `connectors`, `sessions`, `routines`, `stats`, `models`, `doctor`, `skills`, `extensions`, `data`, `logs`, `backup`, `restore`) with a one-line summary of each. You'll use most of them in this course.

Check the command is there:

```bash
bxAgents --version
```

```text
bxAgents v<anything>
```

## The `bxAgents` command

BxAgents declares a native executable in its `box.json`:

```json
"boxlang": { "moduleName": "bxagents", "executable": "bxAgents" }
```

The installer turns that into a `bxAgents` wrapper script on your `PATH`. `bxAgents new my-agent --model=openai/gpt-5` is shorthand for the longer, always-equivalent form:

```bash
boxlang module:bxagents new my-agent --model=openai/gpt-5
```

This course uses the short `bxAgents <verb>` form throughout.

## Optional, for later lessons

* **`serve`** , **`chat --server`** and **`invoke --server`** ([Talking to Your Agent](/next/course/08-talking-to-your-agent/index.html)) additionally need the standalone [`boxlang-miniserver`](https://boxlang.ortusbooks.com/getting-started/running-boxlang/miniserver) binary on `PATH`.

None of them is required to follow along with `build`, plain `chat`, `test`, `package`,
`inspect`, `clean`, `new` or `doctor`. After installing, `bxAgents doctor` inside a project
checks the BoxLang version, whether `bx-ai` is loaded, whether the project validates and
which environment variables it needs are not set.

## Two things to know before you start

* **Flag values do not contain spaces.** BoxLang 1.19.0's launcher splits every quoted argument at its spaces, so `--message="Where is my order"` does not arrive as one value. The course writes `--message=refund` and types sentences into the chat instead. See [Quoting flag values](/next/cli-reference/index.html#quoting-flag-values).
* **What an agent remembers lives outside the project.** Conversations, notes, tokens, the vault, logs and backups are kept in the agent's *data home* , `~/.bxagents/<agent name>/` (the environment variable `BXAGENTS_HOME` moves it). It is created the first time it is needed, and [Logs, Usage and Backups](/next/course/operating-it/index.html) is about looking after it.

See [Installation](/next/getting-started/installation/index.html) for the full reference page.

Next: [A Model That Needs No Key](/next/course/practice-model/index.html)

# instructions.md and the System Prompt

`instructions.md` is **optional** - `bxAgents new` scaffolds a starter one for you to
edit, but you have two equally valid choices for where your agent's system prompt
lives:

1. Set `instructions` inline in `Agent.yml`.
2. Drop an `instructions.md` file beside `Agent.yml` and let the build wire it in.

## Letting the file win

If `instructions.md` exists, the build emits:

```javascript
withInstructions( fileRead( "instructions.md" ) )
```

which wins over an inline `instructions` in `Agent.yml` (or whatever a class set).
This is the more common pattern in
practice - it keeps the prompt as plain text you can edit without touching BoxLang
code, and it's easy to diff in a pull request.

```markdown
# instructions.md
You are a helpful assistant for a small hardware store. Be concise. If a customer
asks about a product you don't have information on, say so rather than guessing.
```

## Setting it inline instead

```yaml
name: my-agent
model: openai/gpt-5
instructions: |
  You are a helpful assistant.
  Keep answers short.
```

Do this for a short prompt, or when you'd rather keep everything about the agent in one
file. If both exist, `instructions.md` wins; if neither exists, the build fails and says
so. A prompt that must be generated or templated in code belongs in the advanced
class-based `Agent.bx` (see the end of [The Agent Definition - Agent.yml](/next/course/05-agent-bx/index.html)).

## Which one should you pick?

Start with `instructions.md` - it's what `bxAgents new` scaffolds, it's the simplest
mental model ("the system prompt is this file"), and it plays nicely with the rest of
this course, which assumes plain-text prompts throughout. Reach for the inline
`instructions` key only for a short prompt, and for code only once you have a concrete
reason to (templating, environment-specific prompts assembled from smaller pieces,
etc.).

## Try it

Write the persona of Acme support. This replaces the starter file:

```markdown
You are Acme's support agent. Answer questions about orders, returns and shipping.
Be brief and friendly. If you do not know something, say so rather than guessing.
```

How do you know the model really received it? The scripted model has a rule that answers with the system message
it was sent, which is the whole of its instructions. Build, then ask for it (the word the rule listens for is
`system`):

```bash
cd ~/bxagents-course/acme-support
bxAgents build
bxAgents invoke --message=system
```

```text
Build succeeded: <anything>/acme-support/.build/app
My instructions are:

Role: Answers questions about orders, returns and shipping for Acme.

Instructions: You are Acme's support agent. Answer questions about orders, returns and shipping.
Be brief and friendly. If you do not know something, say so rather than guessing.
...
```

Your text comes first. What follows it, a list of skills the agent can load, is added by BxAgents (the
[skills lesson](/next/course/10-packaging-skills/index.html) is about those). A real model would not echo its prompt, but with a real
one you can ask the same thing: `What are your instructions?`.

## Checkpoint

`instructions.md` holds the persona above. `kit/resume.sh 06-instructions-and-system-prompt` restores it.

Next: [Building Your Agent](/next/course/07-building-your-agent/index.html)

# Interceptors and Module Dependencies

Three smaller, independent conventions round out the picture: lifecycle hooks into the
generated ColdBox app, extensions for the chat and the served agent, and declared BoxLang
module dependencies.

## `interceptors/` - ColdBox lifecycle hooks

`interceptors/*.bx` are ColdBox interceptors (`preProcess`, `postProcess`, and other
lifecycle hook points), scoped via an `@scope` annotation on the class itself:

```javascript
// interceptors/AuditLogger.bx
/**
 * @scope agent
 */
class {

	function preProcess( event, interceptData ) {
		// ...
	}

}
```

|       Scope       |                                                                            Effect                                                                            |
|-------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `agent` (default) | Copied into the generated app's own `interceptors/` folder - affects only this app.                                                                          |
| `runtime`         | Copied to `.build/runtime-interceptors`, outside the app, for the whole BoxLang runtime rather than just this app. BxAgents does not register these for you. |

An interceptor with no `@scope` at all defaults to `agent` - the narrower, safer
choice, since `runtime` scope has effects beyond one app. An `@scope` value that isn't
`agent` or `runtime` fails the build with a clear error.

You've already seen a **generated** interceptor without writing one yourself - when you list
`users` on the web chat ([The Web App](/next/course/15-the-generated-web-chat-ui/index.html)), its sign-in gate is
registered exactly this way, just written by BxAgents instead of by you.

## `extensions/` - add to the chat and the served agent

An interceptor reacts to the ColdBox request. An **extension** adds to BxAgents itself, without
changing it. One `.bx` file is a whole extension: it reads like a ColdBox `ModuleConfig` (a
`configure()`, an `onLoad()`), and annotated methods become chat commands.

```javascript
// extensions/hello.bx
class {

	@Command( "hello" )
	@Hint( "say hello: /hello <name>" )
	function greet( agentContext, commandArguments ) {
		return agentContext.reply().ok( "Hello, #commandArguments#!" )
	}

}
```

Run `bxAgents chat` and type `/hello Ada`; `/extensions` lists what loaded. The same command runs
in the web page and, if allowed, on chat platforms. A folder with an `Extension.bx` can bring more:
keys (`@Key`), status items (`@Status`), `@` sources and message prefixes for the terminal, web
page slots and the styles and scripts of a `web/` folder, listeners for chat and bx-ai events, schedulers, tools, skills, a new gateway type or
a `bxAgents` verb. Values for an extension go under `extensions:` in `Agent.yml`.

Start one with `bxAgents add extension standup`, which asks what to bring and writes working
stubs. Install someone else's with `bxAgents extensions install <folder, zip, owner/repo, address or ForgeBox slug>`: it shows what the extension adds and asks first, and records it in
`extensions.lock.json`, which you commit. `bxAgents extensions link <folder>` links one you are
working on, and `/reload` picks up your edits. See the [`extensions/`](/next/conventions/extensions/index.html)
reference and the guide [Your first extension](/next/guides/first-extension/index.html).

## `modules/` - BoxLang module dependencies

`modules/` holds BoxLang module dependencies your agent declares - one immediate
subfolder per module, discovered by folder name (not recursive):

```text
modules/
└── my-extra-module/
    ├── module.json
    └── ...
```

A module folder may include a `module.json` with a `dependsOn` array naming other
`modules/*` entries by folder name:

```json
{
	"dependsOn": [ "some-other-module" ]
}
```

This is BxAgents' own dependency-declaration convention for validation purposes - it's
independent of BoxLang's own module-loading mechanism, and today `build` validates and
records these folders in the manifest without loading them into the generated app. **Circular dependencies** are
rejected the same way subagent cycles are (see [Composing Subagents](/next/course/11-composing-subagents/index.html)):
full cycle path reported, no code generation until the graph is acyclic. A
`module.json` is entirely optional - a module folder with none is assumed to have no
declared dependencies.

## Try it

Two small additions to Acme support. First an interceptor that writes a log line for every request. It is `agent`
scope (the default) and says so:

```javascript
/**
 * @scope agent
 */
class {

	function preProcess( event, interceptData ) {
		writeLog( text = "Acme request", type = "information" )
	}

}
```

Second an extension that adds a chat command, `/hello`. One file is a whole extension (the guide
[Your first extension](/next/guides/first-extension/index.html) goes on from here, and `bxAgents add extension standup` writes a
richer frame):

```javascript
class {

	@Command( "hello" )
	@Hint( "say hello: /hello <name>" )
	function greet( agentContext, commandArguments ) {
		return agentContext.reply().ok( "Hello, #commandArguments#!" )
	}

}
```

Build, check that the interceptor was copied into the app, and that the extension loads:

```bash
cd ~/bxagents-course/acme-support
bxAgents build
ls .build/app/interceptors
bxAgents extensions list
```

```text
Build succeeded: <anything>/acme-support/.build/app
RequestLogger.bx
WebUiLoginGate.bx
hello (project, loaded)
    commands:   /hello
```

`WebUiLoginGate.bx` is the interceptor BxAgents wrote itself for the accounts you declared in
[Who Is Allowed](/next/course/users-roles-and-tokens/index.html): the same mechanism, generated instead of written by you.

Now open the terminal chat and type `/hello Ada`: the answer is `Hello, Ada!`, written by your extension, and `/extensions`
lists it. The same command runs in the web app's chat. It never reached the model.

```bash
bxAgents chat
```

## Checkpoint

`acme-support/` has `interceptors/RequestLogger.bx` and `extensions/hello.bx`. `kit/resume.sh 18-interceptors-and-modules`
restores them; rebuild after.

Full reference: [interceptors/](/next/conventions/interceptors/index.html), [extensions/](/next/conventions/extensions/index.html) and
[modules/](/next/conventions/modules/index.html).

Next: [Testing Your Agent](/next/course/19-testing-your-agent/index.html)

title: interceptors/
body: interceptors/ interceptors/*.bx are ColdBox interceptors (lifecycle hook classes - preProcess , postProcess , etc.), scoped via an @scope annotation on the class itself: // interceptors/AuditLogger.bx /** * @scope agent */ class { function preProcess( event, interceptData ) { // ... } } Tip bxAgents add interceptor scaffolds one: pick the scope and the interception points and it writes interceptors/<Name>.bx with a method for each. See add . agent vs runtime scope Scope Effect agent (default) Copied into the generated app's own interceptors/ folder and registered with ColdBox when the app starts - affects only this app. runtime Copied separately to .build/runtime-interceptors (not into the generated app), for the way a BoxLang module registers its own interceptors. BxAgents does not register them for you: loading them is up to you. An interceptor with no @scope annotation at all defaults to agent - the narrower, safer default, since runtime scope has effects beyond this one app. An @scope value that isn't agent or runtime (case-insensitive) fails the build with a clear error - there's no silent fallback for a typo'd scope. Generated wiring For each agent -scope interceptor, the generated base class ( bxagents/Application.bx ) registers an instance with ColdBox's interceptor service from after() , once ColdBox has loaded: application.cbController.getInterceptorService().register( target: application.cbController.getWireBox().getInstance( "app.interceptors.AuditLogger" ), name: "AuditLogger" ) Every agent-scope interceptor is registered exactly once. The generated config/Coldbox.bx has no interceptors array: the registration happens at startup instead. (A declarative array was once measured not to reach ColdBox's interceptor service, but against a config file ColdBox was not loading; that was not measured again, and the registration at startup works.)

> **Tip**
>
> `bxAgents add interceptor` scaffolds one: pick the scope and the interception points and it writes `interceptors/<Name>.bx` with a method for each. See [`add`](/next/cli-reference/index.html#add-interceptor).

## `agent` vs `runtime` scope

|       Scope       |                                                                                                      Effect                                                                                                       |
|-------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `agent` (default) | Copied into the generated app's own `interceptors/` folder and registered with ColdBox when the app starts - affects only this app.                                                                               |
| `runtime`         | Copied separately to `.build/runtime-interceptors` (not into the generated app), for the way a BoxLang module registers its own interceptors. BxAgents does not register them for you: loading them is up to you. |

An interceptor with **no** `@scope` annotation at all defaults to `agent` - the narrower, safer default, since `runtime` scope has effects beyond this one app.

An `@scope` value that isn't `agent` or `runtime` (case-insensitive) fails the build with a clear error - there's no silent fallback for a typo'd scope.

## Generated wiring

For each `agent`-scope interceptor, the generated base class ([`bxagents/Application.bx`](/next/conventions/application-bx/index.html)) registers an instance with ColdBox's interceptor service from `after()`, once ColdBox has loaded:

```javascript
application.cbController.getInterceptorService().register(
	target: application.cbController.getWireBox().getInstance( "app.interceptors.AuditLogger" ),
	name: "AuditLogger"
)
```

Every agent-scope interceptor is registered exactly once. The generated `config/Coldbox.bx` has no `interceptors` array: the registration happens at startup instead. (A declarative array was once measured not to reach ColdBox's interceptor service, but against a config file ColdBox was not loading; that was not measured again, and the registration at startup works.)

# Layered settings

Someone ships a ready-made agent. The person who installs it can override and add to its settings without touching the author's files. All three files are called `Agent.yml`:

```text
<project>/Agent.yml             the author's file
~/.bxagents/Agent.yml           the person's file, for every agent
~/.bxagents/<agent>/Agent.yml   the person's file, for one agent on this machine
```

`<agent>` is the agent's [data home](/next/conventions/data/index.html#the-data-home), which is `~/.bxagents/<name>` unless `data.home` or `BXAGENTS_HOME` says otherwise. `BXAGENTS_USER_CONFIG` names another file in place of the one for every agent (for tests).

```yaml
# ~/.bxagents/Agent.yml
model: ollama/qwen3              # replaces the author's model
tools+: [ "*@bxplaywright" ]     # adds to the author's tools
mcpServers+: [ https://mcp.example.com ]
volumes:
  notes: { path: ~/Notes, mode: rw }
instructions+: |
  Always answer in French.
```

## Precedence

First match wins:

1. the flag of one run
2. `~/.bxagents/<agent>/Agent.yml`
3. `~/.bxagents/Agent.yml`
4. the project: `environments.<env>`, `boxlang.json` and `miniserver.json`, then `Agent.yml`
5. the default

The person's files win over the author's `environments:` block too. The person who runs the agent has the last word.

## When it applies

Both, with one merge (`SettingsLayers`):

* **Build.** `bxAgents build` reads the person's files, merges, and generates from the result. This covers an agent shipped as a project folder that the person builds themselves. The build prints each setting that came from a person's file, with the file.
* **Start.** A built app (a zip or a container, no source on the machine) reads the person's two files as they are *when it starts* and merges them over the author's settings, which the build saved in `config/agent-settings.json`.

At start the files are merged over the *author's* settings, never over what the build baked. A `tools+:` that the build already applied would otherwise be applied twice. The result is the same when the files are unchanged, and the files on the machine decide when they are not.
> **Warning**
>
> A build bakes the files of the machine it runs on. If you ship an agent, build it on a machine without your own `~/.bxagents/Agent.yml`, or look at the lines the build prints.

## Merge rules

|     Written as      |                                                          Result                                                          |
|---------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| a mapping           | merges key by key with the layer below                                                                                   |
| a plain value       | replaces                                                                                                                 |
| a list              | replaces                                                                                                                 |
| `key+:` with a list | appends to the list below                                                                                                |
| `key+:` with text   | appends to the text below, after a blank line (for `instructions`)                                                       |
| `key-:` with a list | removes those entries from the list below. A mapping entry, such as an MCP server, matches by its `name`, else its `url` |
| `key: ~`            | removes the key                                                                                                          |

Inside one file a key is applied in this order: the plain value, then `key-:`, then `key+:`. The markers work at any depth of a mapping. `+:` on a mapping is an error, and so is a marker with nothing after it. A `key-:` on a key nobody set does nothing.

## What a person's file may say

Everything except `name`, `data.home` and `environments`. `data.home` decides where the agent's own file lives, `name` decides which one that is, and `environments` is the author's way to vary a build.

`chat:` is valid only in the person's files, never in a project, so a project can never switch those on for a person. `extensions:` values layer the same way, and the person's win.

Unchanged: an unknown key is an error and the message lists the valid ones. Secrets stay as ``${env.X}` or `${vault.X}`` placeholders, never in the files. A bad value names the file, and a built app that finds a bad file at start refuses to start and names it.

## What a built app can change when it starts

Read from the generators and checked by running a built app with the mock provider.

|                                                                                               Key                                                                                                |                                                                                          At start                                                                                           |
|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `model`, `profile`, `provider`, `params`, `options`, `providers`, `profiles`, `defaultProfile`, `contextWindow`, `vision`, `embeddings`, `speech`, `transcription`, `image`, `security`, `usage` | yes. The settings bx-ai reads are merged into its live settings, and the root agent's model is built from the result                                                                        |
| `instructions`, `description`                                                                                                                                                                    | yes. An `instructions.md` beside the agent is the author's `instructions`, so a person's `instructions:` replaces it and `instructions+:` adds to it                                        |
| `tools`, `toolOptions`, `volumes`, `mcpServers`                                                                                                                                                  | yes. A tool must come from a module the machine has: the app fails at start and names it                                                                                                    |
| `memory`, `checkpointer`, `notes`, `vault`, `skills`, `connectors`                                                                                                                               | yes                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| `extensions` values and `disable`                                                                                                                                                                | yes, in the chat and for the root agent's tools. The person's values win over the project's                                                                                                 |
| `tui`, `chat`                                                                                                                                                                                    | yes, in the chat                                                                                                                                                                            |
| `agentApi`, `gatewaySession`, `routines`, `subAgents`, `data`                                                                                                                                    | **no.** They are generated into the app (routes, gateways, schedulers, the agent tree). The app says so at start, with the file, in the `bxagents-settings` log, and `/info` marks the line |
| `name`, `data.home`, `environments`                                                                                                                                                              | not overridable                                                                                                                                                                             |

Only the root agent reads its person's files. A subagent keeps what the build baked, except for the `volumes` its file tools get, which follow the root's.

A scheduler in `schedules/*.bx` is code, not a setting, so a person's file cannot add one.

A class-based `Agent.bx` is code too. For it the settings bx-ai reads apply at start, but the agent itself is the class, so its own model, tools and the rest are not rebuilt from a person's file.

Removing a setting with `key: ~` takes it out of what the root agent is built from. bx-ai's own live settings only gain values at start, so a baked provider stays the default underneath.

## Seeing and changing it

* **`/info`** lists each setting that came from a person's file, one line each with the file, and marks the ones that need a rebuild. A file for every agent can widen every agent, so nothing is silent.
* **`/settings model ollama/qwen3`** writes any setting of the `Agent.yml` to the agent's own file, and **`--global`** writes it to the file for every agent. `/settings tools+ [ now@bxai ]` adds to the list, and `/settings tools+ reset` takes that entry out of the file. A name that is one of the chat's own settings (`header`, `theme`, `tools` ...) still changes the chat. To write an `Agent.yml` setting that shares such a name, use a marker (`tools+`) or a block (`params.temperature`). It edits only its own lines and keeps the rest of the file, comments included, and puts the file back when the result would not be valid. It applies the next time the agent starts.

## API shape

```text
SettingsLayers( globalFile = "", agentFile = "", flags = {} )
  .load()                   reads and checks the person's files, throws a message naming the file
  .merged( base, baseFile ) the base with the person's layers and the flags applied, rules above
  .files()                  [ { layer, file } ] the person's files that exist
  .provenance()             { "dotted.path": { op, layer, file, value } } for the last merge
  .fromPerson()             the provenance entries that came from a person's file, sorted by path
  .buildOnly()              the ones the built app can not apply at start

RuntimeSettings.start( file )   what a built app calls: merges, applies, logs, returns { config, changed, needsRebuild }
SettingsFileEditor.set / reset  what /settings calls
```

A mapping that nothing below had is one setting, so its path is where the file started writing (`agentApi`). Inside a mapping that exists, each leaf has its own path (`tui.header`).

What a built app can change when it starts

# Logs

An agent writes what it does, and what goes wrong, to log files in the `logs/` folder of its [data home](/next/conventions/data/index.html). There is one file per area, so a broken gateway is not buried in the noise of a busy API:

```text
<data home>/logs/
  agent.log       startup, errors in a turn, tool failures
  gateways.log    every gateway: connect, disconnect, send failures. The gateway's name starts each line
  routines.log    routines: created, changed, run, skipped, failed, delivered
  heartbeat.log   each tick of the routine scheduler that did something
  api.log         refused calls and sign-in failures
```

A file appears when its first line is written. `routines.log` and `heartbeat.log` are written by [routines](/next/conventions/routines/index.html).

A line looks like this:

```text
[2026-11-09T09:15:11,300] [main] [ERROR] [GATEWAYS] [my-agent] [telegram] Could not start: Telegram rejected the configured bot token: Unauthorized
```

![The Logs page: a tab for each log, a level filter and a search box](/next/assets/webui/webui-logs.png)

## Error diagnostics

Local chat errors, `invoke`, `/ping` and `models test` include the exception type and detail, any available cause and source location, and the provider endpoint when available. Model probes capture the endpoint from bx-ai's actual request, not the configured URL, so an ignored setting is visible. Turn and probe failures also write these diagnostics to `agent.log`; remote responses keep their shorter message rather than exposing server paths and endpoints. Diagnostics are bounded and redact known credential patterns, URL userinfo and URL query values; requests and headers are not dumped.

## What is never written

A log is for finding out what happened, not for keeping what was said.

* No message from a person, and no token, password or key. Callers do not pass them, and every line is cleaned all the same: bearer tokens, Telegram, Slack, GitHub and OpenAI style tokens, and the value after a name such as `password`, `secret`, `api_key` or `access_token` are replaced by `***`.
* Writing a log never stops the work it describes. A log that cannot be written is skipped.

## Rotation

The logs are written with BoxLang's own logging, so BoxLang rolls and removes them by its own rules: by default a file rolls at 100 MB, files are kept for 90 days and all logs together are capped at 5 GB. Change that with the `logging` settings of the BoxLang runtime (`maxFileSize`, `maxLogDays`, `totalCapSize` in `boxlang.json`). BX Agents adds no settings of its own for it.

`backup` does not include the logs.

## Reading them

**In the terminal:**

```bash
bxAgents logs                                     # which logs there are and how big
bxAgents logs gateways                            # the last 100 lines of the gateways log
bxAgents logs gateways --tail=500 --level=warn --grep=telegram
bxAgents logs api --json
bxAgents logs gateways --follow --level=warn         # the last lines, then each new one as it is written
bxAgents logs --ui                                # a full-screen viewer: a tab per log, level, search, live lines
bxAgents logs gateways --follow --connect=https://agent.example.com --token=$ADMIN_TOKEN   # a deployed agent
```

`--level` shows that level and anything more serious (`debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error`), `--grep` keeps the lines that contain the text (case does not matter), and `--tail` is how many lines, up to 1000. Only the end of a log is read, so a big log is as quick as a small one.

`--follow` keeps printing new lines until Ctrl+C, and `--ui` opens a viewer with a tab per log, the level (`l`), a search (`/`), scrolling and live lines (keys in the [CLI reference](/next/cli-reference/index.html#logs)). `--connect=URL` reads a served agent's logs over its API with an admin token. In the terminal chat, `/logs` and `/logs <area>` print them too.

**In the web page** , for an admin, the menu has a **Logs** page and a **Gateways** page (see [the web UI](/next/conventions/web-ui/index.html#logs-and-gateways)). The Logs page has a tab for each log, with a red chip when it logged errors since the app started, a level filter, a search, a line count and a **Live** switch: with it on, new lines show as they are written (over `GET /logs/stream`). The tab and the search are in the address, `<path>/logs/gateways?q=telegram`, and **Open log** on the Gateways page links there.

**Over the API** , for an admin: `GET /logs` lists the logs and how many sources logged an error since the app started, and `GET /logs?area=gateways&tail=200&level=warn&q=text` gives lines. `GET /logs/stream?area=gateways&level=warn&q=text` follows one live: an event stream of `lines` frames (`{ area, lines }`, only lines written after it opened) and a `reset` frame when the file was rotated; the server looks at the file every second and ends the stream after ten minutes. The client has `logs()` and `logsStream( area, onEvent, level, q )`. See [the agent API](/next/conventions/agent-bx/index.html).

## Gateways

`GET /gateways` (and **Gateways** in the web page) says, for each gateway the project names:

* whether it is **connected** , **stopped** , **failing** (stopped, with an error logged) or **not registered**;
* which of its credentials are set, by the name of the environment variable and set or not set, never the value;
* when it last had a conversation, and its last error.

The gateways themselves are still set up in `gateways/<name>.bx` and `.env`, and read when the app starts. See [gateways](/next/conventions/gateways/index.html).
