markdown:
# Logs, Usage and Backups

An agent that someone else depends on raises three questions. *What is it doing?* *What does it cost?* *If the disk
dies, what do I lose?* BxAgents answers them from one place, the agent's **data home**, with a command for each.
> **What you will do**
>
> Read the usage the model calls left, look at what the data home holds and at the logs, then back it up, lose a
> note on purpose and restore it. About 20 minutes.

## The data home

Everything an agent *keeps* lives outside the project, in `~/.bxagents/<agent name>/` (set `BXAGENTS_HOME`, or `data.home`
in `Agent.yml`, to put it elsewhere). The project is what you ship; the data home is what accumulated while it ran.
`bxAgents data` shows where it is and how big each part is:

```bash
cd ~/bxagents-course/acme-support
bxAgents data
```

```text
Data home: <anything>/.bxagents/acme-support  (the convention, ~/.bxagents/<agent name>)
Database:  <anything>/chat.db

  chat.db<anything>
  files/<anything>
  skills/<anything>
  routines/<anything>
  logs/<anything>
  backups/<anything>

Volumes:
  files<anything>read and write<anything>
```

|    Part     |                                             Holds                                              |
|-------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `chat.db`   | Conversations, notes, access tokens, accounts, routines, the sealed vault and the usage record |
| `files/`    | What the agent writes with its file tools (the `files` volume)                                 |
| `skills/`   | Skills the agent saved for itself                                                              |
| `routines/` | The reports of every routine                                                                   |
| `logs/`     | The logs below (not part of a backup)                                                          |
| `backups/`  | The backups you make                                                                           |

Volumes, the folders of your machine you let the agent use, are named in `Agent.yml` and are *not* in the data home or in a
backup.

## What is it doing: logs

An agent writes what it does, and what goes wrong, to one log per area: `agent`, `gateways`, `routines`, `heartbeat`
and `api`. Without an area `logs` lists them; with one it prints the last lines:

```bash
bxAgents logs
bxAgents logs routines --tail=3
```

```text
...
```

(What you see depends on what has run: a log file appears when its first line is written.) `--level=warn` and
`--grep=text` filter, `--follow` keeps printing new lines, and `--ui` opens a viewer with a tab per log. An admin sees the
same in the web app on the **Logs** page, with a **Live** switch, and over the API with `--connect=<url> --token=<admin token>`. **A log never holds what a person said, nor a token, password or key** (they are replaced by `***`), and a log
that cannot be written never stops the work it describes.

![The Logs page: a tab for each log, a level filter and a search box](/next/assets/webui/webui-logs.png)

## What does it cost: usage

Set `usage: true` and each model call leaves a row of counts: the time, who asked, the provider, the model and the
tokens in and out. You did that in [The Agent Definition](/next/course/05-agent-bx/index.html), so there is already a record:

Make one more call, so there is something to count, and read the record:

```bash
bxAgents invoke --message=hello > /dev/null
bxAgents stats
```

```text
Last 30 days: <anything> call<anything>, <anything> tokens (<anything> in, <anything> out)

By model<anything>calls<anything>in<anything>out<anything>total
...
Counts only the calls whose provider reported usage.
```

The scripted model reports one token in and one out for every call, so these numbers are small and the same every
time, but the command is the one you would use with a real provider. `--by=provider|day|user` regroups, `--days=7`
narrows, `--user=bo` shows one person's. Only counts are kept, never what was said, and cost in money is not worked out,
because prices change too often to ship a table. The same numbers are on the **Agent** page of the web app (the Usage
tab) and in the chat as `/stats`.

![The Agent page, Usage tab: tokens by day and by model](/next/assets/webui/webui-agent-usage.png)

## Can I get it back: backup and restore

`backup` zips the database (copied whole, so it is safe while a server is running), `files/`, `skills/` and `routines/`.
It does not hold the logs, the volumes, or your **vault key** : keep `BXAGENTS_VAULT_KEY` somewhere safe on its own, because
a backup of sealed secrets is useless without the key.

Prove it works. Add two notes, back up, lose one, and restore:

```bash
bxAgents notes add --text=Prefers-short-answers
bxAgents notes add --text=Loses-this-note
bxAgents backup
```

```text
Noted (user).
Noted (user).
Backed up <anything> to <anything>/backups/backup-<anything>.zip
```

```bash
ID=$(bxAgents notes list --scope=user | grep Loses-this-note | awk '{print $1}')
bxAgents notes remove --id=$ID
bxAgents notes list --scope=user | grep -c Loses-this-note || true
```

```text
Removed.
0
```

Now put the backup back. `restore` stops when a server or a chat looks to have the database open, and SQLite leaves a
`-wal` file behind that looks like one, so when you are sure nothing is running, say so with `--force`. What was there is
kept for one restore as `chat.db.before-restore`:

```bash
BACKUP=$(ls -t ~/.bxagents/acme-support/backups/*.zip | head -1)
bxAgents restore $BACKUP --force
bxAgents notes list --scope=user | grep -c Loses-this-note
```

```text
Restored chat.db<anything> into <anything>
Kept what was there as chat.db.before-restore<anything>. The next restore replaces them.
1
```

The note is back. In the web app the **Data and backups** page (admins only) makes, downloads and schedules the
restore of a backup, and shows the volumes.

![The Data and backups page: where the agent keeps everything, the volumes, and the backups](/next/assets/webui/webui-data.png)

## When something is wrong: doctor

`bxAgents doctor` checks the BoxLang version, that `bx-ai` is loaded, that the project validates, which environment
variables it needs are not set, and that the data home can be written. Run it first, before you read logs.

```bash
bxAgents doctor
```

```text
[ OK ] BoxLang <anything>
...
0 problem(s), <anything>
```

(In this shell it warns that `ACME_ADA_PASSWORD` and `ACME_BO_PASSWORD` are not set: you exported them only for the
server's run in [Who Is Allowed](/next/course/users-roles-and-tokens/index.html). That is `doctor` doing its job, naming a variable the
project needs.)

## Checkpoint

Nothing in the project changed. In the data home there is a backup, and a note you lost and got back.
Nothing to restore with `kit/resume.sh`.

Full reference: [data and volumes](/next/conventions/data/index.html), [logs](/next/conventions/logs/index.html) and the
[CLI reference](/next/cli-reference/index.html#data-backup-and-restore) for `data`, `backup`, `restore`, `logs`, `stats` and `doctor`.

Next: [Interceptors and Module Dependencies](/next/course/18-interceptors-and-modules/index.html)
headings: Can I get it back: backup and restore

title: mcp/
body:
mcp/ MCP (Model Context Protocol) works two directions - consuming remote servers, and hosting your own. flowchart LR subgraph consume["CONSUMING - declared on Agent.yml via mcpServers"] direction LR AG["your agent"] -->|"calls out at runtime"| RM["a remote MCP server
https://example.com/mcp"] end subgraph host["HOSTING - one file per server under mcp/"] direction LR TL["tools/
your @AITool functions"] -->|"a named SUBSET"| MS["mcpServer( 'localServer' )
registered at onApplicationStart()"] MS --> GW["a gateways/ entry with exposes: mcp
route( '/mcp/tools' ).toMCP()"] GW -->|"reachable over HTTP"| OC["some outside MCP client"] end style consume fill:#e7f1ff,stroke:#004085 style host fill:#eaf6ec,stroke:#155724 Nothing links the two: an agent consuming remote servers need not host one, and a hosted server is reachable only if a gateways/ entry exposes it. Tip bxAgents add mcp client github adds a server to Agent.yml with its credential as an environment placeholder, and bxAgents add mcp server writes the mcp/ file and the gateways/ entry that serves it. See add . Consuming remote servers Declared directly on Agent.yml (not a file under mcp/ ), via mcpServers : # Agent.yml name: my-agent model: openai/gpt-5 mcpServers: - https://example.com/mcp - url: https://other.com/mcp name: other Each entry is either a bare URL string or a mapping. A mapping can carry the credentials the server wants: mcpServers: - name: github url: https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/ token: ${env.GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN} - url: https://other.com/mcp headers: X-Api-Key: ${env.OTHER_API_KEY} timeout: 20000 Key Meaning url Required. The server's address name A label for the file. It is not sent to the server token A bearer token. Must be an ${env.NAME} placeholder: a token written in the file is a build error password , user Basic authentication. password must be an ${env.NAME} placeholder headers Extra request headers. Values can use ${env.NAME} timeout Milliseconds oauth The server asks each person to sign in (mail, a calendar). oauth: true or a mapping. Needs a name . See connect allowedHosts The host names the server's address may have, for example [api.example.com, "*.example.com"] . *.example.com matches any subdomain, not example.com itself. A request to any other host is refused before anything is sent redirects false treats a redirect answer as a failure and never follows it maxResponseBytes Refuses an answer longer than this many characters handshake true sends the MCP initialize handshake before the first call prefix Tools are named prefix__tool , so two servers cannot clash toolFilter A list of tool names; only these are given to the agent Placeholders are replaced with the environment variable when the app starts , never at build time, so a secret stays out of the project and out of a packaged .bxa . A variable that is not set fails the agent at startup and names it; one that is set but empty lets the agent start, the server refuses the connection, and bx-ai logs that and carries on without that server's tools. Any other key is a build error that lists the valid ones. The entries are passed into the generated aiAgent(mcpServers: [...]) call. No network connection is ever attempted at build time - reachability is a runtime concern; an unreachable server at build time is not a build error. This section is for servers reached over the web; servers that run as a program on the agent's machine are next. bxAgents new offers GitHub, Stripe, Notion, Atlassian, Cloudflare, Supabase and Git and writes the entry and the .env stub for you. Subagents can declare their own mcpServers independently - each node in the agent tree gets its own resolved list. Servers that run as a program An entry with command starts an MCP server as a program on the machine that runs the agent, and talks to it over the program's standard input and output: mcpServers: - name: git command: [uvx, mcp-server-git] prefix: git toolFilter: [git_status, git_diff, git_log] - name: browser command: [bxplaywright, mcp] env: PLAYWRIGHT_API_KEY: ${env.PLAYWRIGHT_API_KEY} cwd: . Key Meaning command Required. A list: the program, then its arguments. It is never run through a shell name A label for the file env Environment variables for the program. A variable whose name contains KEY , TOKEN , SECRET , PASSWORD or CREDENTIAL must be an ${env.NAME} placeholder cwd The folder the program starts in inheritEnv false starts it with only env . Default true maxRestarts How many times in a row a program that died is started again. Default 2 timeout Milliseconds per request prefix , toolFilter As for web servers The program starts on the first call and is closed when the app stops. command cannot be combined with url , and the keys that only make sense for a web server ( token , headers , user , password , allowedHosts , redirects , maxResponseBytes , handshake ) are a build error on it. When the app starts, the programs your agents declare become bx-ai's mcp.stdio.allowedCommands setting, so the process starts only what the project declared. A list you set yourself (for example in .boxlang.json ) is left alone and must name the programs. bxAgents doctor warns when a program is not on the PATH. A program runs with your user's rights on the machine that hosts the agent. Read what you start, and use toolFilter to limit what the agent may call. Hosting a local server Each mcp/*.bx file is a local MCP server your project hosts, exposing a subset of your tools/ as MCP tools: // mcp/localServer.bx class { function configure() { return { description : "Internal tools MCP server", version : "1.0.0", cors : "*", // optional - CORS origin(s) allowed to call this server; omit for none tools : [ "sayHello" ] // names of tools already declared under tools/ }; } } The entry's discovered name is its filename ( localServer.bx → localServer ), not any name field inside its own configure() struct - a project may still set one for documentation, but it's ignored for naming/registration purposes. cors is optional and defaults to an empty string (no CORS header) when omitted - passed straight through as mcpServer() 's 4th positional argument. # mcp/ MCP (Model Context Protocol) works two directions - consuming remote servers, and hosting your own. ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph consume["CONSUMING - declared on Agent.yml via mcpServers"] direction LR AG["your agent"] -->|"calls out at runtime"| RM["a remote MCP server
https://example.com/mcp"] end subgraph host["HOSTING - one file per server under mcp/"] direction LR TL["tools/
your @AITool functions"] -->|"a named SUBSET"| MS["mcpServer( 'localServer' )
registered at onApplicationStart()"] MS --> GW["a gateways/ entry with exposes: mcp
route( '/mcp/tools' ).toMCP()"] GW -->|"reachable over HTTP"| OC["some outside MCP client"] end style consume fill:#e7f1ff,stroke:#004085 style host fill:#eaf6ec,stroke:#155724 ``` Nothing links the two: an agent consuming remote servers need not host one, and a hosted server is reachable only if a `gateways/` entry exposes it. > **Tip** > > `bxAgents add mcp client github` adds a server to `Agent.yml` with its credential as an environment placeholder, and `bxAgents add mcp server` writes the `mcp/` file and the `gateways/` entry that serves it. The server's address | | `name` | A label for the file. It is not sent to the server | | `token` | A bearer token. Must be an `${env.NAME}` placeholder: a token written in the file is a build error | | `password`, `user` | Basic authentication. `password` must be an `${env.NAME}` placeholder | | `headers` | Extra request headers. Values can use `${env.NAME}` | | `timeout` | Milliseconds | | `oauth` | The server asks each person to sign in (mail, a calendar). `oauth: true` or a mapping. Needs a `name`. # Models and profiles

Which model an agent uses is written in `Agent.yml`. The build maps it onto bx-ai's settings, so you never write a `boxlang.json` for it. The names are bx-ai's own: `provider`, `model`, `params`, `options`, `providers`, `profiles`.

```yaml
provider: openai                 # the default model
model: gpt-5
params: { temperature: 0.2 }

providers:                       # settings for another provider
  claude: { params: { max_tokens: 4000 }, options: { timeout: 90 } }

profiles:                        # named combinations
  fast:    { description: Cheap and quick, provider: openai, model: gpt-5-mini, params: { temperature: 0 } }
  planner: { description: Careful planning, provider: claude, model: claude-opus-4, apiKeyEnv: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }
defaultProfile: fast             # optional

embeddings:    { provider: openai, model: text-embedding-3-small }
speech:        { provider: openai, model: tts-1, voice: nova }
transcription: { provider: openai, model: whisper-1 }
image:         { provider: openai, model: gpt-image-1, size: 1024x1024 }
```

## The default model

`provider`, `model` and `params` are the model every agent uses when it says nothing else. `model: openai/gpt-5` still works as shorthand for `provider: openai` plus `model: gpt-5`. `params` are request parameters such as `temperature` and `max_tokens`. `options` (timeout and similar) apply to the default provider.

`contextWindow` and `vision` say what the default model can do, see [What the project knows about a model](#what-the-project-knows-about-a-model).

## Other providers

`providers` holds `params` and `options` for a provider by name, for the ones you use through a profile or a subagent. `bxAgents add provider` writes one for you. The key for each provider is read from its usual environment variable (`OPENAI_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, ...); `bxAgents doctor` tells you when one is missing.

## Profiles

A profile is a named combination: a provider, a model, params, options and the name of the environment variable that holds its key. It can carry a `description`.

|            Key            |                                                              Meaning                                                              |
|---------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `description`             | For people and the terminal and web pickers.                                                                                      |
| `provider`, `model`       | What it runs on. A profile without a provider uses the default provider.                                                          |
| `params`, `options`       | Layered on top of the provider's and the default's: `params` from the default, then the provider, then the profile.               |
| `apiKeyEnv`               | The **name** of the variable that holds the key. A key itself is never written in `Agent.yml`; a profile that has one is refused. |
| `contextWindow`, `vision` | What the project knows about the model, see below.                                                                                |

A profile cannot be named `default` or like a provider (`openai`, `claude`, ...), because both are selected by name. `defaultProfile` picks which profile is used when nothing asks for another one: it is the default model. If the file also has a top-level `model`, the profile wins and the build and `doctor` warn that the `model` line is ignored. Without a `defaultProfile`, the top-level `provider` and `model` are the default. `bxAgents add profile` writes a profile (and `--default` the `defaultProfile`) without touching the rest of the file; see [`add profile`](/next/cli-reference/index.html#add-profile).

## What the project knows about a model

bx-ai has no way to ask a model how much it can hold or whether it can see images, so you can say so, on the default model and on each profile:

```yaml
contextWindow: 128000      # tokens the default model can hold
vision: true               # the default model can see images
profiles:
  fast:
    provider: openai
    model: gpt-5-mini
    contextWindow: 400000
    vision: false
```

`contextWindow` is a whole number of tokens and `vision` is `true` or `false`; `build` refuses anything else. Both are optional and nothing is guessed: a model with no entry is simply unknown. bx-ai does not read them. The chat shows them in `/info` and `/model`, and uses `contextWindow` for the share of the window the context takes (`/context`, the status bar and the context ring of the web chat). `vision: false` makes the chat refuse a picture before it is sent, with a message instead of a provider error; when `vision` is not set the picture goes through.

## Testing a model

`/ping` in the chat and `bxAgents models test` send a model one tiny question through bx-ai and say whether it answered, and how long it took, so a wrong key or model name shows up before a conversation does. See [`models`](/next/cli-reference/index.html#models) and [Models in the chat](/next/cli-reference/index.html#models-in-the-chat).

## Which agent uses what

An agent uses its own `profile:`, else its own `model:` (a `provider/model` slug), else the default. Every subagent inherits the root's settings, and may set its own `model` or `profile`:

```yaml
# subagents/planner/Agent.yml
name: planner
profile: planner
```

`providers`, `profiles`, `defaultProfile`, `params`, `options` and the capability keys apply to the whole app, so they belong in the project's own `Agent.yml`; a subagent that sets them fails validation.

## Capability defaults

`embeddings`, `speech`, `transcription` and `image` set bx-ai's defaults for `aiEmbed()`, `aiSpeak()`, `aiTranscribe()` and `aiImage()`. They do not take profiles. Each takes `provider` and `model`; `speech` also `voice` and `format`, and `image` also `size`, `quality`, `style` and `instructions`. Any other key fails `build`. bx-ai has one audio provider, so `speech` and `transcription` must name the same one. `bxAgents add capability` writes one; see [`add capability`](/next/cli-reference/index.html#add-capability).

## Validation and tests

`bxAgents build` checks all of the above by bx-ai's own rules and names the file and the key. Under `bxAgents test` every profile runs on the `mock` provider, so a test never reaches the network.

## How it reaches bx-ai

The build writes the settings to `config/bxai-settings.json` in the app, and the app merges them into bx-ai's settings when it starts, before ColdBox boots and builds the agents. They travel with the app wherever it runs (`serve`, a `.bxa`, a container).

# Models and Profiles

When you want more than one model in the same project, you name them: a **profile** is a provider, a model and a few settings under a name such as `fast` or `planner`. Everything lives in `Agent.yml`; you never write a `boxlang.json`.

```yaml
provider: openai
model: gpt-5
params: { temperature: 0.2 }

profiles:
  fast:    { description: Cheap and quick, provider: openai, model: gpt-5-mini, params: { temperature: 0 } }
  planner: { description: Careful planning, provider: claude, model: claude-opus-4, apiKeyEnv: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }
```

A subagent picks one with `profile:`; an agent that says nothing uses the default. A profile cannot be named `default` or like a provider, and a key is never written in the file: `apiKeyEnv` names the environment variable that holds it.

`defaultProfile: fast` makes a profile the default model (when a top-level `model` is written beside it, the profile wins and `build` and `doctor` warn that the model is ignored). `bxAgents add profile` and `add provider` write these blocks for you, with an empty key stub in `.env`.

## What the project can say about a model

`contextWindow` and `vision` on the default model and on each profile say what the model can hold and whether it can see images. Both are optional and nothing is guessed. `/info`, `/model` and the context size in the chat show them, and a picture sent to a profile with `vision: false` is refused with that reason.

## Using and testing profiles

* In the terminal chat, `/model` shows the model, `/profile` picks a profile from a list (or `/profile fast`) and `/default` goes back. The conversation, memory and tools stay.
* A web chat entry or an agent API that lists `profiles` offers them as a picker. Only the listed ones can be chosen, and the page never sees a key.
* `bxAgents models list` shows what the project can talk to, and `bxAgents models test --all` sends each model one tiny question and says whether it answered and how long it took. In the chat, `/ping` does the same.
* Set `usage: true` in `Agent.yml` and `bxAgents stats` (or `/stats`) shows what the model calls used, by model, provider, day or user. It keeps counts only.

## Why bother

A slug is enough for most agents. Reach for profiles when several agents share a configuration (a cheaper model your routing subagents use), or when a model needs settings you do not want to repeat.

## Try it

Give Acme support two models: a quick one for simple questions and a careful one for planning. Add the profiles at
the end of `Agent.yml`. Both name the scripted model, which accepts any model name, so the answers can still tell
them apart:

```yaml

profiles:
  fast:
    description: Quick answers for simple questions
    provider: openai-compatible
    model: fast-model
  planner:
    description: Thinks it through before it answers
    provider: openai-compatible
    model: planner-model
```

```bash
cd ~/bxagents-course/acme-support
bxAgents build
bxAgents models list
```

```text
Build succeeded: <anything>/acme-support/.build/app
default<anything>/fast-model<anything>
fast<anything>openai-compatible/fast-model<anything>
planner<anything>openai-compatible/planner-model<anything>
```

In the terminal chat, `/profile planner` switches the model in the middle of a conversation: same conversation,
same tools, only the model changed. Ask `anything` before and after, and the answer ends with `(Answered by fast-model.)` and then `(Answered by planner-model.)`. `/model` shows which one is in use and `/default` goes back.
Because the web app and the API list the profiles too, a person can pick one per message there.
> **\`models test\` and the scripted model**
>
> `bxAgents models test` sends each model one tiny question. It does not work against the scripted model in this
> course, so the course does not use it; with a real provider it is the quickest way to find a wrong key.

## Checkpoint

`Agent.yml` has the `profiles:` block. `kit/resume.sh 12-named-model-configs` restores it; rebuild after.

Full reference: [Models and profiles](/next/conventions/models/index.html).

Next: [The Web App](/next/course/15-the-generated-web-chat-ui/index.html)

# modules/

`modules/` holds BoxLang module dependencies your agent needs - one immediate subfolder per module, discovered by folder name (not recursive - only the top level of `modules/` is enumerated).

```text
modules/
└── my-extra-module/
    ├── module.json
    └── ...
```

## Declaring dependencies between modules

A module folder may include a `module.json` with a `dependsOn` array naming other `modules/*` entries by folder name:

```json
{
	"dependsOn": [ "some-other-module" ]
}
```

This is BxAgents' own dependency-declaration convention for validation purposes - it is independent of BoxLang's own module-loading mechanism.
> **Info**
>
> Today `build` validates `modules/` and records each entry (with a content hash) in the [manifest](/next/manifest/index.html), but it does not copy the folders into the generated app or load them. To give the generated app a library, use the project `lib/` folder described in [Installation](/next/getting-started/installation/index.html#adding-your-own-libraries).

## Validation

* A `module.json` that isn't valid JSON fails the build with a parse error naming the offending module.
* A `dependsOn` entry naming a module that isn't itself a discovered `modules/*` folder fails validation ("depends on unknown module").
* **Circular dependencies** are rejected the same way [subagent](/next/conventions/subagents/index.html) cycles are - full cycle path reported, DFS-based detection, no code generation happens until the graph is acyclic.
* A `module.json` is entirely optional - a module folder with none is assumed to have no declared dependencies.

markdown:
# Packaging Skills

Where `tools/` gives your agent a single callable function, `skills/` gives it a
packaged, freeform capability - instructions the agent loads on demand rather than a
function it calls directly.

Each immediate subfolder of `skills/` that contains a `SKILL.md` file is one skill,
following the [Claude Agent Skills](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/claude-skills)
convention: YAML frontmatter (`name`, `description`) followed by a body of freeform
instructions.

```text
skills/
└── greeting/
    └── SKILL.md
```

```markdown
---
name: greeting
description: How to greet people warmly.
---

Always greet the user warmly and use their name if known.
```

## Naming

The skill's name is its frontmatter `name:` if present; otherwise it falls back to the
folder name. An explicit `name:` always wins even if it differs from the folder. Two
skills resolving to the same name fail validation with a duplicate-name error.

A folder without a `SKILL.md` inside it isn't discovered as a skill at all - it's
simply ignored, which is handy for scratch subfolders or assets kept alongside a skill
under a different structure.

## Starting one, and installing one

`bxAgents add skill code-review` writes `skills/code-review/SKILL.md` with the frontmatter and
a body to fill in. Skills other people published are installed from skills.boxlang.io:

```bash
bxAgents skills find review
bxAgents skills install <owner/repo/skill>
bxAgents skills list
```

Installed skills go into `.agents/skills/` (kept out of source control) and are recorded in
`.agents/skills.lock.json`, which you commit; `build` restores whatever the lock lists and the
disk lacks. Skills in `skills/` and installed ones both go into the build, and one of your own
with the same name wins. `skills update` and `skills remove` do what they say.

## How it's wired at runtime

`skills/` is copied verbatim into the generated app, the same wipe-then-write,
dotfile-excluding copy as `tools/`. The generated `config/bxai-settings.json` always points
bx-ai's own `skillsDirectory` module setting at `/app/skills` - you never need to set this
yourself, even though bx-ai's own default is a different path (`/.agents/skills`).

## Tools vs. skills - when to reach for which

Use a **tool** when the agent needs to call a specific function with specific
arguments and get a specific return value back (get the weather, look up an order).
Use a **skill** when you want to hand the agent a body of know-how it applies
judgment to (how to write a professional email, how your team formats commit
messages, how to review a pull request against your team's checklist).

## Try it

Acme has a refund policy. A tool would be a function; this is know-how, so it is a skill. Write the folder with its
`SKILL.md` (or let `bxAgents add skill refund-policy` write the frame):

```markdown
---
name: refund-policy
description: What Acme refunds, when, and how to explain a refusal kindly.
---

# Refund policy

- Returns are free for 30 days after delivery.
- Refunds land within 5 working days of the parcel coming back.
- Sale items are final, but a damaged item is always replaced.
```

Rebuild. The agent lists the skills it can load in its system prompt, so asking the scripted model for it (the word
`system` again) shows yours next to the six BxAgents ships:

```bash
cd ~/bxagents-course/acme-support
bxAgents build
bxAgents invoke --message=system
```

```text
Build succeeded: <anything>/acme-support/.build/app
...
- refund-policy: What Acme refunds, when, and how to explain a refusal kindly.
...
```

The six that ship (`bxagents-build-agent`, `bxagents-chat`, `bxagents-gateways-connectors`, `bxagents-operate`,
`bxagents-subagents-routines` and `bxagents-tools-and-skills`) are on by default and teach the agent how BxAgents
itself works; `skills: { builtin: false }` leaves them out. In the terminal chat, `/skills` lists all of them and
where each came from (`project` for yours, `bxagents` for the shipped ones). A model loads a skill on its own when
the question matches its description, which the scripted model does not do: it only answers with what the course
wrote. The agent can also write a skill itself (`skill_save`, with your approval), which the
[approvals lesson](/next/course/approvals/index.html) comes back to.

## Checkpoint

`acme-support/skills/refund-policy/SKILL.md` exists. `kit/resume.sh 10-packaging-skills` restores it; rebuild after.

Next: [Models and Profiles](/next/course/12-named-model-configs/index.html)

title: Packaging, Deploying, and Wrapping Up
body:
Packaging, Deploying, and Wrapping Up You've built Acme support: an agent with tools, skills, subagents, an HTTP route, a web app, routines, people and tokens, a vault, a test suite and a backup. This lesson ships it. The chain, end to end flowchart LR P["your project"] -->|"bxAgents build"| B[".build/
app/ public/ lib/ runtime/"] B -->|"bxAgents package"| A["dist/name-version.bxa
+ .sha256 + redacted manifest.json"] A -->|"bxAgents deploy"| T["a target:
local / ssh / ftp / sftp
docker / digitalocean"] T --> RUN["boxlang-miniserver runs in the unzipped folder"] ENV["environment variables"] -->|"read at RUNTIME by bx-ai"| RUN style A fill:#eaf6ec,stroke:#155724 style ENV fill:#fff3cd,stroke:#856404 Secrets never enter the artifact at any step - .env /dotfiles are excluded from the zip unconditionally, and the manifest is redacted on top of never carrying one. Every API key, token and password is resolved from a real environment variable, live, at runtime. Package bxAgents package --version=1.0.0 Zips the built app ( app/ , lib/ , public/ , runtime/ , boxlang_modules/ and miniserver.json of .build/ ) into dist/{agentName}-{version}.bxa , a .sha256 checksum, and a redacted manifest.json . Packaging twice over the same build produces byte-identical zip bytes - useful for verifying a CI-built artifact matches a locally-built one. An optional .bxaignore (one glob per line) excludes extra paths. Deploy bxAgents deploy --destination=/path/to/somewhere # local, no deploy/ folder needed bxAgents deploy --name=production # any target, via deploy/production.bx Six pluggable targets: local (copy the newest .bxa ), ssh (scp + optional restart), docker (build/push an image), digitalocean (App Platform), and ftp / sftp . Every target resolves credentials from environment variables only - never from deploy/* config itself. // deploy/production.bx class { function configure() { return { target : "digitalocean", appName : "my-agent", registry : { type : "docr", repository : "myorg/my-agent" }, envs : [ { key : "OPENAI_API_KEY", scope : "RUN_TIME", type : "SECRET" } ] }; } } Seeing how the agent is composed bxAgents inspect prints a report of your agent straight from its source - it does not need a build: bxAgents inspect bxAgents inspect --section=tools,env bxAgents inspect --json You get the agent and subagent tree with each model, the tools and skills, what the project is exposed through, the schedule, and every environment variable it needs with a marker for the ones that are not set (names only, never values). --md writes the same thing as Markdown for a pull request. See the CLI Reference for every section. What every build recorded: the manifest Every build also writes .build/manifest.json , a hash-stamped record of exactly what went into the build - agent name, model, environment, and one entry per discovered file with a SHA-256 content hash. This is what makes rebuilding an unchanged project byte-identical, the idea you first met back in What Is BxAgents? . Open it in any editor; inspect shows its version and file count in the build section. Cleaning up bxAgents clean Removes only .build/ and dist/ - your source conventions are never touched. Running it for other people A deployed agent is no longer on your own machine, so decide who may call it. The agent API is open by default, which is right on a laptop and wrong on the internet. Before you deploy, set agentApi in Agent.yml ( Exposing Your Agent over HTTP and MCP ): a shared secret in an environment variable, tokens: true for per-person tokens, and allowedIPs or rateLimit where they fit. Run token where the agent's database is (on the server), make one for each person or program, and talk to the deployment from your own terminal: bxAgents token create --name=laptop --expires=90d bxAgents chat --connect=https://agent.example.com --token= The conversations, notes and tokens live in one SQLite file, chat.db in the agent's data home ( ~/.bxagents// by default, the same place in development and when deployed; BXAGENTS_DB can name another file). bxAgents sessions list and bxAgents notes list read it from a shell, and bxAgents stats shows what the model calls used when usage: true is set. What travels, and what does not A deployed agent is the package plus three things that stay outside it: Stays outside Why How it gets there Environment variables ( OPENAI_API_KEY , ACME_ADA_PASSWORD , BXAGENTS_VAULT_KEY ) Secrets never enter the artifact Set on the server, or by the deploy target's envs The data home ( ~/.bxagents/acme-support/ ) Conversations, notes, tokens, routines and the sealed vault are state , not code bxAgents backup on the old machine, bxAgents restore on the new one The vault key The vault is sealed with it, and a backup is no use without it Set BXAGENTS_VAULT_KEY yourself, kept apart from the backup So moving to a new machine is: install BoxLang and BxAgents there, unpack the .bxa , set the variables, restore the backup, start the server. The vault lesson says why a secret is not written in .env for the model to use, and Logs, Usage and Backups makes and restores a backup. Try it Build, package and deploy Acme support to a folder (the local target needs no server): cd ~/bxagents-course/acme-support bxAgents build bxAgents package --version=1.0.0 ls dist bxAgents deploy --destination=$HOME/acme-deploy ls ~/acme-deploy Build succeeded: /acme-support/.build/app Packaged: /dist/acme-support-1.0.0.bxa acme-support-1.0.0.bxa acme-support-1.0.0.bxa.sha256 manifest.json Deployed acme-support-1.0.0.bxa to acme-support-1.0.0.bxa The .sha256 lets a server check the artifact it received, and the redacted manifest.json records what went in. Packaging the same build twice gives the same bytes. Nothing of your .env , your data home or your vault is in the .bxa . Checkpoint Nothing in the project changed ( dist/ is output, and .gitignore ignores it). Every verb, in one place You've now used new , build , test , chat , invoke , serve , package , deploy , inspect , clean and hash-password across this course. The rest, all in the CLI Reference : add adds one piece to a project that already exists: a tool, skill, subagent, gateway, schedule, interceptor, MCP client or server, profile, provider, capability or extension. doctor is the one you'll reach for when something isn't working - it checks your BoxLang version, whether bx-ai is loaded, whether the project validates and which environment variables are not set, without needing a prior build . models lists the models a project can talk to and tests that they answer ( models test ). token , notes , sessions and stats manage access tokens, the notes the agent keeps, the saved conversations and the usage counts. skills installs skills from skills.boxlang.io, and extensions lists, installs and links extensions. Where to go from here Conventions The full reference for every convention folder this course walked through. The Build Pipeline Exactly what build does, in order, in more depth than Building Your Agent covered. Deployment & Secrets The full packaging and secrets story from this lesson, in depth. One lesson is left: Ship Acme Support runs the whole agent end to end and shows the one-line swap to a real model. Next: Ship Acme Support

# Packaging, Deploying, and Wrapping Up You've built Acme support: an agent with tools, skills, subagents, an HTTP route, a web app, routines, people and tokens, a vault, a test suite and a backup. This lesson ships it. ## The chain, end to end ```mermaid flowchart LR P["your project"] -->|"bxAgents build"| B[".build/
app/ public/ lib/ runtime/"] B -->|"bxAgents package"| A["dist/name-version.bxa
+ .sha256 + redacted manifest.json"] A -->|"bxAgents deploy"| T["a target:
local / ssh / ftp / sftp
docker / digitalocean"] T --> RUN["boxlang-miniserver runs in the unzipped folder"] ENV["environment variables"] -->|"read at RUNTIME by bx-ai"| RUN style A fill:#eaf6ec,stroke:#155724 style ENV fill:#fff3cd,stroke:#856404 ``` Secrets never enter the artifact at any step - `.env`/dotfiles are excluded from the zip unconditionally, and the manifest is redacted on top of never carrying one. Every API key, token and password is resolved from a real environment variable, live, at runtime. ## Package ```bash bxAgents package --version=1.0.0 ``` Zips the built app (`app/`, `lib/`, `public/`, `runtime/`, `boxlang_modules/` and `miniserver.json` of `.build/`) into `dist/{agentName}-{version}.bxa`, a `.sha256` checksum, and a redacted `manifest.json`. An optional `.bxaignore` (one glob per line) excludes extra paths. ## Deploy ```bash bxAgents deploy --destination=/path/to/somewhere # local, no deploy/ folder needed bxAgents deploy --name=production # any target, via deploy/production.bx ``` Six pluggable targets: `local` (copy the newest `.bxa`), `ssh` (scp + optional restart), `docker` (build/push an image), `digitalocean` (App Platform), and `ftp`/`sftp`. Every target resolves credentials from environment variables only - never from `deploy/*` config itself. ```javascript // deploy/production.bx class { function configure() { return { target : "digitalocean", appName : "my-agent", registry : { type : "docr", repository : "myorg/my-agent" }, envs : [ { key : "OPENAI_API_KEY", scope : "RUN_TIME", type : "SECRET" } ] }; } } ``` ## Seeing how the agent is composed `bxAgents inspect` prints a report of your agent straight from its source - it does not need a build: ```bash bxAgents inspect bxAgents inspect --section=tools,env bxAgents inspect --json ``` You get the agent and subagent tree with each model, the tools and skills, what the project is exposed through, the schedule, and every environment variable it needs with a marker for the ones that are not set (names only, never values). `--md` writes the same thing as Markdown for a pull request. This is what makes rebuilding an unchanged project byte-identical, the idea you first met back in [What Is BxAgents?](/next/course/02-what-is-bxagents/index.html). Packaging the same build twice gives the same bytes. Nothing of your `.env`, your data home or your vault is in the `.bxa`. ## Checkpoint Nothing in the project changed (`dist/` is output, and `.gitignore` ignores it). ## Every verb, in one place You've now used `new`, `build`, `test`, `chat`, `invoke`, `serve`, `package`, `deploy`, `inspect`, `clean` and `hash-password` across this course. title: Quick Start
body: Quick Start By the end you will have an agent you can chat with in the terminal and serve over HTTP. This walks through the full lifecycle of a BxAgents project: scaffold, edit, build, run. Before you start you need BoxLang and the module installed (see Installation ) and an API key for the model provider you pick ( OPENAI_API_KEY for openai/gpt-5 ). To run bxAgents test you also need CommandBox (the box command) on your PATH : new runs box install once to fetch TestBox. Without box the project is still created, new prints a warning with the command to run later, and --skipInstall leaves the step out. 1. Scaffold a project bxAgents new my-agent At a terminal this asks what the agent should do (its model, tools, MCP servers (outside tool servers that speak the Model Context Protocol), channels, how people reach it, where it deploys) and writes the project to match; see the new wizard . # Quick Start

![A terminal session: bxAgents new scaffolds a project, bxAgents build assembles a ColdBox app, bxAgents inspect prints the agent and its model, and bxAgents serve starts it on http://127.0.0.1:8080](/next/assets/cli-quickstart.svg)

By the end you will have an agent you can chat with in the terminal and serve over HTTP. This walks through the full lifecycle of a BxAgents project: scaffold, edit, build, run.

Before you start you need BoxLang and the module installed (see [Installation](/next/getting-started/installation/index.html)) and an API key for the model provider you pick (`OPENAI_API_KEY` for `openai/gpt-5`). To run `bxAgents test` you also need [CommandBox](https://commandbox.ortusbooks.com) (the `box` command) on your `PATH`: `new` runs `box install` once to fetch TestBox. Without `box` the project is still created, `new` prints a warning with the command to run later, and `--skipInstall` leaves the step out.

## 1. Scaffold a project

```bash
bxAgents new my-agent
```

At a terminal this asks what the agent should do (its model, tools, MCP servers (outside tool servers that speak the Model Context Protocol), channels, how people reach it, where it deploys) and writes the project to match; see [the new wizard](/next/guides/new-wizard/index.html). It ends by printing the one-line command that builds the same project without questions. To skip the questions, pass a model:

```bash
bxAgents new my-agent --model=openai/gpt-5
```

`--model` is a `provider/model` slug (written to `Agent.yml` as separate `provider:` and `model:` lines) - see [the model slug](/next/conventions/agent-bx/index.html#the-model-slug) for how it's parsed. `--name` and `--description` are optional; `--name` defaults to the target directory's own name.

This creates:

```text
my-agent/
├── Application.bx
├── Agent.yml
├── instructions.md
├── tools/
├── skills/
├── subagents/
├── gateways/
├── schedules/
├── mcp/
├── interceptors/
├── modules/
├── box.json
└── tests/
    └── specs/
        └── AgentSpec.bx
```

Plus a root [`Application.bx`](/next/conventions/application-bx/index.html) that extends the class every build generates (add your own settings and hooks there), a `.env` (secrets live here, so put your provider API keys in it and keep it out of source control), a `.gitignore` and a few dotfiles (`.editorconfig`, `.gitattributes`, `.bxlint.json`, `.markdownlint.json`, `.boxlang.json`). BoxLang loads the `.env` from the project root itself. The root `box.json` lists `testbox` as a development dependency.

This is the `minimal` starter - the default when `--template` is omitted. A template is a preset: the wizard (and flags such as `--with`, `--channels` and `--deploy`) add tools, channels and a deploy target on top of it. `new` can also scaffold one of 7 other built-in starters (`--template=webui-chat|slack-bot|telegram-bot|github-bot|mcp-server|scheduled|multi-agent`), each adding a bit of pre-wired content (a gateway, a scheduler) on top of the same skeleton, or skip scaffolding entirely and create the project from an existing GitHub repo (`--repo=owner/repo`) or a ForgeBox package (`--forgebox=<slug>`) instead - see the [CLI Reference](/next/cli-reference/index.html#new) for the full list and how each one works. The agent is defined by an `Agent.yml` by default; pass `--class` to scaffold the advanced, class-based `Agent.bx` instead (see [Agent.bx](/next/conventions/agent-bx/index.html)).

`Agent.yml` looks like this (`--description` adds a `description:` line):

```yaml
# Your agent. Most agents need nothing more than this file and instructions.md.
# For code in the definition (hooks, dynamic instructions), scaffold with --class.
name: my-agent
provider: openai
model: gpt-5

environments:
  # `bxAgents test` builds against this override by default (see
  # BaseAgentSpec.bx) so a fresh project's tests need no API key or
  # network access - swap the model to test against a real provider.
  test:
    model: mock/mock-model
```

The agent is just this file plus `instructions.md`. See [Agent.yml](/next/conventions/agent-yaml/index.html) for every key.

Every convention folder (a folder whose name tells BxAgents what its files are, such as `tools/` or `gateways/`) is created empty - add files to the ones your agent actually needs and delete (or just ignore) the rest.

## 2. Edit

Open `instructions.md` and write the agent's system prompt, and adjust `name`, `description` or `model` in `Agent.yml` as you like. Add a tool:

```javascript
// tools/Greeter.bx
class {

	@AITool( "Say hello to someone by name." )
	function sayHello( name ) {
		return "Hello, " & arguments.name & "!";
	}

}
```

See the [Conventions](/next/conventions/agent-yaml/index.html) section for every other folder (`skills/`, `subagents/`, `gateways/` (a gateway is a door into the agent: a chat platform, a web page or an HTTP path), `schedules/`, `mcp/`, `interceptors/`, `modules/`). You do not have to write them by hand: `bxAgents add <kind>` (`tool`, `skill`, `subagent`, `gateway`, `schedule`, `interceptor`, `mcp`, `profile` (a named model setup you can switch to in a chat), `provider`, `capability`, `extension`) asks a few questions and writes the files, and `--dry-run` shows them first.

## 3. Test it

```bash
box install        # once, to fetch testbox into lib/testbox (`new` already tried this for you)
bxAgents test
```

The scaffolded `tests/specs/AgentSpec.bx` passes out of the box - it builds your agent against the `mock` provider (no API key or network needed) and asserts on a scripted response. See [tests/](/next/conventions/testing/index.html) for `mockResponses()` and the custom matchers (`toHaveCalledTool`, etc.) available to your own specs.

## 4. Build

```bash
bxAgents build
```

Runs the full [build pipeline](/next/build-pipeline/index.html) - config resolution, discovery, validation, code generation, manifest normalization - and writes a real ColdBox application to `.build/` (the code in `app/`, the web root in `public/`), plus `.build/manifest.json`. Run `bxAgents build --environment=production` to build against an `Agent.yml` environment override (see [Agent.yml](/next/conventions/agent-yaml/index.html#environments)).

If your project fails validation (duplicate tool names, an unknown model provider, a gateway entry with a bad path, ...) `build` fails with every collected error - not just the first one.

## 5. Run it

Two ways to talk to the built agent - both load the exact same `GeneratedAgentFactory.bx` and build the exact same agent tree, so they never diverge:

**Interactively, from the terminal:**

Put your provider key in `.env` first (the file has a commented `OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...` line to uncomment and fill in). Without it the model call fails with the provider's "You didn't provide an API key" error.

```bash
bxAgents chat
```

At a terminal this is a full-screen chat that keeps your scrollback: answers stream in as formatted Markdown, tool calls show as they run, Esc stops the agent, and typing `/` lists the commands (`/sessions`, `/resume`, `/name`, `/fork`, `/export`, `/notes`, `/context` and more). Type `@` to attach a file, or `@picture.png` to send a picture. Conversations are listed in the `chat.db` of the agent's [data home](/next/conventions/data/index.html) (`~/.bxagents/<agent name>/` by default; the messages last as long as the agent's memory does), so `bxAgents chat --continue` can pick up where you left off. See [the terminal UI](/next/guides/terminal-ui/index.html) and [Slash commands](/next/guides/slash-commands/index.html). To chat against the full app (schedulers, interceptors, gateways), use `bxAgents chat --server`, or `--connect=<url>` for a server that is already running (add `--token=<token>` if it wants one).

**Over HTTP** , via a real [`boxlang-miniserver`](https://boxlang.ortusbooks.com/getting-started/running-boxlang/miniserver) process:

```bash
bxAgents serve --port=8080
```

Every served agent has an HTTP API at `/__bxagents` (open on your own machine, behind tokens when you share it), and the web page, the terminal chat and chat platforms all use it. See [Call your agent from code](/next/guides/agent-api/index.html). The root address, `http://localhost:8080/`, redirects to the web page when the project has one, and otherwise points at `/__bxagents/health`.

If your project also has a `gateways/*` entry with `{ exposes: "agent", path: "/api/chat" }`, the agent is reachable at `POST http://localhost:8080/api/chat/invoke` (and `/stream`, `/batch`, `/info` - see [gateways/](/next/conventions/gateways/index.html)). An `exposes: "webui"` entry adds the browser chat page.

### See the web app

If you scaffolded with `--template=webui-chat`, `bxAgents serve` also serves the web app at `/chat`. This is the whole of it, in three minutes:

![The web app: the left menu, a conversation with a tool call and a formatted answer, with the model select in the bar above the conversation](/next/assets/webui/webui-chat.png)

Each page has its own address under `/chat` (`/chat/routines`, `/chat/settings`, ...), and an address there that is no page answers `404`. Every page is described in [the web app guide](/next/conventions/web-ui/index.html#the-pages).

## 6. Inspect, package, deploy

```bash
bxAgents doctor               # runtime, modules, project checks and unset environment variables
bxAgents inspect              # how the agent is composed: agents, tools, env vars, checks
bxAgents package --version=1.0.0   # writes dist/my-agent-1.0.0.bxa + .sha256 (a .bxa is the built agent as one portable file)
bxAgents deploy --destination=/path/to/somewhere   # copies the newest .bxa there
```

See [The Manifest](/next/manifest/index.html) and [Deployment \& Secrets](/next/deployment-and-secrets/index.html).

## 7. Clean up

```bash
bxAgents clean
```

Removes `.build/` and `dist/` only - your source conventions (`Agent.yml`, `tools/`, etc.) are never touched.

## Next steps

* Build one agent end to end, with no account and no key, in the [Introduction to BxAgents](/next/course/index.html) course.
* Walk through every convention folder in [Conventions](/next/conventions/agent-yaml/index.html).
* Look at the working sample projects in [`examples/`](https://github.com/ortus-boxlang/bx-agents/tree/development/examples).
* See every verb's flags in [CLI Reference](/next/cli-reference/index.html).

The settings: Setting Default Meaning enabled false Turns the feature on maxPerUser 20 The most routines one person may have (1 to 200) minInterval 5m The shortest a routine may repeat ( 1m to 1d ) maxParallel 2 How many routines the heartbeat starts in one beat (1 to 10) maxPromptLength 4000 The longest prompt, in characters (200 to 20000). Longer instructions belong in a skill approvalTimeout 24h How long a run waits for a person to approve a tool ( 5m to 7d ) timezone the server's The time zone cron expressions are read in, an IANA name such as Europe/Madrid summaryLength 1500 How many characters of an answer are sent to a gateway (200 to 4000) maxReportSize 256kb The largest report file a routine may save ( 1kb to 5mb ) maxReportFiles 500 The most files in one routine's results folder (10 to 5000) A duration is a whole number with m , h or d , and a size a whole number with kb or mb . A bad value stops the build and doctor names it. Making one Ask the agent: "every weekday at 9, check the build". The agent calls routine_schedule and a person approves it, as for any tool that needs approval. The answer says when it first runs. A schedule is stored in one of two forms: a 5 field cron expression, minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week , such as 0 9 * * 1-5 an interval, every 30m , every 2h or every 1d The model turns plain words into one of these, and the tools answer with the English reading ("weekdays at 09:00") and the next run time, so a mistake is seen straight away. Routines have a page in the web app : list, make, edit, run, pause, resume, delete, and read the reports. The tools Every tool the agent gets from BX Agents is named {type}_{action} , so permissions can match them by pattern later. Tool Does Needs a person's approval routine_schedule Makes a routine, and says where its answer goes Yes routine_list Lists yours, with when each runs next and how the last run went No routine_update Changes the schedule, the prompt, where the answer goes, or any of them Yes routine_pause Stops one without deleting it No routine_resume Starts a paused one again, and clears its failures No routine_run Runs one at the next beat instead of waiting No routine_delete Deletes one. Its conversation and reports stay Yes report_save Saves a report file, for the routine that is running. Refused anywhere else No report_list Lists a routine's report files No report_read Reads one No The tools act as the person in the conversation, never as an admin, and only the root agent has them. A routine's own run is refused the routine_* tools, so a routine cannot make or change routines. There is no tool that deletes a report. A run Every minute the heartbeat , a scheduler the build adds, looks for routines that are due and starts them, at most maxParallel at once. Each run: is a normal turn as the person who owns the routine, so their notes, volumes and tool approvals all apply, and nothing extra is allowed happens in a conversation of its own, routine-<name>-<id> , which the person finds in their conversation list and reads like any other never overlaps itself: a routine still running is skipped, and the skip is logged stops for approval like any chat. The routine shows as waiting, the person answers in its conversation, and after approvalTimeout the run is cancelled and counts as a failure Three failures in a row pause the routine. routine_resume starts it again. If the server was down when a routine was due, it runs once on start, never once per missed time. An admin sees and manages every person's routines. Nobody else can see yours. Where the answer goes Each routine has a destination, set when it is made: Destination Meaning nothing said The gateway chat the person is writing in, if that is where they asked. Otherwise the routine's own conversation routine The routine's own conversation only gateway:telegram (any gateway) A chat on that gateway Gateways belong to the person who runs the agent. A person writing from a gateway may send a routine's answer to their own chat there. Anyone else is limited to the routine's own conversation, and the local user can choose a gateway, naming the chat when it has talked to more than one. A gateway can only write to a chat it has already heard from, because that is when the agent learns its address (and for Teams, the address it needs to reply). If the gateway has talked to nobody, the agent tells the owner to message the bot once. What is sent is a summary: the answer cut to summaryLength characters, headed Routine <name>: , and a last line naming the reports the run saved. The whole answer is in the routine's conversation. A message that cannot be sent (the gateway is not connected, the chat is unknown, the platform refuses) counts as a failed run, so three in a row pause the routine, and routines.log says why. The log never holds the text. A run that stopped for an approval is not sent anywhere once a person answers: its answer is in its conversation. Reports A routine can save what it found as files: report_save( file, content ) while it runs. They go in <data home>/routines/<name>-<id>/ , are never overwritten (a name already used becomes report-2.md ), and are never deleted automatically. A file name is letters, digits, . , _ and - , up to 80 characters, ending in .md , .txt , .json , .csv or .html . A file is at most maxReportSize , and a folder holds at most maxReportFiles ; at the limit the agent is told a person has to clean up. The agent reads reports back with report_list and report_read for the person's own routines. A long file is cut when read. The reports are in a backup . Logs routines.log records each routine made, changed, run, skipped, failed, sent and paused, and each report saved (its name, never its text), and heartbeat.log the beats that started something. A prompt is never logged, only the routine's name and its owner. See logs . Managing routines Making and changing a routine is usually asked of the agent, where a person sees it and approves it. The terminal, the API and the web page can also make and change one directly. Everything else can be done from each surface, and every surface goes through the same service, so they cannot disagree. Surface Does Chat: /routines , /routine <name> [run \| pause \| resume \| delete confirm \| reports \| report <file>] List yours (an admin adds all ), show one, run, pause, resume, delete (only with confirm ), list and read reports Terminal: bxAgents routines list \| show \| add \| edit \| pause \| resume \| run \| delete \| reports \| report \| clean The same, as the local operator, so --all lists every owner's. See the CLI reference API GET /routines and the routes below, for your own program Web page The Routines page of the menu ( <path>/routines ): a list with run, pause, edit, delete, reports and clean-up run marks a routine due. It starts within a minute, by the heartbeat of a served app, so from a terminal that is not serving the app nothing starts until the app is running. The /routines and /routine commands are for the terminal and the web page. They are not on gateways yet: a person there asks the agent, which has the routine_* tools. Reports are removed by a person Nothing in a chat deletes a file, and the agent has no tool for it. A person removes one report, or the old ones, from the terminal, the API or the web page: bxAgents routines clean <name> --older-than=30d (or --all ) only says what it would remove. Add --yes to remove it. The API's POST /routines/reports/clean does the same, and removes only with "apply": true . The web page asks first how many files and bytes it would remove, then asks you to confirm. Deleting a routine keeps its reports. People see only their own routines, and an admin may act on anyone's by id, or by a name only one owner has. An admin may also send a routine's answer to a gateway, which the tools do not allow for a chat-scope person.

# Routines

A routine is a prompt the agent runs on a schedule, as the person who made it. "Every weekday at 9, check the build and tell me what broke" is a routine. A person makes it by asking the agent, and the agent keeps it in the chat database. The answer can go to a gateway, and a routine can keep reports as files.

Routines are not [schedulers](/next/conventions/schedules/index.html). They are for the people who use the agent, not for the developer.

|                |       `schedules/*.bx` scheduler       |                       Routine                        |
|----------------|----------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------|
| Who makes it   | The developer, in a file               | Anyone, by asking the agent                          |
| Where it lives | In the project, shipped with the agent | In the chat database, per person                     |
| Runs as        | The app                                | The person who made it, with their notes and volumes |
| Changed by     | Editing the file and rebuilding        | Asking the agent, while the app runs                 |
| Turned on by   | Existing                               | `routines.enabled: true`                             |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  P[Person asks the agent] --> T[routine_schedule, approved by the person]
  T --> S[(routines table)]
  H[Heartbeat, every minute] --> S
  H --> R[Runner]
  R --> C[The routine's own conversation]
  R --> L[routines.log and heartbeat.log]
```

## Turn it on

Routines are off by default, so a published agent never grows automated work by surprise.

```yaml
routines:
  enabled: true
  minInterval: 5m
  timezone: Europe/Madrid
```

With the feature off there are no routine tools, no heartbeat and no routines capability. The settings:

|      Setting      |   Default    |                                                            Meaning                                                             |
|-------------------|--------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `enabled`         | `false`      | Turns the feature on                                                                                                           |
| `maxPerUser`      | `20`         | The most routines one person may have (1 to 200)                                                                               |
| `minInterval`     | `5m`         | The shortest a routine may repeat (`1m` to `1d`)                                                                               |
| `maxParallel`     | `2`          | How many routines the heartbeat starts in one beat (1 to 10)                                                                   |
| `maxPromptLength` | `4000`       | The longest prompt, in characters (200 to 20000). Longer instructions belong in a [skill](/next/conventions/skills/index.html) |
| `approvalTimeout` | `24h`        | How long a run waits for a person to approve a tool (`5m` to `7d`)                                                             |
| `timezone`        | the server's | The time zone cron expressions are read in, an IANA name such as `Europe/Madrid`                                               |
| `summaryLength`   | `1500`       | How many characters of an answer are sent to a gateway (200 to 4000)                                                           |
| `maxReportSize`   | `256kb`      | The largest report file a routine may save (`1kb` to `5mb`)                                                                    |
| `maxReportFiles`  | `500`        | The most files in one routine's results folder (10 to 5000)                                                                    |

A duration is a whole number with `m`, `h` or `d`, and a size a whole number with `kb` or `mb`. A bad value stops the build and `doctor` names it.

## Making one

Ask the agent: "every weekday at 9, check the build". The agent calls `routine_schedule` and a person approves it, as for any tool that needs approval. The answer says when it first runs.

A schedule is stored in one of two forms:

* a 5 field cron expression, `minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week`, such as `0 9 * * 1-5`
* an interval, `every 30m`, `every 2h` or `every 1d`

The model turns plain words into one of these, and the tools answer with the English reading ("weekdays at 09:00") and the next run time, so a mistake is seen straight away.

![The Routines page in the web app: three routines, one paused, with the schedule in words and the next run](/next/assets/webui/webui-routines.png)

![The reports of one routine, with a report open](/next/assets/webui/webui-routine-reports.png)

Routines have a page in the [web app](/next/conventions/web-ui/index.html#routines): list, make, edit, run, pause, resume, delete, and read the reports.

## The tools

Every tool the agent gets from BX Agents is named `{type}_{action}`, so permissions can match them by pattern later.

|        Tool        |                                    Does                                     | Needs a person's approval |
|--------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------|
| `routine_schedule` | Makes a routine, and says where its answer goes                             | Yes                       |
| `routine_list`     | Lists yours, with when each runs next and how the last run went             | No                        |
| `routine_update`   | Changes the schedule, the prompt, where the answer goes, or any of them     | Yes                       |
| `routine_pause`    | Stops one without deleting it                                               | No                        |
| `routine_resume`   | Starts a paused one again, and clears its failures                          | No                        |
| `routine_run`      | Runs one at the next beat instead of waiting                                | No                        |
| `routine_delete`   | Deletes one. Its conversation and reports stay                              | Yes                       |
| `report_save`      | Saves a report file, for the routine that is running. Refused anywhere else | No                        |
| `report_list`      | Lists a routine's report files                                              | No                        |
| `report_read`      | Reads one                                                                   | No                        |

The tools act as the person in the conversation, never as an admin, and only the root agent has them. A routine's own run is refused the `routine_*` tools, so a routine cannot make or change routines. There is no tool that deletes a report.

## A run

Every minute the **heartbeat** , a scheduler the build adds, looks for routines that are due and starts them, at most `maxParallel` at once. Each run:

* is a normal turn as the person who owns the routine, so their notes, volumes and tool approvals all apply, and nothing extra is allowed
* happens in a conversation of its own, `routine-<name>-<id>`, which the person finds in their conversation list and reads like any other
* never overlaps itself: a routine still running is skipped, and the skip is logged
* stops for approval like any chat. The routine shows as waiting, the person answers in its conversation, and after `approvalTimeout` the run is cancelled and counts as a failure

Three failures in a row pause the routine. `routine_resume` starts it again. If the server was down when a routine was due, it runs once on start, never once per missed time.

An admin sees and manages every person's routines. Nobody else can see yours.

## Where the answer goes

Each routine has a destination, set when it is made:

|           Destination            |                                                     Meaning                                                      |
|----------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| nothing said                     | The gateway chat the person is writing in, if that is where they asked. Otherwise the routine's own conversation |
| `routine`                        | The routine's own conversation only                                                                              |
| `gateway:telegram` (any gateway) | A chat on that [gateway](/next/conventions/gateways/index.html)                                                  |

Gateways belong to the person who runs the agent. A person writing from a gateway may send a routine's answer to their own chat there. Anyone else is limited to the routine's own conversation, and the local user can choose a gateway, naming the chat when it has talked to more than one. A gateway can only write to a chat it has already heard from, because that is when the agent learns its address (and for Teams, the address it needs to reply). If the gateway has talked to nobody, the agent tells the owner to message the bot once.

What is sent is a summary: the answer cut to `summaryLength` characters, headed `Routine <name>:`, and a last line naming the reports the run saved. The whole answer is in the routine's conversation. A message that cannot be sent (the gateway is not connected, the chat is unknown, the platform refuses) counts as a failed run, so three in a row pause the routine, and `routines.log` says why. The log never holds the text.

A run that stopped for an approval is not sent anywhere once a person answers: its answer is in its conversation.

## Reports

A routine can save what it found as files: `report_save( file, content )` while it runs. They go in `<data home>/routines/<name>-<id>/`, are never overwritten (a name already used becomes `report-2.md`), and are never deleted automatically.

* A file name is letters, digits, `.`, `_` and `-`, up to 80 characters, ending in `.md`, `.txt`, `.json`, `.csv` or `.html`.
* A file is at most `maxReportSize`, and a folder holds at most `maxReportFiles`; at the limit the agent is told a person has to clean up.
* The agent reads reports back with `report_list` and `report_read` for the person's own routines. A long file is cut when read.
* The reports are in a [backup](/next/conventions/data/index.html).

## Logs

`routines.log` records each routine made, changed, run, skipped, failed, sent and paused, and each report saved (its name, never its text), and `heartbeat.log` the beats that started something. A prompt is never logged, only the routine's name and its owner. See [logs](/next/conventions/logs/index.html).

## Managing routines

Making and changing a routine is usually asked of the agent, where a person sees it and approves it. The terminal, the API and the web page can also make and change one directly. Everything else can be done from each surface, and every surface goes through the same service, so they cannot disagree.

|                                                           Surface                                                           |                                                               Does                                                                |
|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Chat: `/routines`, `/routine <name> [run \| pause \| resume \| delete confirm \| reports \| report <file>]`                 | List yours (an admin adds `all`), show one, run, pause, resume, delete (only with `confirm`), list and read reports               |
| Terminal: `bxAgents routines list \| show \| add \| edit \| pause \| resume \| run \| delete \| reports \| report \| clean` | The same, as the local operator, so `--all` lists every owner's. See [the CLI reference](/next/cli-reference/index.html#routines) |
| [API](/next/guides/agent-api/index.html#routines)                                                                           | `GET /routines` and the routes below, for your own program                                                                        |
| [Web page](/next/conventions/web-ui/index.html#routines)                                                                    | The **Routines** page of the menu (`<path>/routines`): a list with run, pause, edit, delete, reports and clean-up                 |

`run` marks a routine due. It starts within a minute, by the heartbeat of a served app, so from a terminal that is not serving the app nothing starts until the app is running.

The `/routines` and `/routine` commands are for the terminal and the web page. They are not on [gateways](/next/conventions/gateways/index.html) yet: a person there asks the agent, which has the `routine_*` tools.

### Reports are removed by a person

Nothing in a chat deletes a file, and the agent has no tool for it. A person removes one report, or the old ones, from the terminal, the API or the web page:

* `bxAgents routines clean <name> --older-than=30d` (or `--all`) only says what it would remove. Add `--yes` to remove it.
* The API's `POST /routines/reports/clean` does the same, and removes only with `"apply": true`.
* The web page asks first how many files and bytes it would remove, then asks you to confirm.

Deleting a routine keeps its reports. The count of what a clean-up removed is logged in `routines.log`, never a name or text.

### Routes

|                               Route                               |                                                    Does                                                     |
|-------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `GET /routines` (`all=1` for an admin)                            | List, with the schedule in words, status, next and last run, destination and the routine's `conversationId` |
| `GET /routines/get?name=`                                         | One routine with its full prompt                                                                            |
| `POST /routines`                                                  | Make one: `name`, `schedule`, `prompt`, optional `destination` and `chat`                                   |
| `POST /routines/update`                                           | Change `schedule`, `prompt` or `destination`                                                                |
| `POST /routines/pause`, `/resume`, `/run`, `/delete`              | As the tools, with `name`                                                                                   |
| `GET /routines/reports?name=`, `GET /routines/report?name=&file=` | List and read reports                                                                                       |
| `POST /routines/reports/delete`                                   | Remove one report (`name`, `file`)                                                                          |
| `POST /routines/reports/clean`                                    | `name`, `olderThanDays` or `all`; removes only with `apply`                                                 |

Every route answers `404` with "Routines are not turned on" when the feature is off. People see only their own routines, and an admin may act on anyone's by id, or by a name only one owner has. An admin may also send a routine's answer to a gateway, which the tools do not allow for a chat-scope person.
