# Talking to Your Agent

Once you've built your project ([Building Your Agent](/next/course/07-building-your-agent/index.html)), there are three ways in. They all
load the same generated agent and build the same agent tree, so they never diverge from each other.

|      Way in       |                For                 |               Needs                |
|-------------------|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| `bxAgents chat`   | You, talking to it                 | A terminal                         |
| `bxAgents invoke` | A script, CI, a quick check        | Nothing                            |
| `bxAgents serve`  | A browser, a program, other people | `boxlang-miniserver` on the `PATH` |

## `chat`: the terminal chat

```bash
bxAgents chat                                  # local chat in an isolated runtime
bxAgents chat --server [--port=<port>]         # the full app, on its own throwaway server
bxAgents chat --connect=http://127.0.0.1:8791  # the full app, on a server you already run
bxAgents chat --no-tui                         # a plain line-by-line prompt
```

At a terminal this draws a full-screen chat, not a bare prompt (the whole tour is in
[The terminal UI](/next/guides/terminal-ui/index.html)). Finished turns are ordinary terminal text, so your scrollback and
search keep working. Answers stream in as formatted Markdown, tool calls show their arguments and how long they
took, and a run that needs approval asks in place.

![The terminal chat after two answers, with the message box open for a new command](/next/assets/tui/chat-answer.png)

What you can do in it:

* **Keys.** Enter sends, Shift+Enter adds a line, Up and Down walk your history, Esc stops the agent, and a message typed while it works steers it. `?` or `/keys` lists every key.
* **Slash commands.** Type `/` for a menu: `/help`, `/tools`, `/model`, `/info` and more. Every command is listed in [Slash commands](/next/guides/slash-commands/index.html). Later lessons use `/skills`, `/profile`, `/remember`, `/notes`, `/settings` and `/stats`.
* **Sessions.** Every chat is a conversation kept in the agent's data home (`~/.bxagents/acme-support/`), the same list the web app shows. `/sessions` lists them, `/resume` goes back to one, `/new` starts another, `/name` names it, `/fork` copies it and carries on in the copy, and `/export` saves it as Markdown or HTML. `bxAgents chat --continue` reopens the latest one.
* **Context.** The hint row under the box shows how much of the model's window is used, such as `ctx ~12.4k / 128k 9%`. `/context` shows what it is made of.
* **Files and pictures.** `@` lists files, and `@notes.md` puts a text file's content in your message.
* **Recording.** `bxAgents chat --record=demo.cast` saves the screen as an asciicast file.

The default mode starts a separate BoxLang process using the project's `.build/runtime/boxlang.json` and
`.build/runtime` home, then loads the generated factory directly: no server, but also no ColdBox (no scheduler,
no interceptors, no gateway registry). When those matter, `--server` boots a real miniserver and drives the chat
over HTTP against your project's agent API, and `--connect` does the same against a server you already have
running; both stream the reply and carry the conversation across turns. If the server wants a token
([Who Is Allowed](/next/course/users-roles-and-tokens/index.html)), pass `--token=<token>` or set `BXAGENTS_TOKEN`.

Try it. Open the chat on the project and say hello, then ask for a command menu with `/` and look at `/model`.
Leave with `exit`:

```bash
cd ~/bxagents-course/acme-support
bxAgents chat
```

You see the screen above, with the scripted model's answer: *Hello from the practice model...* A terminal that
cannot draw, or a pipe, gets the plain prompt instead. It echoes what you type as you type it, so piped input
looks untidy, which is one more reason scripts use `invoke`:

```bash
cd ~/bxagents-course/acme-support
printf 'hello\nexit\n' | bxAgents chat --no-tui
```

```text
Chatting with the agent - type 'exit' or 'quit' to leave.
...
agent> Hello from the practice model. I am scripted: I only say what the course told me to say.
...
Chat session ended
```

The plain prompt sends everything, slash commands included, to the model. Slash commands belong to the full-screen
chat, the web app and the chat platforms.

## `invoke`: one turn, no screen

```bash
bxAgents invoke --message=hello
bxAgents invoke --message=hello --json
```

```text
Hello from the practice model. I am scripted: I only say what the course told me to say.
{"response":"Hello from the practice model. I am scripted: I only say what the course told me to say."}
```

`invoke` exists for scripting and CI, where `chat`'s terminal requirement is a hard blocker. By default it loads
the generated factory in the already-started BoxLang process, so there is no `serve` prerequisite. Unlike `chat`,
it does not start a separate process with the project's runtime config and home. `--json` prints
`{"response": "..."}`. Add `--server` to launch a real, throwaway `boxlang-miniserver` and send the message as a
genuine HTTP request to your project's agent API: it exercises the path a browser takes.
> **Flag values without spaces**
>
> With the BoxLang 1.19.0 launcher a quoted value with spaces is split at the spaces, so
> `--message="where is my order"` does not work yet; see
> [Quoting flag values](/next/cli-reference/index.html#quoting-flag-values). That is why this course writes `--message=refund`
> and the scripted model listens for single words.

## `serve`: a real HTTP server

```bash
bxAgents serve --port=8791
```

`serve` requires a prior `build` and `boxlang-miniserver` on the `PATH` ([Installing BxAgents](/next/course/03-installing-bxagents/index.html)).
It launches a real server process that serves `.build/public` (the code in `.build/app` is not reachable from the
web), started in `.build` with its own `.build/runtime` BoxLang home, so each project's compiled-class cache stays
isolated and the BoxLang modules installed on your machine are not loaded into it. The agent API is at
`/__bxagents`, and the web app is the next lesson's subject.

The three ways share what the agent remembers: a conversation started in the terminal shows up in the web app's
list, and the other way round.

## Checkpoint

Nothing changed in `acme-support/`: this lesson was about ways in. From here on the agent gets abilities.

Full reference: [Quick Start](/next/getting-started/quick-start/index.html), [CLI Reference](/next/cli-reference/index.html).

Next: [Giving Your Agent Tools](/next/course/09-giving-your-agent-tools/index.html)

# Testing Your Agent

Every project scaffolded via `bxAgents new` ([Scaffolding Your First Agent](/next/course/04-scaffolding-your-first-agent/index.html))
already has a root `box.json` (TestBox as a development dependency) and a ready-to-run
`tests/` folder with `tests/specs/AgentSpec.bx`, a spec that passes out of the box.

```bash
cd my-agent
box install       # fetches testbox into lib/testbox (new does it too, unless you pass --skipInstall)
bxAgents test
```

## Writing a spec

Extend `bxModules.bxagents.models.testing.BaseAgentSpec` instead of
`testbox.system.BaseSpec` directly:

```javascript
// tests/specs/AgentSpec.bx
class extends="bxModules.bxagents.models.testing.BaseAgentSpec" {

	function run() {
		describe( "my-agent", function() {

			it( "responds to a greeting", function() {
				mockResponses( [ "Hello! How can I help you today?" ] )

				var response = agent.run( "Hi there" )

				expect( response ).toContainText( "Hello" )
			} )

		} )
	}

}
```

`BaseAgentSpec` builds your agent once per spec bundle, against a **throwaway temp
copy** of your project - it never touches your real `.build`, so testing never
clobbers a real `build`/`serve`/`package` cycle. The built agent is exposed as `agent`.

## Testing needs no API key

By default, `bxAgents test` builds your agent using an `Agent.yml` `test` environment
override, scaffolded automatically by `new`:

```yaml
environments:
  test:
    model: mock/mock-model
```

This is the same `mock` provider you met in [The Agent Definition - Agent.yml](/next/course/05-agent-bx/index.html) - no network
call, no API key, deterministic CI.

## `mockResponses()`

Scripts the agent's next replies, consumed in order - one per LLM round-trip,
including the intermediate turns of a tool-calling loop:

```javascript
mockResponses( [
	{ toolCalls: [ { name: "getWeather", arguments: { city: "Miami" } } ] },
	"It's sunny in Miami!"
] )

var response = agent.run( "What's the weather in Miami?" )
```

A plain string scripts a final reply. A `{ toolCalls: [...] }` struct scripts a
tool-call turn - the named tool **actually executes for real** against your real
`tools/` implementation (from [Giving Your Agent Tools](/next/course/09-giving-your-agent-tools/index.html)); only the
LLM's own reply is scripted, never the tool's behavior.

## Matchers built for agent behavior

|                Matcher                 |                                                                Checks                                                                |
|----------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `toContainText( "substring" )`         | The response contains the given text, case-insensitively.                                                                            |
| `toHaveCalledTool( "toolName" )`       | The agent actually decided to invoke the named tool.                                                                                 |
| `toHaveReceivedMessage( "substring" )` | Some message sent to the provider contained the given text - useful for asserting your `instructions.md` actually reached the model. |

```javascript
expect( agent ).toHaveCalledTool( "getWeather" )
expect( agent ).notToHaveCalledTool( "getStockPrice" )
```

## Try it

You made Acme support with `--skipInstall`, so TestBox is not there yet. Install it (this needs the internet; `box` is
the CommandBox command, see [Installing BxAgents](/next/course/03-installing-bxagents/index.html)). The suite `new` wrote passes straight away:

```bash
cd ~/bxagents-course/acme-support
box install
bxAgents test
```

```text
...
Bundles: 1 | Suites: 1 | Specs: 1
Pass: 1 | Fail: 0 | Error: 0 | Skipped: 0
```

Now test what Acme cares about: that a question about an order calls the order tool. The mocked model first asks for the
tool, the tool really runs against your `tools/Orders.bx`, and the mocked model then answers:

```javascript
class extends="bxModules.bxagents.models.testing.BaseAgentSpec" {

	function run() {
		describe( "order lookups", function() {

			it( "calls the order tool and reports the answer", function() {
				mockResponses( [
					{ toolCalls : [ { name : "orderStatus", arguments : { orderNumber : "48213" } } ] },
					"Order 48213 has shipped."
				] )

				var response = agent.run( "Where is order 48213?" )

				expect( agent ).toHaveCalledTool( "orderStatus" )
				expect( response ).toContainText( "shipped" )
			} )

		} )
	}

}
```

```bash
bxAgents test
```

```text
Bundles: 2 | Suites: 2 | Specs: 2
Pass: 2 | Fail: 0 | Error: 0 | Skipped: 0
```

`test` prints pass, fail, error and skipped counts, one line per failure, and exits non-zero on a failure, so it can gate
a deploy in the last lesson. Because the model is mocked, the suite needs no key, no network and no scripted model; the
scripted model of this course is for *talking* to the agent, the mock for *proving* it.

## Checkpoint

`acme-support/tests/specs/` has `AgentSpec.bx` and `OrderSpec.bx`. `kit/resume.sh 19-testing-your-agent` restores them.

Full reference: [tests/](/next/conventions/testing/index.html).

Next: [Packaging, Deploying, and Wrapping Up](/next/course/20-packaging-deploying-and-wrapping-up/index.html)

body: tests/ Every project scaffolded via bxAgents new gets a root box.json (declaring testbox as a development dependency, installed into lib/testbox ) and a ready-to-run tests/ folder with tests/specs/AgentSpec.bx , an example spec that passes out of the box. cd my-agent box install # fetches testbox into lib/testbox (new already ran this for you) bxAgents test Info Inspired by the coldbox-templates/boxlang template's own dedicated tests/ + box.json folder - adapted to BxAgents' own simpler testing story. Testing an agent is about its behavior (what it says, which tools it calls), not HTTP routing, so there's no Application.bx /ColdBox virtual app involved here at all. Writing a spec Extend bxModules.bxagents.models.testing.BaseAgentSpec (a testbox.system.BaseSpec subclass) instead of testbox.system.BaseSpec directly: // tests/specs/AgentSpec.bx class extends="bxModules.bxagents.models.testing.BaseAgentSpec" { function run() { describe( "my-agent", function() { it( "responds to a greeting", function() { mockResponses( [ "Hello! How can I help you today?" ] ) var response = agent.run( "Hi there" ) expect( response ).toContainText( "Hello" ) } ) } ) } } BaseAgentSpec builds your agent once per spec bundle ( beforeAll() ), against a throwaway temp copy of your project - it never touches your real .build , so running tests never clobbers (or is clobbered by) a real build / serve / package cycle. The built agent is exposed as agent . Testing against the mock provider By default, bxAgents test builds your agent using the test environment override in Agent.yml (scaffolded automatically): # Agent.yml environments: test: model: mock/mock-model A class-based Agent.bx expresses the same override as a test() method returning { model : "mock/mock-model" } . In the test environment every profile is pointed at the mock provider too, so a project with profiles needs no key either. This means your tests need no API key and no network access out of the box - the same mock provider convention used throughout BxAgents' own test suite. Edit this override if you want a spec to run against a real provider instead (you'll need a real API key available in the environment running the tests). mockResponses( responses ) Scripts the agent's next replies, consumed in order - one per LLM round-trip, including the intermediate turns of a tool-calling loop: mockResponses( [ { toolCalls: [ { name: "getWeather", arguments: { city: "Miami" } } ] }, "It's sunny in Miami!" ] ) var response = agent.run( "What's the weather in Miami?" ) A plain string scripts a final reply. A { toolCalls: [ { name, arguments } ] } struct scripts a tool-call turn - the named tool actually executes for real (against your real tools/ implementation), and its real return value is what the next round-trip sees; only the LLM's own reply is scripted, never the tool's behavior. Custom matchers BaseAgentSpec registers a few matchers, tailored to testing agent behavior, via TestBox's own addMatchers() extension point - use them exactly like any built-in TestBox matcher, including negation ( notTo... ): Matcher Checks toContainText( "substring" ) The actual value (usually a response string) contains the given text, case-insensitively. toHaveCalledTool( "toolName" ) The agent's own recorded provider requests show it actually decided to invoke the named tool - not just that the tool exists. toHaveReceivedMessage( "substring" ) Some message actually sent to the provider (any role, any round-trip) contained the given text - useful for asserting your system prompt/instructions actually reached the model. expect( agent ).toHaveCalledTool( "getWeather" ) expect( agent ).notToHaveCalledTool( "getStockPrice" ) Running tests bxAgents test Runs your project's tests/specs/** via TestBox, in a fresh child process (so it never fights over BoxLang's own class-mapping caches with anything else you're running). Prints bundle/suite/spec counts and pass/fail/error/skipped totals, plus one line per failure, and exits non-zero if anything failed - suitable as a CI gate before deploy . Warning bxAgents test requires TestBox actually installed in lib/testbox ( box install in the project root; tests/testbox is also found, for projects scaffolded before box.json moved to the root) - it errors clearly, rather than silently reporting zero specs, if that hasn't been done yet.

# tests/

Every project scaffolded via `bxAgents new` gets a root [`box.json`](/next/conventions/box-json/index.html) (declaring `testbox` as a development dependency, installed into `lib/testbox`) and a ready-to-run `tests/` folder with `tests/specs/AgentSpec.bx`, an example spec that passes out of the box.


>
> Inspired by the `coldbox-templates/boxlang` template's own dedicated `tests/` + `box.json` folder - adapted to BxAgents' own simpler testing story. Testing an agent is about its **behavior** (what it says, which tools it calls), not HTTP routing, so there's no `Application.bx`/ColdBox virtual app involved here at all.

## Writing a spec

Extend `bxModules.bxagents.models.testing.BaseAgentSpec` (a `testbox.system.BaseSpec` subclass) instead of `testbox.system.BaseSpec` directly:

```javascript
// tests/specs/AgentSpec.bx
class extends="bxModules.bxagents.models.testing.BaseAgentSpec" {

	function run() {
		describe( "my-agent", function() {

			it( "responds to a greeting", function() {
				mockResponses( [ "Hello! How can I help you today?" ] )

				var response = agent.run( "Hi there" )

				expect( response ).toContainText( "Hello" )
			} )

		} )
	}

}
```

`BaseAgentSpec` builds your agent once per spec bundle (`beforeAll()`), against a **throwaway temp copy** of your project - it never touches your real `.build`, so running tests never clobbers (or is clobbered by) a real `build`/`serve`/`package` cycle. The built agent is exposed as `agent`.

## Testing against the mock provider

By default, `bxAgents test` builds your agent using the `test` environment override in `Agent.yml` (scaffolded automatically):

```yaml
# Agent.yml
environments:
  test:
    model: mock/mock-model
```

A class-based `Agent.bx` expresses the same override as a `test()` method returning `{ model : "mock/mock-model" }`.

In the `test` environment every [profile](/next/conventions/models/index.html#profiles) is pointed at the `mock` provider too, so a project with profiles needs no key either.

This means your tests need **no API key and no network access** out of the box - the same `mock` provider convention used throughout BxAgents' own test suite. Edit this override if you want a spec to run against a real provider instead (you'll need a real API key available in the environment running the tests).

### `mockResponses( responses )`

Scripts the agent's next replies, consumed in order - one per LLM round-trip, including the intermediate turns of a tool-calling loop:

```javascript
mockResponses( [
	{ toolCalls: [ { name: "getWeather", arguments: { city: "Miami" } } ] },
	"It's sunny in Miami!"
] )

var response = agent.run( "What's the weather in Miami?" )
```

A plain string scripts a final reply. A `{ toolCalls: [ { name, arguments } ] }` struct scripts a tool-call turn - the named tool **actually executes for real** (against your real `tools/` implementation), and its real return value is what the next round-trip sees; only the LLM's own reply is scripted, never the tool's behavior.

## Custom matchers

`BaseAgentSpec` registers a few matchers, tailored to testing agent behavior, via TestBox's own `addMatchers()` extension point - use them exactly like any built-in TestBox matcher, including negation (`notTo...`):

|                Matcher                 |                                                                                      Checks                                                                                       |
|----------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `toContainText( "substring" )`         | The actual value (usually a response string) contains the given text, case-insensitively.                                                                                         |
| `toHaveCalledTool( "toolName" )`       | The agent's own recorded provider requests show it actually decided to invoke the named tool - not just that the tool exists.                                                     |
| `toHaveReceivedMessage( "substring" )` | Some message actually sent to the provider (any role, any round-trip) contained the given text - useful for asserting your system prompt/instructions actually reached the model. |

```javascript
expect( agent ).toHaveCalledTool( "getWeather" )
expect( agent ).notToHaveCalledTool( "getStockPrice" )
```

## Running tests

```bash
bxAgents test
```

Runs your project's `tests/specs/**` via TestBox, in a fresh child process (so it never fights over BoxLang's own class-mapping caches with anything else you're running). Prints bundle/suite/spec counts and pass/fail/error/skipped totals, plus one line per failure, and exits non-zero if anything failed - suitable as a CI gate before `deploy`.
> **Warning**
>
> `bxAgents test` requires TestBox actually installed in `lib/testbox` (`box install` in the project root; `tests/testbox` is also found, for projects scaffolded before `box.json` moved to the root) - it errors clearly, rather than silently reporting zero specs, if that hasn't been done yet.

markdown:
# The Agent Asks First

Some things an agent should not do on its own. Saving a routine that will run every morning as you, saving a new
skill into its own memory, forgetting a note: BxAgents makes the run **stop** at those tools, shows the person what
the agent is about to do, and carries on only when the person says so. That pause is *human-in-the-loop*, and it is
what you will meet in this lesson.
> **What you will build**
>
> A turned-on `routines` setting, and an approval you reject and then approve, first from a script and then by
> clicking in the web app. About 20 minutes.

## What asks first

Tools BxAgents gives the agent are named `{type}_{action}`, and the ones that change something lasting need a
person's approval:

|                                                         Tool                                                          |                                       Does                                       |                        Asks first                        |
|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------|
| `routine_schedule`, `routine_update`, `routine_delete`                                                                | Make, change or delete a [routine](/next/course/routines-and-reports/index.html) | Yes                                                      |
| `skill_save`                                                                                                          | Save a skill the agent wrote for itself                                          | Yes, unless `skills.autoApprove: true`                   |
| `note_forget`                                                                                                         | Forget a note                                                                    | Yes, while `notes.approveForget` is `true` (the default) |
| `routine_list`, `routine_pause`, `report_save`, `note_remember` and the other `routine_*`, `report_*`, `note_*` tools | Read, or add                                                                     | No                                                       |

The Registry page of the web app marks the tools that ask first. The tools of your own `tools/` folder run without
asking: the docs do not describe a way for one of them to ask, so this lesson uses the built-in ones.

## 1. Turn routines on

`routine_schedule` only exists when routines are on. They are off by default, so a published agent never grows
automated work by surprise. Add these lines at the end of `Agent.yml`. `minInterval: 1m` lets a routine repeat every
minute, which the course needs; the default is 5 minutes:

```yaml

routines:
  enabled: true
  minInterval: 1m
```

Rebuild and serve it (Terminal 3). Stop the server from the last lesson first, with Ctrl+C there, because a server
runs the app that was built when it started:

```bash
cd ~/bxagents-course/acme-support
bxAgents build
```

```text
Build succeeded: <anything>/acme-support/.build/app
```

```bash
cd ~/bxagents-course/acme-support
bxAgents serve --port=8791
```

## 2. See the run stop

In the web app (`http://127.0.0.1:8791/chat`) type `routine`. The scripted model answers a message with that word by
calling `routine_schedule`. Instead of a result, the chat shows an approval card with the tool, its arguments and
three buttons.

The terminal chat asks the same question in place: approve once, approve for the conversation, or reject. And a
program sees the same thing, because the web page only uses the agent API. Here is the whole exchange from a
script. `invoke` answers with `"type":"suspend"` and a `threadId` instead of an answer:

```bash
B=http://127.0.0.1:8791/__bxagents
curl -s -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"input":"routine"}' $B/invoke
```

```text
{"output":{"reason":"","data":{"pendingActions":[{"toolName":"routine_schedule","toolArgs":{"name":"weekly-report","schedule":"every 5m","prompt":"report"}}],<anything>"type":"suspend"},"threadId":"<anything>","success":true}
```

The run is saved by the agent's *checkpointer* (the default `cache` one is enough here) and waits. Ask what it waits
for with the thread id, then answer with `reject`:

```bash
B=http://127.0.0.1:8791/__bxagents
T=$(curl -s -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"input":"routine"}' $B/invoke | sed 's/.*"threadId":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/')
curl -s "$B/pending?threadId=$T"
echo
curl -s -N -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d "{\"threadId\":\"$T\",\"decision\":\"reject\"}" $B/resume | grep '"content"' | cut -d'"' -f4 | tr -d '\n'
echo
bxAgents routines list
```

```text
{"pendingActions":[{"toolName":"routine_schedule","toolArgs":{"name":"weekly-report","schedule":"every 5m","prompt":"report"}}],"pending":true,"threadId":"<anything>","success":true}
The routine request finished. The tool answered: [Tool call blocked: Rejected by human operator<anything>
No routines yet. Ask the agent to schedule one, or use: bxAgents routines add --name=... --schedule=... --prompt=...
```

The tool never ran, the agent was told it was refused, and no routine exists. Run it again and answer `approve`:

```bash
B=http://127.0.0.1:8791/__bxagents
T=$(curl -s -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"input":"routine"}' $B/invoke | sed 's/.*"threadId":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/')
curl -s -N -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d "{\"threadId\":\"$T\",\"decision\":\"approve\"}" $B/resume | grep '"content"' | cut -d'"' -f4 | tr -d '\n'
echo
bxAgents routines list
```

```text
The routine request finished. The tool answered: <anything>
weekly-report         every 5 minutes           not run yet           next <anything>
```

The answer is the tool's real result: the routine's name, its schedule *in words* ("every 5 minutes", read back so
a mistake is seen straight away) and when it first runs. The next lessons use it.

## The three answers

`resume` takes one of three decisions:

|     Decision      |            Button            |                                  Does                                  |
|-------------------|------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `approve`         | Approve                      | Runs this one call                                                     |
| `approve_session` | Approve for the conversation | Runs it, and does not ask again for the same tool in this conversation |
| `reject`          | Reject                       | Does not run it; the agent is told, and answers accordingly            |

`resume` can also carry `editedData`, an edited set of arguments, and `reason`, which the agent sees on a rejection.

## Who may answer

* **A run belongs to the person or token that started it.** `GET /pending` answers "nothing pending" and `POST /resume` answers `403` to anyone else, so a visitor holding someone else's thread id can neither read the arguments nor approve. [Who Is Allowed](/next/course/users-roles-and-tokens/index.html) comes back to this with two tokens.
* **Who approved is filled in by the server**, from the session, never from the request.
* **A routine's own run** stops for approval like any chat: the routine shows as *waiting for approval* and the person answers in its conversation. After `approvalTimeout` (24 hours by default) the run is cancelled and counts as a failure.
* On a chat platform the approval goes through that platform's own buttons. The `cli` gateway type is the blocking prompt in a terminal.

## Checkpoint

`Agent.yml` has the `routines:` block and the agent now has a routine called `weekly-report`. The routine lives in
the agent's data home, not in the project, so `kit/resume.sh` does not touch it. `kit/resume.sh approvals` restores
the `routines:` lines; rebuild after.

Full reference: [The web app](/next/conventions/web-ui/index.html#human-in-the-loop) and [routines](/next/conventions/routines/index.html#the-tools).

Next: [What It Remembers, and for Whom](/next/course/memory-and-notes/index.html)

Only the active block is applied, on top of the top-level keys. You'll use this exact mechanism for the mock provider in your tests ( Testing Your Agent ), which is why bxAgents new already gives you a test block. Full reference: Agent.yml . When you need code: Agent.bx Agent.yml covers almost every agent. It is a real class extending bx-ai's AiAgent , which the build instantiates: class extends="bxModules.bxai.models.runnables.AiAgent" { function init() { super.init( name : "my-agent", description : "A helpful assistant", instructions: "You are a helpful assistant.", model : aiModel( provider: "openai", params: { model: "gpt-5" } ) ) return this } } Scaffold one with bxAgents new --class , or start in YAML and switch later: create the Agent.bx , move the settings across, and delete the Agent.yml . This replaces the file bxAgents new wrote (its test block stays): # Acme support: the agent this course builds, lesson by lesson. name: acme-support description: Answers questions about orders, returns and shipping for Acme. provider: openai-compatible model: fast-model usage: true environments: test: model: mock/mock-model Ask the agent to check the file still describes a valid agent: cd ~/bxagents-course/acme-support bxAgents inspect --section=agents ... <anything>acme-support openai-compatible/fast-model ... markdown:
# The Agent Definition - Agent.yml

`Agent.yml` is the **only required file** in a BxAgents project (beside the
instructions it points at). It is plain settings - a name, a model, and any optional
extras - and the build turns it into a real
[BX AI agent](https://ai.ortusbooks.com/main-components/agents/class-based-agents).
No code needed.

```yaml
name: my-agent
description: A helpful assistant
model: openai/gpt-5
instructions: |
  You are a helpful assistant.
```

That is a complete agent. `bxAgents new` scaffolds this shape for you (see
[Scaffolding Your First Agent](/next/course/04-scaffolding-your-first-agent/index.html)), with the system prompt in an
`instructions.md` beside it (see [instructions.md and the System Prompt](/next/course/06-instructions-and-system-prompt/index.html)).
> **Info**
>
> A folder holds **one** agent definition. An `Agent.yml` together with an
> `Agent.bx` (or an `Agent.yml`) in the same folder is an error, and the build names
> both files so you can keep one.

## The keys

|                           Key                            |                                                                                                               What it does                                                                                                                |
|----------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `name`                                                   | The agent's name. Also its WireBox binding key, so it must be unique across the whole project.                                                                                                                                            |
| `model`                                                  | A `provider/model` slug (see below).                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| `description`                                            | Optional.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| `instructions`                                           | Inline system prompt. An `instructions.md` beside the file wins when both exist.                                                                                                                                                          |
| `tools`                                                  | Module tools this agent gets, as `item@module` or `*@module` (see [Giving Your Agent Tools](/next/course/09-giving-your-agent-tools/index.html)).                                                                                         |
| `toolOptions`                                            | Options for a module's tools, keyed by module name.                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| `subAgents`                                              | Names of sibling folders under `subagents/` (see [Composing Subagents](/next/course/11-composing-subagents/index.html)).                                                                                                                  |
| `mcpServers`                                             | Remote MCP servers the agent can call (see [Hosting and Consuming MCP Servers](/next/course/17-hosting-mcp-servers/index.html)).                                                                                                          |
| `security`, `memory`, `checkpointer`                     | Guardrails, conversation memory and human-in-the-loop state.                                                                                                                                                                              |
| `gatewaySession`                                         | How chat gateways queue messages, which slash commands they answer and whether they read attachments (see [Connecting Chat Platforms](/next/course/14-connecting-chat-platforms/index.html)).                                             |
| `agentApi`                                               | The always-on agent API: who may call it (tokens, allowed addresses, rate limit) and where it is served (see [Exposing Your Agent over HTTP and MCP](/next/course/13-exposing-http-and-mcp/index.html)).                                  |
| `environments`                                           | Per-environment overrides (see below).                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| `provider`, `params`, `options`, `providers`, `profiles` | The model and its settings (see [Models and Profiles](/next/course/12-named-model-configs/index.html)).                                                                                                                                   |
| `notes`, `routines`, `vault`, `volumes`, `usage`         | What the agent keeps and may do: short notes about people, prompts it runs on a schedule, secrets it may use, folders its file tools may reach, and a record of token counts for `bxAgents stats`. Each has a lesson later in the course. |
| `tui`, `extensions`, and more                            | The look of the terminal chat, values for extensions and the rest, all listed in the [Agent.yml](/next/conventions/agent-yaml/index.html) reference.                                                                                      |

An **unknown key is an error** that lists the valid ones, so a typo such as `modle:`
can never quietly do nothing. Wrong types and empty values are errors too.
> **Info**
>
> The checkpointer is the one thing the build fills in unasked. An agent reachable
> from a gateway with no checkpointer has silently broken human-in-the-loop, so a
> definition that sets none still gets the `cache` default.

## The model slug

`model` is BxAgents' own convention - bx-ai itself takes `provider` and `model` as two
separate arguments. BxAgents splits the slug **on the first `/` only**:

|          `model` value          |   provider   |        model         |
|---------------------------------|--------------|----------------------|
| `openai/gpt-5`                  | `openai`     | `gpt-5`              |
| `openrouter/anthropic/claude-x` | `openrouter` | `anthropic/claude-x` |
| `mock/mock-model`               | `mock`       | `mock-model`         |

`mock` is a real provider that never makes a network call - useful for tests (see
[Testing Your Agent](/next/course/19-testing-your-agent/index.html)). The course itself uses `openai-compatible`
against the scripted model instead, because that one also streams and calls tools like a real
provider does.

## Adding settings

Other settings are just more keys:

```yaml
name: with-mcp-servers-agent
model: openai/gpt-5
mcpServers:
  - https://example.com/mcp
```

## Environment overrides

`environments` maps an environment name (`production`, `development`, or any custom
name) to a block of overrides:

```yaml
name: my-agent
model: openai/gpt-5

environments:
  production:
    model: openai/gpt-5-mini
  test:
    model: mock/mock-model
```

The active environment resolves, highest wins: `--environment` CLI flag \>
`BX_AGENTS_ENV` env var \> `"development"` default. `bxAgents build --environment=production`
picks it up. Only the active block is applied, on top of the top-level keys. You'll use
this exact mechanism for the `mock` provider in your tests ([Testing Your Agent](/next/course/19-testing-your-agent/index.html)),
which is why `bxAgents new` already gives you a `test` block.

Full reference: [Agent.yml](/next/conventions/agent-yaml/index.html).

## When you need code: Agent.bx

`Agent.yml` covers almost every agent. Reach for the advanced class form, `Agent.bx`,
only when the definition itself needs code: hooks, dynamic instructions, tools
registered in code, an overridden method, or computing the environment with
`detectEnvironment()`. It is a real class extending bx-ai's `AiAgent`, which the build
instantiates:

```javascript
class extends="bxModules.bxai.models.runnables.AiAgent" {

	function init() {
		super.init(
			name        : "my-agent",
			description : "A helpful assistant",
			instructions: "You are a helpful assistant.",
			model       : aiModel( provider: "openai", params: { model: "gpt-5" } )
		)
		return this
	}

}
```

Scaffold one with `bxAgents new --class`, or start in YAML and switch later: create the
`Agent.bx`, move the settings across, and delete the `Agent.yml`. Full reference:
[Agent.bx](/next/conventions/agent-bx/index.html).

## Try it

Give Acme support a description, and turn on usage recording now so the later lessons have numbers to show.
This replaces the file `bxAgents new` wrote (its `test` block stays):

```yaml
# Acme support: the agent this course builds, lesson by lesson.
name: acme-support
description: Answers questions about orders, returns and shipping for Acme.
provider: openai-compatible
model: fast-model
usage: true

environments:
  test:
    model: mock/mock-model
```

Ask the agent to check the file still describes a valid agent:

```bash
cd ~/bxagents-course/acme-support
bxAgents inspect --section=agents
```

```text
...
<anything>acme-support  openai-compatible/fast-model
...
```

A typo in a key is an error, not a silent no-op. Try `modle: x` on a new line, run `bxAgents inspect`, read the
message that lists the valid keys, and take the line out again.

## Checkpoint

`acme-support/Agent.yml` is the file above. If it is not, `kit/resume.sh 05-agent-bx` puts it back.

Next: [instructions.md and the System Prompt](/next/course/06-instructions-and-system-prompt/index.html)

title: The Build Pipeline
body:
The Build Pipeline bxAgents build runs a fixed sequence of phases, once, producing a plain ColdBox application laid out like the ColdBox BoxLang application template : the code in .build/app , the web root in .build/public . Nothing here runs again at request time - that's the whole point of build-time assembly. This page walks the phases in the exact order BuildPipeline.bx runs them. What is in .build , and what is served .build/ miniserver.json how boxlang-miniserver finds everything below (paths relative to .build) manifest.json the internal manifest (not served, not packaged) app/ the generated code: handlers, config, agent/, tools/, skills/, models/, interceptors/, modules/bxagentsui/ ... Application.bx the template's guard: `abort;` public/ the web root, and the ONLY folder that is served Application.bx the app's Application.bx (see conventions/application-bx.md) index.bxm the front controller every request is rewritten to robots.txt favicon.ico includes/ images/, i18n/, bxagentsui/build/assets/ (the web page's scripts and styles) lib/ coldbox/, modules/ (qb, cbsecurity, cbauth, cbmailservices), java/ runtime/ the BoxLang home boxlang.json the template's engine config modules/bx-agents/ a copy of the bxagents module, under its installed folder name: the ONLY module the served app loads global/ lib/ logs/ boxlang_modules/ the project's own installed BoxLang modules bxAgents serve starts boxlang-miniserver in .build with BOXLANG_HOME=.build/runtime , using .build/miniserver.json : { "port": 8080, "host": "127.0.0.1", "webRoot": "public", "configPath": "runtime/boxlang.json", "serverHome": "runtime", "rewrites": true, "rewriteFileName": "index.bxm", "healthCheck": true, "passPredicate": "regex( '^/index\\.bxm(/.*)?$' )" } Only public/ is a web root. Nothing in app/ , lib/ , runtime/ or boxlang_modules/ can be fetched by its address: /config/agent-settings.json , /project/Agent.yml , /agent/instructions.md and a listing of /config/ were all downloadable without a token before this layout, and answer 404 now. An address nothing routes is a small JSON 404 , not an error page. Only index.bxm runs. The server's default runs any .bx or .bxm under the web root as a request; the passPredicate limits that to the front controller, so a class under app/ is not callable by address. Only the bxagents module loads. The module is copied into runtime/modules as it is installed, folder name included ( bx-module install bx-agents and a dev build both use bx-agents ), with the BoxLang modules bundled inside it. The internal BoxLang mapping remains bxagents . Any other folder there is removed, and runtime/ is the BoxLang home, so the machine's own ~/.boxlang/modules is never read. The copy is skipped while a stamp (the module's box.json and the hash of its jars) is unchanged. The paths are relative , so a copy of .build anywhere (a packaged .bxa unzipped on another machine) is served by starting the server in it. A folder name with a space in it does not work: the boxlang-miniserver launcher script does not quote BOXLANG_HOME . public/includes/ shows its file names (the server lists a folder that has no index file, and miniserver.json has no switch for it); it holds only what the browser is meant to load. The template is carried inside the module as a pinned snapshot ( src/main/bx/templates/coldbox-boxlang , its VERSION names the version and the exact commit), so a build never reads the network. Its public/ files ( index.bxm , robots.txt , favicon.ico , includes/ ), runtime/boxlang.json and app/Application.bx are laid out unchanged, apart from two settings in runtime/boxlang.json : whitespace compression is off, and clearClassFilesOnStartup is off so repeated starts can reuse the runtime's compiled classes. public/Application.bx is derived from the template's and changed (a thin class extending the generated base, see Application.bx ). On BoxLang 1.19.0 a native SSE() stream is unaffected by the whitespace setting (14 frames with it on or off); only a hand-written writeOutput event stream loses its blank lines when it is on, so that line is a safety net. flowchart TD A["1 · Resolve config
AgentConfigResolver"] --> B["2 · Discover
ProjectDiscoverer"] B --> C{"3 · Validate
ProjectValidator"} C -->|"any error"| X["Build throws.
.build/app is never written or touched"] C -->|"clean
warnings never block"| D["4 · Generate"] D --> D1["1 Interceptors"] --> D2["2 Gateways"] --> D3["3 MCP"] --> D4["4 Router"] D4 --> D5["5 Agent API"] --> D6["6 Web UI"] --> D7["7 Extensions"] --> D8["8 Core app skeleton"] --> D9["9 Tools/skills copy"] D9 --> D10["10 Project modules"] --> D11["11 Runtime libraries"] --> D12["12 Scheduler"] D12 --> E["5 · Normalize + write
ManifestNormalizer"] E --> F[".build/manifest.json
+ .build/app and .build/public - a plain ColdBox application"] style C fill:#fff3cd,stroke:#856404 style X fill:#f8d7da,stroke:#721c24 style F fill:#d4edda,stroke:#155724 Before phase 1, build restores any skill that .agents/skills.lock.json lists and the disk lacks, and any extension that extensions.lock.json lists and the disk lacks; a failed restore stops the build. Validation is the gate: it collects every error rather than failing fast, and nothing is generated until it comes back clean. (Packaging into a .bxa is a deliberately separate step - see Deployment & Secrets - so a fast build → inspect → build again loop never pays a packaging cost it doesn't need.) 1. Resolve config AgentConfigResolver loads the agent definition ( Agent.yml , or the class-based Agent.bx ), applies the active environment's overrides (the environments: block of an Agent.yml , or the override method and configure() of an Agent.bx ), then deep-merges in boxlang.json / boxlang-{env}.json / miniserver.json / miniserver-{env}.json if present. The person's own files then go over the result for the root agent: ~/.bxagents/Agent.yml and the agent's own Agent.yml in its data home ( layered settings ). Produces the single resolved config struct every later phase reads from. 2. Discover ProjectDiscoverer walks the project root and enumerates every convention folder ( tools/ , skills/ and the registry's .agents/skills/ , subagents/ , gateways/ , mcp/ , interceptors/ , modules/ ) into raw { name, path, type } entries. schedules/*.bx are listed the same way, one entry per BoxLang scheduler file. Pure discovery - no interpretation of file contents happens yet. 3. Validate ProjectValidator runs every validator and collects every error (never fail-fast) plus any warnings: duplicate tool/skill/model/subagent names, duplicate agent name s across the whole subagent tree (see subagents/ ), circular subagent/module references, the two gateway entry shapes, remote MCP config completeness, and model/provider validity. If any errors were collected, the build throws immediately here - no .build/app is written or touched. Warnings (e.g. a schedules/ folder with no Scheduler.bx in it) never block the build. 4. Generate Only reached once validation is clean. Any .build/app from an earlier build is deleted first, then the template is laid out: its public/ (replacing the old one), its runtime/boxlang.json , app/Application.bx and the empty folders its conventions name. In order: Interceptors - InterceptorSplitter copies agent -scope interceptors into .build/app/interceptors , runtime -scope ones into a separate .build/runtime-interceptors directory, outside the app (BxAgents does not register those for you). Gateways - GatewayGenerator emits aiGatewayRegistry().register(...) statements for channel-adapter entries, and writes a small .build/app/handlers/*.bx webhook handler for each whatsapp-cloud , teams , twilio or github entry. If any entry is a push-style gateway (e.g. type: "telegram" ), it also produces the start-up statement that builds a single bx-ai GatewaySession (bundling every push-style gateway) bound to the project's root agent. MCP - McpGenerator copies local mcp/* servers into .build/app/mcp and emits their mcpServer(...).registerTool(...) registration statements. Router - RouterGenerator writes .build/app/config/Router.bx : the reserved /__bxagents agent API (at agentApi.path , unless agentApi.enabled is false ), the same four turn routes under the path of each exposes: "agent" entry, one route(path).toMCP(...) per exposes: "mcp" entry, the cbSecurity middleware for agentApi.allowedIPs and agentApi.rateLimit when set, a single route("/gateways").toAiGateway() if the project has any channel-adapter gateway, and one webhook route per whatsapp-cloud (GET+POST), teams , twilio or github push-style gateway present. Agent API - AgentApiGenerator writes .build/app/handlers/AgentApi.bx , every action of the agent API ( invoke , stream , batch , info , and the run-control, conversation, notes, command and token actions such as events , cancel , steer , resume , sessions and command ), all served by the one handler. Skipped when agentApi.enabled is false . Web UI - WebUiGenerator runs for any exposes: "webui" entry, installing the web app module at /modules/bxagentsui with its settings in config/bxagentsui.json (mounted at the entry's path , a client of the agent API , so no handler of its own), models/ChatDb.bx (the sign-in accounts and the store's forward-only migrations, built at boot by a start-up statement rather than on whichever request touches the database first) and the user models ( User , UserService , PasswordHasher ). apiKeyEnvVar becomes the agent API's shared secret. When users are declared it also writes the account seeder, the sign-in form ( config/bxagentsui-login.html , served at /login.html ), interceptors/WebUiLoginGate.bx and handlers/ChatAuth.bx . It returns the resolved database config, which the next step needs. Extensions - ExtensionsGenerator copies the project's extensions/ folder to .build/app/extensions and writes config/extensions.json from the extensions: block of Agent.yml , so the served agent loads them. Skipped when there is no extensions/ folder. Core app skeleton - ColdBoxAppGenerator writes the generated base app/bxagents/Application.bx (see Application.bx ), public/Application.bx (derived from the template's own file, and ending as a thin class that extends the base: what is derived and what is changed ), app/bxagents/Scheduler.bx , config/Coldbox.bx , config/WireBox.bx , handlers/NotFound.bx and agent/GeneratedAgentFactory.bx , threading in every statement gathered above (gateway registrations, the GatewaySession start, MCP registrations, the web UI's store warm-up and account seeding, and - if tools/ has any files - a bare aiToolRegistry().scan("app.tools") call: bx-ai expands the dotted path against a mapping, /app here, so it must be a mapping path and not one relative to the app) into the base's after() , which onApplicationStart() calls once ColdBox has loaded. Class paths in generated code go through the template's /app mapping ( app.schedules.Nightly , app.agent.GeneratedAgentFactory , app.interceptors.AuditLogger ). Interceptors are registered there too, one getInterceptorService().register(...) per agent-scope interceptor and web UI gate: the generated config declares no interceptors array and registers them this way, which works (the note on config/Coldbox.bx below says why the array's old failure was measured against a file ColdBox never loaded). Every generated agent also now always receives a checkpointer ( withCheckpointer(...) , defaulting to a cache -backed aiMemory() if the project declares no checkpointer config and the class set none of its own) - without one, human-in-the-loop approval flows through any gateway other than cli fail outright. config/WireBox.bx maps every agent in the tree (root + every subagent) under its own declared name , not just the fixed root "GeneratedAgent" alias - see schedules/ . Each agent node's instructions.md is copied into the app as part of this step, mirroring the source layout under agent/ - the root project's to .build/app/agent/instructions.md , each subagent's to .build/app/agent/subagents//instructions.md - so every node keeps its own and the built app carries the file it reads at runtime. The factory reads all three of its runtime paths ( instructions.md , its own tools/ , and any class-based agent's copied Agent.bx ) through a small generated resolveAppPath() helper that resolves them relative to the factory's own location on disk, falling back to the build-time absolute path if that self-location doesn't resolve - which is what makes a packaged .bxa genuinely relocatable rather than runnable only on the machine that built it. For a project with a webui exposure it also turns session management on, registers the SQLite datasource (naming it as the app default via this.datasource ), creates the database's parent directory in onApplicationStart() - SQLite creates the file but never the folder holding it - and pins qb's grammar in config/Coldbox.bx . That file is called Coldbox.bx (ColdBox's convention) and assigns variables.coldbox and variables.moduleSettings : it used to be called ColdBox.bx , which ColdBox never loads on a case-sensitive file system, with unscoped assignments that are local to configure() in BoxLang, so the generated app name and qb grammar never applied before. It also sets modulesExternalLocation to /modules (ColdBox finds its modules in .build/lib/modules ) and defaultEvent and invalidEventHandler to the generated NotFound.index , the JSON 404. Tools/skills copy - ToolsSkillsCopier wipes and rewrites .build/app/tools and .build/app/skills verbatim from your project's own folders, adding the registry skills from .agents/skills/ to the app's skills/ . Project modules - BoxLangModulesCopier copies the BoxLang modules installed in the project's boxlang_modules/ into .build/boxlang_modules , leaving out any that box.json lists only as a development dependency. Skipped when there is no boxlang_modules/ folder. Runtime libraries - RuntimeLibsCopier copies the ColdBox runtime bundled inside BxAgents into .build/lib : coldbox/ plus modules/qb , modules/cbsecurity , modules/cbauth , modules/cbmailservices and their dependencies. A lib/ folder in your project (same layout) is copied afterwards and wins, which is how you add or override a library. The bundled copy exists only in an installed or built module, so a source checkout skips this step with a warning. Schedulers - SchedulerGenerator copies each schedules/*.bx to .build/app/schedules/.bx , adding extends="app.bxagents.Scheduler" to a class that names no parent ( bxagents.Scheduler , the name the docs use, means the same class). The base already lists them in this.schedulers , so BoxLang starts them with the app. The bxagents module and the server config - ModuleCopier copies the installed bx-agents module into .build/runtime/modules/bx-agents (to a work folder, then renamed, so an interrupted copy never carries the stamp; skipped while the stamp is unchanged), and MiniServerJson writes .build/miniserver.json (port 8080 on 127.0.0.1 ; serve rewrites it with the port and host asked for). A source checkout has no installed module: the build says so, and BXAGENTS_MODULE_DIR names the built one ( build/modules/bx-agents ). 5. Normalize + write the manifest ManifestNormalizer produces the canonical, hash-stamped internal manifest from the discovery + resolved-config data, and the pipeline writes it to .build/manifest.json . Idempotency Rebuilding an unchanged project produces byte-identical output, down to the manifest's per-file content hashes - the entire point of paying the assembly cost once, at build time, rather than deferring any of this work into request handling.

When `users` are declared it also writes the account seeder, the sign-in form (`config/bxagentsui-login.html`, served at `/login.html`), `interceptors/WebUiLoginGate.bx` and `handlers/ChatAuth.bx`. It returns the resolved database config, which the next step needs. 7. **Extensions** - `ExtensionsGenerator` copies the project's `extensions/` folder to `.build/app/extensions` and writes `config/extensions.json` from the `extensions:` block of `Agent.yml`, so the served agent loads them. Skipped when there is no `extensions/` folder. 8. **Core app skeleton** - `ColdBoxAppGenerator` writes the generated base `app/bxagents/Application.bx` (see [Application.bx](/next/conventions/application-bx/index.html)), `public/Application.bx` (derived from the template's own file, and ending as a thin class that extends the base: [what is derived and what is changed](/next/conventions/application-bx/index.html#where-it-ends-up)), `app/bxagents/Scheduler.bx`, `config/Coldbox.bx`, `config/WireBox.bx`, `handlers/NotFound.bx` and `agent/GeneratedAgentFactory.bx`, threading in every statement gathered above (gateway registrations, the `GatewaySession` start, MCP registrations, the web UI's store warm-up and account seeding, and - if `tools/` has any files - a bare `aiToolRegistry().scan("app.tools")` call: bx-ai expands the dotted path against a mapping, `/app` here, so it must be a mapping path and not one relative to the app) into the base's `after()`, which `onApplicationStart()` calls once ColdBox has loaded. Class paths in generated code go through the template's `/app` mapping (`app.schedules.Nightly`, `app.agent.GeneratedAgentFactory`, `app.interceptors.AuditLogger`). Interceptors are registered there too, one `getInterceptorService().register(...)` per agent-scope interceptor and web UI gate: the generated config declares no `interceptors` array and registers them this way, which works (the note on `config/Coldbox.bx` below says why the array's old failure was measured against a file ColdBox never loaded). Every generated agent also now always receives a checkpointer (`withCheckpointer(...)`, defaulting to a `cache`-backed `aiMemory()` if the project declares no `checkpointer` config and the class set none of its own) - without one, human-in-the-loop approval flows through any gateway other than `cli` fail outright. `config/WireBox.bx` maps every agent in the tree (root + every subagent) under its own declared `name`, not just the fixed root `"GeneratedAgent"` alias - see [schedules/](/next/conventions/schedules/index.html). Each agent node's `instructions.md` is **copied into the app** as part of this step, mirroring the source layout under `agent/` - the root project's to `.build/app/agent/instructions.md`, each subagent's to `.build/app/agent/subagents//instructions.md` - so every node keeps its own and the built app carries the file it reads at runtime. The factory reads all three of its runtime paths (`instructions.md`, its own `tools/`, and any class-based agent's copied `Agent.bx`) through a small generated `resolveAppPath()` helper that resolves them relative to the factory's own location on disk, falling back to the build-time absolute path if that self-location doesn't resolve - which is what makes a packaged `.bxa` genuinely relocatable rather than runnable only on the machine that built it. For a project with a `webui` exposure it also turns session management on, registers the SQLite datasource (naming it as the app default via `this.datasource`), creates the database's parent directory in `onApplicationStart()` - SQLite creates the file but never the folder holding it - and pins qb's grammar in `config/Coldbox.bx`. That file is called `Coldbox.bx` (ColdBox's convention) and assigns `variables.coldbox` and `variables.moduleSettings`: it used to be called `ColdBox.bx`, which ColdBox never loads on a case-sensitive file system, with unscoped assignments that are local to `configure()` in BoxLang, so the generated app name and qb grammar never applied before. It also sets `modulesExternalLocation` to `/modules` (ColdBox finds its modules in `.build/lib/modules`) and `defaultEvent` and `invalidEventHandler` to the generated `NotFound.index`, the JSON 404. 9. **Tools/skills copy** - `ToolsSkillsCopier` wipes and rewrites `.build/app/tools` and `.build/app/skills` verbatim from your project's own folders, adding the registry skills from `.agents/skills/` to the app's `skills/`. 10. **Project modules** - `BoxLangModulesCopier` copies the BoxLang modules installed in the project's `boxlang_modules/` into `.build/boxlang_modules`, leaving out any that `box.json` lists only as a development dependency. Skipped when there is no `boxlang_modules/` folder. 11. **Runtime libraries** - `RuntimeLibsCopier` copies the ColdBox runtime bundled inside BxAgents into `.build/lib`: `coldbox/` plus `modules/qb`, `modules/cbsecurity`, `modules/cbauth`, `modules/cbmailservices` and their dependencies. A `lib/` folder in your project (same layout) is copied afterwards and wins, which is how you add or override a library. The bundled copy exists only in an installed or built module, so a source checkout skips this step with a warning. 12. **Schedulers** - [`SchedulerGenerator`](/next/conventions/schedules/index.html) copies each `schedules/*.bx` to `.build/app/schedules/.bx`, adding `extends="app.bxagents.Scheduler"` to a class that names no parent (`bxagents.Scheduler`, the name the docs use, means the same class). The base already lists them in `this.schedulers`, so BoxLang starts them with the app. 13. **The bxagents module and the server config** - `ModuleCopier` copies the installed `bx-agents` module into `.build/runtime/modules/bx-agents` (to a work folder, then renamed, so an interrupted copy never carries the stamp; skipped while the stamp is unchanged), and `MiniServerJson` writes `.build/miniserver.json` (port 8080 on `127.0.0.1`; `serve` rewrites it with the port and host asked for). A source checkout has no installed module: the build says so, and `BXAGENTS_MODULE_DIR` names the built one (`build/modules/bx-agents`). ## 5. Normalize + write the manifest [`ManifestNormalizer`](/next/manifest/index.html) produces the canonical, hash-stamped internal manifest from the discovery + resolved-config data, and the pipeline writes it to `.build/manifest.json`. ## Idempotency Rebuilding an unchanged project produces byte-identical output, down to the manifest's per-file content hashes - the entire point of paying the assembly cost once, at build time, rather than deferring any of this work into request handling.

# The Manifest

Every `build` writes `.build/manifest.json` - BxAgents' own record of exactly what went into the generated app. `bxAgents inspect` reports whether a project was built and the manifest's version and file count in its `build` section (the manifest itself is a plain file you can open); `bxAgents package` copies a **redacted** version of it alongside the `.bxa` (see [Deployment \& Secrets](/next/deployment-and-secrets/index.html)).

## Schema

```json
{
	"manifestVersion": "1.0.0",
	"generator": { "name": "bx-agents", "version": "dev" },
	"agent": {
		"name": "my-agent",
		"description": "",
		"model": "openai/gpt-5",
		"environment": "development"
	},
	"files": [
		{ "category": "tools", "name": "Greeter", "path": "tools/Greeter.bx", "hash": "..." }
	]
}
```

|                 Field                  |                                                                                                                                                                                         Meaning                                                                                                                                                                                          |
|----------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `manifestVersion`                      | Semver stamp for the manifest schema itself (currently `1.0.0`) - `package` refuses to run if this is unset or malformed.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| `generator.name` / `generator.version` | Always `"bx-agents"` / the version string stamped into the build: `dev` unless `bxAgents build --generatorVersion=...` says otherwise.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| `agent`                                | Only safe, structural fields (`name`, `description`, `model`, `environment`) - **never** secrets. For a class-based `Agent.bx` that sets them in code, `name`, `description` and `model` are read from the class. Secrets are never read into the manifest at all; they're resolved by bx-ai itself, live, at runtime.                                                                   |
| `files`                                | One entry per discovered convention-folder item, each `{ category, name, path, hash }`. The categories are `tools`, `skills` (your own and the ones installed from the registry), `subagents`, `gateways`, `schedules` (one per scheduler file), `mcp`, `interceptors` and `modules`. Sorted by category then path for deterministic ordering - independent of filesystem listing order. |

## Content hashes

Each `files[]` entry's `hash` is a SHA-256 of its content:

* **A file**: the hash of its content, with line endings normalized first (CRLF and LF checkouts of the same content hash identically).
* **A directory** (a skill folder, a subagent folder, a module folder): the hash of every contained file's own `relativePath:contentHash`, recursively, sorted for determinism - so renaming or editing any single file inside changes the whole folder's hash.

This is what makes rebuilding an unchanged project produce an **identical** manifest: same categories, same ordering, same hashes, every time - and it's exactly why changing one tool file's content only ever changes that one entry's hash, nothing else.

## Compatibility policy

`manifestVersion` exists so a future breaking change to this schema can be detected by anything reading `manifest.json` (a deploy target, a future `inspect` version, external tooling) - a tool encountering an unrecognized major version should refuse to guess at the shape and fail clearly, rather than silently misreading fields.
