# Welcome to BxAgents

This is a hands-on course on **BxAgents** , a conventions-based AI agent framework for
[BoxLang](https://www.boxlang.io), built on [ColdBox](https://www.coldbox.org) and [BX AI](https://ai.boxlang.io).
The idea is simple: you describe an agent with **files and folders** , not a framework's API, and one command,
`bxAgents build`, assembles a real, runnable ColdBox application out of it.

```text
acme-support/
├── Agent.yml          # name, model, settings
├── instructions.md    # the system prompt
├── tools/             # @AITool functions
├── skills/            # SKILL.md capabilities
├── subagents/         # nested agent trees
├── gateways/          # HTTP, MCP, web app, chat platforms
├── schedules/         # BoxLang schedulers
├── mcp/               # MCP servers you host
├── interceptors/      # lifecycle hooks
├── extensions/        # chat commands, keys and more
└── modules/           # module dependencies
```

Every folder is optional except `Agent.yml`. Add the ones your agent needs and leave the rest empty.

## What you will build

You build **one** agent, from the first lesson to the last: *Acme support*, an assistant that answers questions about
orders, returns and shipping. By the end it has:

* a persona, a tool that looks up an order, a skill with the refund policy, and two models to switch between
* a researcher and a writer it can delegate to
* a web app, a terminal chat and an HTTP API in front of it
* a routine that runs on its own and saves a report, and approvals where a person has to say yes
* notes it keeps about people, accounts and tokens for who is allowed, and a vault for a secret
* a test suite that runs with no key, a backup, and a packaged `.bxa` ready to deploy

## You need no account and no key

The agent talks to a **scripted model** : a small server on your machine that speaks the same protocol as a real model
but only says what the course told it to. [A Model That Needs No Key](/next/course/practice-model/index.html) sets it up in five minutes, and
from then on every command in the course gives the output the lesson shows. When you do have a key, swapping it in is two
lines, and the [last lesson](/next/course/capstone/index.html) shows them. What you need:

* A terminal with a Unix shell (macOS, Linux, or WSL on Windows).
* About 20 minutes per lesson if you type along. There are 29 lessons, so plan a weekend rather than an evening, and stop wherever a lesson ends: each one leaves the project working.
* No BoxLang or ColdBox experience. [Installing BxAgents](/next/course/03-installing-bxagents/index.html) installs everything.

## How the lessons work

Each lesson explains one thing and then has you do it. The parts of a lesson:

* **Try it** holds what you type. A grey block titled `Terminal 2` is a command, a block titled with a path such as `acme-support/Agent.yml` is a file to create, and a block titled `You see` is what the command prints. A `<anything>` in it stands for the part that differs on your machine (a path, a time).
* **Checkpoint** says what `acme-support/` holds now. If your project gets out of step, `kit/resume.sh <lesson>` puts it back to the state after that lesson, and you rebuild.
* A link to the reference page for the deep dive. The course is the guided path; [Conventions](/next/conventions/agent-yaml/index.html) is the exhaustive reference you will come back to.

You will use up to three terminals: **Terminal 1** runs the scripted model and stays open, **Terminal 2** is where you
work, and **Terminal 3** runs `bxAgents serve` from the web app lesson on.

Every command and every output in the course is replayed against the scripted model by a checker in the repository
(`tools/course/check-course.bxs`), so the text cannot drift from what the software does. The few steps that need a
person and a screen (the terminal chat, clicking in the web app) are marked as manual and shown with screenshots.

## The parts of the course

1. **Start** : [what BxAgents is](/next/course/02-what-is-bxagents/index.html), [installing it](/next/course/03-installing-bxagents/index.html), the [scripted model](/next/course/practice-model/index.html) and your [first project](/next/course/04-scaffolding-your-first-agent/index.html).
2. **The agent** : [Agent.yml](/next/course/05-agent-bx/index.html), [the persona](/next/course/06-instructions-and-system-prompt/index.html), [building](/next/course/07-building-your-agent/index.html) and [talking to it](/next/course/08-talking-to-your-agent/index.html).
3. **Teach it** : [tools](/next/course/09-giving-your-agent-tools/index.html), [skills](/next/course/10-packaging-skills/index.html) and [models and profiles](/next/course/12-named-model-configs/index.html).
4. **The web app** : [the web app](/next/course/15-the-generated-web-chat-ui/index.html), [approvals](/next/course/approvals/index.html), [memory and notes](/next/course/memory-and-notes/index.html) and [subagents](/next/course/11-composing-subagents/index.html).
5. **On its own** : [routines and reports](/next/course/routines-and-reports/index.html) and [schedulers](/next/course/16-scheduling-background-work/index.html).
6. **Reach people** : [HTTP and MCP](/next/course/13-exposing-http-and-mcp/index.html), [chat platforms](/next/course/14-connecting-chat-platforms/index.html) and [MCP servers and connectors](/next/course/17-hosting-mcp-servers/index.html).
7. **Run it for a team** : [who is allowed](/next/course/users-roles-and-tokens/index.html), [the vault](/next/course/the-vault/index.html), [each person's settings](/next/course/layered-settings/index.html) and [logs, usage and backups](/next/course/operating-it/index.html).
8. **Extend and ship** : [interceptors and extensions](/next/course/18-interceptors-and-modules/index.html), [testing](/next/course/19-testing-your-agent/index.html), [packaging and deploying](/next/course/20-packaging-deploying-and-wrapping-up/index.html) and the [capstone](/next/course/capstone/index.html).

Next: [What Is BxAgents?](/next/course/02-what-is-bxagents/index.html)

title: What Is BxAgents?
body:
What Is BxAgents? Most agent frameworks wire tools, skills, routes and schedules together at request time , on every boot. BxAgents does the opposite: bxAgents build runs discovery, validation and code generation exactly once , producing a plain ColdBox application in .build/ , laid out like the ColdBox BoxLang template: the code in app/ , the web root in public/ . Starting it afterwards - via bxAgents serve , a real boxlang-miniserver process, or a portable .bxa deployed anywhere BoxLang runs - is then just booting an ordinary app. No convention scanning, no dynamic file walking, no build-time work deferred into the request path. flowchart LR A["your convention tree
Agent.yml, tools/, skills/, ..."] -->|"bxAgents build"| B[".build/
app/ + public/: a plain ColdBox application"] B -->|"bxAgents serve / chat / invoke"| C["running agent"] B -->|"bxAgents package"| D["dist/name-version.bxa"] D -->|"bxAgents deploy"| E["a real target"] style B fill:#d4edda,stroke:#155724 Folders are the API Agent.yml and instructions.md are the only files that matter to get started. Every other convention folder - tools/ , skills/ , subagents/ , gateways/ , schedules/ , mcp/ , interceptors/ , extensions/ , modules/ - is optional and only shapes the generated output if it exists and has content in it . You add conventions as you actually need them, not up front. Agent.yml defines the agent Agent.yml is plain settings - a name, a model, and any optional extras - and the build turns it into a real BX AI agent. No code is needed for most agents. You'll write your first one in The Agent Definition - Agent.yml . When the definition itself needs code (hooks, dynamic instructions, tools registered in code), there is an advanced option: a class-based Agent.bx that extends BX AI's own AiAgent , which the build instantiates as-is. The Agent Definition ends with when to reach for it. What build actually produces Your convention tree on the left, the plain ColdBox application build turns it into on the right: your-agent/ ├── Application.bx ├── Agent.yml ├── instructions.md ├── tools/ ├── skills/ ├── subagents/ ├── gateways/ ├── schedules/ ├── mcp/ ├── interceptors/ └── modules/ .build/ ├── miniserver.json ├── app/ the code (not served) │ ├── bxagents/ Application.bx Scheduler.bx │ ├── config/ Coldbox.bx WireBox.bx Router.bx │ ├── schedules/ agent/ tools/ skills/ mcp/ │ └── handlers/ interceptors/ ├── public/ the web root: the only served folder │ ├── Application.bx │ └── index.bxm ├── lib/ coldbox/ modules/ └── runtime/ boxlang.json modules/bx-agents What build does not produce: the data home A built agent also keeps things while it runs: conversations, notes, access tokens, routines and their reports, the sealed vault, usage counts and logs. They are not in the project and not in .build/ : they live in the agent's data home , ~/.bxagents// , so rebuilding or redeploying never loses them and a backup can copy them. ~/.bxagents/acme-support/ ├── chat.db conversations, notes, tokens, accounts, routines, the sealed vault ├── files/ what the agent writes ├── skills/ skills the agent saved for itself ├── routines/ the reports of each routine ├── logs/ agent, gateways, routines, heartbeat, api └── backups/ made by bxAgents backup That split (what you ship, and what accumulates) comes back in Logs, Usage and Backups . Why this matters Rebuilding an unchanged project produces byte-identical output, down to a hash- stamped manifest recording exactly what went into the build (more on that in Packaging, Deploying, and Wrapping Up ). That's the whole point of paying the assembly cost once, at build time, rather than deferring any of it into request handling. See BxAgents home and The Build Pipeline for more detail whenever you want it. Next: Installing BxAgents

title: What It Remembers, and for Whom
body: What It Remembers, and for Whom "Does it remember me?" has three answers, and an agent that mixes them up is either forgetful or creepy. This lesson separates them and gives Acme support the ones it needs. What you will build notes turned on; one note about a person, one note shared by everyone, and a look at how a second person stays apart. About 20 minutes. markdown:
# What It Remembers, and for Whom

"Does it remember me?" has three answers, and an agent that mixes them up is either forgetful or creepy. This lesson
separates them and gives Acme support the ones it needs.
> **What you will build**
>
> `notes` turned on; one note about a person, one note shared by everyone, and a look at how a second person
> stays apart. About 20 minutes.

## The three kinds

|                   What                   |           Belongs to            |                                       Lasts                                       |                     Where you manage it                     |
|------------------------------------------|---------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Conversation memory**                  | One person and one conversation | As long as the conversation, up to `memory.maxMessages` messages (500 by default) | The Conversations page, `/sessions`, `/clear`, `/compact`   |
| **Notes about a person** (*user* scope)  | One person                      | Across conversations                                                              | The Memory page, `/remember` and `/notes`, `bxAgents notes` |
| **Notes about the work** (*agent* scope) | The agent, so everyone          | Across conversations                                                              | The same, and removing one needs an admin                   |

Conversation memory is on for every agent: the terminal, the web app and the API share one list of conversations in
the agent's data home, so the person finds the same conversation from any of them. Notes are off until you ask. They
are short lines the agent reads at the start of **each conversation**, so a note saved now shows from the next
conversation, not the current one.

## 1. Turn notes on

Add this at the end of `Agent.yml` (`notes: {}` turns them on with the defaults: 1400 characters of notes per
person, 2200 for the agent, and the agent gets `note_remember` and `note_forget` tools):

```yaml

notes: {}
```

```bash
cd ~/bxagents-course/acme-support
bxAgents build
bxAgents notes list
```

```text
Build succeeded: <anything>/acme-support/.build/app
Notes about local: 0 of 1400 characters, 0 notes
  (none yet)
Agent notes (acme-support): 0 of 2200 characters, 0 notes
  (none yet)
```

`local` is who you are on your own machine: the terminal and an open server both call the person `local`. Once
there are tokens or accounts ([Who Is Allowed](/next/course/users-roles-and-tokens/index.html)), the person is the token's name or the
account.

## 2. Add notes yourself

A person manages their notes from a shell. The agent's notes use `--scope=agent`. (The values have no spaces because
of the launcher rule from [A Model That Needs No Key](/next/course/practice-model/index.html); in a chat you would write whole
sentences.)

```bash
bxAgents notes add --text=Prefers-short-answers
bxAgents notes add --text=Orders-ship-from-Leeds --scope=agent
bxAgents notes list
```

```text
Noted (user).
Noted (agent).
Notes about local: 21 of 1400 characters, 1 note
  <anything>  Prefers-short-answers
Agent notes (acme-support): 22 of 2200 characters, 1 note
  <anything>  Orders-ship-from-Leeds
```

Now a second person. Their user notes are their own, and the agent's notes are the same for both:

```bash
bxAgents notes list --user=ada
```

```text
Notes about ada: 0 of 1400 characters, 0 notes
  (none yet)
Agent notes (acme-support): 22 of 2200 characters, 1 note
  <anything>  Orders-ship-from-Leeds
```

In the terminal chat the same person is chosen with `bxAgents chat --user=ada`, and inside the chat `/remember <text>`
and `/notes` do what `notes add` and `notes list` do.

## 3. Let the agent keep one

The agent can save a note itself with `note_remember`, with a scope of `user` or `agent` and a note of one short
line. The scripted model has a rule for the word `remember`. Serve the app (Terminal 3, after stopping the previous
server) and ask through the API, as the open server's one user, `local`:

```bash
cd ~/bxagents-course/acme-support
bxAgents serve --port=8791
```

```bash
curl -s -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"input":"remember"}' http://127.0.0.1:8791/__bxagents/invoke
echo
bxAgents notes list --scope=user
```

```text
{"output":"Noted. I will keep my answers short.","threadId":"<anything>","success":true}
Notes about local: 42 of 1400 characters, 2 notes
  <anything>  Prefers-short-answers
  <anything>  Prefers short answers
```

> **\`invoke\` in the terminal does not save to \`local\`**
>
> `bxAgents invoke` runs the agent in this process, and a note the agent saves there is not saved under `local`.
> To exercise the agent's note tool, go through a server (this lesson's curl), or `invoke --server`.

Saving a note needs no approval. Forgetting one does, by default (`approveForget: true`, see
[The Agent Asks First](/next/course/approvals/index.html)), so an agent cannot quietly erase what a person wrote.

## 4. The Memory page

Open `http://127.0.0.1:8791/chat/memory`. The page has three parts: **About you** (your user notes, which you can add
to, edit and remove), **About the agent** (the shared notes; a member can add and edit, only an admin removes) and
**Conversation memory** (clear the messages of one conversation, or of all).

![The Memory page: your notes, the agent's shared notes and conversation memory](/next/assets/webui/webui-memory.png)

The notes also go over the API (`GET /__bxagents/notes`), which is what the page uses.

## What goes where

* **The data home.** Conversations and notes live in `chat.db` of the agent's data home (`~/.bxagents/acme-support/`), not in the project. `kit/resume.sh` never touches them, and [Logs, Usage and Backups](/next/course/operating-it/index.html) backs them up.
* **Limits.** A note is one line of at most 500 characters. A note that does not fit the limit is refused, and the agent is told how full the notes are so it can replace or forget an older one. Nothing is dropped silently.
* **Compacting.** `/compact` in the chat summarizes the older messages of a conversation and keeps the recent ones (`memory.keepRecent`), and needs a summary model to do it.

## Checkpoint

`Agent.yml` has `notes: {}`. In your data home there is a note about `local` and one about the agent, which a
checkpoint cannot hold. `kit/resume.sh memory-and-notes` restores the project files.

Full reference: [Notes](/next/conventions/agent-yaml/index.html#notes), the [CLI reference](/next/cli-reference/index.html#notes) and
[the web app's Memory page](/next/conventions/web-ui/index.html#memory).

Next: [Composing Subagents](/next/course/11-composing-subagents/index.html)

title: Who Is Allowed
markdown:
# Who Is Allowed

So far the agent has been open: anyone who could reach port 8791 was `local`, and `local` could do everything. That is
right on your own machine and wrong on a network. This lesson closes it, in two ways that fit two kinds of caller:
**people** sign in to the web app with an account, and **programs** (a script, the terminal chat on another machine,
CI) send an access **token**.
> **What you will build**
>
> The web app with two accounts, `ada` (an admin) and `bo` (a member), the agent API behind tokens, and a token
> for a laptop, a script and a phone, one of which you revoke. About 25 minutes.

## What changes when it is closed

|                         |         Open (so far)         |                   With accounts and tokens                   |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------|
| Who the caller is       | `local`, always               | The signed-in account, or the token's name                   |
| Conversations and notes | One shared set                | Each person's own                                            |
| The agent API           | Anyone who can reach the port | A sign-in cookie or an `x-bxagents-token` header, else `401` |
| Admin pages and routes  | Everyone                      | Admins only (`403` to the rest)                              |

There are two roles. A **member** talks to the agent and sees only their own conversations, notes and preferences. An
**admin** can also do what the operator of the app does: see everyone's conversations, manage access tokens, change
the agent's own notes and the secrets, see where the agent keeps its data. The terminal on the server and an admin
token are admins too.

## 1. Two accounts

Accounts are written in the web gateway. A password is never written in the file: an account names the *environment
variable* that holds it (or carries an already-hashed value; `bxAgents hash-password` makes one). Replace the gateway
file from [The Web App](/next/course/15-the-generated-web-chat-ui/index.html) with this one:

```javascript
class {

	function configure() {
		return {
			exposes : "webui",
			path    : "/chat",
			users   : [
				{ username : "ada", passwordEnvVar : "ACME_ADA_PASSWORD", displayName : "Ada Lovelace", admin : true },
				{ username : "bo",  passwordEnvVar : "ACME_BO_PASSWORD",  displayName : "Bo Park" }
			]
		};
	}

}
```

An account whose variable is not set is skipped, with a warning in the `webui-auth` log: it fails closed on purpose,
because an account with an empty password would be far worse than none.

## 2. Tokens for programs

Tokens are made and kept by the agent itself. Turn them on, and let an admin manage them over the API too, with these
lines at the end of `Agent.yml` (`agentApi` is the agent's HTTP API, [the one you called](/next/course/13-exposing-http-and-mcp/index.html)
from curl):

```yaml

agentApi:
  tokens: true
  manageTokens: true
```

Rebuild and serve it (Terminal 3), after stopping the old server. The two `export` lines give the accounts their
passwords for this run only; use your own words for a real deployment:

```bash
cd ~/bxagents-course/acme-support
bxAgents build
```

```text
Build succeeded: <anything>/acme-support/.build/app
```

```bash
cd ~/bxagents-course/acme-support
export ACME_ADA_PASSWORD=ada-demo-pw ACME_BO_PASSWORD=bo-demo-pw
bxAgents serve --port=8791
```

The agent API has stopped being open. A call with no credentials is refused, and the accounts exist:

```bash
B=http://127.0.0.1:8791/__bxagents
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' $B/whoami
bxAgents users list
```

```text
401
USERNAME<anything>ROLE<anything>STATUS<anything>NAME
ada<anything>admin<anything>active<anything>Ada Lovelace
bo<anything>member<anything>active<anything>Bo Park
```

`admin: true` in the file made `ada` an admin when her account was created. After that the database keeps the flag,
and `bxAgents users admin --name=bo` or `users member --name=bo` changes it (the last admin cannot be demoted).

Now make a token. It is printed **once**, and only a hash is stored:

```bash
bxAgents token create --name=laptop
```

```text
Token for [laptop] (chat, never expires):

  bxa_<anything>

Copy it now: it is not stored and cannot be shown again. A caller sends it in the x-bxagents-token header;
...
```

A token has a **scope** , `chat` (talk to the agent, the default) or `admin`, and may expire (`--expires=90d`). Make one of
each, call the API with them, and see what the scope allows. The token's *name* is who the caller is, so it is also
the owner of the conversations and notes it creates:

```bash
B=http://127.0.0.1:8791/__bxagents
ADMIN=$(bxAgents token create --name=desk --scope=admin | grep -o 'bxa_[A-Za-z0-9_-]*')
CHAT=$(bxAgents token create --name=phone | grep -o 'bxa_[A-Za-z0-9_-]*')
curl -s -H "x-bxagents-token: $ADMIN" $B/whoami
echo
curl -s -H "x-bxagents-token: $CHAT" $B/whoami
echo
for T in $CHAT $ADMIN; do curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} ' -H "x-bxagents-token: $T" $B/logs; done
echo
```

```text
{<anything>"scope":"admin"<anything>"id":"desk"<anything>}
{<anything>"scope":"chat"<anything>"id":"phone"<anything>}
403 200
```

The `logs` route is for admins: the chat token gets `403`, the admin token `200`. Take a token back, and it stops at
once, on the running server. `token list` shows each token's name, scope, status and when it was last used, never the
token itself:

```bash
B=http://127.0.0.1:8791/__bxagents
PHONE=$(bxAgents token create --name=old-phone | grep -o 'bxa_[A-Za-z0-9_-]*')
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -H "x-bxagents-token: $PHONE" $B/whoami
bxAgents token revoke --name=old-phone
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -H "x-bxagents-token: $PHONE" $B/whoami
bxAgents token list
```

```text
200
Revoked [old-phone]. It stops working at once.
401
NAME<anything>SCOPE<anything>STATUS<anything>CREATED<anything>LAST USED<anything>EXPIRES
...
old-phone<anything>chat<anything>revoked<anything>
...
laptop<anything>chat<anything>active<anything>
```

Use a token with the terminal chat on another machine:

```bash
bxAgents chat --connect=http://127.0.0.1:8791 --token=<the token>
```

## 3. Sign in as a person

Open `http://127.0.0.1:8791/chat` in a browser. You are sent to the sign-in form. Sign in as `bo` with `bo-demo-pw`:
the chat works, the menu has the Main group only, and an address under the Admin group answers `403`. Sign out (the
header) and sign in as `ada`: the **Admin** group appears, and the **Access** page lists the tokens you made (a
**Tokens** tab, because `manageTokens` is on) and the accounts (**People**).

![Sign in with the accounts declared in users](/next/assets/webui/login.png)

![The Access page: the token list and the form that makes a token](/next/assets/webui/webui-access.png)

A conversation `bo` starts is invisible to `ada`'s own list (an admin can switch to **Everyone** ), and `bo`'s notes are
`bo`'s. A run that stops for an [approval](/next/course/approvals/index.html) belongs to whoever started it: `ada` cannot approve `bo`'s
pending routine from her own session.

## What to remember

* **Passwords are never in the file** , only the name of a variable or a hash. A password in a command line stays in your shell history, which is why `bxAgents hash-password --password=...` is for throwaway passwords or a hash you paste once.
* **Accounts close the API too.** With `users`, `/__bxagents` needs the sign-in cookie or a token, whatever `agentApi` says. The rest of the course therefore sends a token when it calls the API.
* **Tokens are secrets.** Shown once, kept as a hash, revocable, optionally expiring. `agentApi.tokenEnvVar` adds one shared secret that acts as an admin, for a deployment you manage through an environment variable.
* **It is a fixed roster.** No self-registration, no password reset and no roles beyond admin and member; for your own identity system see [the web app reference](/next/conventions/web-ui/index.html#what-this-is-not).

## Checkpoint

`gateways/web.bx` has the two accounts and `Agent.yml` ends with the `agentApi` block. The tokens are in your data
home. `kit/resume.sh users-roles-and-tokens` restores the project files; rebuild after.

Full reference: [Users and sign-in](/next/conventions/web-ui/index.html#users-and-sign-in), [access tokens](/next/conventions/agent-bx/index.html#access-tokens-for-a-deployed-agent)
and [`token`](/next/cli-reference/index.html#token), [`users`](/next/cli-reference/index.html#users) and [`hash-password`](/next/cli-reference/index.html#hash-password).

Next: [Secrets the Agent May Use](/next/course/the-vault/index.html)
